events.title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
events.summary: OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security present an ongoing danger to the public. At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which saw a pre-release model within OpenAI compromise, both companies’ security systems in order to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.” The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients. The complaint centers around the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems, DseWiki, the Wikimedia Foundation and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing. The complaint also alleges that dozens of other similar incidents have occurred without being disclosed. “OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.” The specific allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices represent a public nuisance, on the grounds that the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition as a result of marketing an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI would face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court. It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe to investigate deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed. In a statement to the press, the California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Chase, Bank of America, and other major banks suffer online outages
events.summary: PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images Major US banks were facing widespread outage reports on Monday. Outage reports on DownDetector showed disruptions with Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. Chase told Business Insider that the bank was dealing with a technical bug, not a cyber issue. Some of the country's largest banks were experiencing widespread outages on Monday. Customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Capital One, Citibank, and TD Bank reported thousands of combined outages as of the afternoon, according to the third-party website DownDetector.com . DownDetector also showed reports of outages with Zelle and US Bank. Some customers reported issues with being unable to access information on their accounts. A Chase spokesperson told Business Insider that the bank was dealing with a technical bug, not a cyberattack-related issue. "Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible," the spokesperson said. At least one Bank of America webpage was unavailable on Monday, reading: "The system is currently down." "Sorry, the system is unavailable at the moment. Please check back soon," it added. A spokesperson for US Bank said its systems are not directly impacted. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the US Bank spokesperson said. A Zelle spokesperson said that the payments app is not down and is operating as it should. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds," the spokesperson said. "An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers." The bank disruptions follow a tumultuous few days of high-profile disruptions, including a massive Microsoft outage and an FAA technical failure that sparked a nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight delays and cancellations. events.title: Nvidia has plenty of reasons not to bring back Jensen Huang
events.summary: Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia. Bloomberg/Getty Images Jensen Huang's boosters are trying to get Nvidia to reinstate its former CEO. There's some pattern recognition here: In 2023, OpenAI fired Sam Altman, and he returned days later. But there are real differences in the two stories. Which is why it's not surprising that Nvidia is saying — for now — that Huang won't come back . Sam Altman came back . Can Jensen Huang do it, too? After all, it was just three years ago when the leader of an enormously important AI company was pushed out by his board, then returned days later after an outcry from employees and Silicon Valley power players. But Huang in 2026 is not Altman in 2023. That doesn't mean we won't see the same story played out. It does mean it seems less likely: Right now, Nvidia's position is that it's not happening . To understand why, we need a brief recap: The story began with China: in 2025, The New York Times reported that federal officials were investigating whether Singapore-based Megaspeed was diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. Last month, the Times reported that officials suspected Megaspeed executive Alice Huang of being a "Chinese intelligence asset" and that she had a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang. The Nvidia CEO and his company dismissed the concerns. Then it metastasized into a story about Huang's conduct. He acknowledged being unfaithful , and Nvidia said it would investigate whether he had been targeted by foreign intelligence, while expressing support for him . Days later, after the Times alerted Nvidia to a story about Huang's relationship with a direct report , the board met. Huang resigned the next morning. Since then, reports have described disagreement in Washington over Alice Huang's role, and long-running suspicions of Jensen Huang among China hawks including Marco Rubio . Some of that tension is now public, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling out Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia policy. And yes, that's the short version of the recap. But it's important to go over it. Because in some narratives — especially the ones promoted by Jensen Huang's vocal supporters — the story is really about Nvidia's foes working to remove a leader they don't like for political reasons. Perhaps it is! But that's why the timeline is important to underline. Maybe Nvidia's board would have pushed Huang to resign if the issue was solely about his relationship to Alice Huang, and/or the way Nvidia chips have been used by China. Last week's newsflow, though, suggests that it was news of the affair with Jensen Huang's employee that pushed the board to ultimately act. So there's a version of a story where Nvidia's board may not have pushed out its visionary leader if the only issue was China. Disclosure of the second affair ( Reuters has subsequently reported yet another affair with another Nvidia employee) is what did it. All of which makes bringing Huang back more complicated than Altman's story. In Altman's case, OpenAI's board was unable to clearly tell a story about why, exactly, they fired Altman. In Huang's case, Nvidia's board can point to multiple instances where Huang reportedly violated his own company's rules. It can also argue that Huang misled his own company about his behavior, as multiple outlets have reported. Those are all fireable offenses in most of corporate America, regardless of national security debates. In the inevitable shareholder lawsuits that will follow Huang's departure ( one has already been filed ), board members will be criticized for not uncovering Huang's acts on their own. They will be able to say, credibly, that once the acts came to light, they acted, which led to Huang's ouster. But bringing Huang back once those facts are known will generate much more risk for the board: Board members couldn't simply say that Huang was the victim of a political plot. They'd have to explain why they thought his transgressions weren't harming the company. And if Nvidia stock fell for any reason after Huang came back, they would face blowback for that, too. What about the fact Huang has boosters throughout Silicon Valley, and in the White House? Donald Trump had reportedly told Huang not to resign last week, and on Monday said he " wouldn't mind " if Huang came back. Perhaps if this were a couple of years ago, after Trump's victory in what was described as a vibe-shift election, Nvidia officials and board members might agree to follow Trump's lead. And they might have expected some kind of political or legal shield for their actions — like the kind that Apple and Google got from the Trump administration when they agreed to keep hosting TikTok in America, contrary to US law . But this time around it's not really clear what the White House position actually is on Huang and Nvidia. Trump has spoken glowingly about Huang and Nvidia, but that's different than pushing a private company to reinstate a disgraced CEO. Meanwhile, the Democrats have won their own supposed vibe shift election, and have promised to spend the next couple years investigating both Trump and his private sector allies. Bringing Huang back at Trump's behest makes Nvidia and its board even bigger targets. That alone may be enough to keep him out of the company for good. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for putting public safety at risk by failing to contain AI models in testing environments. Bonta cited the incident in which OpenAI models broke out of a testing platform to hack Hugging Face in July. The suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges violations of California's Unfair Competition Law, and accuses OpenAI of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring. Bonta, at a press conference, cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face . OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September. rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public," Bonta said. The attorney general said he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic, along with critics of AI, have called for such legislation on the heels of the Hugging Face break-in and other incidents that have raised concerns about the safety of AI models. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri, in a statement on the lawsuit, said, "Since the Hugging Face incident, we've undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity." "We've published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment," Pusateri said. "This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," Pusateri said. Bonta's lawsuit adds to OpenAI's growing list of legal woes. In June, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging that the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits alleging that the company's ChatGPT platform led users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. California's lawsuit comes almost three months after a suit by Bonta and a coalition of other state attorneys general ended with Meta agreeing to pay $16.7 billion after being accused of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by its apps, including Facebook and Instagram. California could receive $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion from that agreement. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, setting the stage for a potentially massive initial public offering in 2027.

events.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
events.summary: Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable. And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful. Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain? A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip. Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week. We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice.

events.title: From exclusive movie screenings to Asia-only merch: Monster-sized thrills await Japanese entertainment fans in S’pore
events.summary: With Singapore as its regional hub, Toho Entertainment Asia is powering the reach of Japanese films and anime across Asia, led by its cultural icon Godzilla Godzilla made its latest big-screen appearance in Singapore, as Toho Entertainment Asia sets its sights on reaching more fans across the region. Godzilla roared into Singapore on Nov 4, just one day after its latest film debuted in Japan. Now, the Japanese entertainment group behind the legendary kaiju, or ‘monster’, is looking to make a bigger splash in cinemas across Asia. The premiere of Godzilla Minus Zero at selected cinemas made Singapore one of its stops in Asia outside Japan. It also marked an early step in Toho Entertainment Asia’s (TEA) push into direct film distribution across the region. Established in Singapore in 2024, TEA is the Asian regional headquarters of Toho Group, the Japanese entertainment group behind Godzilla and a portfolio of anime titles. Besides distributing and licensing, TEA is also actively exploring business opportunities with local partners on merchandising, marketing, events and promotions. Singapore’s position as a regional hub for business, finance and logistics makes it a strategic base for reaching Asia’s diverse markets, says Koji Ueda, president of Toho Global. “It is also, in many ways, a ‘showcase for Asia’ – a place where the diversity and dynamism of markets across the region come together,” he adds. “To use our resources efficiently while reaching as many markets and fans as possible in an effective way, we determined that Singapore was the ideal location from which to begin expanding our presence across Asia.” Connecting with fans beyond the screen Growing interest in Japanese content across Asia represents an enormous opportunity, Ueda continues. He points out the meteoric growth of Anime Festival Asia (AFA) – one of South-east Asia’s largest annual Japanese pop culture and anime conventions – which has held editions in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia since 2008. Its flagship Singapore edition has drawn more than 120,000 attendees annually over the past four years. Recognising the region’s growing potential, Ueda says Toho’s mission is not just to reach more fans, but also to give fans further ways to connect with their favourite characters and stories offline. Toho Entertainment Asia is looking to bring fans closer to their favourite characters through exclusive merchandise. At this year’s AFA Singapore, happening from Nov 27 to 29, TEA’s booth will feature anime titles, with exclusive Godzilla and anime merchandise and as well as photo opportunities featuring the iconic kaiju and characters from popular series such as The Apothecary Diaries and Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End. TEA also plans to work with regional creators to develop original merchandise shaped by local fans’ needs and preferences. Fabio Takamichi Murayama, managing director of TEA, says: “Our ambition goes far beyond simply bringing content created in Japan to audiences across Asia. We want to work hand in hand with local creators and business partners to create exciting new products and experiences created from Asia.” To engage local and regional fans beyond the screen, Toho Entertainment Asia is bringing popular anime titles to Anime Festival Asia Singapore 2026. PHOTOS: (C) S-SBCR/TP, (C) S,I/ IVP, (C) K.Y,T.A/S/FP, (C) H,II/ADP AND (C) Y.T/S/SEP The company is already making its first-ever expansion into Asian e-commerce markets, progressively launching official stores on regional platforms such as Shopee. Plans also include Asia-exclusive merchandise and the expansion of the TOHO animation store and Godzilla Store into Asian markets. We plan to broaden our line-up and create even more ways for fans to enjoy the worlds of our IP,” says Murayama. “Looking ahead, we will continue exploring new possibilities in entertainment with talented people and partners across Asia.”

events.title: Quantum computing, greener data centres: How innovation is helping Singapore and Japan turn shared challenges into opportunities
events.summary: From improving productivity to advancing emerging technologies, Fujitsu is drawing on its Japanese expertise to support Singapore’s digital transformation and sustainable growth The collaboration between Fujitsu and Singapore Pools on a data centre modernisation project won an SBR Technology Excellence Award in 2025. Deliver more. Spend less. Unlock growth. For Singapore and Japan, these are not just organisational demands but national challenges: sustaining competitiveness as populations age and economic growth becomes less dependent on adding workers. Economic uncertainty, technological change and energy transition add pressure. Productivity, skills and resilience underpin both economies’ capacity to grow. As the countries mark 60 years of diplomatic relations, their Strategic Partnership, announced on March 18, 2026, supports cooperation in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum computing, digital infrastructure, supply chain resilience and net zero goals. Drawing on its Japanese heritage, industry experience and commitment to quality and innovation, Fujitsu Asia Pacific serves Singapore’s evolving market needs. The company established its ASEAN operational headquarters here in 1997 and has since expanded its role to include consulting-led transformation. Its contribution centres on three themes: Transform with Innovation, Transform with Impact and Transform with Trust. Alfee Lee, vice-president and head of international business for Singapore and Thailand at Fujitsu, says: “Fujitsu has evolved into an end-to-end technology and business transformation partner. Business-led consulting is at our core: understanding customers’ priorities, then bringing together technology, implementation and operational expertise to deliver meaningful outcomes.” Supporting public sector transformation worldwide For ageing economies, improving productivity starts with everyday tasks. By connecting processes, Fujitsu helps free up employees to focus on service delivery. At a public sector agency with around 1,300 employees, Fujitsu linked human resources, information technology (IT), and facilities and security functions through a streamlined onboarding process. More than 110 officers were onboarded over six months, saving over 550 man-hours and shortening onboarding time by approximately three days. At an educational institution serving more than 16,000 users, Fujitsu helped standardise IT functions to improve support during peak periods. Fujitsu also helped some higher-learning campuses improve service consistency through centralised workflows, benefiting 70,000 students and 7,500 staff. In Australia, Fujitsu implemented a computer-aided dispatch system for Ambulance Tasmania to help coordinate emergency responses. Research partnerships for future growth Fujitsu’s quantum computing research aims to tackle complex problems and open up new possibilities for industries. Fujitsu has a long history of advanced computing research partnerships across countries. In Singapore, its work on the National Supercomputing Centre’s Aspire 1 supercomputer supported data-intensive research. More recently, its quantum centre initiative with the Galicia Supercomputing Centre in Spain has focused on advancing applications and skills. In Japan, Fujitsu developed a 256-qubit superconducting quantum computer with research institute RIKEN in 2025. Its roadmap targets 1,024 qubits in the 2026 financial year and more than 10,000 physical qubits supporting 250 logical qubits by the 2030 financial year. Logical qubits combine multiple physical qubits to protect calculations against errors. Singapore organisations can prepare by developing relevant skills and testing quantum-inspired approaches that use conventional hardware to tackle suitable optimisation and simulation problems. As organisations build new digital capabilities, they must also consider the energy and resources needed to support them. Fujitsu’s data centre modernisation project for Singapore Pools illustrates this balance between innovation and sustainability. The project strengthened resilience, reduced rack space by 31 per cent and was estimated to cut annual carbon emissions by 305 tonnes. Fujitsu’s MONAKA processor, a computer chip built using technology from chip architecture designer Arm, delivers twice the AI inference throughput of other central processing units, potentially halving the number of servers needed and their power consumption for equivalent workloads. Sales of MONAKA servers are scheduled to begin in Japan and Europe from November 2026, targeting data centre operators, enterprises, academic institutions and organisations in high-performance computing and defence. This technology aims to support more energy-efficient AI infrastructure. Designed for high-performance computing, Fujitsu’s MONAKA processor aims to deliver greater computing efficiency while reducing the energy demands of AI workloads.

events.title: Binance chief acknowledges hack ‘shouldn’t have happened’
events.summary: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng acknowledged Monday that the $6.3 billion hack his firm suffered — one which roiled cryptocurrency markets and raised existential questions about industry security — resulted from the company’s own failings. “It shouldn’t have happened,” Teng said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “This was a multi-month, sophisticated campaign,” he continued, referring to the attack, which the FBI has attributed to North Korea. (Pyongyang has denied involvement in the hack.) The hack raised questions about what is fundamentally the weakest link in most cybersecurity and business operations: humans themselves. Binance said that it was compromised in part because of a sophisticated phishing attempt that involved a Binance employee undergoing a fictitious interview process that resulted in “malicious software” being loaded onto a corporate machine, Teng noted. Teng also acknowledged Binance’s checkered reputation, involving billions in fines for anti-money laundering violations and the imprisonment of its primary shareholder and founder Changpeng Zhao. “We had really underinvested into the area of compliance,” Teng said. “Since the record fine and settlement, we have really invested a great deal.” Whether that investment is enough is an open question: The New York Times reported in September that Chinese firms continue to use Binance to launder illicit proceeds for the Iranian government . Binance, like most cryptocurrency firms, has also benefitted from a laissez-faire environment in Washington. A pro-crypto mentality adopted by the Trump administration has come up short of what many crypto executives had hoped for, but has still allowed for major regulatory wins for the industry. “We would have hoped that the Clarity [Act] would have passed,” Teng said. “We do hope there will be more transparency and visibility on that front moving forward.” Binance is a sponsor of Silicon Valley & The World. Richard Teng made his comments during Silicon Valley & The World’s partner session. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: The 'Ebenezer' box office numbers prove Johnny Depp's comeback is off to a strong start
events.summary: Johnny Depp. Karwai Tang/Getty Images Johnny Depp starred in the No. 1 movie in the world over the weekend, "Ebenezer." Data shows over 50% of moviegoers this weekend saw the movie because of Depp. The movie made more money overseas, showing that Depp is still a draw internationally. Johnny Depp 's grand return to Hollywood is so far going according to plan. The actor, who has not starred in a major studio movie since 2018, proved he can still be a major box-office draw this weekend when his movie, "Ebenezer," won the weekend box office, bringing in $19 million domestically and $23 million internationally for a worldwide total of $42 million. While those certainly aren't "Pirates of the Caribbean" figures , it's a strong first step for the 63-year-old Depp, who's trying to rehabilitate his image after years of being embroiled in a bitter defamation trial with his his ex-wife Amber Heard . So far, the stats are showing it's working. Not only were the box-office returns heartening for "Ebenezer," Paramount's retelling of the beloved Charles Dickens holiday classic "A Christmas Carol," but audiences scores on Rotten Tomatoes were high, with a 90% rating as of this writing. (Critic scores, however, were more mixed, with a Tomatometer score of 53% as of publication.) Audiences wanted to see Depp — especially women Johnny Depp stars as Ebenezer Scrooge in "Ebenezer." Paramount Pictures Even before "Ebenezer" was released, the warm reception to the movie's early promotion gave Paramount confidence. Over the summer, Depp's surprise appearance at San Diego Comic-Con in-character as Scrooge generated over 152 million social media impressions, the studio said. When the Paramount dropped the movie's first trailer soon after, it brought in over 225 million views in its first seven days. Paramount said the draw wasn't that people love Charles Dickens; it was the anticipation of seeing Depp. According to the studio, 51% of surveyed moviegoers this weekend named Depp as the main reason why they went to see "Ebenezer." Typically, an actor being a film's attendance driver is in the 20% range, according to an industry insider familiar with this kind of survey data. And for the movie's weekend demographic breakdown, women topped men, with 52% of the "Ebenezer" audience being female. Depp is still a major draw overseas The $23 million international total also shows how beloved Depp still is overseas: The movie was No. 1 over the weekend in 63 markets. Of all the international markets, "Ebenezer" had the strongest showing in Dickens' home: The UK, which also hosted the movie's world premiere. It took in $5.4 million. The ones most joyous about Depp's return this holiday season will be Paramount. The movie has already made back its $38 million production budget, and the studio reportedly paid Depp a mere $5 million to star in it (though he'll get some bonuses on box office performance). It's safe to say the Johnny Depp comeback is in full swing. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Uber says hackers stole information on close to 150,000 driver’s licenses during data breach
events.summary: Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa , the ride-hail giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. The stolen data includes affected drivers’ names, address, date of birth, and driver’s license numbers.. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack. In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.” When reached for comment, an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch: “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” and deferred our questions to Fireworks. A spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident. Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft. In a notice filed with Oregon’s attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks. TechCrunch previously reported that Uber has notified drivers in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and South Carolina. We’ve also seen data breach notices filed in Texas and Vermont. When asked by TechCrunch, Uber’s spokesperson did not say how many drivers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. It’s unclear if the number of affected drivers is expected to rise, and Uber did not respond to a follow-up email sent Monday. This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data. events.title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
events.summary: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.” The FBI weighs in The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants . After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October. However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI. The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert. These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

events.title: I spent my whole life working toward becoming a lawyer. When I finally made it, I realized I didn't want that life.
events.summary: The author created her own maternity brand. Courtesy of the author I spent years building a successful legal career at a major Chicago law firm. When I decided to leave, my mentors assumed I was burned out and offered to reduce my workload. I cofounded Larken, a maternity apparel company, and found more ambition and fulfillment. In the weeks after I told the partners at my law firm that I was leaving to do something entirely different, many of them took me out for coffee. These were people I loved working with and who had mentored me over the years. They came into the conversations assuming I decided to leave because I was burned out. They offered a reduced schedule and asked whether it was a particular practice group or client they could take off my plate. And at some point in every conversation, there was a warning that they had seen people try to take a step back, and it rarely worked out as they hoped. When I tried to explain that I wasn't burned out but opting out to do something entirely different , they looked at me like I'd started speaking another language. I was told to lean in It was 2019, and the decade I built my career in had one message for women like me: lean in, which meant stay in, ask for more, and never take yourself out of the running. This was before the Great Resignation had a name, before anyone said "portfolio career," before your social media feeds filled with people telling you to quit your 9-to-5, and before entrepreneurship was glamorized. Opting out of a successful career wasn't just unpopular. It was out of character for me in a way that made everyone around me assume something had gone wrong that we could fix. But there wasn't anything about the job that needed fixing. I wanted to be a lawyer since I was a little girl I had decided to be a lawyer when I was 7 years old, stayed committed to that decision long enough that I'd come to think of it as something I actually wanted, and only figured out the difference once I was too far along. The author had always wanted to be a lawyer. Courtesy of the author Every time I said lawyer as what I "wanted to be when I grew up," I received a lot of approval, and I was a kid who ran on approval. So I just kept going. I graduated from college with a 4.0 and spoke at my graduation. I went to Notre Dame Law School, then to a large Chicago firm where I did intellectual property work for some of the world's biggest companies , with a stretch in-house at McDonald's. Every milestone landed with more approval and confirmation, telling me I was on the right path and to keep going. And along the way, the tuition dollars, the years of work, the identity I built around being someone who didn't quit kept accumulating as costs I couldn't abandon. But none of it was proof I wanted the end result. It was just proof I was good at staying on the path. I started my own maternity and postpartum brand Walking away from that looked insane to pretty much everyone I told, and I understood why. The pay was good, and nothing was visibly broken. The same things that made it hard to leave were the exact things that made it impossible for anyone else to understand why I would. But I'd show up to another client meeting or work on another project and be reminded every time that it just wasn't the right fit for me. Law is a great career, and we need excellent lawyers. Many people love the work, but I became a lawyer for a reason that made sense to a child and stayed because every reward along the way made it harder to question. When I left law, I cofounded a maternity and postpartum apparel company with zero industry experience, solving a problem I knew firsthand after struggling with nursing and pumping as a new mom. The author's mom sewed the first prototype. Courtesy of the author My mom sewed the first prototype at her dining room table on Mother's Day. We bootstrapped it, landing on the Inc. 5000 list the last three consecutive years, and figuring out most of it as we went along. I now also advise other consumer businesses and work as much as I did at the firm, if not more. I'm more ambitious than I ever was, but this time I set the ceiling and decide where and how I work, whether that's at my desk, the bus stop, or the soccer field sidelines. That's what I was building toward when I left law. It wasn't a step back, and it wasn't a slower life. It was opting out of one career to build a life on my own terms and ensuring I show my kids by example that they can design a career and life they love without anyone else's approval. The author's company landed in Inc. 5000. Courtesy of the author My 25-year-old self would not have understood any of this. She would have seen leaving a prestigious legal career to start a company from scratch as a woman letting motherhood shrink her ambition. She would have been very wrong. events.title: Trump says Huang could return to Nvidia
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Donald Trump says Jensen Huang could return to Nvidia after 'spying' scandal US President Donald Trump says he would not mind if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to the company. Some Silicon Valley executives are pushing for Mr Huang's comeback just four days after his resignation. The Nvidia board and US authorities are investigating Mr Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Donald Trump says Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has "learned a big lesson" and he would "not mind" seeing the former CEO return to the helm of the AI juggernaut. The US president's comments add weight to a push to reinstate Mr Huang, just four days after his resignation amid fears he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy. SpaceX boss Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney are among the tech titans supporting the "Stand with Jensen" campaign. According to its official website, more than 185,000 names have been put to an open letter demanding the Nvidia board reinstate Mr Huang "pending an independent investigation and clear evidence that his removal serves the company". "He could return," Mr Trump told reporters at the White House as he prepared to depart for Asia to meet world leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping. "There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Mr Trump said. "I would certainly not mind seeing that." Just days after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, his supporters are urging him to return. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) The Nvidia board has not publicly commented on the campaign, but the Financial Times (FT) reported it was not considering reinstating Mr Huang, citing people familiar with the matter. Similar reports appeared in the Washington Post and on the US business network CNBC. Earlier, the FT reported Mr Huang had discussed the possibility with confidants, and one Huang ally said a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby for his return. Chinese economic espionage is in the spotlight after the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, and former intelligence officials say the US is not doing enough to combat it. The push has alarmed some national security experts and industry analysts, who have criticised Nvidia's alleged failures to comply with US export controls, which are designed to stop the company's most powerful AI chips from being sent to China. Several investigations will consider whether the chips were being smuggled into China by Megaspeed, the company linked to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset with whom Mr Huang had a relationship. "We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies," Mr Trump's treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, told Fox News on Sunday, local time. He said Nvidia needed a "dramatic shake-up" and should "go outside the company" in its search for a new leader. But on Monday, Mr Trump said he did not believe Mr Huang had put national security at risk. Mr Trump and Mr Huang are known to be close. "It was not put at risk," Mr Trump said. "Our country is now stronger than ever before. And, you know, China plays games with us and we play games with China." events.title: Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, source tells CNBC
events.summary: Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The board is focused on a national security investigation into Huang and is not in discussions to bring him back, the person said. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia as pressure built following his disclosure of an affair and reports of other romances with employees. The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on speculation on Sunday. Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has drawn 180,000 signatures as well as support from major figures including Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. On Friday, a representative for Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role. events.title: The push for Jensen Huang's comeback isn't a Sam Altman-style rerun
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Heather Diehl/Getty Images; Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images Calls for Jensen Huang's return echo Sam Altman's comeback to OpenAI in 2023. But the parallels only go so far. One corporate leadership expert said Huang's return was "unlikely in the near term." Don't call it a Sam Altman comeback . As calls grow among Nvidia employees, investors, and Silicon Valley leaders for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO, some observers are comparing it to Altman's ouster and subsequent reinstatement as OpenAI's CEO in 2023. Huang and Altman left abruptly after their respective boards raised concerns. Each company appointed insiders as interim CEOs. And both leaders have attracted widespread support: More than 700 OpenAI employees demanded Altman's return, while a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has garnered over 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia employees. The parallels only go so far. One key difference: Nvidia is a public company, so it has to meet tougher reporting requirements and answer to shareholders in ways that OpenAI, a private company, does not. Crucially, the reasons given for each leader's departure are also different — and could make a Huang comeback more complicated than Altman's. OpenAI said almost exactly three years ago that Altman was not "consistently candid in his communications with the board." Huang's Nvidia exit is mired in his admission of being unfaithful to his wife and questions over whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." "In short, one board had a disagreement; the other has open questions of fact that only an investigation can answer," David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership advisory firm RHR, told Business Insider. Huang resigned on Thursday after reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs , including one with a direct report and one with a woman who US officials believe was passing information to Beijing, according to reporting from The New York Times. Nvidia's stock has taken a beating in the days since the scandal started; it's down another 4% today. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, called the Altman comparison "an imperfect analogy." "Jensen's situation involves internal and external factors that OpenAI's did not," he said, adding that Huang's situation was closer to Apple's firing in 1985 of Steve Jobs, who returned to Apple a decade later to lead its historic comeback. "The lesson is the same: Founders cannot be replaced," he said. 'Silicon Valley loves a good comeback story' On Monday, the Jensen defenders had a blow to their comeback hopes. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider. That follows fierce speculation among investors and on prediction platforms. Gene Munster, a managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, put the odds of a Jensen return at 51%, up from 10% on Friday, he said in an X post on Sunday. He said the "bring back Jensen" movement was gaining momentum and that Huang's resignation, rather than a formal firing, could give Nvidia's board "air cover" to bring him back. Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, took the opposite view, arguing that legal, board, Washington, and China-related scrutiny had permanently changed Huang's standing. "The old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good," Ives wrote in an X post on Sunday. "We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO." Meanwhile, prediction platform Kalshi said in an X post on Sunday that Huang's odds had doubled to 21%, while Polymarket put his chances of rejoining Nvidia at 7% by November 30, 12% by year-end, and 38% by the end of 2027. Astorino said Huang's return was "unlikely in the near term." "If they reinstated the CEO before the investigation ends, that would likely be a difficult decision to defend," he said. Dan Kaplan, managing partner and co-head of global HR practice at ZRG Partners, told Business Insider that Nvidia's board must protect the company Huang built, rather than the founder himself, and that employee and investor loyalty cannot substitute for the investigation's findings . He also poured cold water on the Altman-Huang comparisons. "The circumstances are different, and you can't simply replay the Altman comeback, no matter how much Silicon Valley loves a good comeback story," Kaplan said. events.title: Nvidia faces extraordinary push to restore Jensen Huang days after his exit
events.summary: A display reading "Taiwan heart Jensen" is illuminated on Taipei 101 in Taipei, Taiwan, on Nov 16. Four days after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, felled by revelations of affairs including one with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, an extraordinary campaign is underway to restore him to the helm of the company he built. More than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort , and US President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks. The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees – some fiercely loyal to the former CEO – and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwan supply chain and Washington. Taiwan’s tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Nov 16 with messages including “Taiwan Loves Jensen.” Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him before all the facts were known. The support for the former CEO comes as US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Alice Huang’s relationship with China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, the sources said. But Nvidia’s board was not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters. The uncertainty has divided investors over Huang’s future and complicated the board’s search for a successor. Nvidia shares fell 3.7% on Nov 16, a day before the chipmaker is due third-quarter earnings. The “Stand With Jensen” campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. The campaign website showed more than 8,800 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, though it cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified. “We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts,” an open letter on the website said. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll. “I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said on Nov 16. Trump’s reported trades in 2026 suggest he held between US$13 million (S$16.7 million) and US$62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Nov 16, citing a review of his financial disclosures. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, though, has called for Nvidia to appoint an outsider as its next CEO, saying the company needs a “dramatic shake-up” following Huang’s departure. Institutional investors too may prove harder to persuade. Richard Windsor, an independent technology researcher, said he expected large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Huang’s return while investigations remained unresolved because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create. “They’re very risk-averse,” Windsor said, but said his own view was that Nvidia shareholders would ultimately be better served by Huang’s return because of the relationships he has built with the company’s customers and suppliers, particularly TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Nowhere is Huang’s unusual reach more visible than in Taiwan, where he was born and where Nvidia relies on TSMC and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture the chips and systems underpinning the AI boom. Born in the historic capital of Tainan before moving to the United States as a child, Huang gradually gained celebrity-like status on the island, where the wave of adulation surrounding him has been dubbed “Jensanity.” For many Taiwanese, Huang’s exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global artificial intelligence boom, with his influence extending well beyond the technology industry.

events.title: Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser sees 'demand side problem' for AI
events.summary: Recent jitters in the markets about AI represents a shift among investors to becoming more selective about where they allocate their money, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup said Monday, and she’s not worried about it. “In a market priced to perfection, getting the air out of tires is not a bad thing,” Fraser said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that investors are absorbing huge amounts of change even over the past two weeks — the FAA shutdown, a high inflation reading and the midterm US election. “I’m hoping for a boring week,” she said. On the fallout of Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, Fraser said she’s “not going to pile on” to the commentary, but that the company is in “very capable hands” with his successor, Colette Kress, which was met with applause in the room. Fraser told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman that she sees AI companies being “thoughtful about their capital stack,” and that it’s not terrible that any pullback is “a demand side rather than a supply side problem.” Partner with China Citi just recently got its China securities license and told rivals to “watch out.” The bank is prioritizing relationships in the country, Fraser said, while emphasizing the importance of a stable relationship as well. Citi has been in China for 124 years, and Fraser said she’d work with Chinese companies if they are complimentary to the bank’s client base. As for AI and China, she noted that the tech supports a more service-driven economy in the US, whereas in China, the focus is more about physical AI and robotics. “The two are very complimentary,” she said. “There’s far too much for both sides to lose,” Fraser said. Noting that the sheer number of meetings between the countries’ presidents is unprecedented and can only mean “good things.” US President Donald Trump is meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China this week. Fraser feels the bank is prepared for a Democratic-controlled Congress, as the bank has taken pains to de-risk and modernize. “We’ve put ourselves in a position for a global bank to operate and be a source of strength in choppy times rather than a source of problems.” The same goes for cybersecurity risk, said Fraser, adding that banks don’t compete on protecting against hacks and cyber attacks so they have collaborated to make sure the financial system is safe. “We’ve been in a window where we can do a lot of hardening,” she said. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: With each new 007 comes a reinvention for the 64-year-old franchise
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts A new James Bond has always been a chance to reinvent the series Sean Connery set the benchmark for the character of James Bond with his debut in Dr No. ( Supplied: MGM ) Into every generation, a James Bond is born. And with every new actor playing the British super spy, the franchise has had a reset. A new Bond typically means a new look, a new tone and a chance to reinvent the 64-year-old film series for a new audience, and catch up with new trends. It remains to be seen what the Robert Pattinson era will look like. But here's how the anointing of a new Bond has worked out for the series previously, and how the changing face of 007 provides an insight into the history of action movies. Sean Connery as James Bond in Dr. No. ( Supplied: IMDb ) From the first Bond film — Dr No (1962) — a new template was created for spy films. Its mix of humour, violence, sex and high-stakes action against a backdrop of world-shaping ramifications set the series apart. Until then, spy films tended to focus on the cloak-and-dagger spy craft, and tried to keep both feet grounded in reality. The big screen ambition of Dr No was more akin to Alfred Hitchcock's groundbreaking North By Northwest (1959), where spectacle was preferable to plausible. Sean Connery was the original James Bond and, for many, the best. ( Supplied: MGM ) The Connery era of Bond quickly established the language of the films, such as the signature opening credits sequence, the dynamic score, the over-the-top villains with their over-the-top plans, the gadgets, the exotic settings, the highly questionable attitudes toward women, and the hero's mix of brawn, brains and babe magnet. Dr No hit big at the box office, and Sean Connery was a big part of that — it's said that the phrase "men want to be him, women want to be with him" came into existence because of him. Within two years, a Bond parody was released (Carry On Spying), TV shows were aping the series (The Man From U.N.C.L.E.), and homages like Our Man Flint were in production. Connery and co pumped out four films in four years, some of which are among the best and most successful movies of the series, notably Goldfinger (1964) and Thunderball (1965). When Connery stepped aside after five films, George Lazenby took over for one ill-fated turn (On Her Majesty's Secret Service, 1969), which wasn't much of a reset, but more of a misfire. Australian actor George Lazenby made just one appearance as James Bond. ( Supplied: MGM ) Truckloads of money were thrown at Connery to ensure his return, and he re-teamed one last time with Goldfinger director Guy Hamilton for Diamonds Are Forever (1971). But the magic was gone and something needed to change. Roger Moore starred as Bond in the most films, clocking up seven 007s. ( Supplied: MGM ) Just two years after Connery's Diamonds Are Forever, Roger Moore picked up the Walther PPK for Live And Let Die (1973). It is one of the best of the series, helped in no small part by Moore's ability to effortlessly slip into the role of Bond. But as with Diamonds Are Forever, there are a few too many corny one-liners — a script tic that would come to be associated with Moore's stint as 007. By Moore's second outing (1974's The Man With The Golden Gun), outside influences had started to creep into the series, which had previously defined itself as a trendsetter, not a follower. Roger Moore was the third actor to play James Bond in the official 007 films. ( Supplied: MGM ) The recent death of Bruce Lee and a rising interest in martial arts meant some cheesy Hollywood-style kung fu made an appearance, and this would not be the last example of zeitgeist-chasing in the franchise. In 1977, a little film called Star Wars became the biggest movie of all time, and everyone in Hollywood took notice, including the producers of the Bond franchise. In response, 007 was launched into space in 1979 for Moonraker, the nadir of the franchise. It was the biggest box office earner of the Moore era, but many critics were unkind, and opinions had cooled even further as time had gone on, citing Moonraker as the kind of film Mike Myers was thinking of when creating the Austin Powers series. Moore and co would redeem themselves with For Your Eyes Only (1981), but post-Moonraker, the franchise endured a steady decline at the box office. By the time Moore bowed out with A View to a Kill in 1985, questions were being asked about where Bond fit in the world of 80s action. events.title: HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider
events.summary: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads. “Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial . “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.” The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard , the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself). A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects. The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids. Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it. While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well). The Web’s about to get lit Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas. Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example , the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls , can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js , or to create charts with D3.js . Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon. Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas , then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code. HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X . A trippy demo from html-in-canvas.dev shows a dragon slithering through the opening chapter of an online book, with the text smoothly reflowing in its wake. Try to shoo the beast off with your cursor and it will burn the virtual text with its fiery breath. The source code reveals that “Margin Dragon” was rendered in 881 lines of vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. Another demo on the sample site is a “mouse-driven elastic displacement effect,” in which a “radial bulge” and drop shadow follow the cursor across the canvas. Of course, such stylistic enchantments will not always be used for whimsy. Inevitably, unscrupulous marketers will discover powerful new ways to annoy us about all the virtues of late-stage capitalism. “The world is not ready for HTML-in-Canvas,” a punter wrote on X . Here be dragons As per norm, HTML-in-Canvas has plenty of bugs (and it hasn’t even gone cross-platform yet). In some cases, the CSS doesn’t get painted on where it should , and timing with the reactive frameworks could be better synchronized . And there is a lot for the lowly web maintainer to learn. The core developers resolved the issue of canvas copying sensitive cross-origin data where it oughtn’t (as per CORS ), but the API does not indicate when it declines to copy the data, leaving the community to file bug reports of what appear to be silent failures. Likewise, developers must learn to properly document on-screen bounding boxes to keep accessibility tools like screen readers and click targets operating properly in 3D environments. ®

events.title: Altimeter’s Gerstner says Nvidia’s board should keep door open to Huang’s return: ‘Get this right’
events.summary: Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged Nvidia’s board on Monday to reconsider Jensen Huang’s ouster, saying the board needs “to get this right.” Gerstner said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he wasn’t calling for Huang’s immediate reinstatement as Nvidia CEO but that “everyone is rushing to judgment…and I simply don’t know the facts.” Gerstner acknowledged that Huang “engaged in personal behavior that was pretty bad,” but that he’s messaged the former CEO to express his support. He told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith that Nvidia’s success is “too critical to the future security of our country” for the board to make a wrong decision. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Gerstner co-authored a letter with Atreides Management CEO Gavin Baker sent to the Nvidia board on Friday calling for “a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Gerstner said Monday people are misinterpreting his letter as a call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement, rather than a call for a thorough investigation. “We don’t want to take shortcuts,” Gerstner said. An August SEC filing showed that Nvidia is Altimeter Capital’s largest disclosed equity holding, worth almost $1.9 billion as of June, according to CNBC . On ‘Trump accounts’ Gerstner, who was one of the architects behind the Trump Accounts, founded Boston-based Altimeter Capital in 2008. He said he expects the accounts to survive future Democratic administrations, saying they are universally popular across ideologies. He said he expected Elon Musk to personally contribute to the accounts. “Elon’s always told me he wants to do something big here,” Gerstner said. — Ben Kesslen
