events.title: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
events.summary: A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide. Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel. Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said , with thousands more delayed. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday. Read more below. What caused the nationwide groundstop? What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds." Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal . The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris , has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide. After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement. How did a router disrupt flights nationwide? How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft. The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft. A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications. The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds. The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights. What to know about radio frequency outages One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions. Some reports described this as a " rolling frequency outage ," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time. This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers. Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy. What happens to pilots during the outages? Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail. These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual . The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage. Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities. Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected. What does this mean for flights? Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions. Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports. Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft. What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris. The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.

events.title: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
events.summary: One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup. With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade. To be clear, this feature is not Face ID. Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay. The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is close. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity. The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it. Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images. The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness. Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month . Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a webpage, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify. Apple is also expanding access to Apple News puzzles for News+ subscribers in Australia, the U.K., and for French-Canadian users. Australian News+ subscribers will get access to a daily quick crossword, crossword mini, and Sudoku, as well as Apple’s original puzzles, Quartiles and Emoji Game . U.K. users will get the quick crossword, the crossword mini, and Sudoku, while French-Canadian subscribers will get access to Apple’s original puzzles. The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete. events.title: Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
events.summary: In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to ​abandon the Rwanda plan. Five European countries have announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a processing centre in Rwanda as early as next year, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse. The planned scheme, which is still being negotiated with Rwanda, would send people to a centre where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said on Monday. list 1 of 4 Rwanda sues UK over scrapped asylum seeker deal list 2 of 4 Greece pushes EU to suspend asylum during mass migration surges list 3 of 4 US reports record number of deportations and arrests in 2026 list 4 of 4 Record number of migrants arrive in Spain’s Canary Islands Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands said that the plan aimed to deter more people from migrating to Europe. The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, reduce the number of asylum seekers arriving and increase deportations of migrants who are not entitled to stay. “I think this will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.” Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe. He added that arrivals would be able “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference”. When asked how Kigali would ensure refugees’ human rights, Biruta said, “There will be an independent monitoring mechanism” and that it would cooperate with the United Nations’ refugee agency. Human rights groups criticised the plans, saying that EU countries could not guarantee their rights would be respected there. In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s. The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups. A Human Rights Watch researcher said the deal “would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad”. Germany’s interior minister said the European plan was not comparable to a scrapped 2022 deal with the United Kingdom because only those whose asylum claims are rejected will be sent to Rwanda. The UK’s Supreme Court ruled that the 2022 deal was unlawful because Rwanda was not considered a safe third country to which migrants could be sent.

events.title: Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis
events.summary: Move comes as government forces withdraw from Red Sea coast to halt Houthi approach to interim capital Aden. Saudi Arabia has replaced the commander overseeing its coalition forces as they battle the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen. King Salman issued a decree on Monday assigning General Fayyad al-Ruwaili to the command, according to Saudi state media. The removal of Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman came as coalition forces were forced to abandon their recent push to recapture regions along the Red Sea coast in order to reinforce the Yemeni government’s interim capital, Aden. list 1 of 4 Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb list 2 of 4 Fighting intensifies in Yemen as Houthis deny targeting Mecca list 3 of 4 Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones list 4 of 4 Siege fuels disease fears in Yemen’s Taiz Al-Salman was appointed as a military adviser to the Saudi defence minister a day after coalition forces were forced to withdraw. Yemen’s internationally recognised government said on Sunday that coalition forces were withdrawing from areas near the key Bab al-Mandeb strait – via which Saudi oil exports have been flowing while the United States-Iran war stifles traffic through the Strait of Hormuz – to focus on defending Aden. The retreat marked a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against the Houthis, who have been firing ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities since Yemen’s civil war restarted in July. A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha . Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis. Government forces – backed by the Saudi-led coalition – quickly retook key positions near Bab al-Mandeb after the Houthi advance on the strait and the Red Sea coast this summer, but have been unable to retake Mocha. They have said they killed or wounded 173 Houthi fighters as part of Operation Dawn of Yemen and engaged the Houthis in Marib, Lahij and in al-Jawf. However, they are now retreating from theterritory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait and preparing to fortify defences around Aden, after the Houthis advanced to an area 60 kilometres (37 miles) north of the city. Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre. “[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X. As the fighting continues, civilians remain exposed. Houthi-affiliated media reported coalition air strikes on the capital Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group took in 2014, and said one person was killed in an attack on a school in Taiz. Authorities in the besieged city of Taiz have called for humanitarian corridors to allow civilians to evacuate, as medical officials warned hospitals could be forced to end operations within two days due to a lack of fuel and oxygen. Earlier on Monday, Saudi Arabia said it had shot down two Houthi drones targeting the Mecca and Riyadh regions.

events.title: SCOTUS gives DEI a boost after national assault
events.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear three conservative appeals tied to battles over diversity, equity and inclusion , leaving lower-court rulings intact in disputes over federal research grants, medical training and transgender-related speech. The big picture: The denials mark a reprieve after years of backlash against DEI, though the justices stopped short of settling the underlying constitutional debates. One of those Monday decisions set back President Trump's administration push to cancel swaths of DEI-related research grants. Driving the news: The justices rejected President Trump's bid to revive cuts to federal research grants awarded to University of California researchers over their perceived DEI-related viewpoints. A U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel ruled in May that challengers were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim that their grants were terminated because of the "perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints." That decision partly upheld a preliminary injunction from U.S. District Judge Rita Lin reinstating grants terminated over perceived DEI-related viewpoint, while reversing relief for a separate group. What they're saying: Trump's DOJ argued to the high court that allowing the grants to continue would force taxpayers to fund ideologies "their public stewards reject." A DOJ spokesperson told Axios the department will continue fighting the preliminary injunction and "will continue to advocate for the Executive Branch's lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives." Catch up quick: The challenged funding represents just a slice of the DEI-related grants ensnared in the administration's terminations and ensuing litigation. Trump has led a top-down campaign to undermine federal and corporate DEI efforts, disputes over state policies have also crept onto the national stage. Case in point: The Supreme Court also declined to hear a challenge from the anti-trans Gays Against Groomers against Colorado lawmakers' restrictions on misgendering and deadnaming during legislative hearings. The Tenth Circuit had found lawmakers were shielded by legislative immunity. Meanwhile: The justices also declined to hear a challenge to required implicit bias training for California continuing medical education courses. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated he would've heard the appeal brought by an ophthalmologist and a conservative medical advocacy group. Justice Clarence Thomas penned a dissent, joined by Justice Samuel Alito. Thomas' argument indicates there may be an appetite for a similar question about government speech in the future: "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny," he wrote. What we're watching: Both in the courts and in the public arena , disputes over the federal administration and state leaders' handling of DEI initiatives are still playing out with many more sure to come. But on Monday, a high court that hasn't always sided with DEI initiatives declined to further some key debates — for now. Go deeper: Trump says he "ended DEI." Courts disagree

events.title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
events.summary: Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year Published 16 November 2026, 11:45 GMT US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated. Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees. It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang. Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia. Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back". The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. "I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House. The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models. The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping. The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China. The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process". Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy. However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. 'China plays games with us, so we play games with China' On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China. "They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said. The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump. Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X. , external "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question.

events.title: How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment
events.summary: Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”. The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions. Many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill. That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable. On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people. Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work. In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line. After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity. Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them. “Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.” He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard. Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip. Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead. Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market. Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment. His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”. The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term. The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have. His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs. So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people.

events.title: There's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costs. How it could impact your bill
events.summary: As Americans wrestle with inflation, there's a growing "property tax revolt" to reduce or limit property taxes amid rising home values. In 2020, the median sales price for U.S. single-family homes was about $300,000, compared with roughly $419,000 in 2025, according to the National Association of Realtors. During the midterm election, property taxes were on the ballot in several states, including Florida, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Property tax relief could impact local government services and infrastructure, experts say. Affordable housing was a key midterm election issue , and as Americans wrestle with rising home costs , there's a growing movement to reduce or limit property taxes. Amid soaring home values , some states want to cap how much local governments can collect from homeowners. Experts have described the trend as a " property tax revolt ." During the Nov. 3 midterm election, Florida voters approved Amendment 3 , which increases the portion of primary residences exempt from property tax for non-school levies and lowers the cap on yearly assessments for certain properties. North Carolina voters approved an amendment to require the state legislature to enact limits on property tax increases, while voters in Oklahoma and Wyoming rejected other property tax measures. IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors Social Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 In Ohio, an amendment to abolish property taxes didn't have enough signatures to make the November ballot, but supporters plan to try again in 2027. Despite the "mixed bag" on midterm ballot initiative results, "I think we'll continue to see property tax reforms," said Matthew Chase, CEO of the National Association of Counties, or NACo, a nonprofit organization that represents county governments. Property taxes are levied as a percentage of a home's assessed value, based on its estimated market rate. Some municipalities use a millage rate — with one mill equaling $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable assessed value — to calculate property tax bills. That rate can adjust up or down based on changes in home values and the local government's budget needs. In some cases, property tax bills can be bigger due to higher assessments, even when local governments lower the millage rate, experts say. Property taxes vary widely throughout the U.S., with yearly bills ranging from less than $250 in some rural counties to more than $10,000 in areas near large cities, according to 2026 data from the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research organization. Affordability concerns prompt tax cuts Nationwide, the property tax cut movement has been "driven by affordability," according to NACo's Chase. As "home values have gone up, property taxes have gone up with it," he said. In 2020, the median sales price for U.S. single-family homes was about $300,000, compared with roughly $419,000 in 2025 , according to the National Association of Realtors. Last year, the median property tax bill for owner-occupied homes was around $3,300 , the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey reported. Higher property tax bills have been a burden, experts say, as homeowners have wrestled with rising costs for groceries, gasoline and other living expenses. That's sparked more demand for property tax relief. From January 2020 to June 2026, state lawmakers enacted at least 168 property tax measures — including exemptions, credits, refunds and more — across 40 states and the District of Columbia, according to an October report from NACo. Property tax cut proponents argue local governments should rein in spending . But other experts say the relief will cause revenue shortfalls that impact local schools, police and fire services, roads and other infrastructure. "There's no realistic way to replace property taxes in most states," said Jared Walczak, a senior fellow at the Tax Foundation. Typically, property taxes are a more stable revenue source compared to income or sales taxes, which can decline during an economic downturn as consumers earn and spend less, experts say. Reliance on the tax varies, but property taxes are the single largest local levy revenue source for most local governments, accounting for about 28% of local funding nationally in 2024, according to the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, an independent, nonpartisan foundation and think tank. "It's easy to savor property tax cuts in abstract," Walczak said. "It can often be much more challenging to define a replacement system that anyone actually likes.

events.title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
events.summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement. The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers. In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.” But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union. Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already. Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said. “We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal. Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely. Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration. “We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said. In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later. But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court. Goldman Sachs said in a Sunday note it expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and fall to $78 by December 2027 as the market returns to a surplus. The bank believes Middle East supply to rise above its 2025 average as producers use ship-to-ship transfers and add pipeline capacity.

events.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy. “He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did… That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims. The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report. Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator President & CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang. “A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. events.title: Altimeter's Brad Gerstner aims to invest $5 billion in Anthropic IPO
events.summary: Altimeter Capital is aiming to invest $5 billion in the Anthropic, Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday. That's five times as much as he's ever put into an IPO. "I think this is a cornerstone compounder for a long time," Gerstner said. Altimeter Capital is aiming to invest $5 billion in the Anthropic IPO, Brad Gerstner told CNBC's "Halftime Report" on Monday. "I think this is a cornerstone compounder for a long time," Gerstner said, noting that his investment would be five times the amount he's ever put into an IPO. "It's where the trade is going." Anthropic is expected to go on Nasdaq on Thursday in a milestone event for the artificial intelligence industry. It would be the first major AI lab to go public, beating OpenAI, which has said it's targeting an IPO next year. Gerstner is investing alongside the leading chipmakers and cloud providers, many of which count on Anthropic as a customer. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Anthropic is planning to offer 825 million shares at a valuation of about $1.4 trillion. Gerstner is friends with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , and sent a letter to the board of directors last week pushing them to take their time and run a full investigation on Huang's tenure before deciding who should run the company. Gerstner said he has confidence in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress , and noted that Huang had not discussed a comeback as CEO with him. While Anthropic is hitting the market at a particularly tough moment — coming after a downturn in semiconductors, a massive anti-AI swing in Washington, D.C., and the Huang saga — Gerstner said he's still optimistic. "They have done such an excellent job presenting this company, they're in such an excellent position on the financials," Gerstner said, "that folks like me are making this a major order."

events.title: US won’t restrict foreign tech companies in allied countries, State Dept. official says
events.summary: The US government has “no plans” to target or “orchestrate the deep pruning” of technology companies headquartered in allied countries from American supply chains, Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg said Monday. Speaking alongside ASML’s President and CEO Christophe Fouquet at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Helberg rejected “top-down government-mandated plans that intentionally discriminate” against companies based on their country of origin in comments to Semafor’s Ashley Gold. He named ASML, Samsung, and SK Hynix as key partners to US firms in the technology supply chain. Discussing Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains, Helberg said that the Trump administration wants to ensure companies across allied economies benefit from a “level playing field.” He described the initiative as a “capability-centric coalition” that draws on the comparative strength of participating countries. Helberg also argued that Washington must balance technological leadership with global market share of AI-focused companies, warning that innovation alone will not secure America’s dominance in the fast-growing technology field. “We need both in order to win the AI race,” Helberg said. “We need to lead the world qualitatively and have the best innovation out there. But we also need market share, and those two things need to happen in conjunction.” Helberg also stopped short of endorsing three bipartisan bills that lawmakers are considering including in the year-end defense bill that would tighten AI chip export controls following the Nvidia controversy. Asked about the investigation involving Nvidia, Helberg described the company as critical to US technological leadership, saying “there is a really compelling argument for national security to have Nvidia continue to be a leading beacon of innovation.” He called for investigations to establish the facts quickly, adding, “Our hope is obviously to see serious work being done through the investigations to uncover the facts and get to the truth quickly in order to get to the right outcome.” Nvidia has attracted scrutiny from Congress as well as the administration amid revelations that now-former CEO Jensen Huang had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Is Israel’s Eisenkot bloc less right wing than Netanyahu?
events.summary: An Israeli government without caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may be close, but a government without his politics is far less certain. As the long and complex negotiations to form Israel’s next government drag on, hopes are high that former military chief Gadi Eisenkot will be able to form a coalition that marks a break from the far-right and divisive politics of the previous administration. The coalition brought together by the now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu brought figures from Israel’s far right into government. Beyond the genocidal war on Gaza following the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, and repeated military strikes against neighbouring countries, the government sought to weaken judicial oversight and pursued an aggressive policy of illegal settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. There, settler pogroms against Palestinian communities have continued with near impunity. list 1 of 4 Israel coalition talks put Arab party leader under pressure over Hamas list 2 of 4 Can Netanyahu and Eisenkot form a ‘unity’ government in Israel? list 3 of 4 Who can force Israel to implement Gaza ceasefire deal? list 4 of 4 Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling “Likud sits further to the right than most conservative parties in Europe. Although historically it was thought of as something like the Conservative Party, today it looks like something of a far-right party,” said Roi Zur, an Israeli academic at the University of Essex, who has researched the comparison between Israeli parties and their international equivalents. In contrast, Eisenkot and his opposition bloc have said that they will repeal the judicial overhaul legislation introduced by Netanyahu, establishing a state commission of inquiry into the security failings ahead of the October 7 attack, and ending the draft exemption offered to many ultra-Orthodox youth in defiance of a 2024 ruling by the Supreme Court. But will a new government under Eisenkot – made up of a number of right-wing figures – really be any different from what has come before? What parties and politicians are likely to sit in government with Eisenkot? As it stands, before any fresh alliances are brokered, there are five main political leaders of the opposition bloc. Its leader, Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar Party, is generally regarded as a centrist security hawk. Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid of the B’Yachad Party are considered right-wing and centre-liberal, respectively. Avigdor Lieberman, the head of Yisrael Beiteinu, is secular and right-wing, while Yair Golan of the Democrats sits as the sole outlier on the left. What do we know about Eisenkot’s politics? Many observers regard Eisenkot’s politics as difficult to read. While he has been broadly supportive of the genocidal war on Gaza, in which more than 74,600 Palestinians have been killed, and attacks on countries across the region, including the current war on Iran, little is known of his domestic politics. His Yashar Party’s economic platform points towards a broadly pro-market approach, prioritising tax cuts over wealth redistribution. On security, there is less ambiguity. Eisenkot is the architect of the Dahiya doctrine, an Israeli military strategy that calls for overwhelming force against areas from which Israel comes under attack. Eisenkot warned in 2008 that Israel’s destruction of large parts of southern Beirut’s Dahiya area during the 2006 war on Lebanon “will happen in every village from which fire is launched toward Israel”. In March, he said the doctrine should again be used in Lebanon, noting it had “never been more relevant”. Eisenkot has also firmly rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state, and supports the continued existence of illegal settlements in the West Bank, even though he has pledged to tackle settler violence. How about the others in Eisenkot’s bloc? The bloc may be viewed internationally as more moderate than Netanyahu, but its members also largely adopt right-wing positions towards Palestinians. Bennett, a former settler council chief, opposes Palestinian statehood and has previously said that he favours annexing 60 percent of the West Bank. His political partner, Lapid, backs a two-state solution, but without any firm details, and then only in the long term. Netanyahu’s former ally and now one of his fiercest critics, Lieberman has been vocal in his support of the expansion of illegal settlements. Both Bennett and Lieberman have made incendiary comments about Palestinians. Bennett defended cutting off water and electricity to Palestinians in Gaza in October 2023, while Lieberman said in December 2023 that there were “no innocents in Gaza”. Bennett and Lapid have led a government in the past: their 2021 coalition included the United Arab List (Ra’am), a party representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.

events.title: Prediction market odds for Tesla-SpaceX merger by April 2027 top 60%
events.summary: Odds of a merger of Elon Musk's SpaceX, a rocket and satellite company, and Tesla, an electric vehicle manufacturer, have risen on multiple Kalshi markets since late last week. On Friday, Walter Isaacson, a CNBC contributor and author of a Musk biography, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that he is confident a merger is coming. He cited Terafab, the semiconductor project involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, as a potential catalyst. Odds of a SpaceX and Tesla merger before March 2027 have climbed to 62% from 27% on Kalshi since Thursday. Chances that Elon Musk's two companies, SpaceX, a satellite and rocket maker, and Tesla, an electric vehicle manufacturer, will soon integrate have jumped since late last week across multiple Kalshi markets. The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and would be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database. On Friday, Walter Isaacson , a CNBC contributor and author of a Musk biography, told CNBC's " Squawk Box " he's confident a merger is coming. He cited Terafab, the semiconductor project involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, as a catalyst. "I think you have to have a merger. Makes no sense otherwise," Isaacson said. Tesla's 2026 annual shareholder meeting, set for Dec. 3, may provide more insight into a potential linkup, Isaacson said. While speculators are anticipating an announcement of a merger this year, a research note from Jefferies last week said a deal will likely face backlash after the Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships in the midterm elections earlier this month. "We understand there is higher risk of scrutiny post elections, but the vision of a combined SpaceX and Tesla as proxies for longer-term U.S. national strategies of independence and leadership in space, energy, manufacturing or semiconductors, in our view, remain highly relevant regardless of which party controls Congress," wrote Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois. Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democrat, said a possible merger between Musk's two companies would face "tremendous scrutiny," Bloomberg reported Thursday. events.title: This Anthropic proxy play is getting traders' attention – here's where they see it going
events.summary: The Destiny Tech100 fund is experiencing 30 times its average-daily volume, with 41,000 calls versus 150 puts traded. 14% of the Destiny Tech100 assets are tied to Anthropic. Anthropic perpetual futures imply a big first-day pop. Who says you can't tailgate an IPO? Traders are preparing for this week's blockbuster Anthropic IPO in different ways, including buying options on one publicly-traded fund that invests in private assets. The Destiny Tech100 (DXYZ) is a publicly-traded, closed-end fund that invests in equity, equity-linked instruments, or shares of private funds and venture companies to gain exposure to private companies. Currently, 14% of the fund's assets are tied to Anthropic, according to the company's website. Options volume on the fund jumped to more than 10x the 30-day average Monday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Of the 42,300 contracts traded by midday, 41,800 were calls, with just 141 puts likely opened by buyers. Just shy of $5.5 million in options premium on DXYZ traded on Monday, with almost all of it tied to calls, but just marginally more spent buying than selling calls, according to SpotGamma. The highest-volume contract is currently the 30-strike call expiring Friday, a 90-cent contract that needs the fund to rally 19% into the weekend to pay off. Traders may want to be wary of how the fund traded around the SpaceX IPO: DXYZ surged almost 150% in May before unwinding all the gains in the weeks ahead of SpaceX's debut. Since then, the fund has barely moved, trading around $26. There are other bullish signs surrounding Anthropic's IPO in the derivatives markets. Current prices for perpetual futures on the blockchain exchange Hyperliquid are implying an opening price of $98, a big pop from the $70-$78 price range quoted in the company's amended S1 filing. The AI giant is expected to price Wednesday evening and begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

events.title: I started a handbag company at 22 and grew it into a fashion sportswear brand with partners like MLB. Here's what I've learned.
events.summary: Zara Terez Tisch is the founder of Terez, a fashion sportswear company based in New York City. Natalie Keyssar for BI At 22, Zara Terez Tisch launched a handbag company called Terez from her parents' home. Terez evolved into a fashion and sportswear brand with MLB partnerships. Her advice is to build an excellent product with a distinct point of view — not just a story. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Zara Terez Tisch, the founder of Terez, a fashion sportswear company based in New York City. It has been edited for length and clarity. I started Terez as a handbag company, from my parents' home on Long Island when I was 22. After college, I was fortunate to live at home without paying rent, which allowed me to save money while my friends moved to Manhattan. I worked in marketing and branding and had always been a creative person, but I was going through a difficult period in my life. I had experienced a lot of loss and was trying to get on my feet. I knew I wanted to create something that made me feel good about myself, and Terez was born. The business has taken several turns over the years. After handbags, I moved into activewear and eventually found an opportunity to bring fashion to professional sports by partnering with major leagues. Today, Terez sits at the intersection of sports and fashion. Natalie Keyssar for BI The early days of building Terez In 2008, when I was still working in marketing, which I quit later that year, I was walking through the West Village in Manhattan on an errand. I came across a leather shop with a sign that said, "Customize your own leather handbags." I walked in and asked, "Do I just draw a handbag and you make it?" I also asked whether they could make 500 bags, or even 1,000. They thought I was crazy, but said they could do it. I decided to work with them to start a business. I started with handbags with fun interiors, including comic-book strips and disco sequins. I wanted to get the happiness inside me out again while representing New York City. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch I started gaining some traction I was doing it all myself, carrying samples with me. I didn't sell them on a website. Instead, I did trunk shows at people's homes. The first one was at my sister's friend's house on Long Island. Not long after I started, I asked my father to come back with me to meet the manufacturers. I thought it would help them take me more seriously. Zara's father, Richard Zimmerman, and sister, Darlene Barzilay, at his Budget Dress showroom during Darlene's 21st birthday celebration in 1986. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch My dad was a garment manufacturer — a 'garmento,' as people in the industry called it. He had worked in the industry in the 1970s, 1980s, and into the 1990s. As manufacturing moved to China and overseas, he had to close his company. I witnessed that, and bringing manufacturing back to New York became part of my story. In 2012, the business took another turn The linings I used in my handbags were made of spandex. I was wearing leggings all the time, so I started making them out of the same spandex at a factory in Queens. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch My parents had started a business manufacturing clothing for tweens. I brought the leggings to one of their children's trade shows to see if it would stick. A store called Lester's picked them up and put them in its store over Thanksgiving weekend. The buyer called me on Monday and said, "You really have something here." The leggings started taking off. We became a popular brand for tweens and teens We created prints and styles that made them feel confident in who they were. We started with galaxy leggings and star-themed designs, then added emojis to them. We would drop new designs every month. Natalie Keyssar for BI The next decade was a period of significant growth for Terez. As demand for activewear grew, department-store buyers began creating dedicated categories for it, and Terez became a key brand in that expansion. We partnered with SoulCycle on limited-edition drops and with Bloomingdale's. We opened our first store in 2022 In the fall of 2022, we opened our first physical store on the Upper East Side. It's the smallest part of the business in terms of revenue, but it's the heart and soul of the brand. Soon after the store opened, a woman came in, and I helped her shop. I showed her our whole collection and told her everything about the brand. When she was checking out, she asked, "Have you ever thought about working with Major League Baseball?" I hadn't. She pointed out that nobody was really focusing on women's clothing for the fans. The options were mostly bubblegum V-neck T-shirts with sequin script logos. Natalie Keyssar for BI The next day, I got a text from an exec at Major League Baseball. The woman who had come into the store was associated with the organization. He told me they wanted Terez to shape the look of the women's collection. I immediately called our head of design and said, " We have to stop everything that we're doing right now and focus on a women's collection for Major League Baseball." Working with professional sports opened up new ways to reach customers Today, we work with multiple professional sports teams and leagues. We sell through our own site, our Upper East Side store, licensed sports channels, and fashion retail partners like Revolve. Natalie Keyssar for BI Partnering with sports has opened up completely new channels for us. Since making our debut with Major League Baseball, our revenue has tripled. I've learned that hiring more people doesn't necessarily make a business more efficient When we were first doing activewear, we had a period of high growth, and the company grew to around 40-something people in 2018 and 2019. Up until that point, I hadn't felt confident enough in myself to run the business side and manage the company's numbers. I always thought I should surround myself with people who were smarter than me. What I realized was that people weren't always efficient in their roles, so we would hire more people to do the same job, sometimes two or three times. I called them Band-Aids. By the end of 2020, we narrowed down to a team of around 10 people. I picked up all the pieces after a rocky situation with one employee and told everyone, "We're either going to do this all together, and we're going to succeed together, or we're going to fail together." Natalie Keyssar for BI Since then, I haven't wanted to grow our team. The majority of the people on my team now were on my team 10 years ago. To have people on your team who care as much as you do is extremely rare. I want the business to reflect what we believe in When people ask me for advice about starting a business, I always come back to the product and deeply caring about your team. You can only tell a story for so long. You need to make sure your product is excellent, high-quality, and has a distinct point of view. What differentiat

events.title: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
events.summary: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind. The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan . But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs , each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz. The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer , built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking. Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger. ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs. Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64. As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale. In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with enough vector and matrix units to put more than a few modern GPUs to shame. With enough of them – by which we mean 22,680 dual-socket nodes – NSCS catapulted China to the top of the Top500 for the first time in nearly a decade. Not the benchmark it used to be The US has no shortage of systems capable of eclipsing El Capitan or even LineShine’s performance if someone were motivated enough to get HPL running on them. SpaceXAI’s 300 megawatt Colossus supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, boasts 200,000 Hopper GPUs each good for 34-67 (vector/matrix) teraFLOPS of FP64 grunt. Even assuming an abysmal 25% efficiency, the cluster should be more than capable of breaking three exaFLOPs in HPL. It might need 10x the power of El Capitan, but the thing is, beyond winning points with the White House — a ship that has almost certainly sailed for Elon Musk after the DOGE fiasco — renting out the cluster to Anthropic to train and run Claude is a far more lucrative endeavor. The same could be said of any number of AI clusters, from Meta’s Prometheus to OpenAI’s Starship. It used to be that the systems to summit the Top500 were among the largest computers humanity has ever built. But this hasn’t been true in some time. The US is starving for compute. HPL or even its sibling High-Performance Gradient Conjugate just aren’t the benchmarks to beat any longer. The new battleground isn’t nuclear proliferation; it’s one of AI models, agents, and the means to harness them. We’re not talking about tokens, LLMs, or chatbots, but the ability to harness these models to automate laboratories and formulate and test hypotheses long after the scientists they serve have gone home for dinner. It’s why the US’s Genesis mission puts such a strong emphasis on AI. AI-driven labs present an opportunity for researchers to iterate faster. Rather than running hundreds or thousands or simulations trying to find a needle in a haystack, a task for which a bigger iron is warranted, AI analysis and automation could focus that search. High-performance computing (HPC), and by extension the Top500, will remain relevant as long as more FLOPS means more simulations per unit of time. But these systems can only move as fast as the men and women who operate them. ®

events.title: Every actor who has played James Bond, ranked from worst to best
events.summary: Daniel Craig, Sean Connery and Pierce Brosnan as James Bond. MGM Robert Pattinson is the newest James Bond. Before he gets his license to kill, let's celebrate who came before him. Business Insider ranked all seven actors who have portrayed Bond in film. Over 60 years and 25 movies, seven actors have played the legendary spy James Bond on screen. Daniel Craig was the latest to take on the character created by novelist Ian Fleming, bringing a darker, grittier tone to the franchise. His run came to an end in 2021's " No Time To Die ," when his Bond, well, died. Now a new 007 has emerged. Robert Pattinson is officially the next James Bond . Before he debuts his version of Bond, here's where all the best Bonds rank. Zac Ntim, Eammon Jacobs, and Ayomikun Adekaiyero contributed to previous versions of this story. David Niven (1967-1967) David Niven as James Bond in 1967's "Casino Royale." Columbia Pictures While most audiences automatically think of Daniel Craig when thinking of " Casino Royale ," there was actually another version of the story that arrived on the big screen back in 1967. (Yes, in the same year as Sean Connery's "You Only Live Twice.") Columbia Pictures' "Casino Royale" starred David Niven as James Bond, and takes a more comedic approach to Ian Fleming's book of the same name. The parody movie isn't connected to any of the other films, nor was it made by Eon Productions and Albert Broccoli. It was only made because Fleming sold the singular rights to the book before it was published in 1953. Niven's Bond is a much older agent who's brought out of retirement to fight a nefarious organization called S.M.E.R.S.H. The Oscar-winning actor brings some charm to the role, but the absurd story — which ends with him going to heaven — ruins the character and sucks all the suave out of 007. George Lazenby (1969-1969) George Lansbury as James Bond. MGM Australian actor George Lazenby is on this list as another matter of courtesy. He was drafted by Eon Productions, the film's producers, to play Bond once in 1969's "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" after Sean Connery decided to step away. He was promptly replaced by Roger Moore when the series resumed in 1973 with "Live and Let Die."  Pierce Brosnan (1995-2002) Pierce Brosnan filming "007" in 1997. Markus Beck/picture alliance via Getty Images After 15 years of Daniel Craig — who is eulogized later in this list — it is easy to forget the damage Pierce Brosnan did to the James Bond franchise. But it's important to revisit our lowest moments so we can grow. So here, I humbly ask, do we remember the unfortunate orange spray tan Brosnan sported throughout his time as 007? Or the awkward hyperpop theme songs like Madonna's awful "Die Another Day"? It's important to note that Brosnan's first Bond film, "GoldenEye," was also the first film in the franchise not produced by Albert R. Broccoli: His daughter, Barbara Broccoli, and his stepson, Michael G. Wilson, took over. But it's been reported that Brosnan was favored by Albert Broccoli. Nonetheless, across his four-film run, Brosnan pushed Bond away from its steely, cool origins to something more Hollywood and less interesting.   Roger Moore (1973-1985) British actor Roger Moore, playing the title role of secret service agent 007, James Bond, is shown on location in England in 1972. AP Photo Roger Moore suited up as James Bond a record seven times. The bulk of his films were helmed by the British director John Glen, who had an unparalleled skill for capturing pure chaos on screen. And that is what Moore's Bond was best known for. In his seven-film run, Moore went to space, fought off a pack of crocodiles, and defused a nuclear bomb. While Moore's Bond was charismatic and entertaining, there was rarely any substance to what he said, and there was even less plot to hold together the big-budget stunts. For this reason, Moore's seven films don't make for great rewatching.  Timothy Dalton (1987-1989) Timothy Dalton as James Bond. MGM The sole reason Timothy Dalton is not at the top of this list is that he portrayed Bond only twice. This wasn't due to bad ratings or box-office numbers, however. His films, "The Living Daylights" (1987) and "Licence to Kill" (1989), are two of the most beloved Bond films, and Dalton's dark and often serious take on 007 is widely considered the most accurate interpretation of Fleming's books.  "I wanted to make him human," Dalton said of his interpretation of Bond during an interview in 2008 . "He's not a superman; you can't identify with a superman. You can identify with the James Bond of the books. He's a tarnished man, really. I wanted to capture that occasional sense of vulnerability and I wanted to capture the spirit of Ian Fleming." As many people have stated before, Dalton's grounding of Bond paved the way for the franchise's most profitable period of releases with Daniel Craig's 007. Dalton's tenure, however, was cut short due to complex legal wrangling between the film's producers MGM and Eon Productions, which halted production until 1994, when his contract expired.  Sean Connery (1962-1967) Sean Connery as the original movie James Bond. United Artists Sean Connery had a legendary acting career that spanned over 50 movies and included appearances in some of Hollywood's most iconic films like 1964's "Marnie," 1989's "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade," and 1987's "The Untouchables," for which he won an Oscar for best supporting actor. But when he died in 2020, he was best remembered as the first 007.  According to Connery, however, his interpretation of 007 managed to charm everyone but Fleming. "I never got introduced to Fleming until I was well into the movie, but I know he was not happy with me as the choice," Connery said on "The South Bank Show" in 2008. Despite Fleming's reservations, Connery played the secret agent in seven films from 1962 to 1983, and his version is remembered as not only the coolest in the franchise but one of the coolest characters in cinematic history.  Connery's powers as 007 came from his own charisma. As Barbara Walters described him in a 1987 interview, the Scotsman was someone who didn't try to be sexy; he simply oozed class. Connery can also claim to be the only Bond actor who actually managed to pull off the famous catchphrase, "Martini, shaken, not stirred" and make it sound cool. Best: Daniel Craig (2006-2021) Daniel Craig as James Bond in "No Time to Die" MGM Daniel Craig's Bond films are dark, physical, and entertaining. But it is Craig's commercial success that has landed him atop this list. events.title: Market's Nvidia obsession obscuring an opportunity in this name
events.summary: Disney reports earnings Tuesday before the bell. Options are implying a 5.6% move, lover that the last eight quarter median move of 7.4% Look for short premium strategies into the print. The market is unable to divert its attention from anything not related to the ongoing saga that is Nvidia and its embattled former CEO Jensen Huang. It's understandable, given both the detail of the story and Nvidia impact on the market. It remains the tech story du jour, and it's getting plenty of ink. I think investors should remember there are other big names reporting this week outside of Nvidia that deserve time and attention. One such name is The Walt Disney Company (DIS) . After a prolonged period of strategic transitions, the company may finally be turning the corner. Driven by a renewed focus on the bottom line, management's cost discipline now supports a runway for double-digit earnings-per-share (EPS) gains through fiscal 2027, even as it continues to trade at about its 5-year average forward multiple of 14.3x, well below the broad market multiple of more than 18x. Trading back to a market multiple, justified if it establishes above-market EPS growth, suggests ~26% upside, which is also consistent with a sum-of-the-parts analysis that points to an intrinsic valuation of $140 to $160 per share versus the Friday, November 13th closing price of $118.97. Disney reports Tuesday before the bell. Despite broader macroeconomic anxieties, the theme park and cruise divisions are showing surprisingly resilient demand. Domestically, the metrics are highly encouraging: attendance is climbing, and more importantly, per-capita spending continues to rise. On the digital front, Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) Disney's streaming margins currently sit in the low teens, respectable given the segment's previous lack of profits. But the real upside scenario requires looking ahead: if Disney can scale these DTC margins to 20% or higher, the stock could at least trade at a multiple comparable to streaming king Netflix (which would imply a share price of ~ $139 or so. Part of the reason the studio segment remains a mixed bag is that, while there are periodic blockbuster bright spots, Disney's theatrical recovery remains uneven overall. Furthermore, legacy media continues its secular decline. The pay-TV industry has likely lost around 40 million subscribers—representing a staggering 40% erosion of the user base since 2015—and will likely lose more this year. However, the critical takeaway for investors is that the pace of cord-cutting is finally slowing down. With linear TV stabilizing, the parks firing on all cylinders, and streaming marching toward higher profitability, Disney offers a highly asymmetric risk-reward profile. The magic is returning to Disney's financials, and the current share price heavily discounts a business fundamentally engineered for double-digit growth. Right now, the options market is pricing a ~6% move by the end of the week (the company reports Tuesday, pre-open), which is below the 8 quarter median move of 7.4%. Anticipating a "vol crush" after earnings, I like selling December premium to help finance the purchase of a longer-dated call - a diagonal call/spread risk reversal. When selecting an option trade consider the key things that affect its value and how those things differ from simply buying (or selling) the underlying asset. For these option trades, let's consider three sensitivities (Greeks): Delta, the rate at which the option position changes in value for changes in the underlying price. Theta, or decay, which measures how much the value of an option declines as time passes, and Vega, the change in an option's price associated with changes in the implied volatility of an option. In the case of the diagonal risk reversal each of these factors plays into the structure to our benefit. The delta of the structure is less than 100, meaning that the p&l associated with moves up or down will be less for one spread than they would be for 100 shares of stock. We like this because the stock has already had a decent run recently, and the option structure will lose less than the stock will if it gives that back. Because nearer dated expiration decay more rapidly as a percentage of the options value than longer dated options do (and out of the money options also exhibit accelerated decay), the shorter dated December options we're selling should decay in value more quickly than the longer dated March options we are buying, even though the March option has a higher premium. Vega can work in our favor as well due to "vol crush". When option premiums are elevated due to a catalyst such as earnings we should expect that much of that premium will be sucked out or crushed once the event has passed.
