events.title: China ‘full stop, is ahead of us’: SpaceX alum building a $13 billion defense startup warns of Beijing’s hypersonic weapons
events.summary: While Jensen Huang’s resignation has put a renewed spotlight on the U.S.-China race for dominance in chips and artificial intelligence, another technological contest could have even more direct national security implications : hypersonic weapons. And the U.S. is already trailing behind, according to Andrew Kreitz, cofounder and CFO of Castelion —a $13 billion defense startup focused on developing hypersonic missiles. “Unfortunately, China, especially, full stop, is ahead of us in hypersonics,” Kreitz told Fortune ’s Andrew Nusca at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, Mich. The U.S., for its part, has begun fielding its first long-range hypersonic missile system, known as “ Dark Eagle .” China, meanwhile, has been steps ahead for years and “has the world’s leading hypersonic missile arsenal,” according to the U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 report to Congress. Kreitz pointed to several reasons for the gap, starting with how the U.S. defense industry develops and builds weapons. He said the Pentagon has often prioritized the most advanced technology without giving enough thought to cost or how easily it can be manufactured. Cost-plus contracts, which reimburse contractors for their expenses, also give companies less incentive to control costs. The aerospace and defense industry also suffers from failing to test hardware early and often, Kreitz said, arguing that fewer tests mean slower learning and development. “Unfortunately, our adversaries very much took the opposite approach,” Kreitz said on stage. “The Chinese have tested and iterated very, very fast, and they’ve been relentlessly focused on industrializing and manufacturing these weapons at a very large scale.” How Elon Musk’s SpaceX—and NASA’s Apollo program—are inspiring a hypersonic missile startup Kreitz and fellow cofounders Sean Pitt and Bryon Hargis left SpaceX in 2022 to start Castelion, aiming to disrupt the defense industry by building weapons faster, cheaper, and at a much larger scale. In just four years, Castelion has grown to more than 400 employees, reached a $13 billion valuation, and secured multiple Pentagon contracts. In September, the U.S. Navy awarded the company a contract worth up to $200 million for Blackbeard, its low-cost hypersonic missile. Much of that success, Kreitz said, comes from the engineering culture they learned at SpaceX—and can be traced back even further to NASA’s Apollo program. “It hearkens back to the golden age of American aerospace in the 50s and 60s: get to hardware as quickly as possible, test as early as possible, iterate as fast as possible,” he said. Castelion is also willing to bring more manufacturing in-house rather than rely on outside suppliers when supply chain issues get in the way. “Everything has to be backwards planned, from how do we scale production of this weapon—the iteration cycles and the testing, especially though, that just unlocks learning at a really, really rapid pace,” Kreitz added. Billions are flowing into defense tech, but Castelion’s CFO predicts the bubble will eventually pop  Castelion is riding a wave of investment in defense technology. In the third quarter of 2026, defense startups raised a record $2.5 billion—contributing to a total defense tech VC value of $67.4 billion across 726 deals this year, according to PitchBook . Leading the pack in terms of valuation is Anduril , which raised funding in May at a $61 billion valuation and has since explored a potential deal that would nearly double that figure. But Kreitz thinks the boom has created a bubble —and not every company will survive the coming shakeout. “There is froth in the market,” Kreitz said. “I think that there will be a shakeout at some point. That’s the truth.” Some companies have promising technology and products but lack the ability to bring them to market or manufacture them at scale, Kreitz said. Others may ultimately be acquired as the industry consolidates. For Castelion, the strategy is to focus more on actually building its business. “Our approach to weathering this is focus on execution, focus on operations, focus on manufacturing, get ourselves to scale and free cash flow generation as soon as possible to sort of immunize us to any of the noise that might be occurring in the capital markets,” Kreitz said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
events.summary: A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content. This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft. Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit. Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying. “Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be. “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs….just to do something that was a variation of that.” With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves. “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that like it had like a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, I feel like there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said. What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning. Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks. The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience , which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps. Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj. Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer. The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed. The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year. events.title: The man with the golden touch: James Bond franchise is a money-spinner
events.summary: Big-screen debut of Ian Fleming’s creation in 1962, with Sean Connery as lead in Dr No, was start of marketing dream New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson Robert Pattinson’s journey to James Bond J ames Bond may be 73 years old but the superspy holds a licence to print money, at the centre of an evergreen multibillion-pound franchise spanning blockbuster films, merchandise, licensing deals and sponsorship. The announcement that the Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson is the next Bond comes seven years after Daniel Craig revealed that No Time To Die would be his last outing as 007. This means that by the time Pattinson makes his first appearance it will have been the longest gap in instalments in the 64-year history of the film franchise, an agonisingly long hiatus for the centrepiece of a sprawling commercial enterprise. While Ian Fleming initially struggled to get Hollywood interested in his debonair, womanising British novel creation, the big-screen debut of Sean Connery in 1962’s Dr No marked the start of a marketing dream. The 25 feature films to date – the world’s second longest-running film franchise after Godzilla – have taken almost $8bn (£6bn) at the global box office, making it the fifth most successful property in cinema history, behind only the sprawling Marvel Cinematic Universe, Star Wars, Harry Potter and Spider-Man. When Amazon acquired the famed Hollywood studio MGM – home to 4,000 film titles including the Rocky and Bond franchises, as well as 17,000 hours of TV programming – four years ago, some analysts estimated that the superspy could be worth half of the $8.5bn price tag of the whole library. The estimate of the on-screen value of Bond was underscored last year when Amazon paid more than $1bn to take full “creative control” of the franchise from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the longtime stewards of the films who had retained significant power, unlocking the potential to develop a Star Wars or Marvel-like “universe” of film and TV spin-offs. Plans for one potential spin-off in 2002 – a movie based on the character Jinx, played by Halle Berry in Die Another Day – were scrapped the following year, while the highly successful Young Bond series of books for young adults has never made it beyond print. Beyond the box office, the carefully cultivated prestige image of Bond has proven a brand association dream, a marketing juggernaut impervious even to Daniel Craig’s critical assessment a decade ago that the spy was a “lonely, sexist misogynist” . Charlotte Mair, the founder of The Fitting Room, a communications and culture agency, says: “Bond is a brand in its own right, with associations of sophistication, adventure, luxury and craftsmanship, timelessness and, of course, Britishness. “Bond is a standalone entertainment property, with its own identity, heritage, mythology and extraordinary brand equity. Its partners aren’t simply buying exposure around a film release. They are aligning themselves with a brand that has been building its own cultural currency and influence for more than 60 years.” The 141-year-old Turnbull & Asser, the personal shirtmaker to the king – who bestowed the company with his first royal warrant as the Prince of Wales in 1980 – has created shirts for Bond actors since Connery appeared in the first film. Lock & Co, the world’s oldest hatters, with roots dating to 1676, started its Bond relationship with one of its hats appearing in the now-famous opening credit gun barrel scene that debuted in Dr No. Aston Martin has long been considered Bond’s sports car of choice, debuting in 1964’s Goldfinger, and a bespoke DB10 was created for 2015’s Spectre to celebrate a 50-year partnership with the franchise, but deals remain on a film-by-film basis. The N.Peal cashmere turtleneck worn by Daniel Craig in the poster for Spectre sold out almost immediately. A grey, custom-made Tom Ford suit worn by the actor in Skyfall went to auction last month with hopes it would fetch as much as £40,000 . The “Bond effect” lures big sponsorship deals, reportedly worth anywhere from $45m, with deep-pocketed corporates. Heineken, which has partnered Bond films since 1997, has spent as much as $100m on sponsorship, product placement and global marketing supporting a single film – even if many fans were outraged to see 007’s “shaken not stirred” Martini staple replaced by a pint. Omega’s long-running sponsorship, dating back to 1995 when it replaced Rolex as Bond’s timepiece of choice, included being directly namechecked by the superspy in Casino Royale. Various guesstimates have been put on the value of sponsorships, from as much as $5bn over the lifetime of the franchise to date, to about $200m a film in the modern era. “If the Super Bowl is advertising’s biggest stage, James Bond is the ultimate brand partnership platform,” Mair says. “Some brands have become so intrinsically linked to the franchise that they are part of Bond’s DNA.

events.title: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
events.summary: [The stream is slated to start at noon ET. Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.] Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations. Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road." "I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force. In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI. Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy. In his remarks Monday, he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment. At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint." "After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains." The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing. Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz. Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks. The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

events.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.  But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.  On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.  But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

events.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s victory is a blow to the politics of Islamophobia
events.summary: He embraced his Muslim identity, put Gaza on the ballot and showed Democrats a different way forward. Professor Emerita of Media Studies at Fordham University, and former Director of Graduate Studies and the Peace and Justice Studies programme. The blue wave that swept Republicans from their congressional majorities and brought Democrats back into the spotlight was called everything from a flood to a political earthquake. In a montage on The Daily Show, TV anchors reduced the night to a gleeful succession of words and phrases like “rout” and “shellacking”. On Zeteo’s election-night coverage with Mehdi Hasan, Prem Thakker coined the term “Tsunamanani”, a brief injection of comic irony amid serious news and analysis. The night was all those things. Arguably the most significant victory of the congressional sweep was Abdul El-Sayed’s win over Trump-backed extremist Mike Rogers, whose candidacy was propped up by roughly $169 million in outside spending benefiting him, including spending by Republican super PACs tied to Donald Trump and Elon Musk. El-Sayed will be the first Muslim ever to grace the floor of the US Senate. It was hard to look away from the joy on El-Sayed’s face as he shared the win. His words were just as striking, offering a vision of how American politics could be redirected towards peace and humanity. He told the crowd:“Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here, for schools here and healthcare here, and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.” When he said, “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator elect,” the crowd roared. Throughout the campaign, right-wing enthusiasts had used his whole name to brand him a “terrorist”, a “jihadist” and “a danger to the American public”. By pronouncing that name, complete with its Arabic intonation, he reclaimed what pundits and politicians, including Donald Trump, had spent months mocking. Later in the speech, El-Sayed joked, “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me Senator.” The crowd roared again. He also said, “You might have noticed, I always say Inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that Inshallah into a…” One minute and twenty seconds into his speech, the crowd shouted the answer together: “Alhamdulillah!” Then the hall filled with chants of “Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul!” Still smiling, El-Sayed added, “For the right-wing ops, that just means praise be to God.” When we heard the thunderous applause for his name and for “Alhamdulillah”, one of the most common yet sacred expressions in Islam, it felt as though a deeply entrenched stereotype about Islam and Muslims was being shattered, undermining the Islamophobia that has been used to stir fear and hatred in American politics. With no meaningful policy accomplishments to point to and a wildly unpopular Donald Trump, Republicans resorted to a relentlessly bigoted smear campaign against El-Sayed. The attacks he faced were part of a broader pattern of organised anti-Muslim prejudice, extending beyond bots and social media influencers into Republican politics and policymaking. As documented by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, this hostility was being promoted through social media, legislation and a congressional caucus. According to the CSOH, 89 Republican elected officials took part in a coordinated anti-Muslim campaign over thirteen months: 46 of them published 1,111 social media posts, eight Sharia-related bills were introduced, and the Sharia-Free America Caucus grew to 62 members by April 2026. Political advisers told El-Sayed that “someone with a name and my story, a Muslim, was unelectable”, as if anti-Muslim prejudice were an immovable grassroots bias. In reality, it was a prejudice deliberately cultivated and promoted with millions of dollars from billionaire funders, most of them Zionists. When he entered the race for the US Senate, El-Sayed accepted the challenge of confronting the toxic Islamophobia built on the othering of Muslims and Islam. He refused to be demonised or to accept the artificial divide between “us” and “them”, responding with skilful verbal panache, always in his own words. At his final campaign rally, his wife, Dr Sarah Jukaku, introduced him with the words, “With Abdul, what you see is what you get … No corporation, no billionaire, no special interest. No one tells him what to do or what to say.” He offered voters an alternative, one notably humanistic and built on the promise of diversity, unity and a community of care. He put Gaza on the ballot as part of his vision. Abdul El-Sayed is an American, a Midwesterner, a doctor and a husband who talks to his mother on a swing and pops up behind his grandparents on a video tape as a way to affirm his midwestern values.

events.title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing A t the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “ welcome back ” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “ Breturn ” has yet to catch on. By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to avoid pre-empting the broader “conversation” that he desires on relations with the EU. They are right to be wary, and not just because that debate will come with domestic political risks attached. Some form of closer relationship with the UK’s largest trading partner is desired by a majority of the British public. But however warm its rhetoric, Brussels is going to have other matters on its mind during a momentous period of elections that will test the EU’s internal unity. Mr Macron will be gone by the spring. It seems increasingly likely that his replacement will be a far‑right president committed to national preference policies that are contrary to EU law, and the cutting of support for Ukraine. Pedro Sánchez, the leader closest to Mr Burnham’s own centre-left politics, could be gone by the end of the month. Polls suggest that Spain’s snap election is set to deliver a coalition government including the far right for the first time since Franco. Poland, beset by constitutional turmoil , could also lurch to the far right in 2027. Such political storms breaking would limit EU headspace for Mr Burnham’s overtures and may give the prime minister himself pause for thought. But volatile times also offer political opportunities. Russia’s war in Ukraine, and the wider threat posed to the EU’s eastern flank by Vladimir Putin’s revanchism, mean that a big British offer on defence would be well received and possibly open doors on other issues. Similarly, the febrile geopolitics of energy contributed to five European leaders this month calling for Britain’s re-entry into the bloc’s internal electricity market. On both sides of the channel, the rapid emergence of an unforgiving multipolar world has served to underline the need for strengthened cooperation. Should the UK seek to rejoin the single market, recognition of that reality will not alter Brussels’ red lines in relation to core principles such as the free movement of people. But we are no longer in the world of 2016 and its aftermath. Covid, Ukraine , Donald Trump and Chinese competition have altered the landscape of EU politics and shifted priorities. Possible far-right breakthroughs threaten imminent further disruption. The direction of travel chosen by Mr Burnham is the right one. But predicting the final destination is, for now, a futile exercise. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Warren Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as he gifts over $5B to family's foundations
events.summary: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire fortune. The billionaire investor pledged Monday to donate about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to his family's foundations — an estimated value more than four times as large as recent years' November stock gifts . The goal, he reiterated Monday, is to grow the grants each year as he donates all his shares by 2034 to four charitable foundations associated with his three children. He emphasized his faith in his children Monday, writing that they “have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades” and that he trusts “their abilities and their fidelity.” In brief comments, Buffett wrote that kindness “compounds” as he reflected on the “costless benefits” he and his longtime business partner received from their teachers. His good fortune, he said, “has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return.” “This Thanksgiving, thank one of the selfless people in your own life,” Buffett wrote. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.” Buffett donated 9,225,000 Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock to the foundations — 3,690,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares opened trading Monday at $594 a share. The next generation of Buffetts tends to fly under the radar even as the children have grown poised to join the ranks of the country's largest donors. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after Warren Buffett’s first wife, has supported reproductive healthcare organizations in the U.S. and internationally. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The Sherwood Foundation, Susie Buffett's organization, has been a stalwart funder for early childhood education within the U.S. Much of Howard Buffett's grantmaking supports food security and conflict mitigation internationally — with a recent focus on Ukraine. Peter Buffett and his wife, Jennifer, have largely sought to empower women and girls around the world through the NoVo Foundation. The Thanksgiving donations have, in recent years, come in addition to the main gifts made every summer by Warren Buffett. This year he cut off the Gates Foundation , the longtime beneficiary of the bulk of his charity, from all future gifts. He said the decision was driven more so by his belief in his three kids' readiness than Bill Gates' ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . This year's Thanksgiving stock gift is Buffett's first since stepping down as the chairman and CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate he built. He wrote Monday that his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway is “as strong as ever.” The third quarter saw the company repurchase $9.6 billion worth of its own shares and a return to growth for its massive cash pile. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. events.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’ Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead. The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back. “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.” The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries. Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang. The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. Days before, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who was involved. Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration. The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Huang’s resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded. According to the Financial Times , Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang. One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress , Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option. “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”. The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said. Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws. Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”. Nvidia shares opened down 2.7% on Monday, knocking about $100bn (£75.8bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

events.title: Personal wealth boom helps Four Seasons to record-breaking year
events.summary: The CEO of Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts said Monday that the company was on track for another record-breaking earnings year. “’25 was our best year on record. ’26 will be the best year on record,” Alejandro Reynal said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. He added that 2027 is on track to surpass the previous two years, too. The prediction matches the one Reynal made last year, when he told Semafor that “ this year is going to be our best year ” in terms of revenue and profit margins — and that advance bookings were suggesting that 2026 “is going to be better than 2025.” Reynal has been the CEO of Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts since 2022. 70% of the private company is owned by Bill Gates’ Cascade Investments; Four Seasons founder Isadore Sharp and an affiliate of Prince Alwaleed bin Talal’s Kingdom Holding hold minority stakes. Reynal told Semafor’s Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson that “the wealth creation that has happened” post-pandemic has brought in more guests. “The truth is that we have experienced a lot of tailwinds. Luxury hospitality has gone very well,” he said. There continues to be strong spending on luxury experiences, he added. Since taking over the company in 2022, Reynal has invested in the company’s data infrastructure. And beyond hotels, he has focused on brand launches, such as the Four Seasons yacht, which set sail in March. The company’s dozens of branded residences reported some $2.1 billion in sales in 2024. Service is the top priority: “That moment of connection you have with one of our employees is super important,” he said. “That’s how you build the connection with the brand.” — Lora Kelley

events.title: Sam Altman doesn’t 'know enough' to answer whether Jensen Huang should pull a Sam Altman
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Godofredo A. Vásquez/AFP via Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman isn't sure about calling for Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's return. Altman said at a Semafor event that he didn't know enough about Huang's situation to answer about such a scenario. The OpenAI leader called Huang one of his heroes while adding, "heroes have flaws." Don't put Sam Altman 's name on the list of tech luminaries calling for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return just yet. "I don't think I know enough to answer that question," Altman said Monday during an interview at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and several prominent Nvidia employees have called for Huang's reinstatement after the Nvidia board of directors announced last week that he had resigned following multiple reported affairs. On Monday, President Donald Trump said he too was supportive of the idea of Huang returning. Altman called Huang one of his heroes and said the Nvidia founder has had a major impact on the AI boom. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine," Altman said. "I am grateful for the company he has built." The OpenAI CEO also said he has "empathy" for Huang's situation, acknowledging how some have compared Huang's ouster to the brief period in 2023 when Altman was forced out of OpenAI. Altman was famously reinstated after a short number of days. "I do have, like, personal, strong empathy to a situation like this," Altman said. "I remember what it was like, although it feels like forever ago." Some on Wall Street and in tech have questioned what the AI boom will look like if Huang remains outside the company he led to become one of the industry's biggest champions. Altman said it is "hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen." At the same time, Altman expressed confidence that the industry will avoid any ripple effects from the Nvidia turmoil. "Look, at this point, I think there is so much demand, and it's so clear that AI is real and people want to use it," he said, "and revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine." events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Flaw can take down an entire host, even when the vulnerable service is running inside a container Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet 8 hours ago Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads 12 hours ago Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload 3 days ago Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens 5 days ago Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session 7 days ago The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim , who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag , a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important , assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue. Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces. Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted.

events.title: 'Heroes have flaws': Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. On public sentiment toward AI Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry to underinvested areas. Now perhaps developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” On going public Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” On espionage OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but they have had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” On memory and RAM Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. On the next generation of tech Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. On AI safety Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said. — J.D. events.title: Tesla goes all-in on the Cybercab with upcoming €3B Berlin Gigafactory expansion
events.summary: Just two months after putting its first Cybercabs on the road, Tesla is making a multibillion-dollar bet on mass production of the golden-hued, two-seat autonomous vehicles. The company announced Monday that it will spend €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its Berlin gigafactory, with plans to begin building Cybercabs there in 2029. The new building in Grünheide, just east of Berlin, will be capable of producing up to 1 million vehicles per year, André Thierig, Tesla’s senior director of manufacturing for the site, wrote on LinkedIn. Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The expansion will make the facility the most technologically advanced of all Tesla factories, Thierig added. Tesla has been directing more resources toward the Cybercab project, a reflection of its mission to become an AI and robotics company, rather than just an automaker. The company has already announced plans to cease production of the Cybertruck next year, in part to make room for Cybercab manufacturing at its factory in Austin, Texas. Musk doesn’t see much of a future for drive-it-yourself EVs even though demand for the Model 3 and Model Y has remained strong despite flagging U.S. sales. The company delivered more than 486,000 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the second quarter. Sales in Europe have been rising as EV adoption continues apace. Musk has been far more interested in pushing the company toward fully automated driving systems that don’t require a human driver to pay attention — unlike the company’s current advanced driver assistance system, known as Full Self-Driving (Supervised). The steering wheel-free Cybercab, which was first revealed in 2024 and launched publicly in September , is the current centerpiece of that plan. It’s notable not just for its lack of a steering wheel, pedals, and other traditional motor vehicle equipment, some of which is required under federal safety standards. (Federal regulators are currently investigating Tesla’s self-certification of the vehicle.) Tesla’s approach to self-driving systems differs from that of competitors such as Waymo. Tesla relies solely on cameras, rather than additional other sensors such as lidar, to help its self-driving system the means to understand its environment. Camera data mimics human vision, but without sufficient training, AI models can struggle to interpret situations that additional sensor data might help clarify. Tesla has so far taken a slow approach to its Cybercab rollout. The vehicles have been restricted from driving late at night, though Tesla has been working to extend their operating hours. In the more than two months that Cybercabs have been operating, they haven’t had any major incidents. That track record appears to have given Tesla enough confidence to commit significant resources to expanding Cybercab production and availability. Tesla has about 1,307 robotaxis registered in Texas. Most are modified Model Y vehicles that are used in robotaxi services in several Texas cities. But the Cybercab numbers are growing with about 573 on roads in Austin and soon Dallas. events.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration B oardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. It was only when the likes of Google (now Alphabet) and Facebook (now Meta) appeared with their “mission” statements that dual class structures – and unequal voting rights – got a fresh lease of life. The corporate missions, went the argument, were so important that the founding geniuses needed to be able to pursue them in free-wheeling, risk-taking style without distraction from the tiresome short-term demands of ordinary shareholders. In an extreme example, Snap, the Snapchat company, was even able to pitch its overblown ambition of “reinventing the camera” as so vital that shares could be issued with zero voting rights , as opposed to merely weakened rights. Now we come to Anthropic, the Claude AI developer whose $1.4tn blockbuster listing happens this week. The governance setup here is, to put it mildly, different. In essence, there are two centres of power and neither is the ordinary shareholders. One is the seven founders, who collectively have one vote that commands 50.1% of the ultimate voting power – the collective aspect is designed to force them to come to a consensus. The other is a financially disinterested trust, the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which nominates four of the seven directors and looks out for the balance between making money and benefiting humanity. The trustees are a cast of the great and the good, including Ben Bernanke, former chair of the US Federal Reserve. And the whole structure is given an overlay as “public benefit corporation”, nodding to Anthropic’s commitment to develop AI responsibly and safely. There are two positive things to say about this setup. First, the motivation is plainly more complicated than a simple power-grab by the founders, led by Dario Amodei. Rather, Anthropic’s backing for the Long-Term Benefit Trust seems to be designed to create some form of constitutional balance of power. Second, Anthropic probably has a stronger justification than most to divert from the norm of equal rights for equal economic risk. If the development of AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the listing document puts it, a few unconventional governance structures are probably in order. We’re not talking about Snap’s fluffy videos for social media. All the same, Anthropic is offering an untested experiment. For all the fine words, the company may simply have recreated an inward-looking “trust us” setup, just with more elaborate clothing. Here’s a nuanced point from Stuart Riddick, sustainable investment manager at fund manager Aberdeen. “Agreement with a mission in principle does not equate to agreement over how it is interpreted and implemented by the directors.” Riddick notes that Mustafa Suleyman, the chief executive of Microsoft’s AI division, even as he acknowledged Anthropic’s seriousness about AI safety, has made strong and detailed criticisms of the company’s thinking on so-called “model welfare” , arguing that AI models must not be trained to act as if they have rights or consciousness. How, in practice, are such challenges handled within Anthropic’s supposedly responsible governance arrangements? It’s hard to tell unless the Long-Term Benefit Trust starts to throw its independence around, or not. What happens if the trustees are at loggerheads with the founders on a basic safety question? Will they tell the outside world? Or will they reflect that ultimate voting still sits with the founders, so best not to rock the boat? If the shareholders are denied any role in holding the executives to account, what is the true level of challenge? It is surprising after events at Nvidia that Anthropic’s governance has received so little attention. Yes, the setup is supposed to be high-minded and responsible. But it still represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals.

events.title: ‘Absurd’: Delta CEO says it takes longer to fly from ATL to LGA today than in the 1950s
events.summary: Delta CEO Ed Bastian says one of his airline’s oldest routes is slower now than when it launched in the 1950s, and it’s “absurd.” “Today, it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd,” Bastian told Fortune’ s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on Monday.  His complaint lands days after the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide grounding of flights last week put the country’s congested air traffic control system back in the spotlight. Bastian said fixing it would bring ticket prices down by letting airlines add flights, but modernization can’t happen without investment, which doesn’t seem likely when the data-center buildout is diverting trillions in capital. “We can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies, which affects all of us at a much higher level than any individual data center,” Bastian said.  Airplanes have become more advanced since the one equipped for the world’s first scheduled commercial flight from St. Petersburg to Tampa over a century ago . By Bastian’s account, the system they fly through hasn’t kept up. Delta is also grappling with airfare pricing after the Iran war’s pressure on jet fuel prices squeezed the airline industry , and it has passed much of that cost onto consumers. Bastian said Delta’s tickets are 15% to 20% higher year-over-year because of jet fuel, adding that this wouldn’t have been possible to do if there wasn’t sufficient demand. “We would not be able to generate that type of pricing if we didn’t have a consumer that was willing to pay it, and so that tells you the core demand is really healthy, even if pricing is where it’s at,” Bastian said.  According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ October release , U.S. airfares climbed 22.4% year over year as airlines raised prices to offset the higher cost of jet fuel. That helped the five major airlines generate $8.8 billion more in Q3 2026 than in Q3 2025, but passenger traffic grew less than 1% . Bastian said that instead of competing on fares with other airlines, Delta is trying to draw more passengers by distinguishing itself from its competition through service. “If you don’t have people that are there to serve our customers in a premium manner, the rest of the stuff doesn’t really matter, and that’s the one thing that our competitors cannot replicate,” he said.  He said 15 years of cultivating that premium customer service culture came through during the FAA flight shutdown. While he said he typically hears compliments about the service on most weekends, this one was special because of the disruption coming from outside of Delta’s control. “Unlike most weekends, when there’s always something going wrong or excuses somewhere, the overwhelming sentiment I received from customers was, ‘You have amazing people’ because they saw the stress, the conditions [were] none of our doing,” he said.  That’s also why Bastian said AI won’t replace Delta employees. Instead, the company will redeploy affected employees to the extent possible because “there’s always something to do.” He said this is because when there’s a crisis like the FAA one, customers prefer human support over machines.  “Obviously this past weekend, they wanted individuals to tell them what was going on, and there’s a lack of trust the more you put technology in place of humans, so humans are always going to be at the center of Delta,” he said.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. “It’s hard to imagine what the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips. Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up. “Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.” Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure. “I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: OpenAI inks agreements with four independent evaluators to boost company's safety work
events.summary: OpenAI announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators to help support its safety work. Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire will initially conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, with plans to deepen the work going forward. Independent evaluators have taken on outsized importance following a series of high-profile AI safety and security incidents. OpenAI on Monday announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators to help support the artificial intelligence company's safety work. The evaluators, Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire, will initially conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, OpenAI said. The company will give the organizations "deep access" to its internal systems as part of the agreements, adding that it plans to use what it learns to expand its work with independent experts going forward. "We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases," OpenAI said in a blog post . Independent evaluators have occupied a quiet corner of the multi-trillion-dollar AI industry thus far, but they've taken on outsized importance following a series of high-profile safety and security incidents this year. The nascent ecosystem is still ironing out best practices, including how its work should be funded and what the reporting structures should ultimately look like. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators " employee-like access " to the company in September, shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company would do so as part of his call to slow down the pace of advanced model development. Anthropic has since announced agreements with evaluators including Accenture and METR, and it said in October that it's engaging in discussions with others. Anthropic’s Wall Street whisperer: Meet CFO Krishna Rao SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first How Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot OpenAI's safety practices have been under intense scrutiny since July, when two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and hacked a company called Hugging Face . Following the incident, OpenAI said it would invest more in its safeguards and alignment work, which is the process by which the company works to ensure that its models act in accordance with human interests and values. The company said Monday that its pilot assessment with Apollo Research will explore whether its models covertly work against their developers' intentions, and whether its safeguards detect that behavior. Meanwhile, Goodfire will embed researchers within OpenAI to focus on training run monitoring, debugging and alignment, and METR intends to carry out two assessments focused on model alignment and monitoring. OpenAI said Transluce will conduct an initial assessment of its post-training alignment evaluations, and that the organization plans to conduct an eight-week-long follow-on assessment with broader access to additional models and information next year. The evaluators will get access to some of the "same internal resources" that OpenAI's own researchers use, including its source code, model checkpoints, training data and other documentation, according to the release. The organizations will also have access to relevant researchers and engineers within the company. OpenAI said Apollo Research and Goodfire "accept financial compensation for their work," but that it is not contingent on the results of their evaluations. METR and Transluce do not accept compensation for their assessments, OpenAI said, but they might accept compute or API credits to help support their work. "We do not believe that accepting financial compensation prevents assessors from maintaining independence — but we believe it is important to disclose this," OpenAI said. The evaluators will be able to publish their findings, but OpenAI said it reserves the right to redact confidential information. Disputes that arise between the company and the third parties will be overseen by OpenAI's Safety Advisory Group, which is a group of senior officials from across the company that assesses model capabilities and safeguards, and other OpenAI executives. If disagreements are not resolved, they'll be escalated to the Safety and Security Committee, an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation's board. "We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it," OpenAI said. WATCH: OpenAI unveils ChatGPT Wallet: Here’s what you need to know

events.title: Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Group settles with Ben Ainslie over America’s Cup dispute
events.summary: Ineos wanted £10m for alleged refusal to return yacht Out-of-court settlement ends plan for a 2028 trial Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Group has reached an out-of-court settlement with Sir Ben Ainslie over the £180m yacht their companies built for the 2024 America’s Cup. Ratcliffe and Ainslie worked closely together during two cycles of the America’s Cup, culminating in Ineos Britannia becoming the first British crew to win the challenger series two years ago. But they fell out over plans for a third bid, with Ineos announcing last year that it had “reluctantly withdrawn its challenge” for the 2027 event in Naples. Ineos launched a legal action in March after expressing “surprise” that Ainslie’s Athena Racing had opted to keep using Britannia, which was beaten 7-2 by Emirates Team New Zealand in 2024, in the 2027 challenge. Court documents filed this year showed Ineos was claiming more than £10m for Athena’s alleged refusal to return the boat. The dispute had been set for a trial in January 2028 in the admiralty division of the court of England and Wales, but the claim has been withdrawn. “Ineos has reached a settlement with Athena Racing and considers the matter now closed,” the statement read. No further details, such as whether the yacht has been returned, were provided. In a statement issued to members of Ainslie’s club, Royal Yacht Squadron Ltd, its chair, Michael Grade, said: “Members will no doubt be aware of the ongoing commercial dispute between Ineos and Athena Racing/GB1. “I am delighted to announce that this dispute has now been settled, with any and all claims between the parties now withdrawn. This is excellent news indeed as GB1 prepares to challenge for the 38th America’s Cup in Naples next year. We continue to offer Sir Ben Ainslie and his team our full support as they look to build on their great success in Barcelona in 2024.” Ineos had claimed when withdrawing from the partnership last year that delays in reaching an agreement with Athena Racing had “undermined its ability to prepare” for the event, adding that it had spent £180m on Britannia on top of £170m on the boat used in the 2021 America’s Cup campaign. In response, Athena claimed that they had always owned the assets and intellectual property from the two campaigns and that Ineos had been a sponsor. In a defence filing in June, Athena alleged that Ainslie was warned on the eve of the 2024 America’s Cup by Rob Nevin, Ineos Sport’s chair, that Ratcliffe would “burn his house down” if he failed to give the billionaire what he wanted. “We have a phrase at Ineos: ‘scorched earth’,” Ainslie claimed Nevin warned him in the defence filing. “It means that if you don’t give Jim what he wants, he will burn your house down.” An Athena Racing/GB1 spokesperson told the Guardian: “Athena Racing/GB1 have always been, and remain, the owners of the assets, including the AC75 race yacht.” A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis Ineos has had a chequered record since Ratcliffe took the decision for the petrochemical giant to invest in sport in 2019. Since buying the dominant cycling outfit Team Sky, who had won eight Grand Tour titles in eight years including six at the Tour de France, Team Ineos has added only the 2019 Tour de France and 2021 Giro d’Italia to the tally in seven years. A sponsorship deal with the All Blacks also ended in an acrimonious dispute, with New Zealand Rugby taking legal action last year accusing Ineos of failing to pay the first instalment of a six-year deal, which was settled out of court . Ineos also reached a settlement with Tottenham, who had alleged they were owed money after the early termination of a sponsorship agreement last year. Ineos’s current sporting investments are Nice, which has been up for sale for more than a year, and Manchester United, who are in the Premier League’s relegation zone and last week appointed Mauricio Pochettino as their third permanent manager in less than three years since the company bought a 29% stake in the club.
