events.title: Sam Bankman-Fried’s former employer Jane Street poised for $35 billion windfall from purchase of Anthropic shares in FTX bankruptcy
events.summary: When Anthropic goes public this week, several big players will enjoy a windfall after having snapped up shares at firesale prices in 2024 at the bankruptcy liquidation of collapsed crypto exchange FTX. Those include the quant giant Jane Street, which spent $1.34 billion to purchase Anthropic shares at the time—a stake that is likely to be worth over $35 million after the IPO. And, in a twist of fate, Jane Street is the first employer of Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced founder of FTX, who is now serving a 25-year sentence for fraud in federal prison. Bankman-Fried expressed frustration over the sale in a recent interview with The New York Times , criticizing the bankruptcy administrators who took control of FTX after its collapse. In addition to Jane Street, other buyers of FTX’s Anthropic shares are an investment vehicle linked to Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala and the Ford Foundation, both of which are also poised to share in the windfall. Bankman-Fried became one of Anthropic’s earliest investors in late 2021, when he put $500 million into the little-known startup for a 13.5% stake that later shrank as the company raised more money, according to The New York Times . Nearly five years later, Anthropic is just two days away from pricing what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history, with trading on the Nasdaq expected to begin Thursday. Its proposed price range of $70 to $78 per share would value the company at up to roughly $1.4 trillion . The company behind the Claude chatbot generated $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter alone, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier, according to earlier Fortune reporting. Bankman-Fried’s interest in the company stemmed in part from his connections to its cofounder, former OpenAI executive Dario Amodei. The two moved in the same tech circles and shared concerns about the risks of powerful AI, according to the Times . Mutual acquaintances connected them shortly after Amodei left OpenAI to start Anthropic. At the time of FTX’s investment into Anthropic, Bankman-Fried was also illegally using his customers’ money to make numerous other bets and spraying funds to several politicians in Washington, DC in a bid to gain political influence. FTX, though, would not survive to see the early bet on Anthropic mature. In November 2022, the exchange collapsed after a run on deposits exposed an $8 billion hole in customer accounts—a scandal that ultimately led to Bankman-Fried’s conviction on fraud and conspiracy charges and a hefty prison sentence . The bankruptcy administrators who took control sold the Anthropic shares in 2024 to raise money to repay customers. By then, Anthropic had launched Claude and attracted billions of dollars from investors, including Amazon . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: I travel alone all the time, but taking my first cruise solo surprised me in 6 ways
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter took a solo cruise on Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I'd traveled across the world and back on long-haul flights by myself. I'd booked cabins for one on overnight trains. So why not try cruising alone? I was used to traveling solo by plane and train, but I'd never even seen a cruise ship in real life. In April 2022, I went on my first cruise by myself. I booked a seven-night voyage for one on board Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas. My ship sailed from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, to Roatán, Honduras; Cozumel and Costa Maya, Mexico; and Perfect Day at CocoCay, Royal Caribbean's private island in the Bahamas. As a longtime solo traveler and first-time cruiser, my inaugural voyage came with some surprises. From booking the trip to setting sail, here's what I didn't see coming. When booking my cruise, I was surprised to find that the room rate was higher for just one person than for two. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Typically, most cruise ship staterooms sleep at least two people, and booking a room by yourself often means you still have to pay higher prices. Some cruise ships have solo cabins for one person, but mine didn't.  I learned this while booking my cruise. The listed rates for my ship were per person, not per room. When I changed the number of guests in my search from two to one, the per-person cost doubled. This is known as paying a " single supplement ," as it helps the cruise line recoup the revenue it would have generated from a second person on board. For $2,000, I got an ocean-view stateroom to myself. It would have cost about half the price per person if I had brought someone with me. I thought it would be harder to socialize with other cruisers as a solo traveler. Joey Hadden/Business Insider As someone who is typically shy around new people, I was surprised by how easy it was to talk to other travelers on the ship. Couples, families, and solo cruisers seemed open to chatting and sharing their experiences with me on the pool decks and in various eateries and common spaces. After all, we had at least one thing in common — being on this epic vacation.  I expected navigating the ports to be a challenge, but it wasn't since I booked excursions through the cruise line. Joey Hadden/Business Insider At each cruise port, passengers may disembark to spend their time as they wish. They might sightsee independently, take a taxi to a beach, link up with a local tour guide, or join an official cruise-line excursion. I joined a cruise-line excursion at every port and was nervous about finding my group amid the large crowds. However, I was given clear directions on where to meet my group each time, and there were so many posted signs that it was easy to find.  The easiest way to get to know fellow cruisers wasn't on board. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I figured that since I was a solo traveler, I'd experience the ports alone, but I found that many people on excursions were looking to meet new people. Since we were together for hours sharing an experience, I built deeper connections with people on excursions than on the ship. With group activities like hiking and plenty of downtime on bus rides to and from the tour locations, I spent most of my time socializing. On a guided hike in Roatán, Honduras , I met couples, families, and one other solo traveler. I was shocked to be mistaken for a child every time I entered or exited the ship. The author at a cruise port. Joey Hadden/Business Insider "Where are your parents?" was a question I had to answer nearly every day of my cruise. Cruise-line workers were quick to assume that I was a lost child rather than a solo cruiser each time I entered and exited the ship. This could be because I look young (in my opinion), but it also made me think that solo cruising might be less common at 26, my age at the time. Even as a single person on one of the world's largest cruise ships, it was hard to find a chair on the pool deck after noon. A crowded pool deck on the ship. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Wonder of the Seas is one of the largest cruise ships in the world, so I thought that it would be pretty easy to find a single pool chair on the ship at any time. But by midday, most of the chairs were occupied or covered with towels. While saving chairs with towels wasn't allowed on my ship, I didn't see the rule enforced, so I had to arrive early to secure a good spot.  While I thought my first cruise was enjoyable on my own, if I were to take another one, I'd prefer to bring a buddy. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Despite the social activities and friendly cruisers who loved to chat with random strangers like me, I still found myself feeling lonely on the ship. I longed to have a conversation with someone who knew me or to share my experiences in new places with a loved one. Being surrounded by so many families and groups of friends made me wish I could be with mine. If I cruise again, I'll definitely bring my own crew. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest | Letters
events.summary: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest Joanna Elson of the Independent Age charity is concerned about poverty among pensioners and says ministers need to think hard before making changes You report ( 11 November ) Torsten Bell’s suggestion that the Conservatives would need to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock. It is well known that raising the state pension age increases poverty rates among those who have to wait longer for it, with those on the lowest incomes hit the hardest. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported that when the age rose from 65 to 66, the poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled, with renters and those with lower levels of education among those more likely to struggle. Our helpline already hears from too many older people on low incomes having to cut back on essentials to pay their bills. With poverty in later life on the rise, and healthy life expectancy reversing (with lows of 50.9 years for men and 51.8 years for women, both in Blackpool at the last count, according to the Office for National Statistics ) we need to think very hard indeed about how to mitigate these impacts if we contemplate further rises. Joanna Elson CEO, Independent Age charity Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Opt-in Edge archive gives Pro subscribers early access before full testing, while normal updates remain human-validated Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn 14 minutes ago ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years 1 hour ago NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making 1 hour ago Crook turns free trials into phishing factory, as LearnWorlds sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices 3 hours ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 3 hours ago Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering. Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive , an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework. As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive." Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated. Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company . At the previous such event in June , the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious. The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team. Ubuntu Summit 26.10 Thursday keynotes – Pierre Guillemin's begins at 27 minutes in. It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism ). It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022 , Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings. We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30 , surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world. Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money .

events.title: At 17, South Carolina-bound GG Banks is building a brand before her first college game
events.summary: Jezelle “GG” Banks doesn’t turn 18 until Nov. 27, but she already has a logo. The senior at The St. James Academy, just outside Washington, D.C., is a five-star guard ranked No. 4 in the class of 2027 and committed to South Carolina, the No. 1 team in the AP poll. She’s as at home slicing past defenders as she is hosting long livestreams on social media. Banks is also building a business. In a growing number of states, high school athletes can now be paid for their name, image, and likeness (NIL), just like college athletes. In an exclusive interview with Fortune , she revealed her personal logo publicly for the first time. “I love it! It really fits me,” Banks said. “Everything in the logo has special meaning to me. I think the logo speaks to my personality—spikes of energy boosting everything, and then towards the bottom you’ve got a dollar sign, because, of course, banks.” Logo Design & Branding: THE·TEAM The dollar sign plays on her last name. Banks worked on the design with her agency, THE·TEAM , the sports and entertainment firm formerly known as Wasserman. Coming just weeks before her 18th birthday, it’s a birthday present of sorts. “This was a dream,” Banks said. THE·TEAM showed her mockups of the logo on sneakers and in Times Square. “That’s what I envisioned when I was younger, me having the logo.” Building who she was on the court Custom logos are still rare among high school players, but Banks has been dreaming big for a while. “I saw this coming a little bit, not just for me, but I think just the women’s era—people paying more attention to women’s basketball,” she said. “And I think when I was 14 or 15, I honestly started to, I wouldn’t say build my brand, but build who I was on the court… I learned pretty early on how to manage myself in a mature way.” Her agent, Lindsay Kagawa Colas, executive vice president of talent representation at THE·TEAM, has represented some of the game’s biggest names, including Diana Taurasi, Paige Bueckers , and 2026 WNBA Finals MVP Gabby Williams. “In establishing an elevated mark like this, I think our goal, with (the logo) and her business, was to make sure that she was building something big enough to match her potential,” Kagawa Colas said. Donovan Chew In viral highlight videos, Banks is equally adept at dribbling past opponents to score and dishing to teammates for easy buckets. She finishes with a flourish, usually with a winning smile. That’s a combination brands notice. She’s clearly been working on her handle off the court, too. She has more than 120,000 followers on TikTok and about 84,000 on Instagram. “She had a real clear understanding about the value of building her audience as she was building her resume,” Kagawa Colas said. A commitment streamed on Twitch Last month, Banks partnered with Amazon-owned Twitch on an exclusive livestream of her commitment to South Carolina. The Saturday-afternoon stream followed her through the day and ended with her announcement in her high school’s gym, packed with friends and family. “For me to be the first high school hooper to have this on Twitch, it just shows what I’m trying to build, not only for me, but for the younger generation behind me, anything is possible,” Banks said. “I think it was awesome!” Kagawa Colas sees a generational shift. “I think she is certainly emblematic of a generation where she’s becoming the media we used to wait for, where she knows that fans believe in her and will invest emotionally if you let them get close and provide that sense of connection,” she said. Why South Carolina fit the plan Under coach Dawn Staley , South Carolina has become a powerhouse. The Gamecocks have won three national titles since 2017, most recently in 2024, and finished runner-up in each of the past two seasons. “It’s clear that GG wants to be the best and that she is not afraid of high expectations and hard work. So that was really the first focus,” Kagawa Colas said. “We’ll be looking for partnerships that build on that, but establishing who she is in that direction, through that (college) choice, we thought was very clear.” Kagawa Colas knows what it takes for athletes to reach the top, on and off the court. “With GG, it’s been rewarding to see her plan gain traction so quickly, because it’s driven by her joy, her love of the game and her natural ability to connect with people,” she said. events.title: Rudd-era mining tax could have boosted budget by $135b
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Kevin Rudd-era mining 'super profits' tax could have improved budget by $135b Kevin Rudd (left) attempted to introduce a tax on resources super profits, but it led in part to his removal as prime minister. ( Alan Porritt: AAP ) Parliamentary Budget Office analysis commissioned by the Greens has found a mining super profits tax proposed by former PM Kevin Rudd could have raised $135 billion if it had been kept. The proposed tax became deeply unpopular and led to Mr Rudd's removal as prime minister in 2010. The Greens continue to call for a tax on gas export profits, saying the public is missing out. Labor's abandoned mining tax, which led to the 2010 toppling of then-prime minister Kevin Rudd, could have improved the budget by $135 billion if it had been kept, a Parliamentary Budget Office analysis has concluded. Mr Rudd's proposal to tax 40 per cent of mining company "super profits" sparked a fierce $22 million industry campaign against the tax that continued until he was ousted by his then-deputy, Julia Gillard. The unpopularity of the Resources Super Profits Tax partly prompted the leadership challenge by Ms Gillard, who replaced the super profits tax with a lighter-taxing scheme. That was also eventually scrapped when the Coalition — under Tony Abbott — won government at the 2013 election. Since 2012, when the super profits tax was meant to begin, the federal budget has been in deficit most years. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has warned the pressures on the budget are mounting — with borrowing costs growing, and aged care and other social payments becoming more expensive — even with measures to save $38 billion over four years from the National Disability Insurance Scheme. The federal government is also under pressure to slow down spending, as the Reserve Bank warns a lack of "domestic capacity" is driving up inflation, alongside international pressures including the war in Iran. The Greens have called for a 25 per cent tax on gas export profits and an increase in the rent tax levied on offshore petroleum companies, saying both could help to fund the budget. Senator Steph Hodgins-May said the PBO modelling showed the missed opportunity by not pursuing revenue from the resources giants. "We were interested to see what other revenue has been lost as a consequence of our government not being willing to stare down those big gas exporters, those big resources industry players, to make them pay what they owe," the senator said. "They jump with fright as soon as there are a couple of billboards at the airport warning them off going after these profits. "We're sick of the government telling us we can't have nice things, nice essential things, like free early childhood education, like wiping HECS debt, like having a well-funded National Disability Insurance Scheme, and being told those things aren't possible when they are leaving in the realm of $135 billion on the table because they are unwilling to stare down a few mining and gas corporations." Steph Hodgins-May says the government could have raised tens of billions of dollars if it had held firm against resources industry lobbying. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) On Monday, Resources Minister Madeleine King dismissed the Greens' gas tax push. "Our focus is on getting more gas available to Australians at affordable prices. I'm not aware of any policy where you put a tax of that magnitude on a product that would make it more affordable to everyday Australians," she said. The government has previously warned a gas export tax could also damage Australia's relationships with Asia, which depends on Australian gas, and which Australia depends on for petrol and diesel. The PBO suggested the mining tax would have raised a net $24 billion last financial year if it had been kept, which would have eliminated the government's $22.3 billion budget deficit, with all else being equal. It found over the 14 years that the tax would have operated, it could have improved the overall budget position by $135 billion — assuming that the major reform would not impact mining company behaviour. Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who was a senior adviser to then-treasurer Wayne Swan when the resources super profits tax was introduced, declined to comment. But the ABC was told the government is not considering reinstating the resource rent tax.

events.title: New warning about antibiotic resistance as world 'looks off cliff'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Antibiotic resistance on track to kill 39 million people in coming decades, doctors warn Antibiotic resistance means standard medical procedures can become high-risk or life threatening. ( ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills ) The peak body for doctors says increasing antibiotic resistance in Australia could threaten the foundations of modern medicine. Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats. Doctors and experts are calling for governments to act and scale up solutions. Millions of people are expected to die because of rising antimicrobial resistance over the coming decades, the peak body for Australian doctors has warned. The latest Australian figures show reports of critical resistance jumped by more than 25 per cent in 2024 alone, and if current trends continue, antimicrobial resistance will cause the deaths of 39 million people globally by 2050 — more than the total deaths projected for all cancers. Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats and occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites adapt to the medicines designed to treat them, most commonly, antibiotics. It means infections become difficult or impossible to treat, which increases the risk of disease spread and death. A new report released today by the Australian Medical Association (AMA) said the scale of the threat in Australia was rising and resistance was outpacing the national response. AMA president Michael Bonning said antibiotic resistance was already having devastating consequences and threatened to undermine the foundations of modern medicine. Michael Bonning says antibiotic resistance is already having serious impacts. ( ABC News: Rahni Sadler ) The World Health Organization (WHO) last year warned resistance to essential antibiotics was "widespread, increasing and unevenly distributed". The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a similarly stark warning last month, saying drug-resistant germs caused an estimated 50,800 deaths in the country each year. The latest figures show in 2020, more than 1,000 Australians died because of infections caused by five common antimicrobial-resistant bacteria. Although antimicrobial stewardship, which is specialised programs to promote responsible use of antimicrobials in the health system, has reduced overall antibiotic use by about 21 per cent in the past decade, prescribing has risen in residential aged care. Dr Bonning said such stewardship needed to be scaled up across hospitals, primary care and aged care, as well as agriculture and the environment. "We know what needs to be done. What we need now is coordinated action from governments and proper investment to implement those commitments and turn plans into results," he said. Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria and parasites adapt to the drugs meant to kill them. ( Pixabay ) The AMA report also took aim at state and federal initiatives allowing pharmacies to prescribe antibiotics for urinary tract infections without a script from a GP. It said evidence showed E. coli, which causes urinary tract infections, had developed resistance to Trimethoprim, an antibiotic available through some pharmacy prescribing programs. A spokesperson for the Pharmacy Guild of Australia said suggestions that pharmacies were independently choosing which antibiotics to prescribe were wrong, as they followed the same therapeutic guidelines as doctors. "Antimicrobial resistance is a whole-of-health-system challenge. The answer is strong antimicrobial stewardship by every prescriber …. not scaremongering and old turf wars," they said. Only a 'handful' of new antibiotics being explored Molecular biologist Amy Cain, who has dedicated her career to finding solutions for antimicrobial resistance, said the situation was getting increasingly "dangerous" and the world was "looking off a cliff". "I think anyone that's had a really nasty infection, especially one that hasn't responded to treatment, will understand how scary it is." Dr Cain, who works to find new antibiotics at the Galleria Research Facility at Macquarie University, said there were only a "handful" of new antibiotics in the pipeline globally and urgent funding was needed to turbocharge development. She said the pressure to develop new treatments fell heavily on academics and small research organisations, with pharmaceutical companies unmotivated to find breakthroughs as they did not stand to make significant financial gains from new antibiotics. Amy Cain wants to see a reduction in antibiotic use in agriculture.

events.title: Cargo ship capsizes off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast
events.summary: Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry says that all 12 of the ship’s crew members were saved in a rescue operation. A cargo ship has capsized off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, the country’s Transport Ministry has said. The ship’s crew, eight Turkish citizens and four Azerbaijani nationals, were rescued from the Somali-flagged Betul 8 in an operation on Monday that involved four ships, two from Bulgaria, one from Romania and one from Turkiye. list 1 of 3 Russia expels Moldovan diplomat in tit-for-tat move list 2 of 3 US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline list 3 of 3 At least 12 people killed in Bulgaria motorway pile-up Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry confirmed that one of its helicopters repatriated them to shore and that the crew was in good health. Speaking to journalists after being brought to the port city of Varna, crew members said their ship had been hit by two sea drones. The incident comes after three ships were hit off Romania over the weekend, according to authorities in Bucharest, though no casualties were reported. Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said on Monday the latest incidents were “unacceptable”. The ship was carrying 3,000 metric tons of wheat and was headed to Egypt from Romania. Bulgaria received a distress signal early on Monday that the ship was sinking approximately 40 nautical miles (74km) southeast of Cape Kaliakra. Betul 8 is the 17th vessel to be attacked off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania since mid-July, according to Diaplous, a maritime security firm. The waters off the coasts of the two countries, both of them NATO members, have become the primary route for shipments from Ukraine, one of the world’s largest grain exporters, whose own Black Sea ports have come under fire since Russia’s full-scale invasion more than four years ago. Ukraine has also been accused of targeting Russian vessels in other areas of the Black Sea. Romanian and Bulgarian officials have both pointed the finger at Russia over the attacks, though Bulgaria has underlined that there is no proof of who was behind them. Russia has previously denied it was responsible for deadly drone attacks in the region.

events.title: Bitcoin slides to $62,000 following liquidation cascade, then rebounds slightly
events.summary: Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite. The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level. Bitcoin's ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week, breaking below its 200-day moving average of about $73,000 and triggering the cascade of long liquidations, forcing traders to sell their assets at market price to settle their debts, pushing prices lower. On Saturday night, exchanges tracked by CoinGlass saw more than $165 million in liquidated bitcoin long positions, following $629 million on Friday and nearly $700 million on Thursday. Bitcoin was also facing potential selling pressure ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering, with the listing drawing speculative capital away from riskier assets. On Friday, the dollar index — which has an inverse relationship with bitcoin — reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening. That pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold, despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. "A break below $60,000 is possible if Nvidia's results add to the tech selling," he said. "The catalysts for a move higher are mostly macro, and a softer dollar with falling real yields would ease the pressure on every risk asset at once. If that happens, bitcoin goes into the recovery with less leverage than it carried in October, and a close back above $73,000 would be the first sign that the selling is over." Edwin Mata, CEO of tokenization platform Brickken, said he's monitoring whether spot buyers step in once the forced selling subsides. "Clearing out leveraged longs can slow the selling," he said. "For a recovery to hold, spot buyers need to keep showing up after the forced selling has passed."

events.title: Several companies are using Trump tariff refunds for corporate bonuses
events.summary: Some firms are directing refunds to corporate leadership instead of reimbursing consumers, ProPublica finds Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump ’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found. After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they are receiving tariff refunds and noted they are directing some of those funds to their leadership. Stanley Black & Decker, a tool company that makes common household products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, told its consumers they were forced to raise prices because of Trump’s import fees, ProPublica reported. The company is expected to receive at least $298m in tariff reimbursements and indicated some of it will go to bonuses. Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, discount department stores that are set to receive tariff refunds, also said the same. A spokesperson for TJ Maxx and Marshalls, which are owned by the same TJX parent company, confirmed ProPublica’s reporting, and said that the company received an aggregate of $331m in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered in the supreme court ruling. Because of these refunds, the company now has “accrue incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”, the spokesperson said. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” the company spokesperson said. In financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, according to ProPublica. Stanley Black & Decker, TJMaxx and Marshalls did not immediately respond to request for comment. The Trump administration has refunded at least $100bn to companies since August, about 60% of roughly $131bn in tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs were illegal. The court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful because they overstepped his executive authority and should have required congressional approval. Some companies immediately sued the US government for refunds after the ruling, though Trump signaled that he would “remember” which companies requested reimbursements and praised companies for holding off. The Trump administration has not specified which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica. Though many companies said publicly that they had to increase prices because of tariffs, it has largely been unclear what companies are doing with their tariff refunds. In its analysis, ProPublica found that almost all the companies that have publicly said they plan to use their tariff reimbursements to refund customers are those that deal directly with other businesses, rather than directly consumers. Some companies have remained “vague” about their plans for the reimbursements and have not specified whether those funds will go towards price decreases or holding back on future increases, according to the report. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Research has shown that US consumers have shouldered some of the cost of tariffs, with the New York Federal Reserve estimating that 26% of tariff increases pass through to consumer prices. The Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost households about $900 annually under current laws. Tariffs are one of several of Trump’s economic policies that have proven unpopular with voters, reflected in the widespread victories Democrats notched in the November midterms. A year after Trump’s tariffs were announced, a survey from the Pew Research Center found that 63% of Americans felt little or no confidence in his handling of tariffs. Republican candidates across the country were largely punished for Trump’s tariffs and other White House decisions that have led to greater inflation. In the Associated Press’s survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, two-thirds said that Trump’s decisions had fueled inflation, about half of the number of 2022 midterm voters who said the same thing about former president Joe Biden.

events.title: Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjar
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Occupied West Bank land defender is set to remain in detention until at least February 26 next year, with the possibility that the term could be extended. An Israeli military court has upheld a four–month administrative detention order against Palestinian land activist and farmer Ghassan Najjar. Najjar appeared at Ofer Military Court on Monday. He was arrested during a pre–dawn raid on Burin village, south of Nablus, in the occupied West Bank on October 27, and has been held in administrative detention since. list 1 of 3 Netanyahu may fall, but his far-right legacy in Israel is going nowhere list 2 of 3 Israel takes measures to crush Palestinian business in occupied West Bank list 3 of 3 As homes seized, Jericho’s Palestinian residents fear settler takeover The Israeli authorities have not given a reason for Najjar’s arrest, as administrative detention allows them. The Palestinian human rights defender, farmer and veteran grassroots organiser has a long history of arrest, having spent nearly a decade in Israeli prisons, much of it under administrative detention. He has been subjected to a travel ban since 2011. The Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) told Al Jazeera that Najjar was arrested because he intended to harvest olives on his land and planned to help other Palestinian farmers do the same. Israel’s security agency Shin Bet reportedly warned Najjar, cofounder of Burin’s Land and Farming Agricultural Cooperative, that he would be arrested if he did not stop organising with grassroots groups and Western activists. The olive harvest in the occupied West Bank is a key target of pogroms by Israeli settlers. The attacks have surged during this year’s harvest and have already surpassed last year’s figures. The United Nations and international voices have long urged Israel to guarantee Palestinian farmers’ protection and safe access to their land. Administrative detention allows Israel to detain people without charge or trial, notes B’Tselem, an Israeli human rights group. It adds that the absence of legal proceedings leaves detainees “helpless”. Following the court’s confirmation of the detention order, Najjar will remain in Ofer Prison until at least 26 February, his sister, Suha Najjar, told Al Jazeera. However, in the meantime, an Israeli military court will review his case and decide whether to extend the term. “It is an unjust decision, and it is deeply upsetting that my brother has been subjected to such a great injustice,” Suha said. “He has been placed under administrative detention for four months, without any charges [lodged] against him. Even more concerning is that this detention could be renewed when the four months come to an end.” Earlier this month, Amnesty International demanded Israeli authorities release Najjar immediately. The rights group accused Israel of detaining him “solely because of his peaceful activism to protect the olive harvest season in Burin”. “I am extremely worried, especially because we are not allowed to visit him or even see him. This makes our anxiety as a family even greater, as we have no way of knowing how he is doing, either physically or psychologically,” Suha said. “We are aware of the cruel methods used by the Israeli occupation to torture Palestinian prisoners, both physically and psychologically, and this makes us even more fearful for his safety and wellbeing.” In a statement released earlier this month, Amnesty called on states with leverage to pressure Israel to release Najjar. “Like Palestinian human rights defender Ayman Bani Owda and countless other Palestinians, Ghassan Najjar is being hounded by a discriminatory justice system that has played a key role in legitimising and maintaining Israel’s system of apartheid and unlawful occupation,” it said. “States with influence on Israel must use their leverage to pressure Israeli authorities into releasing all arbitrarily detained Palestinians, including Ghassan Najjar, and finally end their use of administrative detention.”

events.title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
events.summary: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country T his week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old. There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service , careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation , scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold , the leisure centres closed , the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back . That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. Let that begin here. It is the central purpose and the meaning of Tuesday’s report by Alan Milburn, commissioned by Keir Starmer and keenly adopted by Andy Burnham. This is the hardest of social projects, yet the government nonetheless sets itself to be judged by it, despite the high upfront cost, with no payback for years. How will this land? There will, no doubt, be protest from right and left. But never has a policy been so pitch-rolled to flatten critics and sceptics with undeniable evidence that it will be to the good. There is a cornucopia of plans for schools, colleges, the NHS, councils and early years education. Ideas come from visits to see what works elsewhere, notably the Netherlands and Denmark. Seeing proportionally far fewer Neets in those countries, Milburn asked what they did about school and college drop-outs. “They didn’t understand that term,” he tells me. In those countries, if children start to struggle with school attendance, “they go straight round to find them and work out their problem. Here they disappear.” Politically, this duty will fall on local mayors (or councils, where mayors have not yet been introduced). Their colossal task is to pull together schools, FE colleges, jobcentres, NHS services and local employers. Heaving them out of their silos to collaborate will test mayoral devolution to its limits. With extra funding comes accountability for creating a continuous decline in the number of Neets in their area. Everywhere, this will be delivered through youth hubs – welcoming places, “not jobcentres where they’re met by security guards, but places only for young people,” Milburn tells me. Last week he visited a model hub in Liverpool , Merseyside Youth Association . Hiring and training a new cohort of work coaches and advisers has begun, so hubs can offer supported internships, short flexi-jobs to ease people into work and experience for those with none on their CVs. Incentives to employers to hire them may include cuts to employers’ national insurance contributions for those aged 21-24 in retail and hospitality. Ordinary earners under 21 are already NI-free. GPs will not mourn the passing of the “fit notes” with which they were expected to sign people off work. That task goes to hubs’ community teams of occupational therapists, work coaches, mental health and job advisers, who offer counselling and personal “return to work plans” instead. Neets will be fast-tracked through NHS mental health queues. Milburn is searching for obstacles to knock down. Care leavers will get back the education maintenance allowances (EMA) for staying in school or college, with plans to spread this to all who used to qualify before the Tories axed them – that is, every sixth-former on free school meals. “Just paying for buses to stay in college is £4 a day, £20 a week: too much for those families,” he tells me. Abolishing another obstacle, the government will end young people’s loss of 55p from their benefit for every £1 they earn when they do get a job. A good omen is the optimism of FE colleges, after years of despair at turning away 16- and 17-year-olds for lack of spaces and teachers. These neglected gardens of second chances for all those failed by Gove-stricken schools are the mainstay of this whole plan. Today, they celebrate being told they can now take as many students as they want. David Hughes, head of the Association of Colleges, closely involved in the Milburn plan, expects colleges to be funded to take tens of thousands more. He wants funding for colleges to do their own social outreach to missing young people. “We can go and find them,” he says. “Many have no adult to ask what to do.

events.title: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
events.summary: Buffett converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation. He also gave 1,845,000 shares to each of The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. The Berkshire chairman emeritus still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion — following the donations. Billionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year. Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett. Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion. "Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message. The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023. Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500's decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the artificial intelligence buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk. The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points. In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year. Buffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel: "My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity. ... You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever," he said. Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received." "Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us," said CEO Abel of the letter. Buffett closes his message with this advice: "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."

events.title: All 25 James Bond movies are on Prime Video. Here are 15 you need to see and 10 you can skip.
events.summary: "Goldfinger." 20th Century Fox All the James Bond movies are now available on Prime Video. Make sure to watch "Goldfinger," "A View to a Kill," and "Skyfall." Skip "On Her Majesty's Secret Service," "The World is Not Enough," and "Spectre." Now that the world has a new James Bond in Robert Pattinson , there's no better time to dive back into the 007 franchise. Lucky for you, all 25 movies (plus the one that isn't part of the canon, "Never Say Never Again") are all available on Amazon Prime. Here are the ones you should watch, and the ones you can skip. Must-see: "Dr. No" (1962) United Artists The classic first movie in the franchise didn't just introduce us to the dashing spy character based on the Ian Fleming novels, but also to the first 007 in movie history, Sean Connery. Thanks to his good looks, charming Scottish accent, and action moves, he became the blueprint of a movie hero in the early 1960s. Tying it all together was the story, which was just damn good. He faces the OG villain in the franchise, Dr. No. Must-see: "From Russia With Love" (1963) United Artists Connery returned to play Bond in the second movie in the franchise. This time, he's fighting bad guys on the Orient Express and Istanbul. And the gadgets he uses became a hallmark for most of the 007 movies going forward.  Must-see: "Goldfinger" (1964) United Artists Arguably the greatest Bond movie in the Connery era, here he takes on the villain Auric Goldfinger ("No, Mr. Bond, I expect you to die"), drives around in an Aston Martin, and saves Fort Knox from blowing up. Must-see: "Thunderball" (1965) Sean Connery in "Thunderball." Eon Productions Connery is at it again, and though this one isn't as good as "Goldfinger," it still has top-notch action. Eye-patch villain Emilio Largo is one of the best in the franchise, too. Also, this is the movie where Bond flies around on a jet pack! Must-see: "You Only Live Twice" (1967) (L-R) Sean Connery and Donald Pleasence in "You Only Live Twice." Eon Productions With the story set in Japan, the sights are dazzling. And with the SPECTRE's Number One Blofeld (played perfectly by Donald Pleasence) as the movie's villain, things couldn't get any better with his lair featuring piranhas and battles with ninjas. Must-see: "Diamonds Are Forever" (1971) 20th Century Fox After retiring from the Bond role, which only lasted one movie ("On Her Majesty's Secret Service"), Connery returned and proved he is the true Bond when he breaks up a diamond smuggling ring while also breaking some hearts. Then he retired from the role. Sort of (more on that at the end). Must-see: "The Spy Who Loved Me" (1977) (L-R) Roger Moore and Richard Kiel in "The Spy Who Loved Me." Eon Productions For the third movie in the Roger Moore era, he finally hit his stride as Bond. Teaming with a KGB agent, he has to track down missing submarines that are armed with ballistic missiles. And he also has to run from the clutches of the giant henchman Jaws, named that way thanks to his giant metal teeth. Jaws, played by Richard Kiel, quickly became a fan favorite. Must-see: "Moonraker" (1979) United Artists Trying to compete with the popularity of "Star Wars," 007 goes to space in this mission. It's cheesy but lots of fun. Moore once again faces off with Jaws, which we can't get enough of. Sadly, it's their final showdown. Not because Bond kills him, but because Jaws finds love by the end of the movie. Must-see: "A View to a Kill" (1985) Christopher Walken and Grace Jones in "A View to a Kill." Eon Productions The Moore era closed with perhaps Bond's most 1980s story. Christopher Walken plays the villain, who chases Bond in a giant blimp. Grace Jones is the fantastic henchwoman, dressed throughout in amazing outfits. And the movie features the best Bond song of them all , performed by '80s icons Duran Duran. Must-see: "The Living Daylights" (1987) United Artists This movie marks the start of the Timothy Dalton era, and it began with a bang as he fits nicely in the 007 role here. Like one of Moore's movies, this one is set around the KGB, but unlike Moore, Dalton gave the character a ferocious edge — which was fitting as the character was headed into the 1990s. Must-see: "Tomorrow Never Dies" (1997) YouTube Moving to the Pierce Brosnan era (Dalton only stuck around for two movies), Bond is more dashing, the Bond girls are ravishing (hi, Michelle Yeoh!), and the action is hitting Hollywood-blockbuster level with lots of explosions of gun fire. Must-see: "Die Another Day" (2002) 20th Century Fox This movie marks Bond's 40th anniversary and arguably the best one in the Brosnan era. Entering the 2000s, the franchise, like all blockbusters, is using more CGI. But there's still a grounded action feel in this one as Bond battles it out in North Korea with Halle Berry as the Bond girl. Must-see: "Casino Royale" (2006) "Casino Royale" was directed Martin Campbell. Sony Pictures Releasing Four years after "Die Another Day," the franchise gets a reboot and a new Bond. Daniel Craig joins the party and introduces the most serious 007 yet. Must-see: "Skyfall" (2012) "Skyfall" was Craig's third appearance as 007. MGM Studios Craig finds his groove in this movie, which, for us, is in the top five of the best Bond movies of all time. Directed by Sam Mendes, starring Javier Bardem in the villain role, and shot beautifully by legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins, the movie has a real high-stakes feel by the end (if you've never seen the movie we won't give away why). Must-see: "No Time to Die" (2021) Daniel Craig as James Bond in "No Time to Die" MGM The latest Bond movie closes out the Craig era in grand fashion. The movie's action is some of the best in years and the final half hour is some of the most thrilling you'll find in the franchise. Skip: "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" (1969) 20th Century Fox After "You Only Live Twice," Connery said he was retiring from playing Bond, opening the door for George Lazenby. It didn't turn out well as the model-turned-actor felt the wrath of fans and critics who wanted Connery back. Lazenby has his moments, but the movie itself is a dull one. Skip: "Live and Let Die" (1973) United Artists Roger Moore's first Bond movie has one of the best Bond songs, performed by Paul and Linda McCartney's band Wings , but in the movie's attempt to cash in on the popular blaxploitation genre, it feels bland and at times more like a cop procedural than a spy movie. Skip: "The Man with the Golden Gun" (1974) United Artists Though featuring the likes of Christopher Lee and Hervé Villechaize as the villains, once again Moore finds himself navigating a dull story. Though, this is the movie that features the cool corkscrew car jump

events.title: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
events.summary: The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry. In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open-source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks. Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.” The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease. Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people. The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers. The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim. Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials. “Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer Arve Kjoelen. A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers. After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks. It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea. events.title: Beckham firm sues after fragrance found for sale in discount store
events.summary: Brand reacted with ‘shock and dismay’ after products were also found in a ‘bargain bin inside a gas station’ David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in the British discount store Poundland, court documents have revealed. The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon. DB Ventures claimed to have discovered the perfumes for sale in the troubled UK budget retailer and in a “bargain bin inside a gas station” at an unspecified location, according to court papers filed in New York. Lawyers acting for Beckham’s company said it reflected “desperation and greed” by the perfume company, Coty. Coty, which is headquartered in the Netherlands, has worked with Beckham’s brand for more than a decade and has produced more than 30 different fragrances bearing his name. In the UK, they sell at about £20 a bottle. Lawyers claimed that Coty sold at least $24m (£18m) of Beckham products through “unapproved distribution channels”. In the court filing, they said: “DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades. “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.” The legal documents, filed at the supreme court in New York and first reported by the Daily Mail, allege that Coty had “distributed David Beckham fragrances through the budget retailer Poundland , allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.” The lawyers asked for compensation and damages totalling $41m. They also claimed Coty under-reported net sales by $123m, which would mean that DB Ventures lost $6m in unpaid royalties. Coty filed its defence, asking for the case to be dismissed. It denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland , but argued that it had the right to decide where it wanted to sell its David Beckham range. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Beckham, who retired from professional football in 2013, has built a multimillion-pound business empire, DRJB Holdings, around his brand. The group is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his commercial partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss. The Seven Global division contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas, and the remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production studio that made Netflix documentaries about the lives of himself and of his wife, the former Spice Girl and fashion designer Victoria Beckham. This year David Beckham received a $51m dividend from the group, after a series of lucrative brand deals for the Fifa World Cup. He appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns during the tournament this summer, working with brands such as Lenovo, McDonald’s and Bank of America. The Beckhams are together worth an estimated £1.2bn, according to the most recent Sunday Times Rich List. DB Ventures and Coty were approached for comment.

events.title: Silicon Valley’s head-on collision
events.summary: The timing of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World this week, which brings together global business and political leaders at the intersection of technology and geopolitics, could not feel more urgent. When we came up with the name of the California convening this spring, the phrase was meant to represent a broad sense that AI and geopolitics were on a collision course. Policymakers and CEOs were starting to come to terms with the pressing need to talk to one another. Then, here in the US, they spent a long bitter summer campaigning for and against each other. Thirteen days ago, that collision course became a head-on collision. The US is preparing to inaugurate a new Congress deeply skeptical of the tech industry and its leaders, and — perhaps more consequential — new governors from Texas to Ohio who have pledged to stop data center construction. Similar sentiments are rising in Europe, but much of the rest of the world is rushing to get in on the action, and eager to pick up data-center investments forced out of North America. And now Washington is facing questions about how it managed the interactions between its main geostrategic rival, China, and one of the world’s most valuable companies, Nvidia, and what, if any, involvement it had in the undoing of the CEO atop an American chip champion. There are, of course, far more than two sides to this story: Silicon Valley is divided on the fundamental questions of how fast to develop new technology, on open- versus closed-weight models, on the role of startups and hyperscalers, and on the correct place for regulation. Washington, too, is balancing the promise of AI against the impact it could have on citizens. And senior officials from Singapore to South Africa bring their own pressing agendas. You can join us live here for conversations with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, and dozens of other CEOs and world leaders. We don’t have all the answers, but you can be sure we’ll be asking the right questions.

events.title: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond
events.summary: Robert Pattinson will star in the 26th James Bond film, the first installment since Amazon MGM took control of the franchise. Denis Villeneuve will direct the film with producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman. Pattinson has been in major films this year including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and will soon appear in "Dune: Part Three." Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise. Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement . "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team." Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime ," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic. The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin," Villeneuve said. In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios , which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion . Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

events.title: All 32 Robert Pattinson movies, ranked
events.summary: Pattinson. Robert Pattinson. Jeff Spicer/BAFTA/Getty Images for BAFTA Robert Pattinson skyrocketed to fame with his role as Edward Cullen in "Twilight." Now, he's one of our biggest movie stars, starring in four films this year. But perhaps his biggest films are yet to come: He was officially cast as James Bond this week. 2026 has been the year of Robert Pattinson . This year alone, he's appeared in "The Drama," "The Odyssey," "Primetime," and will appear in the highly anticipated " Dune: Part Three ," which is scheduled for a December release. And, to cap it all off, he was announced as Denis Villeneuve's pick for the suavest spy in cinema, James Bond, in November. He's come a long way since the 2000s, when he appeared in two of the biggest franchises of this century: first as the minor (but pivotal) Cedric Diggory in " Harry Potter, " and then as millennials' biggest heartthrob, Edward Cullen, in " Twilight ." To celebrate his casting as Bond, here's a look at how critics have rated Pattinson's movies throughout his career, from his film debut in 2005 to now. 31. "Queen of the Desert" (2017) IFC Films Rotten Tomatoes score: 17% Based on a true story, "Queen of the Desert" follows Gertrude Bell (Nicole Kidman) as she leaves life in England behind and travels across the Middle East, forming a love affair with a British officer (James Franco) along the way. Pattinson appears as the famous archaeologist T.E. Lawrence, who was the subject of "Lawrence of Arabia." "An emotionally empty, thematically ill-defined, and listless affair. It is never able to communicate the complexity of the woman at its center," wrote Angelica Jade Bastién for RogerEbert.com. 30 (tie). "Little Ashes" (2009) "Little Ashes." Kaleidoscope Entertainment Rotten Tomatoes score: 25% In the period drama "Little Ashes," renowned artist Salvador Dalí (Pattinson) and poet Frederic García Lorca fall in love during the pre-Spanish Civil War era. "The drawcard of Robert 'Twilight' Pattinson as Dalí is a mixed blessing for the filmmakers, given how ill-at-ease he is in the role. Javier Beltran, as Garcia Lorca, cast as the heroic center of the film, cuts a more confident figure," wrote Philippa Hawker for The Age. 30 (tie). "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1" (2011) "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1." Summit Entertainment Rotten Tomatoes score: 25% The first part of a two-part adaptation of "Breaking Dawn," the final novel in Stephenie Meyer's series, "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1," focuses on Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) and Edward (Pattinson) as they go from wedded bliss to chaos. "The last twenty minutes of 'Breaking Dawn' are so harrowing that it's possible to forget that most of the acting is soap-operatic (the guy who plays Carlisle is aging to look like Liberace) and the dialogue from hunger," wrote David Edelstein for New York Magazine . 28 (tie). "Remember Me" (2010) Summit Entertainment Rotten Tomatoes score: 27% In the coming-of-age drama "Remember Me," Pattinson plays Tyler Hawkins, a man who struggles to connect with his father (Pierce Brosnan) following a tragic loss. He finds solace in Ally (Emilie de Ravin), but outward influences threaten the future of their relationship. This movie's lasting legacy, though, is its twist ending — even calling it a twist feels kind of icky. "Be warned, if you're vulnerable to outrageous, cringe-inducing implausibilities — not least the ludicrous stand-up row between Tyler and his father in the latter's Twin Towers boardroom — you'd best give this one a miss," Time Out's Wally Hammond wrote. 28 (tie). "Bel Ami" (2012) StudioCanal Rotten Tomatoes score: 27% "Bel Ami" is a drama about Georges Duroy (Pattinson), a clever traveler who rises through the ranks of Parisian society in the 1890s. As he goes from extreme poverty to settings of extravagant wealth, Duroy becomes entrenched in a world of lies and seduction.  "The women are all elegant and intelligent, they know the ways of the world, and they know Georges' history. Why do they find him attractive? We don't, and that failure is the downfall of the film," wrote Roger Ebert. 27. "The Twilight Saga: New Moon" (2009) Summit Entertainment Rotten Tomatoes score: 28% In the second installment of the popular "Twilight" book series, "The Twilight Saga: New Moon" begins with Edward (Pattinson) leaving Bella (Stewart) behind in an effort to protect her. Heartbroken, Bella grows closer to her friend Jacob (Taylor Lautner) only to discover that vampires aren't the only supernatural creatures in their small town of Forks.  "If you buy into the central romance, you'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll swoon. Otherwise, the lingering glances, lip-chewing, and regular de-shirting may cause uncontrollable giggles," wrote Helen O'Hara for Empire Magazine . 26. "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse" (2010) "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse." Summit Entertainment Rotten Tomatoes score: 46% Upon Edward's return to Forks in "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse," Bella (Stewart) struggles to grapple with her love for him and her burgeoning attraction to Jacob (Lautner). Amid the love triangle that develops, Edward and Jacob attempt to put their feelings aside to protect Bella from a group of malevolent vampires . "I wanted 'terrible/AWESOME' and all we got was painfully terrible. I am upset," wrote Autostraddle's Alex Vega. 25. "Twilight" (2008) Summit Entertainment Rotten Tomatoes score: 48% It's the one that started it all. In the first "Twilight" film, high schooler Bella Swan (Stewart) transfers to a new school in rainy Forks, Washington, and is immediately drawn to otherworldly student Edward Cullen (Pattinson). As Bella becomes more certain that Edward is a vampire, her love for him grows as well.   The New York Times' Manohla Dargis called it "a deeply sincere, outright goofy vampire romance for the hot-not-to-trot abstinence set." 24. "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 2" (2012) Summit Rotten Tomatoes score: 49% In the final installment of the "Twilight" franchise, Bella (Stewart) acclimates to her new life as a vampire as she and Edward (Cullen) come together to protect their supernaturally gifted daughter, Renesmee (Mackenzie Foy), whose very existence draws the unwelcome attention of the Volturi, who are looking for any excuse to take the Cullens down. "You're going to hear a lot about 'Breaking Dawn Part 2' being the best of the 'Twilight' movies. events.title: McKinsey and Cognition are trying to prove AI coding pays off
events.summary: AI is reshaping software engineers' work across industries. Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images McKinsey and Cognition want to show companies that AI coding is worth the cost. A McKinsey survey found AI productivity surged at a quarter of organizations, while it fell at others. Choosing the right model can help: You don't always need a Ferrari, said a Cognition VP. McKinsey & Company and the AI lab Cognition want to show that AI coding is worth the cost. Under a partnership announced Monday, McKinsey will advise clients on which engineering projects to target and how to redesign teams and workflows around AI. Cognition will provide its AI coding agent, Devin, which the company says can understand, plan, write, and test code. The launch of Devin in early 2024 set off jitters among some software engineers about whether AI tools would upend their workflows and perhaps overtake their livelihoods. In the years since, developers' work across industries has shifted dramatically — from writing code to guiding AI's output. AI coding tools are getting more capable Some of the biggest changes for developers have come in the past year, said Lari Hämäläinen, a senior partner in McKinsey & Company's technology, media, and telecommunications practice. Until the final months of 2025, he said, many AI coding tools were most useful for narrow tasks, such as looking up technical guidance or syntax details. "That was about it," Hämäläinen said. Since then, he said, more capable AI models have made it possible to hand off longer, more autonomous coding work. That can create a challenge for companies trying to adopt the tools broadly, Hämäläinen said. The technology might be improving faster than organizations can redesign the processes around it. "This is really a step-change phenomenon" that "requires a complete rethink" of software- and product-development processes, Hämäläinen said. That reinvention isn't necessarily easy. In a recent McKinsey survey of more than 300 product and engineering leaders, the top quarter of organizations saw productivity more than double due to AI, while nearly 30% said it had dropped. One common pitfall is that while it's straightforward to have a small team experiment with an AI tool, "it's a completely different thing to scale it across 2,000 developers or 20,000 developers," he said. The challenge is proving the payoff The hunt for AI returns, and for ways to manage its costs, has prompted a range of large companies, including Goldman Sachs, Cisco, and JPMorgan , to become more selective about who gets access to which tools and how they are used. Art Levy, VP of global partnerships at Cognition, said Devin can draw on multiple AI models. That might mean using pricier frontier tools for harder engineering work and cheaper models elsewhere. "You don't need to drive a Ferrari to the grocery store," he said. AI routing tools are becoming a popular way for companies to manage AI costs by directing different tasks to models based on their capabilities and costs. Levy said Devin's approach can be useful for large software modernization projects that companies have put off. He pointed to one client where work to update enterprise resource planning software, expected to take five years, is being compressed into 18 months. "It's no longer, 'Can you get the job done?'" Levy said. "It's, 'Can you get the job done, and are you cheap at doing it?'" Read the original article on Business Insider
