events.title: Musk, Silicon Valley insiders urge Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Nvidia faces potential 30 percent value loss without Jensen Huang, say market analysts amid stock downturn. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley insiders are calling on chipmaker Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned last week from the company he cofounded. Musk is one of the 177,000 signatories to a petition titled “Stand With Jensen”, calling for the reinstatement of the executive, who resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. list 1 of 4 When tech founders leave, what happens to their companies? list 2 of 4 US Treasury chief calls for outsider to lead embattled tech firm Nvidia list 3 of 4 Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, says Alice Huang left in 2025 list 4 of 4 ‘Stand with Jensen’: Why US tech titans are backing Nvidia ex-CEO Huang “We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” the letter published on the petition’s website said. More privately, a group of Silicon Valley insiders is pushing to get Huang back in the role, with the Financial Times reporting that Huang is considering a comeback. The paper reported that an unnamed group of Silicon Valley insiders has put together a so-called war room and is lobbying the White House for support which is a move that may have been successful. “A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday. Trump’s reported trades this year suggest he held between $13m and $62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures. But Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing Jensen back, the Reuters news agency reported citing three unnamed people. Much of Nvidia’s value is tied to Huang, with analysts estimating that the company could lose as much as 25 to 30 percent of its value without him . Nvidia’s stock was trending downward in early trading on Wall Street, with US markets opening down 2.3 percent on the day. Over the last five days, the stock has dropped 8.5 percent and is down more than 25.7 percent over the last month. The developments come as the White House moves to designate Nvidia, along with more than two dozen other companies, as “national champions” in the artificial intelligence industry, a new initiative intended to help the company secure more business overseas, according to reporting by The Wall Street Journal. They also come as the Trump administration issued a rule on Monday that it would restrict China’s access to chips made by companies including Nvidia, as Trump begins a trip to China where he will meet with President Xi Jinping. The restrictions are aimed at preventing Chinese companies from “circumventing” existing limits by using data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia and Thailand to train their AI models. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the Department of Commerce said in a statement. The new rule comes as the Commerce Department is scrambling to demonstrate that it is cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive US technology, following reports that the agency under Secretary Howard Lutnick turned a blind eye to the smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips into China.

events.title: Nvidia fallout: Commerce targets loophole for China's data center use
events.summary: The Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's computing power from locations in other countries. Commerce's action is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week. It came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. The Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive chip technology being exported to China . The interim final rule from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal that led Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week after reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who worked for Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's biggest Asian customers. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release. The rule came after growing criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on its "entity list," which would restrict certain exports to it. Trump says Nvidia scandal did not put U.S. national security 'at risk,' defends Lutnick Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on China workaround of restrictions Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe The rule is designed "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," according to the text of the rule. The new restrictions "will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using" advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors produced by U.S. companies to train advanced AI models, the rule says. The rule also says that a license will now "be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion." The New York Times reported on Nov. 9 that American authorities began investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed and one of its executives, Alice Huang, in 2024, "after the company started importing billions of dollars' worth of advanced Nvidia A.I. equipment into Malaysia." "Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant," The Times reported that day. "While that behavior is legal, U.S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China." Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, and that she was a spy working for China. The two are not related. China's government has denied the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, as national security advisor, leads the National Security Council, warned President Donald Trump last spring that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, The Times has reported. Chris McGuire, a former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council, in a post on X called the new rule "a major step forward to countering Chinese smuggling of and access to advanced AI chips." "The work here is not done, as there are some critical loopholes that remain open and need to be closed in a follow-up rule (namely those related to activities inside the United States)," wrote McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. "Commerce should move extremely quickly to close these. But this is the first time in over 18 months that the administration is starting to take export controls seriously, and does represent a meaningful step forward." McGuire said that the fact that the new rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the NSC "is remarkable and unprecedented." "I have never seen a BIS rule that was not written by BIS," he wrote.

events.title: I'm a financial advisor who has worked with wealthy clients for 20 years. Here are the 10 money habits everyone should avoid.
events.summary: Sathya Chey Patterson is the cofounder of Arise Private Wealth. Courtesy of Sathya Chey Patterson. Wealth manager Sathya Chey Patterson explains the money habits that lead to out-of-control spending. She says it's not necessarily about cutting your daily Starbucks habit. Here are 10 ways people spend money without realizing it — and ways to spend more intentionally. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sathya Chey Patterson, 42, a Los Angeles-based certified financial planner (CFP) and cofounder of Arise Private Wealth. I have been in wealth management for 20 years. My family immigrated to the US from Cambodia. I was born in a refugee camp in Thailand, so I came here with nothing. I've worked since I was 9 years old, but I grew up learning core money habits that allowed my parents to retire in their 50s, despite never graduating from high school and barely speaking English. I grew up wondering why I saw so many Americans living paycheck to paycheck when I came from a war-torn country. I really wanted to help people bridge the gap between what they value and financial planning. I was raised Buddhist , and that's why mindfulness and meditation are so natural to me and connect with me. It's something I apply to my practice as a wealth manager. My philosophy around money is about living within your means and being mindful and intentional about how you spend your money. Here are 10 money mistakes I think people should avoid. 1. Not identifying what you value Wipada Wipawin/Getty Images If you really enjoy that $7 Starbucks coffee , buy that coffee and feel good about spending money on it. But really first, take a step back and say, what do I really value? Unless you have an endless trust fund, you have to prioritize what is important to you and what you like to spend money on. I created a concept called the "Six Money Love Languages": experiences, material things, time-saving services, generosity, security and stability, or comfort and well-being. Most people have one dominant and one secondary priority. If you're not making enough money, prioritize one or two things first. 2. Spending money on your imaginary future self Try a more affordable gym membership first to see if it's a habit you can stick to. Liliia Lytvyn/Getty Images We all get caught up in this idea of things we want to do and accomplish. People say, "I want to be a runner," so they go buy a Garmin before they've even started running, or they want to play pickleball, so they buy all the outfits, but they don't have time in their schedule to play consistently. First, build the habit before buying all the stuff. If you want to start going to the gym, for example, start with something more affordable. See if you really have the discipline to make it a habit before spending more money on a premium gym membership . 3. Spending money to buy the appearance of wealth Prostock-Studio/Getty Images I think people try to keep up an appearance of wealth, but I will say most of my wealthiest clients don't look wealthy. They don't have a Birkin bag or drive a Rolls-Royce. They like high-quality things, but much of their money goes toward travel, comfort, and freedom. I think the wealthiest people have it locked in when it comes to their version of success — and it's not usually the luxury bag. Before making an expensive purchase, ask yourself: Would I still want this if I wasn't posting about it, or if no one saw me wearing it? 4. Replacing things that already work There is no need to upgrade or replace something that's still working fine. Sorapop/Getty Images We often feel like we need to have the newest thing. With most tech, we upgrade it because we see it has 15 more options, none of which we end up using. Before upgrading your phone , ask yourself: Is the new device actually solving a problem you have, or is what you have right now not fulfilling it? Again, it's that pausing to think: Do I really need this? Otherwise, it's just another expense. 5. Paying too much for convenience CentralITAlliance/Getty Images One of the most powerful financial tools we have is our attention, and companies are playing into that. I call this the "distraction tax." When we're distracted, we end up paying for conveniences we could have avoided with a little planning. For example, you might say you're too busy to go to the store and meal plan. But then you're just sitting on your couch, mindlessly scrolling for an hour. There's an upcharge for that, as you will pay more through delivery app fees. Or you don't want to wait around during commercials, so you pay for a premium streaming service subscription. These conveniences add up. 6. Forgetting about subscriptions Rokas91/Getty Images When something renews automatically, you stop thinking about it. It's called the "default effect." And when you start making more money, it's easy to become careless and stop paying attention to these little expenses. I would recommend reviewing your subscriptions and insurance at least every six months. Think about whether you really need a certain subscription. You could even cancel it and see if you miss it, right? 7. Not scheduling time to review your finances YakobchukOlena/Getty Images/iStockphoto It's easy to bury your head in the sand about your finances. I would schedule a money date with yourself. Just as people have a wellness day, I think you need a money wellness day , too. I'd like to see people set aside at least 30 minutes a week to review all their accounts and transactions. Make it a little ritual you actually look forward to. I personally use Simplifi, a budgeting app that lets me review my transactions for the week. 8. Justifying purchases by saying 'I deserve it' apichat panyakaew/Getty Images The "I deserve it, YOLO" attitude can become our throwaway line for "I'm going to do something really irresponsible." I caution how often we use it when spending money. I really want people to be mindful about what's triggering their spending. Not every stressful day needs to end with an Amazon delivery. Sometimes, instead of making a purchase, you might just need a day off , better boundaries with your friends, or a good night's sleep. 9. Shopping without taking a moment to think stockbusters/Getty Images As your income grows, it's easy to spend hundreds here and there without thinking about whether those purchases actually matter to you. Meditation or simply slowing down can help you become more aware of your emotional spending triggers. Take a five-minute pause before a purchase. Once in a while, try a 30-day no-purchase challenge , or a one-week challenge if that's too long, where you only spend money on essentials such as groceries. The goal isn't deprivation. It's to reset your habits so you can make healthier, more mindful spending decisions afterward. 10. events.title: Digital-only banks could be forced to fund high street banking
events.summary: Treasury-backed review says customers of banks such as Monzo and Revolut often rely on physical cash services Digital banks like Monzo and Revolut could be forced to pay towards high street banking facilities, after a government-backed review outlined plans to protect face-to-face financial services across the UK. The access to banking review, which was released on Monday, was commissioned by the Treasury earlier this year, and addresses the dwindling options for nearly 3 million people who regularly rely on in-person banking across the UK. That includes many older and disabled customers, and people with mental health challenges, who struggle to navigate online banking but have been left with little choice after the closure of almost 7,000 branches since 2015. Banks have been closing branches at pace over the past decade to cut costs after the 2008 banking crash. The trend accelerated during the digital push seen in Covid-era lockdowns, against the backdrop of growing competition from digital-only banks such as Monzo, Revolut, Starling and JP Morgan’s Chase bank. It has left customers struggling to access in-person banking for everyday tasks such as handling cash, deposits, payments, as well as more complex issues such as fraud, debt, power of attorney, and handling the accounts left behind by family members after they have died. The government said on Monday it would adopt the review’s recommendation to introduce new laws protecting essential face-to-face banking services across the UK. However, many details still need to be hammered out, including which lenders will be expected to maintain and pay for those services. That includes whether digital-only banks, which have never operated in-person services, would be forced to contribute. The review, led by former Which? director Richard Lloyd, said many customers now held accounts at more than one bank, and that “large numbers of customers of digital-only banks frequently rely on physical cash services”. That has meant leaning on existing services offered by traditional high street lenders, such as NatWest, Barclays, and Lloyds. The report said the banks responsible for safeguarding these services should be up for “regular review to ensure relevant market developments and changing consumer needs are taken into account”. It added: “There is also recognition that vulnerable consumers of all banks may struggle to have their more complex needs met, and this can be expected to become more significant as the profile of customers changes, for example through ageing or vulnerabilities.” Monzo, Revolut and Innovate Finance, which represents digital banks and fintechs, were approached for comment.

events.title: Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
events.summary: US pressure on Iraq to curb Tehran’s influence leaves potential for direct confrontation with Iran-linked armed group around the town of Jurf al-Nasr. Iraq has ordered its armed forces to move into a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, amid an investigation into suspected oil smuggling. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the military to enter the town of Jurf al-Nasr, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi said on Monday, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA). The Iraqi leader has also set a deadline for the armed faction, which has been implicated in the oil probe, to leave the area. list 1 of 4 From the UK to the Gulf, are US overseas bases becoming liabilities? list 2 of 4 Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold list 3 of 4 Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict? list 4 of 4 Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’ The order comes amid pressure on Baghdad from the United States and some of its Gulf-state allies to counter Tehran’s influence in Iraq. Al-Aboudi told local media the “deadline is not far off”. A senior Iraqi official told Al Jazeera Arabic that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, which sits south of Baghdad in the centre of the country and was previously known as Jurf al-Sakhar. Al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group. Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area. Iraq recently launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries. Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, denied the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines. “We are therefore being subjected to the greatest campaign of blackmail aimed at forcing us to relinquish the weapons of dignity that have upheld sovereignty and protected the rights of Iraqis at multiple stages,” the group said in a statement. The campaign to stamp out the oil smuggling trade has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of senior government officials and security directors. Al-Aboudi said an investigative committee, following an intelligence agency report, had “detected clear tampering with pipelines passing through the area, as well as attempts to bury and conceal traces of that tampering”. Sources told the Reuters news agency that the smuggling , carried out with accomplices among some security and oil officials, has robbed the government of hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021. While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds, analysts believe the oil probe is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus. Iranian-backed armed groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have resisted repeated calls by both al-Zaidi and ‌‌‌‌his ally, US President Donald Trump, to disarm. They have struck US troops and targets in Saudi Arabia and the UAE in solidarity with Tehran since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

events.title: Billy Evans says he gave up a ‘pretty silly’ profit share from ‘You Can See Everything’. He won’t say where the money went.
events.summary: Former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans. Philip Pacheco/Getty Images Billy Evans gave his first TV interview, speaking with CBS News' Matt Gutman. He said his profit share from "You Can See Everything" would be worth tens of millions of dollars. He said he "wasn't unhappy" about giving it up because he knows where the money is going. Warning: This article contains spoilers for the movie "You Can See Everything." Billy Evans said he gave up a profit share worth tens of millions of dollars from the smash-hit documentary " You Can See Everything ," but declined to say where the money went. The A24-produced film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, follows Evans' relationship with Elizabeth Holmes , the Theranos founder, in the days before she begins her prison sentence. It has grossed about $90 million at the box office on a $7 million budget. In his first TV interview ever, with CBS News' Matt Gutman, Evans was asked why he had not taken a share of the profits. One of the film's key scenes depicts   the filmmakers reluctantly negotiating a profit-sharing agreement with Evans. However, at the end, the film says that Evans gave up his right to any profits. "The number's pretty silly," Evans told CBS News in Sunday's interview, adding that it would be in the tens of millions of dollars. Asked why he gave it up, Evans said: "I don't know how much I can talk about it, but what I can say is, knowing where the money's going, I'm not unhappy about that decision." When Gutman asked whether that meant the filmmakers weren't getting the money, Evans declined to elaborate. "That's all I can say about it," he said. A24 and representatives for Fielder and Oppenheim did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Evans said he earns little from working for himself running the blood-testing startup Haemanthus, and that he has spent considerable sums on childcare and legal bills. "The amount of money spent on lawyers would blow your mind," he said. That's why he thought asking for a share of profits was "reasonable," he added. "I think the disappointing thing is that giving it up was to demonstrate that this was not about the money. This was about people seeing Liz," Evans said. "But then they make it about the money." Holmes is serving an 11-year, three-month sentence after being convicted of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud by lying to investors to raise money for Theranos. The hit film dropped in theaters on October 16. It grossed $15 million in the US and Canada during its opening weekend, marking the best opening weekend for a documentary so far this year. events.title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
events.summary: Robot startup Foundation has failed to pay employees since missing its Oct. 30 payroll, angering some workers after its CEO borrowed $4.6 million from the firm last year to buy a luxury home, according to people familiar with the matter. Co-founder and CEO Sankaet Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, raising governance concerns among prospective investors. Foundation's widely reported $24 million in Pentagon contracts actually stems from its 2024 acquisition of Boardwalk Robotics, which held some existing government research contracts, the people said. Pathak's previous company, Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of customers without access to deposits. Pathak reportedly took loans from Synapse as it neared bankruptcy. Foundation Future Industries , a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company. The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said. Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025. A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts . Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation. The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts. "What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview. That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is. Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business. "We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands." Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism. "Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight." Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts." While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets. Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said. Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

events.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
events.summary: Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York. I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense , but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him. It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on Quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”) You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July , noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year. But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.) Now, he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”). Belfort says the platform, called Tone , is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice. It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer). But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard. Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. What have you built? It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically. Is this effectively trained on you? It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made. How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together? Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own. Who are your customers, and how do they use it? We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale.

events.title: Ukraine's naval drones are now fighting Russian ones in gun battles
events.summary: Ukraine's naval forces say its drone boats have started taking out Russia's naval drones in sea battles. Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Ukraine's naval drones have begun engaging Russian sea drones. Ukraine's navy has revealed two drone-on-drone fights at sea. Russia, it says, has lost both. Naval drones have already been used against Russian ships, helicopters, jets, and ground targets. Ukraine's naval drones are getting into fights with Russia's drone boats, taking them on in gun battles at sea. Ukraine's navy said Monday that a Sargan 3000 naval drone destroyed a Russian naval drone using an automated gun turret. The sea service wrote that the score in naval drone battles stands at two to zero. The Ukrainian navy reported "the first-ever battle between uncrewed surface vessels" in September. Another of Ukraine's Sargan 3000 naval drones destroyed a Russian naval drone in an operation involving Ukraine's naval forces and Ukraine's Main Intelligence Directorate, the GUR. During the September engagement, the drone was equipped with a Protector remote weapons station with a mounted 12.7mm machine gun. The station, developed by Norwegian defense company Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, can also work with other weaponry, including grenade launchers. Ukraine has used its growing fleet of naval drones to hit, damage, and destroy Russian warships. These attacks, along with missile strikes, drove the Russians to relocate their battered Black Sea Fleet away from the occupied Ukrainian region of Crimea. Ukrainian naval drones equipped with missiles have also shot down Russian helicopters and fighter jets , while other drone boats functioning as maritime motherships have been used to launch aerial drones capable of prosecuting ground targets. Drone boats often deliver an asymmetric advantage. In the case of Russia's Black Sea Fleet, relatively inexpensive sea drones devastated conventional warships and patrol boats that were significantly more expensive. Ukraine's Western partner nations have taken note of both the opportunity and the threat. Ukraine has not said much about the Sargan 3000 naval drone, but President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the weapon in April as "a multipurpose platform" that is "capable of carrying out strike missions." Not only has it been used to engage enemy drone boats, but the Ukrainian navy said in October that a Sargan 3000 equipped with a gun turret shot down a Russian Shahed-style attack drone. Automated turrets are weapon mounts that can be controlled and aimed without a person physically operating the gun. They are newer additions to Ukraine's naval drones, which were initially used primarily as one-way explosive weapons, piloted remotely into targets before detonating. Ukraine's naval drones have received more weaponry, including turrets and Grad multiple-launch rocket systems. Vitalii Nosach/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Ukraine's naval drones have received more weaponry, including turrets and Grad multiple-launch rocket systems. Vitalii Nosach/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Many Ukrainian naval drones now carry turrets. The Magura, made by UFORCE, for example, can be equipped with the company's Predator remote weapons station to fire machine guns and other weapon systems. Oleg Rogynskyy, the founder and CEO of UFORCE, told Business Insider that turrets, which can also be mounted on ground robots, are "where we're seeing a lot of growth," adding that they are "probably one of the largest markets on the planet" because of their potential to counter drones. Russia is a relative newcomer to naval drone warfare, but its growing use of the weapons presents another threat to Ukrainian vessels. Armed turrets could help Ukraine defend against those attacks. Ukraine's navy wrote on Monday that "each such operation is another step towards a safe Ukrainian sea and the protection of our borders!" Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Crook turns free trials into phishing factory, as LearnWorlds sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices
events.summary: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register . According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame , who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X , referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.” The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts. “The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.” According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same. Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks. These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it. LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue. The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

events.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
events.summary: OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing. OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI. The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat. The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user. Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions. Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers. With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI. Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organizations also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release. At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits. Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations. Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work. Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.

events.title: Exclusive: White House requires signoff before staffers testify to Congress
events.summary: The White House counsel has instructed all executive branch agencies to get permission from their chief legal counsel and legislative affairs offices before allowing any employee to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Monday's memo from White House Counsel Will Scharf is the latest sign President Trump is ready to fight the many investigations being promised by Democrats, who will have significant majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. "The Trump administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations," a White House official said. Zoom in: Scharf's memo to staffers follows a letter he sent last week to the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif). In that letter, Scharf warned Democrats to limit their investigations to "legitimate" inquiries. "The Supreme Court has held that '[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to 'punish ' those investigated are indefensible," Scharf warned. "Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary," the letter said. Between the lines: Partisans will likely differ on what's "legitimate," but it's clear that Scharf's office will use its interpretation in deciding whether to allow executive branch employees to testify. "We are ready to engage with Congress," the White House official said, "This process ensures reasonable requests are respected, but baseless political attempts to undermine our mission will not be accepted as the status quo by Democrats' who want to slow the administration down from its historic work." In his Monday memo, Scharf said the administration "will remain disciplined in pursuing the work and service the American people deserve by ensuring that all Executive Departments and Agencies follow the established White House consultation process ... before any agency personnel may agree to appear before any congressional committee." Zoom out: For more than a year, Trump's administration has planned for the day congressional investigations ramp up. Trump knows he also faces the prospect of impeachment. But advisers say that's no longer threatening to Trump, and he doesn't believe there would be the 67 votes needed in the Senate to remove him. "The president can count, and he won't be cowed," a Trump adviser said. Trump also has promised to pre-emptively pardon staffers and allies he believes will be unfairly targeted by Congress or prosecutors in future Democratic administrations.

events.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
events.summary: OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement. The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM. OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images. What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users towards specialized support to stop harmful behaviour, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently. OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages. The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI. OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Saftey-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children . The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropritate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens . events.title: Instagram now lets creators add Amazon affiliate links in reels and feed posts
events.summary: Instagram announced on Monday that it’s launching an integration that will give creators a new way to earn by adding Amazon affiliate links directly in reels and feed posts. Creators can add up to 30 products per reel or 20 per feed post, which makes it possible for them to earn from multiple products through one piece of content. While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app. The Meta-owned company told TechCrunch in an email that it has seen product links directly on creators’ reels and posts draw about twice as many clicks as the links in their bio. By allowing creators to embed multiple product links directly in Reels and feed posts, the platform is expanding their opportunities to monetize content, while also giving them more flexibility in how they share recommendations. The change also strengthens the platform’s appeal to creators, as it continues to compete with rivals like TikTok and YouTube for their attention and content. Instagram says adding products and affiliate links is free, and that it doesn’t take a commission on purchases or charge transaction fees. Eligible creators can now connect their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts through the Monetization section of their Professional Dashboard. Once connected, Instagram automatically adds affiliate links when creators tag Amazon products in their content, with links directing viewers to the Amazon Shopping app. Connected affiliates also unlock image previews for their links, making it easier for viewers to recognize the products. When creators connect their Amazon Associates account to Instagram, affiliate attribution is automatically applied to any Amazon product they add, even when they paste a regular product link, which wasn’t the case before, as they were required to add an affiliate URL. Instagram says creators can also see each product’s estimated commission rate before adding it to a post or reel, with commissions continuing to be paid out by Amazon. The new integration marks another step in Instagram’s efforts to expand its monetization tools while also making affiliate marketing more accessible for creators on its platform. events.title: Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance
events.summary: The gas infrastructure in Iran has suffered from underdevelopment and sanctions, and now damage from the war. Tehran, Iran – Iran is heading into winter with warnings of natural gas shortages, as damage from strikes by the United States and Israel deepens an energy imbalance that has plagued the resource-rich country for years. Iran holds the second-largest proven natural gas reserves in the world, only behind Russia, but its government last week forecast a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day for winter that could impact both households and industries. list 1 of 3 Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb list 2 of 3 Lebanon’s second airport could provide economic and political benefits list 3 of 3 USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume? The country’s ageing energy infrastructure has long suffered from underinvestment and international sanctions that have restricted finances and equipment. Authorities say that inefficient consumption and limited storage capacity are also to blame, in addition to the damage from the ongoing war. Saeed Tavakoli, head of the National Iranian Gas Company, told local media last week that 26 projectiles struck six refineries on March 18, knocking out 28 percent of Iran’s gas production capacity in the immediate aftermath of the strikes. According to the government, about 100 million cubic metres per day of processing capacity has since been restored, but fully bringing back the additional 130 million cubic metres lost in the US and Israeli attacks could extend into 2028. Hashem Oraee, head of the Iranian Energy Associations Union, told local media last week that Iran was not able to rely on any gas imports to plug the gap. Gas shortages could also lead to electricity blackouts if the gas feeding some power plants goes out, something that has repeatedly happened in recent years. To avoid electricity shortages, those power plants resort to burning cheap fuel , predominantly a heavy oil alternative called mazut, which significantly pollutes the air. Despite that, Mostafa Rajabi Mashhadi, a deputy energy minister, told the state-linked ILNA outlet on Saturday that mazut burning would continue this year. Umud Shokri, energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said that if the problems facing Iran’s gas industry remain unresolved over the coming years, the consequences would extend beyond the energy sector, affecting industrial production, employment, inflation, and living standards. “In my view, Iran’s biggest challenge is not a lack of energy resources, but its inability to turn those resources into reliable supplies for its people and economy,” Shokri told Al Jazeera. “Without serious reforms, sustained investment, and better energy management, what is now largely a seasonal crisis could gradually become a year-round problem.” Gas accounts for 73 percent of Iran’s energy mix, the gas company’s Tavakoli said last week, adding that household consumption had reached 480 million cubic metres per day and was expected to sharply rise as the cold season approaches. Last winter’s peak consumption for households, businesses and small industries was recorded at 737 million. The National Iranian Gas Company identifies 11 of Iran’s 31 provinces as considerably vulnerable to shortages this winter, particularly some provinces to the north of the country, including Mazandaran, Golestan and North Khorasan. High consumption due to cold temperatures, as well as locations near the ends of transmission lines, increase gas pressure problems in those provinces. Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani explicitly warned during a press conference last week that if consumption grows, gas might be cut off across the country, including Tehran. “Unlike electricity, which can be reconnected quickly after being cut off, bringing back gas after cutoff is a time-consuming process,” she said. “So, network stability is of utmost importance and we must work to prevent any disruptions.” The government has said it will do its best not to let households or industries go offline due to gas shortages. But on Saturday, the Zagros Petrochemical Company, operating in southern Iran’s energy production hub of Asaluyeh, notified its shareholders that it shut down a methanol production unit until further notice in line with directives from the National Iranian Gas Company David Jalilvand, managing director at Orient Matters, a geopolitical research consultancy in Germany, said the industrial sector would bear the brunt of the shortages as the authorities prioritise households, which rely on gas for heating. “Prioritising households, however, does not guarantee that residential supplies will remain uninterrupted if shortages become severe,” he told Al Jazeera. To help save on gas, the government has tasked its affiliated executive bodies with reducing their gas consumption by 20 percent.

events.title: More drops for Nvidia and other AI stocks drag the US market lower
events.summary: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — More drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia . The S & P 500 fell 1.1% and was on track for a third straight loss . The weakness for tech stocks pulled the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.6%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time. Nvidia sank 2.5% and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership . Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow. Now, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities. It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaky because of criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centers. “The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.” Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.8% and was on track for a second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. So was Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 4.5%. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 5%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, fell 3.3%. The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations. Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 2.5% after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation. Summit Therapeutics sank 13.4% after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Tyson Foods helped to limit the market’s losses and rose 7.5% after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier. The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what's been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S & P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet. It's the third straight quarter of growth above 25% for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week's jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation . The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80% reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates . Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 2.1% to $93.81. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% for two of the world’s sharpest losses because of weakness for tech and AI-related stocks.

events.title: The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia
events.summary: When Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday , critics of the U.S.’s policy of restricting chip sales to China lost one of their biggest allies. In addition to being one of the industry’s biggest proponents of the AI buildout, Huang remains one of the most vocal critics of U.S. policies that bar the sale of advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China. He claimed that these measures would encourage the creation of a competing Chinese chip industry, and that it was better for the U.S. to keep Chinese companies hooked on U.S. technology.  Nvidia’s CEO was also a strong supporter of open-source AI models—many of which came from Chinese developers like DeepSeek—in the face of criticism that such models posed a serious cybersecurity threat.  Revelations that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation)—a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company suspected of funnelling controlled chips to China—has torched the Nvidia CEO’s credibility on the issue of export controls. (Some reports claim U.S. intelligence considered Alice Huang to be part of a Chinese espionage campaign against Nvidia, but others have cast doubt on that assessment). On Monday morning, the U.S. Department of Commerce released the first update to its export control regime since the scandal broke, issuing an interim final rule that closes a longstanding loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access AI chips based in overseas data centers, and expands export controls to an array of Southeast Asian countries. Congress, too, is debating several laws that would codify and expand existing export controls.  Yet tighter rules may also complicate matters for other countries trying to forge a more neutral path between the U.S. and China How likely are tighter export controls? Current export controls block the most advanced AI processors—made by companies like Nvidia, AMD , and Intel—from being sold to Chinese companies, though the Trump administration has allowed sales of Nvidia’s H200 to approved Chinese customers. Chipmaking equipment and high-bandwidth memory are also blocked.  Commerce’s new rule—which will go into effect immediately once it’s included in the Federal Register—would require licenses to export advanced AI chips to data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. It would also require a license if large data center operators anywhere in the world want to grant access to companies headquartered in China, effectively closing the remote access loophole . Data centers already serving such companies will have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to get a license. The Trump administration may remain split on how to act against chip smuggling; interestingly, the press release from the Commerce Department notes the rules were “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.” But Congress may act if the Trump administration remains divided.  “The regulatory path in Washington is going to be harder and bumpier,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told Fortune before the rule’s release. She pointed out that several bills have been included in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act. The Huang scandal “adds momentum to push those bills through, and the chance of those passing are likelier than ever.”  “No matter what Trump does, it’s possible that Congress should be able to provide limitations,” Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said before the rule’s release. “It’s not only about Trump anymore.” Congress, meanwhile, is closer than ever to locking those controls into law.  The first bill, the Remote Access Security Act, also seeks to close the remote access loophole, giving the Commerce Department authority to license and penalize foreign companies tapping advanced U.S. AI chips from abroad. (The House passed the bill in January and is still awaiting consideration in the Senate). The second bill, the Chip Security Act, would require advanced chips to ship with  security measures, like location tracking, to ensure processors aren’t diverted upon export. It also requires exporters to promptly disclose evidence of diversion or smuggling. Yet the act does not go as far as to mandate kill switches or more aggressive measures to stop smuggling. The third, the AI Overwatch Act, would treat advanced chips like weapons: before any sale to China or other adversaries, the administration would have to notify Congress, which could then block the deal with a joint resolution of disapproval. It also carries an “America First AI” provision requiring Commerce to certify that exports won’t leave U.S. customers short of computing power. The fourth, the MATCH Act, may be the most aggressive. The act would largely ban the sale and servicing of deep ultraviolet lithography tools across China, and imposes broader restrictions on facilities associated with major Chinese chipmakers like SMIC and CXMT. It gives allies like Japan and the Netherlands 150 days to align their own controls with Washington’s; if they fail, the U.S. can extend controls to equipment supplied from those countries, even if they contain no U.S.-made components.  Still, Dohmen pointed out that changing the rules alone won’t be enough to entirely halt chip smuggling. Several measures still require follow-on enforcement by either the U.S. or third parties; she pointed out that knowing that a chip was smuggled matters little if the Bureau of Industry and Security doesn’t act. How might third parties respond? Much of the attention during the Nvidia scandal has fallen on Southeast Asia, and Singapore and Malaysia in particular . Megaspeed, the company accused of funnelling Nvidia chips to China, is based in Singapore; Malaysia was also reportedly the home of Megaspeed’s data centers. Megaspeed has denied sending chips to China. “The administration wants to encourage Malaysia and Singapore to remain in the American AI ecosystem, but it doesn’t want them to become conduits through which Chinese firms can obtain advanced chips—or remotely access the computing power those chips provide,” Jennifer Lind, associate professor of government at Dartmouth College, said. “That has been its policy so far and I don’t anticipate this changing.” The new Commerce Department rule does offer a carve-out for end-users that are, or are owned by, a U.S.-headquartered company. The region has attracted billions of dollars of investment from U.S. tech companies such as Microsoft , Oracle , and Amazon , which should qualify for that exemption, though the rule’s remote access limits still apply to them. While both Singapore and Malaysia have made some public moves against chip smuggling, Kurlantzick said he’s “more inclined” to believe the Singaporean government was taking the matter seriously. events.title: UEFA backs France’s Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino in FIFA election
events.summary: French Football Federation chief Diallo emerges as a strong challenger in FIFA’s upcoming presidential election. European football’s governing body UEFA has given its “unanimous” backing to French Football Federation chief Philippe Diallo to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino in the FIFA presidential election. UEFA invited Diallo to “stand as a candidate in the FIFA presidential election in March 2027”, the continental body said in a statement on Monday, adding that European national associations had “unanimously pledged their full support”. The deadline for rival candidates to declare themselves is Wednesday, November 18. The Union of European Football Associations (UEFA), which boasts 55 member associations, said Diallo “has accepted the invitation to stand” and that his candidature is set to be confirmed at a meeting of the French Football Federation (FFF) on Tuesday. Diallo, the 63-year-old son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the FFF since January 2023. He was initially appointed to the post on an interim basis when previous chief Noel Le Graet was forced to stand down following a series of controversies. Diallo, from Saint-Nazaire on France’s Atlantic coast, was then elected to the role by a large majority in June of that year, before being re-elected in December 2024 for a new four-year term. UEFA’s months-long Infantino opposition Under its Slovenian president Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA has led the opposition to Infantino since his announcement in late July of a project to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of widespread uproar, but UEFA has since gone to court in the US state of Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the FIFA president in Switzerland. UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in the election, which will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat. Confederation of North, Central American and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) chief Victor Montagliani had been mooted as a candidate, but the Canadian later announced his desire to stand for a new term as the head of his confederation. The Asian Football Confederation, which consists of 47 member associations, announced last month that it was backing Infantino for re-election. Diallo said in September that the FFF was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election. “We believe that the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed, and that the way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us,” he said at the time. Infantino, a former UEFA secretary general, has been in charge of FIFA since 2016.
