events.title: I bought a house with my sister. Her husband lives with us, and we're planning for our parents to move in, too.
events.summary: Buying a house with my sister and her husband has been great for all of us. Mindy McNamara Last year, I decided to buy a house with my older sister and her husband. Splitting the mortgage and living on separate floors makes the arrangement work. This unconventional living situation has brought us closer while still giving us our independence. As children, my older sister, Kayla, and I spent many afternoons daydreaming about our future homes. We drew pictures of ideal floor plans, but while other kids would probably opt for elaborate slides between floors and in-ground pools, we were designing connected houses — because if there was one nonnegotiable feature, it was that we'd both live together. That childhood vision stayed with us, even as adulthood made it feel less and less realistic. After graduating from college , we moved back into our shared childhood bedroom with full-time jobs, student loans, and considerably more clothes. Throughout our 20s, we chipped away at those loans, traveled, and enjoyed nights out together. Though life got busier, we always prioritized our sisterhood. Eventually, Kayla moved out to live with her now-husband. Suddenly, spending time together required coordinating schedules, driving somewhere, and eventually going home without her. After years of saving, we started looking for our own places, both with very different wish lists. I wanted a low-maintenance condo with beautiful finishes, and Kayla and her husband wanted a family home with a yard and room to grow — but neither of us could find a perfect match. As the search continued, we thought of a solution: what if we pooled our resources for a forever home, with private spaces for each household and perhaps even an in-law apartment for our parents? We share a mortgage, but not every moment of our lives We decided I would cover 40% of the home's cost, and my sister and her husband would handle the remaining 60%. Mindy McNamara During our search for a prospective home, we came across a promising new two-story listing in New England . Immediately upon entering, we fell in love with the soaring ceilings, natural light, and floor plan. Before purchasing, we discussed what living together would look like, including how finances and household responsibilities would be handled, to make sure we were all on the same page. We decided that I would cover 40% of the cost, and Kayla and her husband would handle the remaining 60%. We agreed to use the same percentage for general finances and maintenance costs. Additionally, before moving forward, we figured how we'd best optimize the layout of the home. We agreed that I would have the first-floor primary suite , which has a bedroom, a closet, an office, and ample closet space. Kayla and her husband would have the second floor, with their own bedroom, two bathrooms, an office, and two additional guest rooms to use when they eventually have children. I have the first-floor primary suite, which features a bedroom, a bathroom, an office, and ample closet space. Mindy McNamara The shared spaces — like the kitchen and the living room — would then allow us to spend time together, while the private ones would provide the breathing room we might need. After a competitive bidding process, we closed in November 2025 and began moving in. We were so excited to live together again, but it still took some time to adjust to being under one roof. When furnishing and decorating the home, we didn't always see eye to eye on every purchase because of our different tastes and ideas about what's worth splurging on. Fortunately, we were able to work through them as a team, learning when to compromise and when to give each other a little creative freedom. Our home has room for our sisterhood — and eventually, our parents I love that this space has allowed my sister and me to bond while also having our independence. Mindy McNamara Now, nearly a year later, our evenings have settled into an easy rhythm. After dinner, if Kayla's husband wants to relax on his own, my sister and I will hang out in the living room for "cozy time," where we meet in our pajamas and watch TV together before bed. Some evenings, we talk for hours. Others, we're doing completely different things in the same room, occasionally sharing a funny video on our phones or catching up on plans for the week, at ease in the quiet comfort of our sisterhood. Like we've always hoped, our house is now a gathering place for friends and family, from Friday happy hours to themed parties and holidays. Looking ahead, we're exploring the construction of a detached in-law suite so our parents can join us. As Kayla and her husband plan for kids, we're all excited to be present and share in their daily lives rather than just occasional visits. Living together has fulfilled our childhood dream. Mindy McNamara We know our living arrangement doesn't appeal to everyone, but for us, it offers the close sisterhood we cherish without sacrificing our independence. Although housing affordability was a consideration, we ultimately chose this lifestyle for the closeness and joy we'd miss if we lived separately. Life is short, and we want to spend as much of it as we can with the people we love — and our shared home has been a wonderful way to do just that. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 5 of the best and 4 of the worst looks at the 2026 Governors Awards
events.summary: Florence Pugh at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images The 2026 Governors Awards were hosted in Hollywood on Sunday night. Florence Pugh was one of the best-dressed stars there in a pink princess gown. Tom Holland, on the other hand, made a fashion mistake. We're one step closer to the 2027 Oscars. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences hosted the annual Governors Awards in Hollywood on Sunday. A-list stars were in attendance, and legends were honored. Actor Glenn Close, director Ridley Scott, and Disney animator Floyd Norman were among the latter, taking home honorary Oscars for their contributions to film. The red carpet leading into the event was another highlight. Sharp suits and sparkling gowns were everywhere. Here are some of the best and worst looks we saw. Zendaya stepped out in an archival look. Zendaya at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Michael Buckner/WWD/Getty Images She looked stunning in the brown, fringe-covered Giles Deacon gown from 2007. Its strapless neckline highlighted her statement earrings and pixie haircut, while its hip pads gave it a unique shape. No one else wore anything like Zendaya's look on the red carpet. Inde Navarrette chose the wrong color and silhouette. Inde Navarrette at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images The "Obsession" star attended her first Governors Awards in a shapeless Dior design. The sleeveless dress had a pleated bodice with deep side cutouts and a straight, floor-length skirt. Unfortunately, the gown's gold-toned coloring was too light to complement Navarrette, and its loose-fitting shape wasn't ideal for her small frame. Florence Pugh looked like a princess in pink. Florence Pugh at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images Pugh might be known for her daring fashion , but she can also pull off glamorous looks. She arrived in a custom Valentino gown with off-the-shoulder sleeves, a bedazzled bodice, and a ruffled skirt that tapered into a short train. The dress was fun, feminine, and accessorized perfectly with a diamond necklace. Olivia Wilde's gown was missing something. Olivia Wilde at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images "The Invite" actor arrived at the Governors Awards in a black velvet gown from Valentino. It had long sleeves and shoulder pads, a plunging V-neckline that reached her hips, and ruffles along the hem of its skirt. Worn alone, the gown didn't stand out on the red carpet. It should have been styled on Wilde the way it was styled on the Valentino red carpet, with statement accessories like gloves and bold jewelry. The dress needed a pop of color or two. Alexander Skarsgård added a bold touch to a classic suit. Alexander Skarsgård at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Monica Schipper/Getty Images Tom Ford designed the "Wicker" star's suit. It comprised a classic black blazer, pleated trousers in the same color, and a sparkling silver vest that matched his shimmering top. The suit was tailored to Skarsgård perfectly, and the deeply scooped neckline of his top gave the look a daring edge. Andrew Scott probably should have opted for a different suit. Andrew Scott at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Monica Schipper/Getty Images Scott, who stars in the coming film "Elsinore," wore Louis Vuitton. The designer look was overly simple: black trousers and a matching blazer with only a single button. The two pieces blended together and needed a brooch or other accessory to bring them to life. Tessa Thompson wore one of the night's most daring looks. Tessa Thompson at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Amy Sussman/Getty Images The "His & Hers" actor stood out in Schiaparelli. Her sleeveless look featured two spotted prints on three different-colored fabrics, a plunging neckline, and cutouts across its bodice. The ruffled gown was also see-through and embellished with a golden floral piece at the chest. Thompson completed the look with gold pumps, large earrings, and rosy makeup. Tom Holland should have changed one simple element of his outfit. Tom Holland at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Monica Schipper/Getty Images The "Spider-Man" actor's custom Louis Vuitton tuxedo fit him perfectly and could have earned him a spot on this list as one of the best-dressed attendees. However, he wore the wrong shoes. Instead of wearing classic black dress shoes, Holland opted for brown leather boots. They simply didn't match his tux and distracted from the look. Jung Ho-yeon proved that you can never go wrong with a sparkling black dress. Jung Ho-yeon at the 2026 Governors Awards in Hollywood. Amy Sussman/Getty Images The "Squid Game" star walked the red carpet in a black gown from Louis Vuitton. The velvet dress had off-the-shoulder straps, a squared neckline, and a form-fitting bodice that extended into a mermaid skirt. Its silhouette suited Jung well, and the gown's star-shaped sequins gave it a whimsical feel. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I tried stuffing recipes from 4 celebrity chefs. The best used a boxed mix and beat Ina Garten's.
events.summary: I followed four stuffing recipes from famous chefs Ina Garten, Paula Deen, Ree Drummond, and Sunny Anderson, then compared the results. Paige Bennett I tried making stuffing recipes from Ina Garten , Paula Deen, Ree Drummond, and Sunny Anderson. Both Deen and Drummond's stuffing required the extra step of baking homemade cornbread. Anderson's recipe was my favorite because of its mostly savory flavor and easy preparation.  For many Thanksgiving menus , stuffing is a must — but it can feel overwhelming trying to figure out which recipe and technique to use when making this classic side. To narrow down my options, I turned to recipes from celebrity chefs Ina Garten, Paula Deen, Ree Drummond, and Sunny Anderson. Here's how they stacked up, and which stuffing was my favorite. Garten's herb-and-apple stuffing features plenty of fresh ingredients The ingredients for Ina Garten's stuffing recipe included apples and celery. Paige Bennett Unlike the other recipes I tested, Garten's stuffing requires only one type of bread — baguettes — which made it easier to prepare. The recipe, found on the Food Network website, also includes celery, yellow onion, Granny Smith apples, flat-leaf parsley, butter, rosemary, chicken stock, salt, and pepper. Toasted sliced, blanched almonds were optional. I also appreciated the addition of fresh herbs , but was unsure how I'd like the apples and almonds combined with the savory onions and celery.  This recipe yields a huge portion, so I cut it in half. This stuffing was quite easy to make I cooked the onions and celery while the bread dried in the oven. Paige Bennett Overall, the process was pretty simple. While my cubed bread was drying in the oven at 300 degrees Fahrenheit for about 10 minutes, I sautéed the veggies, apples, and herbs in a saucepan with butter. Once the mixture was combined, I poured it over the bread cubes, along with the vegetable stock. The longest part of the process was cooking the onions, celery, and apples, which only took about 10 minutes. Paige Bennett This recipe calls for cooking the filling inside a turkey cavity for two-and-a-half hours at 350 degrees Fahrenheit. I wasn't making a turkey for this taste test, so I baked the stuffing at the same temperature in a shallow dish for an hour instead.  I enjoyed the apples but not the almonds The stuffing I made using Ina Garten's recipe came out nicely crisp. Paige Bennett The final dish was pretty crispy and golden on top, but its center looked less appetizing.  The texture was OK, and the insides definitely seemed soggy. I probably could've avoided this by adding a little less broth than instructed.  I served myself a large portion of Ina Garten's stuffing. Paige Bennett Next time, I'd definitely omit the nuts. I used slivered almonds, and their crunchiness, size, and shape threw off the dish's overall texture. The crusty, breaded exterior was delicious and added all of the crunch this dish needed.  I could definitely taste the rosemary, and I actually enjoyed the apples, which added a slight sweetness to the stuffing that balanced the other savory flavors. Deen's recipe calls for a lot of butter and homemade cornbread The ingredients for Paula Deen's stuffing recipe. Paige Bennett In true Deen fashion, this stuffing recipe from the chef's website calls for a full stick of butter.  Other ingredients include white bread, cornbread, saltine crackers, celery, onion, chicken stock, eggs, salt, and pepper. Sage and poultry seasoning were optional. I was also unsure about the mixture of carbs here — saltine crackers, white bread, and cornbread, which I made from scratch using Deen's recipe. My stuffing mix ended up with too much broth, some of which I had to carefully pour out before baking For the carbs, I started by making cornbread — a quick and easy process that resulted in a savory, slightly dense dish. In the meantime, I dried my white-bread slices in the oven. I then sautéed the veggies with the stick of butter and mixed all of the prepared ingredients in a bowl.  I sautéed the onions and celery. Paige Bennett When adding the vegetable stock, I stopped after about five cups because the mixture already looked far too soggy. I was shocked that the recipe asked for seven cups. Paula Deen's recipe called for too much vegetable broth. Paige Bennett Still concerned about the texture, I poured out more broth before adding five eggs to the mix. I then transferred everything into a shallow, glass baking dish. It took about an hour in the oven for the mix to really crisp up. The flavor was fine, but the texture was disappointing I pulled the finished stuffing out of the oven once it was browned. Paige Bennett The top of the stuffing was slightly golden, but it didn't get as crispy as the other recipes I tested.  When I took a bite, I found the interior was far too soggy — there was definitely too much broth, and the crackers turned mushy after absorbing the liquid.  The mushy texture made Paula Deen's stuffing unappetizing to me. Paige Bennett The flavor was OK — very savory and buttery — but the super-soggy texture was not appetizing. If I made this again, I'd swap some of the crackers for more bread and use significantly less broth.   Drummond's stuffing recipe requires 3 kinds of bread The ingredients for Ree Drummond's stuffing recipe. Paige Bennett The Pioneer Woman's recipe calls for a lot of bread — three different types — including cornbread, French bread, and Italian bread. Since I already had the ingredients for Deen's cornbread, I made it for this dish as well.  The stuffing recipe also asks for butter, onion, celery, chicken broth, parsley, rosemary, basil, thyme, salt, pepper, and (optional) turmeric. I omitted thyme from this recipe and others as a personal preference. The process involved making cornbread and carefully ladling broth onto the cubed carbs Once the bread mixture was saturated, I baked the stuffing for 40 minutes. Paige Bennett In general, this recipe had a similar process to the other two, from making the cornbread and dehydrating the other carbs to sautéeing the veggies. I noticed a little too late that I was supposed to let the bread dry for one to two days. Instead, I threw it in the oven at 300 degrees Fahrenheit for 15 minutes, and it still firmed up really well.  The recipe instructed me to add six cups of broth to the sautéed vegetables, then ladle this mixture onto the tossed bread cubes until they were soaked to my liking. I preferred this approach because it was easier to control and prevent the stuffing from getting soggy.  My stuffing took about 40 minutes in the oven — not the 20 to 30 minutes the recipe called for — but the extra time helped it achieve a crisp, golden top. events.title: Why NJ’s governor thinks Republicans are trapped in an X bubble
events.summary: Today I’m talking with Mikie Sherrill, who’s been New Jersey governor for just a little under a year, and you’ll hear her say her election was a preview of the huge Democratic victories in these recent midterms because she ran on the dual themes of affordability and accountability. So I wanted to ask the governor exactly how corruption became such an animating issue for voters, in an era of tech billionaires who own platforms like X and TikTok and who also now control huge swaths of local media and even national broadcast media like CBS News. You’ll hear us get into the new era of influencer politics, which plays out as social video and takes its cues from rising stars like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and how I think influence on platforms like Elon Musk’s X is starting to backfire in big ways for conservatives. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . But the real story this election cycle might be the states. With President Donald Trump concentrating power in the executive branch, governors like Sherrill are starting to exercise their own power in ways that haven’t been tested in a long time. This runs right into tech policy and anti-AI backlash, as states around the country try to address topics like child safety and Big Tech overreach in lieu of any form of meaningful federal regulation. That’s how politicians like Sherrill have found themselves at the forefront of the data center fight, online privacy, and age verification — all topics you’ll hear us dive into here. We also dig into the Meta settlement, why Sherrill expects more Big Tech litigation, and what happens to privacy in the Flock and AI era. She had a lot of questions about the last one, and honestly, so do I. It’s a conversation I think we’re all going to be having for a while. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Governor Mikie Sherrill, you’re the governor of New Jersey. Welcome to Decoder . Well, thanks so much for having me. I really appreciate it. I’m excited to talk to you. It’s after the midterms; there’s a huge blue wave, and you’re a Democrat. I noticed. Yeah. I noticed that you were saying, “New Jersey is like the bellwether,” and you “paved the way…” This is your big quote . Tell me about that, and tell me how you’re feeling about the midterms. I’ll answer the easy question first. I feel great about the midterms. I feel absolutely fantastic about the midterms. And yeah, I was thinking about it because New Jersey has those off-year elections. So, there are very few statewide races — really only two in that cycle: New Jersey and Virginia. Right after Trump won, we started our campaign. And by right after, I mean, he won in November of 2024, and we started our campaign in November of 2024. What’s so interesting about New Jersey is that, even for a governor of this state, it’s still so retail. I don’t think a lot of other big states do as much retail, meaning I’m getting in front of thousands and thousands of people, sometimes per day, at small business stops, at diners, in their community… We have so many municipalities. I am able to go to gatherings of people up and down my state. And that means that we always have a real pulse on what’s going on very quickly. After 2024, we had to get the vibe because it was different; people were furious. They wanted movement, they wanted change, and then suddenly you have Elon Musk with a chainsaw. People are scared, they don’t like what’s happening, and they want a leader who’s going to address it. And I think what we did in that time, because we heard from everyone, is really centered on what the race was about, and it was about affordability and accountability. I know now that seems obvious… Yeah, it’s about affordability, and everyone knows that. I don’t think it was obvious in 2024 what it was all about. What was driving people? And in New Jersey, we were able to figure that out, and I think because the campaign was so incredibly successful, and we had such a huge win at the end of the day, that people then thought, oh yeah, that’s exactly the path. We’re all going to run on affordability and accountability, and that’s powerful in the Democratic Party. I think we’re at the center of our power when we’re fighting for working families, and that’s where we are right now, and I think it bodes really well for the future. I feel like I can connect corruption to all the tech CEOs being at the White House all the time, and to data centers. Is that a real connection, or is that just because I happen to live in the tech bubble? So, as somebody who has worked with polling, good, bad, and everything in between, I would say, and not to sound like a broken record, we were talking about… And that corruption piece was part of the accountability, the affordability. And I was hearing about that anger at corruption on the trail, even from very small, modest businesses, tying it to Trump pocketing billions of dollars as their costs are going up. I think you’re exactly right. People are very upset at the tech billionaires, and when they’re hanging out at the White House, especially those flip-floppers. events.title: International student enrollment drops sharply, putting more U.S. colleges in financial jeopardy
events.summary: Changing immigration policies have contributed to a sharp decline in the number of international students in U.S. colleges this year, according to the Institute of International Education. International enrollment is an important source of revenue for colleges and universities, experts say. Institutions with large graduate and STEM programs may be hardest hit, according to an analysis from Fitch Ratings. Amid changing visa policies and rising degree costs, significantly fewer new international students enrolled at U.S. colleges this year — a shift that could have financial repercussions for colleges, students and the broader economy. In the fall 2026 semester, the tally of new international students studying in the U.S. fell 15% compared with the prior academic year, according to a fall snapshot released Monday by the nonprofit Institute of International Education. Over the 2025-26 academic year, the number of new international students in the U.S. fell more than 17%, largely because fewer graduate students came from countries such as India and China, the IIE's report found. A growing number of U.S. colleges said international student recruitment was a top concern, but the report also cited as significant barriers the high cost of a U.S. degree relative to other countries and uncertainty around new rules ending the traditional "duration of status" system and limiting most F-1 and J-1 visas to four years. IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors Social Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Even though the Department of Homeland Security's new visa restrictions are currently on hold under a federal court injunction, experts say questions about the changing policies may have already discouraged some prospective international students. "At a time when countries around the world are competing for talent, the United States should be strengthening our ability to attract the best and brightest, not creating new barriers to it," Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said in a Sept. 14 statement after a federal court temporarily blocked the Department of Homeland Security's new visa rules. Foreign students typically pay full tuition, making international enrollment an important revenue source for colleges and universities, according to Robert Franek, editor-in-chief of The Princeton Review. With fewer tuition dollars coming in, there are fewer resources for U.S. students, particularly for financial aid, he said: "There are going to be fewer research dollars, fewer scholarship dollars for students here in the states." International students also contributed nearly $40 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2025-26 academic year, according to a NAFSA analysis . This year's enrollment decline is expected to cost the economy roughly $2.4 billion. "The data again reflect the harsh reality that the barriers the U.S. government is putting in place to block talented international students are having a real impact," NAFSA's Aw said. "All Americans will feel the effects as international students' tuition payments, local spending, and contributions to U.S. excellence in research and innovation diminish." Although the fallout extends well beyond college campuses, other research shows that colleges and the students they serve will bear the brunt of the impact. An analysis by Fitch Ratings released in August said recent changes to F-1 student visa rules could heighten financial risks for some U.S. colleges and universities, particularly those that rely heavily on students from abroad. "Sustained drops in new international student enrollment can have outsized revenue effects, as international students often pay full tuition or receive less institutional aid than domestic students," Fitch analysts said in the report. "Lost revenue is hard to replace quickly." Specifically, universities with large graduate and STEM — science, technology, engineering and math — programs, in which time to degree completion can exceed four years, will have a harder time sustaining the enrollment pipeline and "may incur higher costs to address overseas recruitment challenges," the analysts wrote. Most international students — 57% — study in STEM fields, according to IIE's report, so enrollment declines can have an outsized financial impact on schools with large engineering and computer science programs. Underscoring the importance of those students, 91% of colleges and universities said recruiting international students in STEM fields is now a key priority, according to IIE's fall snapshot, which was based on a survey of 809 institutions.

events.title: US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough)
events.summary: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration , signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities. Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy. But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains." The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together." It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains." This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants." Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon. The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom. "The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times . "What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility." This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing. It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms. American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration , and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership . A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs. It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
events.summary: I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind. These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy. WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event , and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind? LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025. It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has. Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way. There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”? It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into. Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable. I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise. What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate. You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board? I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue. I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company.

events.title: Anthropic’s Wall Street whisperer: Meet CFO Krishna Rao
events.summary: Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao has been integral to the company's rise, according to investors and former colleagues. Rao joined the company in 2024, and is leading the AI giant through what is widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO this week. He's helped Anthropic raise billions of dollars through the private markets, and he works closely with the company's seven co-founders. It's been a busy year for Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao . After closing a $65 billion funding round in May, he's been readying the artificial intelligence company for what's widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO . The listing could value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion , instantly making it one of the largest tech companies in the world. Rao joined Anthropic in 2024, when the company was still considered an underdog to OpenAI , now its chief rival. He's known as a straight shooter and a deft operator with a relentless work ethic, according to Anthropic investors and former colleagues, and he's played a crucial role in fueling the company's historic rise. The 43-year-old finance chief has largely stayed out of the public eye, opting to yield the spotlight to Anthropic's seven co-founders , including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei . But Anthropic's upcoming Nasdaq debut, which is expected to take place on Thursday, will likely push him to center stage, as public market investors and analysts hang on his every word for insight into the AI trade. Rao has nearly two decades of experience in finance across a range of companies, including Fanatics Commerce, a sports merchandise retailer, Cedar, a health care payments and billing platform, Airbnb and Blackstone . But he's never taken a company public as a CFO, and the stakes are high. Investors are still reeling after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia following shocking reports of three extramarital affairs . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates would make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases. Against that backdrop, Rao is under pressure to deliver. "He's a committed professional. He's integrity-based, and he's had this meteoric rise in a very, very complex set of companies," Jonathan Mildenhall, Airbnb's former marketing chief and a Fanatics board member, told CNBC in an interview. "There was nothing easy about Airbnb. There was nothing easy about Fanatics. There's nothing easy about Anthropic, and yet he makes it look so." CNBC spoke to current Anthropic investors, Rao's friends and former colleagues for this story, many of whom asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Rao declined to participate in an interview through an Anthropic spokesperson. As Anthropic's first CFO, Rao has been instrumental in helping the company raise tens of billions of dollars over the last two years. He has made himself easily accessible to Anthropic's backers, even during fast-moving, tense discussions about allocation sizes and valuations, according to investors. He often communicates in short bursts of texts or via quick phone calls, sometimes late into the night and through weekends. "He will communicate even bad news very directly, and I think that's important in this role, especially as they're launching into the public life," Byron Deeter , a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, a repeat Anthropic investor, told CNBC in an interview. "He doesn't let the important stuff go unsaid, and he's very good at giving you headlights into what's coming." Rao has a deep mastery of the nuts and bolts of Anthropic's business, as well as its broader strategy, and he's able to translate the complexities into language that financiers understand, according to investors and a former colleague. That's been especially useful ahead of the IPO, while Wall Street has been working to digest Anthropic's ambitious infrastructure plans , the people said. Anthropic has to secure massive amounts of computing power to train AI models and serve customers, and has entered into a range of purchase and lease agreements to try to meet anticipated demand. The company said in an amended prospectus last week that its aggregate spend commitments total roughly $900 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure." "The compute that we procure, it's the lifeblood of our business," Rao said during a rare podcast appearance on "Invest Like The Best" in May. "It is the most important thing in the company. It's like the canvas on which everything else gets built." Rao's frank communication style is different from that of Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive, who's known for penning long essays and opining about AI's transformative potential and grave risks. But the pair complement one another well, according to investors, and Rao has earned Amodei's trust.

events.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
events.summary: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest. Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark. The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do. Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle. The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. events.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
events.summary: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics. Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail. Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines. The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity. NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster. Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails. Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path. Explore NVIDIA Photonics and read Lambda’s deployment announcement . events.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
events.summary: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions. For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need. Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month. Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform: CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server . A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard. CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months. CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation. The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink. At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built. Learn more about NVIDIA quantum computing technologies . events.title: Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds
events.summary: ‘Hyperscaler’ datacenters across country draw upon dirtier power sources to meet vast energy needs, research shows The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found. In that period, 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study. This is equivalent to the entire annual carbon pollution of Denmark, a country of 6 million people, and is about two to three times more than a previous estimate of hyperscale emissions in 2018. The latest research, published in Nature Sustainability , found that these datacenters were responsible for about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption. Researchers said this vast datacenter energy demand, centered on states such as Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, is almost certainly a conservative estimate. The study used federal government data to determine emissions from the facilities over a year until April 2025. Since then, the rapid expansion of datacenters has only accelerated further. “There has been an explosion in these datacenters and the CO2 emissions are pretty substantial,” said Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard University and co-author of the study, which was led by Gianluca Guidi. “Since 2025 there have been many, many more datacenters so we need to think of this level of emissions as a lower bound. This is something that needs study and for policymakers to think about how to do this in a responsible way.” Datacenters use an enormous amount of energy – the new study estimates the hyperscale group consumed 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year – and largely draws upon dirtier sources of power to meet this demand. More than half of the generation used by hyperscalers came from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet, the research found. The growth of AI is being underpinned by a rise in new gas-fired power, sometimes built at the site of the facilities themselves, which is being favored over installed renewables such as solar and wind. “Sadly, it doesn’t surprise me that the majority of hyperscale datacenters rely on fossil fuels for their power generation despite the profound and lasting climate and health impacts that could be, and should be, avoided,” said Gina McCarthy, a former climate adviser to Joe Biden’s administration who said that the study is an “important step” to assessing the impact of datacenters. The rise of datacenters has caused alarm among climate groups amid worsening global heating that may surpass previously agreed “safe” levels and cause an acceleration of the sort of deadly events seen this year, such as roasting heatwaves in Europe, wildfire smoke in North America and the disastrous landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border. In the US, the epicenter of this AI boom, developers have defended the use of energy and water used by the facilities as marginal when compared with other industries, such as agriculture, and have touted associated jobs and raised local taxes as beneficial for communities. Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of the AI industry, has said people who oppose the growth of datacenters will end up “backwards and poor”. But a bipartisan public backlash against datacenters shows little sign of abating in the US. Local opposition has focused on several big developments, such as a cluster of datacenters in the greater Memphis, Tennessee, region that are central to Elon Musk’s AI ambitions but have faced protests and lawsuits over their noise and air pollution. Musk’s AI company has responded to this by buying the homes of those who live nearby. The vast water use of one of the world’s largest planned datacenters in drought-hit Utah, meanwhile, has mobilized grassroots opprobrium . The site, called Stratos , will also emit a large amount of air pollution, a separate study recently found . Stratos could cause health-related economic costs of up to $690m each year if it uses the dirtiest of the fossil fuel options to power itself, this research concluded. Burning this fuel will release up to 3,140 tons of soot-like particulate matter, linked to an array of cardiovascular and respiratory problems in people, in plumes that will waft across Utah and into Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado and Illinois. “Stratos is a modern-day Trojan horse that would unleash deadly air pollution linked to serious, life-threatening health damages upon Utah communities and millions of people living downwind of this massive datacenter,” said John Walke, director of federal clean air at the Natural Resources Defense Council, which commissioned the report. “Pollution from Stratos will contaminate the air and compromise the ability to live a healthy life both around the facility and in states hundreds of miles from the datacenter.

events.title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
events.summary: In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference. NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power. These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack , so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time. AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights , advancing scientific research. Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster. MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy. The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation. NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four. NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems. Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times. NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task. Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates. MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks. For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed. Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster. Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure , Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus , Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE , Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida . Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance. Vera Rubin also delivers leading performance on independent benchmarks including SemiAnalysis AgentX and Artificial Analysis AgentPerf, showcasing how the same NVIDIA infrastructure can productively run everything from pretraining and post-training to agentic inference, as well as workloads beyond AI, such as the high-performance computing showcased at SC26 this week. Dive deeper into the results in the MLPerf Training and MLPerf Endpoints technical blogs. events.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
events.summary: With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever. Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process. With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit , black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes. By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull. Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results. Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge. The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron -powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design. Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research , accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions. NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER , NAMD , GROMACS , LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows. Cadence , Fathom Therapeutics , Topos Bio , Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery. Daviator , a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs. At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory , the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken. The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments. The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center , with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs. Codeveloped with scverse , the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, Therna Biosciences processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. 10x Genomics integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights. And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research , benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models. events.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
events.summary: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films . Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack. Honoring the Architects of Progress Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI: At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics , tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters , one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time. In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition , helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning. That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution . These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more. Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26 . events.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
events.summary: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions. These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes. And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates. Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.
