events.title: NVIDIA Announces Collaboration With IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory to Launch Quantum-Classical Codesign Platform, Plus Error-Correction Breakthrough to Advance Practical Quantum Computing
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA and IBM announce a growing quantum supercomputing collaboration combining NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to advance quantum error-correction research, scientific applications and integration into supercomputing workflows. NVIDIA DGX B200 systems will connect with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the most powerful processor IBM has yet built. A quantum computing codesign platform with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, alongside IBM and NVIDIA, will support quantum error-correction and applications research for future systems. NVIDIA releases TCBP-JOBS, a new decoding algorithm part of the CUDA-Q platform, that delivers up to a 13,000x speedup for quantum error-correction research, accelerating fault-tolerant quantum computation. NVIDIA is expanding Slurm to simplify scheduling quantum processors within supercomputing workflows, with IBM contributing integration through its Quantum Resource Management Interface. NVIDIA today announced plans for new collaborations with IBM and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory that will span research into next-generation modular architectures for quantum computers, scientific applications and supercomputing integration. These efforts, including a new modular quantum computing codesign platform with IBM and Fermilab, combine NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to help researchers scale quantum computers and explore their scientific capabilities. Separately, NVIDIA also announced a new quantum algorithm that delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms — cutting the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to just 45 minutes. The collaboration with IBM also brings together new Slurm capabilities integrations to simplify how quantum computers can be added into supercomputing workflows. Modular Quantum Computing Codesign Platform IBM and NVIDIA are colocating NVIDIA DGX™ B200 systems with state-of-the-art IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the fastest quantum processor IBM has ever delivered. This integrated system is supporting a jointly developed IBM, Fermilab and NVIDIA modular quantum codesign platform. The codesign platform will allow researchers to develop and evaluate error-correction codes, decoding algorithms and quantum-classical applications driving scientific discoveries in high-energy and nuclear physics (HENP), as well as how classical systems can scale alongside multiple linked quantum processors within modular architectures. Fermilab’s expertise will allow work at the platform to focus on quantum error correction and HENP applications — helping define requirements for future fault-tolerant quantum computers and the science that can be achieved with them. “Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together,” said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at NVIDIA. “NVIDIA’s research software and our collaboration with IBM give scientists more powerful tools to investigate quantum designs and develop applications across these systems.” “Some of the most fundamental problems in science remain out of reach without access to quantum computing. Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond,” said Jerry Chow, IBM Fellow and chief technology officer of quantum-centric computing. “With Fermilab and NVIDIA, we plan to explore how these real-world problems can help us shape the modular, interconnected architectures that will define the next generation of quantum computers and accelerated classical computing.” “The future of quantum computing depends on more than advances in quantum hardware alone,” said Anna Grassellino, Fermilab chief technology officer and director of the SQMS Center. “Accelerated computing and superintelligence will play an important role in how we design algorithms, study errors and coordinate increasingly complex quantum systems. This proposed platform would combine NVIDIA’s computing capabilities with IBM’s quantum technologies and Fermilab’s scientific expertise, and would enable researchers to explore new approaches to codesigning quantum computers that meet the needs of challenging HENP science problems.” Advancing Quantum Error-Correction Research Errors inherent to quantum processors limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform. Quantum error correction protects quantum information by encoding it across multiple physical qubits. A classical algorithm called a decoder interprets measurement data to identify likely errors so they can be corrected. Available through the NVIDIA CUDA-Q™ QEC 0.9.0 library today, NVIDIA’s new TCBP-JOBS decoding algorithm accelerates the computationally intensive parts of quantum error-correction research by up to 13,000x while delivering high accuracy. Faster decoding in research workloads allows scientists to evaluate candidate error-correction approaches more efficiently and explore how different codes and decoder configurations perform. The new decoding algorithm provides researchers with tools to identify designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, and better measure their performance improvements, shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing. Advancing Quantum Chemistry  IBM and RIKEN are advancing quantum-classical chemistry research powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. The work, which combines IBM’s quantum computer with RIKEN’s JHPC-quantum GPU supercomputer ROQUO, has been named a finalist for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The researchers calculated binding energies for two protein-ligand complexes to study interactions relevant to drug discovery. By dividing the systems into fragments and combining quantum sampling with GPU-accelerated calculations, they modeled complexes containing up to 12,635 atoms — more than 40x the size of the previous 303-atom quantum-classical benchmark.  ROQUO uses NVIDIA GB200 systems and NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking to support research in quantum algorithms, simulation and hybrid computing. This research is supported by NEDO (New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization), an organization under the jurisdiction of Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry’s “Research and Development of Quantum-Supercomputers Hybrid Platform for Exploration of Uncharted Computable Capabilities.” Bringing Quantum Into Supercomputing Workflows NVIDIA is expanding the open source Slurm workload

events.title: NVIDIA Expands Vera CPU Platform to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
events.summary: The NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform combines NVIDIA processors, NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking and breakthrough scientific software to boost weather, climate and molecular simulations. DKRZ has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer for climate science. The full Vera CPU platform is coming from Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro. NVIDIA today announced the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform for high-performance computing — combining NVIDIA’s first fully custom data center CPU with the gold standard for HPC networking to drive extreme efficiency and throughput for state-of-the-art scientific modeling, simulation and agentic science. The rack-scale platform brings together 192 Vera CPUs interconnected by NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking to meet the massive performance demands of climate modeling, molecular dynamics and other unaccelerated, next-generation scientific workloads. The liquid-cooled system delivers more than 200TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth to support scientific simulation and AI workflows. “Scientific simulations need CPUs that can keep large datasets moving and sustain performance as applications scale,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Vera brings custom CPU cores, high-bandwidth memory and InfiniBand networking together to address those bottlenecks. With compilers and libraries optimized for Vera, researchers can run demanding simulations more efficiently and explore more complex scientific problems.” Engineered for Memory-Intensive HPC Each Vera CPU features 88 custom NVIDIA Olympus cores, 176 threads and compact, serviceable SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory delivering up to 1.2TB/s of bandwidth to accelerate data-intensive scientific applications. The rack combines 192 Vera CPUs with approximately 300TB of memory and 1 petabyte of storage in a fully liquid-cooled NVIDIA MGX™ design. Each 1U tray integrates eight Vera CPUs, and NVMe storage and management. The platform reuses NVL72 rack components, including chassis, power distribution and cooling infrastructure, to simplify deployment and service. NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking connects the system, and NVIDIA SHARP™ In-Network Computing helps scientists finish complex simulations faster by reducing the time processors spend coordinating their work. In NVIDIA’s tests, Vera delivered 1.9x the performance and 2.4x the performance per watt of x86 systems on OpenFOAM’s motorBike Large airflow simulation. Advancing Climate Science Research NVIDIA has benchmarked the open source Weather Research and Forecasting model on Vera CPUs, with projected performance gains of 1.6x and energy-efficiency gains of 2x compared with x86. DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, alongside NVIDIA GB200 Grace Blackwell systems and NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand networking. Built by Bull and expected to be available in early 2028, the system will support climate simulation and AI research, enabling global kilometer-scale climate simulations with lower energy consumption than on the current system. Software and Availability To help researchers speed scientific applications, NVIDIA HPC SDK 26.11 is available now, providing compilers and libraries optimized for Vera. NVIDIA is also introducing a public beta of its next-generation Fortran compiler, which was built in collaboration with leading HPC centers and national labs. The new compiler gives developers a way to run their existing programs built on Fortran — the language that scientific computing was built on — with greater speed on NVIDIA platforms, without needing to rewrite their code. Vera CPU racks are expected to be available from Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro beginning in early 2027. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU . events.title: NVIDIA Introduces Nemotron for Science to Accelerate Discoveries With Agents
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA Nemotron for Science brings together the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model, scientific evaluations, a new open chemistry dataset and recipes to help researchers build domain-specific science agents. LitmusBench v0.2 supports both evaluation and post-training for chemistry reasoning, helping researchers assess model capabilities and adapt models to scientific tasks. NVIDIA DGX Spark and data center infrastructure take Nemotron 3.5 Super VL from researchers’ desktops to supercomputing centers, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. Leading global research institutions, including the U.S. Department of Energy’s Argonne National Laboratory, are using Nemotron to build agents to speed scientific discovery. NVIDIA today introduced NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, bringing together scientific applications of its NVIDIA Nemotron™ 3.5 Super VL open model, a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes to help researchers build specialized agents for scientific discovery. Built on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Nemotron for Science helps researchers develop agents that reason through scientific problems and put specialized research tools to work. With post-training, scientists can adapt the model to specialized tasks such as conducting experiments for chemistry, protein design and more. Part of Nemotron for Science, LitmusBench v0.2 is a new open dataset with nearly 50,000 questions for training and evaluating language models on chemistry reasoning. Drawing on molecular properties and experimental drug discovery data, it helps researchers improve models’ ability to predict how molecules behave, including their solubility and how the human body processes them. Life sciences companies Lila Sciences, Terray Therapeutics and Therna are using and customizing NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for science applications. Use cases include extracting chemical knowledge, planning experiments and designing therapeutics and laboratory protocols. Major research centers like Argonne and Jülich Supercomputing Centre are integrating it into their drug and scientific discovery AI agents. “Accelerated computing is transforming how scientists tackle the world’s most complex challenges,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Nemotron for Science gives researchers open models, scientific data and post-training recipes to build specialized agents that reason through scientific problems and use CUDA-X accelerated tools to turn ideas into discoveries.” Post-Training Nemotron Open Models for Scientific Discovery Researchers can post-train Nemotron open models with domain-specific data to improve performance on specialized scientific tasks. They can integrate the resulting model into agent workflows that interpret scientific information, generate code and call computational tools. These workflows can use NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ accelerated tools to perform scientific computation. Terray Therapeutics post-trained Nemotron to extract reactants, products and reaction conditions from scientific diagrams, surpassing previously published results on two benchmarks. On the RxnScribe test, it recovered about 76% of annotated reactions under the benchmark’s matching criteria, helping turn published chemistry discoveries into structured data for synthesis planning and scientific agents. Lila Sciences used Nemotron to design execution-ready laboratory protocols for its automated labs, matching frontier-level performance without requiring additional fine-tuning. Post-training with laboratory feedback nearly doubled the model’s accuracy for making quantum dots — nanoscale crystals used in screens and solar panels — to 61%, exceeding GPT-6 Astra’s 54% at 10-20x lower inference cost. These gains help agents and materials scientists translate desired material properties into synthesis recipes, advancing the discovery of new materials. Therna collaborated with NVIDIA to post-train Nemotron for agentic mRNA therapeutic design, nearly doubling accuracy in predicting protein-expression ranges over frontier models. Scientists preferred its explanations over those from the base model in 96% of comparisons. These gains could help scientists tailor mRNA designs for the desired protein production in specific cell types as they scale to human use. Researchers Speed Science With Nemotron Models and Datasets Leading research institutions are using NVIDIA Nemotron models and datasets to advance scientific discovery at every scale, from individual researchers’ desktops to labs and supercomputing centers. By helping researchers rapidly design and evaluate novel molecules across the periodic table, the work has the potential to open new pathways for applications in critical materials and minerals, national security and cancer treatment. Argonne is integrating Nemotron into its StructBioReasoner multi-agent system to design and evaluate protein-based therapeutic candidates for treatment of cancer and other diseases. KTH Royal Institute of Technology has built an AI agent on Nemotron that repairs broken GROMACS molecular dynamics setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single NVIDIA DGX Spark ™ system, the agent fixed 81% of test cases with reasoning enabled, and every fix was checked independently by GROMACS itself. RIKEN has made NVIDIA Nemotron, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, available on its RIKYU AI supercomputing platform through RiVault, its inference gateway, enabling researchers to access the models for scientific research and the development of accelerated applications. Availability NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and the LitmusBench v0.2 chemistry dataset are available now on Hugging Face. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model was also optimized to run locally on a 128GB NVIDIA DGX Spark system . Learn more in this technical blog on post-training NVIDIA Nemotron to increase accuracy across scientific domains. ]]>

events.title: Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code?
events.summary: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application. Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet. Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded. A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work. In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100. These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first. Security has to become every developer’s responsibility Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them. Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do. A new approach to securing your code CodeRabbit Secure uses s emantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes. Three main use cases that improve your code security: this works across the SDLC: reviewing each commit in a new PR and flag its security risks; finding vulnerabilities across the repo with a Deep Scan; rechecking code with incremental scans and validating findings at runtime. Find vulnerabilities already in committed code Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it. I tried CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan against ast-grep and was impressed by its precision. Proving vulnerabilities before flagging them makes every finding far more actionable. Herrington Darkholme, creator of ast-grep Review incoming changes before merge PR security reviews assess each incoming change, including agent-generated code, for vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable in the existing application. CodeRabbit’s Security Architecture Review examines how architecture-level changes affect permissions, sensitive data flows, and trust boundaries. The Security Blast Radius map connects changed components to their dependencies and the code that relies on them, helping reviewers trace the potential security impact beyond the PR diff. On GitHub, administrators can enable CodeRabbit Security check and require it through branch protection or a ruleset. It blocks merges when PR security comments at or above the configured severity threshold remain unresolved. Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Delta scans then check changed files and areas of the map that are out of date or unverified, so teams know how much of the codebase has been security-reviewed and when it was last reviewed. Individual findings can also be rechecked to determine whether a fix addressed them. For eligible Deep Scan findings on GitHub Cloud with CodeRabbit Cloud, runtime verification generates a reproduction guide and can run it in an isolated environment to confirm whether the vulnerable path is reached. Results are “reproduced”, “not reproduced” or “inconclusive” for the tested revision and environment, however a failure to reproduce may not mean the finding is fixed. Carry the investigation through to a fix Developers can ask CodeRabbit Agent to implement a fix and open a PR, then inspect the finding, proposed fix, and supporting evidence. Teams can also configure severity thresholds to create Jira or Linear tickets automatically and track remediation in their existing workflow. Connecting the vulnerability finding, its supporting evidence, and a proposed fix helps engineering and security teams act while the context is still fresh and carry the change through review, testing and release. Teams can use CodeRabbit Agent to act on that context or easily hand it off to your preferred coding agent with a shareable markdown file. events.title: 'We slept here': Flight delays linger as airlines recover from ground stop, but schedule improves Monday
events.summary: U.S. flights disruptions eased Monday, but hundreds of additional flights were canceled. Flight disruptions continued through the weekend after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours. Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issue on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday. Nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the issue that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to update copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies . FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic. Officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. ET on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m. ET, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11. Hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware. Over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop. On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve. "We slept here," said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue. DOT Sec. events.title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
events.summary: Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample. The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says. The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews. The feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets. Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews. But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.) Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata. The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books. The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said. “Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added. events.title: Delta CEO Ed Bastian believes ‘human error’ and faulty equipment led to FAA ground stop
events.summary: Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian thinks Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop came from “a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error.” He dismissed other explanations as currently lacking evidence. “There’s no evidence that there’s [an] AI trigger. There’s no evidence that there’s cyber at play.” Bastian, speaking with Fortune’ s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, said he has no information beyond what has been reported. “We’ll find out when it comes in,” he said. The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, canceling roughly 12,500 flights that day and thousands more on Saturday. It was the first nationwide stop since a January 2023 system outage, and only the second since 9/11. What led to the FAA ground stop Bastian said he has talked to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and that Duffy “has been very transparent.” Duffy has said the trouble started during a copper-to-fiber switch at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Ark. A router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, then “started to flood our system.” Contractor L3Harris did the installation, and Duffy has asked publicly whether the fault was the install or the router itself. L3Harris says it is supporting the investigation. Bedford said there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related.” Bastian said the router work wasn’t new. “I think they’ve replaced, I understand, close to 70% of the routers already,” he said. L3Harris says the switch to fiber is more than 70% done. “So I don’t know. I can’t explain it.” He said the system came back once the routers were taken offline, but finding them “took hours.” He put the cost of the disruption “in the billions.” Asked if more nationwide stops are coming, he called Friday “clearly an anomaly” and said he wouldn’t extrapolate “until we know what happened.” The $50 billion pitch Bastian used the outage to argue for spending. Investors are putting “hundreds of billions, if not trillions of dollars” into AI and data centers, he said, but “we can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies.” Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control last year. Duffy has said he wants $50 billion on top of that. President Trump has asked for $30 billion. “The terrible thing would be if we use this instance to ‘lose confidence in what we’re doing,” Bastian said. He also pointed out that it takes longer to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia today than it did when Delta launched the route in the 1950s. He said more capacity in the skies is the only way to lower fares. “We’re congested, we’re gridlocked.” Fuel, fares and the K -shaped economy Bastian said Delta’s profit this year will be “pretty similar” to last year’s despite a $6 billion jump in its fuel bill. Delta’s ticket prices are up 15% to 20% year-over-year, he remarked with amazement: “We have never seen that dramatic growth.” Delta’s adjusted revenue rose 16% in the third quarter, and the company expects about 20% growth in the fourth. Delta could either raise prices or cut flights, he said, arguing that “people are willing to pay more rather than have their options limited.” Most of its customers, he said, live “in the upper end of the K” and want to spend on travel, he said, referring to what economists call the “K-shaped economy.” Shontell noted that a planned Delta route to Riyadh, first revealed at the Fortune Global Forum in October 2025, was pushed back after missile attacks on the Riyadh airport. Bastian said service hadn’t started yet when the airport was hit. Musk and the Wi-Fi fight Shontell also asked about Elon Musk, who has been going after Delta on X since the airline picked Amazon’s Leo satellite service over SpaceX’s Starlink. In early October, Musk posted that Bastian “will lose his job over this” and that “Delta will lose a lot of customers.” He also joked that a Delta flight was a good place to sandbox an AI model because there’s no internet. Delta announced the Amazon deal in March. Leo is slated for 500 Delta planes starting in 2028. United is already installing Starlink across its fleet. Bastian said Delta “helped them get started in aviation,” giving SpaceX planes to test on during COVID. “We just couldn’t come to an agreement on a business model.” He said customers don’t pick airlines based on Wi-Fi, and that when Leo arrives, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink, if not better.” Leo has a new problem, though. On Sunday, a United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit and lost all 40 Amazon Leo satellites it was carrying. Amazon had about 400 in orbit before the launch. On AI, Bastian stuck to his line that the technology is there to help Delta’s roughly 100,000 workers, not replace them. “I’m not getting on any planes operated by AI with one pilot,” he said. Bastian previously told Fortune that he hates the phrase AI and prefers to use “augmented intelligence” instead. Customers who call about the AI never praise it, he said. “They always complain about the AI.” The biggest issue with AI in the U.S. is trust, he said. Workers whose jobs change will be moved “to the extent capable into service, at airports or on the phones. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
events.summary: Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland. Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”. Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays. It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021. Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped. All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade. That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday. The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households. But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make? EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made. In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies. The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker. But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules. A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power. "The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said. The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit. The reset means they will be dismantled. The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU. Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves". He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling. Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats. The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling. The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP. Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included. Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said. But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules. He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found. UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D. Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations. Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area. Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK. "I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said. Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said. Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations. "The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

events.title: U.S. attorney targets another Democrat over congressional investigtions
events.summary: A U.S. attorney put likely incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on notice about her intent to investigate corporations and expected probes into the president's inner circle. Why it matters: The letter demanding Warren preserve documents related to her congressional oversight is the latest in a string of threats levied against congressional Democrats ahead of the party assuming the congressional majority — and gavels — next year. Congress' authority to investigate, hold hearings and gather testimony is a core legislative power. Analysts have long forecasted a Democratic subpoena storm into President Trump's lucrative presidency. But Democrats' plan to exercise that power and hone their focus on the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption," as reported by Axios' Hans Nichols, is already facing Justice Department pushback. Driving the news: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas contended in his Sunday letter that Warren appeared "eager to wield" her "gavel like a tomahawk," instructing her to preserve oversight records. In the strongly worded letter, he warned Warren about targeting private citizens close to the president and reiterated that any probes must serve a legislative purpose or risk violating those individuals' First Amendment rights. Those arguments echo his prior letters to Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller , shared Reitz's letter and referenced two civil rights statutes. Warren's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: Reitz's letter referenced Warren, Blumenthal and incoming Oversight chair Rep. Robert Garcia's (D-Calif.) recent inquiry into Trump fundraiser Meredith O'Rourke's role in coordinating contributions for the president's ballroom and other projects. It also referenced letters Warren, with Slotkin and other lawmakers, sent to tech CEOs probing the extent to which their AI investments were subsidized by GOP-led tax breaks. What they're saying: The White House did not respond to detailed questions but referred Axios to White House counsel Will Scharf's letter to Garcia that argued Democratic threats of investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality." Asked if Warren was the subject of a criminal probe or other proceedings, a Justice Department spokesperson told Axios that "the Department does not confirm or deny the existence of ongoing investigations." "The Department has both the statutory authority and the responsibility to examine potential violations of the law," the spokesperson added. Asked if DOJ leadership authorized or reviewed the letter, the DOJ referred Axios to Attorney General Todd Blanche's prior statement that "DOJ leadership is working with every U.S. attorney, including U.S. Attorney Reitz, on ongoing investigations." Friction point: Blanche refused to rule out prosecuting Democrats set on investigating administration officials in an interview earlier this month, claiming lawmakers' rhetoric had overstepped their authority. That came after Trump demanded the DOJ look into what he labeled as "Weaponization and Lawfare" from his political opponents. What we're watching: Reitz asked Warren to respond to his letter by next Monday. He described the letter as his "first arrow shot." Go deeper: Corporate America's Trump trap

La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste. Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer. According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year. The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September. The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva service disruption for six days. A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October. Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend. Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data. However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently. In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions. According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates. Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years. La Poste said in a statement to The Register : "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients." The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year. On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year. La Poste described the DDoS attack as "unprecedented in its scale and power," and while it had mostly subsided by December 24, the attackers restarted it in the early hours of New Year’s Day. The organization said the second wave comprised "several billion connection attempts per second," sent from several million IP addresses. More than 300 cybersecurity specialists were involved in defending and remediating the attack.

events.title: French football head Philippe Diallo to fight Infantino for Fifa presidency
events.summary: Diallo confirmed by Uefa as its chosen candidate He accused Infantino of seriously damaging football The French Football Federation president, Philippe Diallo, has been confirmed as Uefa’s surprise late choice to run for the Fifa presidency. The search for a Uefa-backed candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino was taken to the wire, with Wednesday the deadline for those planning to contest the Fifa election in March. “At a meeting held today and chaired by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin, the national associations represented on the Uefa executive committee and the Fifa council invited Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), to stand as a candidate in the Fifa presidential election in March 2027 and unanimously pledged their full support,” a statement said. Diallo emerged as the favourite after plans to enlist a decorated former player or manager did not reach fruition. Uefa said the 63-year-old had accepted the invitation and that his candidacy was due to be ratified by the FFF on Tuesday. Diallo strongly criticised Infantino in September, saying he had “seriously damaged the image and unity of football”. He continued: “His initiatives during and after the World Cup have seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.” It is unclear whether the move to back Diallo will spell the end of the campaign begun by Kozo Tashima , the honorary president of the Japanese Football Association, to challenge Infantino. Tashima, a Fifa council member, has influential backers within Uefa but its hierarchy appears to feel Diallo has a greater chance of wooing voters in other areas of the world. Diallo is expected to win the backing of the vast majority of Uefa’s member associations and there are hopes he could pick up votes from Francophone members of the Confederation of African Football, which has been steadfast in its support for Infantino. There are concerns that having multiple challengers to Infantino will strengthen his position and play into the hands of a campaign that will present the incumbent as the unity candidate after months of in-fighting. Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, has been reluctant to endorse an alternative candidate, despite opposing Infantino, with some federations arguing that a boycott of the election would send the strongest message regarding the need for governance reform. Diallo getting Uefa’s backing represents a marked departure from its original approach, in which it sought to coalesce behind a more high-profile figure who had made their name on the pitch or in the dugout. There had been late hope that Arsène Wenger, Fifa’s chief of global development, would throw put himself forward, but it would have required a major change of heart from him. Former players such as Mikaël Silvestre and, belatedly, Didier Drogba are understood to have expressed interest that never came to anything. He was elected president two years later in what was regarded in France as a shock victory, having initially stepped up in an interim capacity. Diallo joined Uefa’s executive committee in the same year. Germany’s head coach, Jürgen Klopp , has said he would welcome a new president. “The general consensus is that a change might make sense. But what would interest me even more in this context, from a football perspective, is that we never thought things could get any worse after Sepp Blatter, and yet someone actually managed to make it worse. “Right now, we’re thinking that if Mr Infantino were to leave, it would be cool if the next person could just do a better job. Because I believe it should be possible to do better.”

events.title: At least 17 killed in two South Africa mass shootings
events.summary: Eight men killed in shooting near Pietermaritzburg while six men and three women shot dead near Pretoria. At least 17 people have been killed in two separate mass shootings in South Africa, police said. Eight men were found dead late on Sunday in a “bullet-riddled” vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, police said. list 1 of 3 More than 900 arrested during South Africa’s antimigrant protests list 2 of 3 At least 11 people killed in South Africa township shooting list 3 of 3 Dozens killed in two mass shootings in South Africa Hours later, nine people were found dead in Jeffsville, an informal settlement near South Africa’s capital, Pretoria, police said. The bodies of six men and three women were discovered inside a shack with gunshot wounds. National Police Commissioner Fannie Masemola said on Monday that investigators had not established motives for the crimes that took place 530 kilometres (330 miles) apart. “The ongoing mass shootings which we encounter are unacceptable. Definitely, we have to find these criminals. We cannot allow them to terrorise communities or determine how people live their lives,” Masemola said. South Africa has struggled for years with high rates of violent crime, but has had a recent surge in mass shootings with high death tolls. Reporting from Pretoria, Al Jazeera’s Clement Manyathela said the community was “gripped by fear” as it waits for answers about the shooting. He said the victims were found in a four-room shack, where the killings happened just before midnight. A young child who went into the shack looking for a relative made the discovery, he said. Pathologists, investigators and officers were working to establish what happened. Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said one of those killed was a “person of interest” in a shooting last year in the nearby informal settlement of Saulsville, in which 12 people were killed and 13 wounded, the Associated Press news agency reported. “We cannot rule out that they may be linked, and may possibly have been a retaliation attack,” Mthombeni said. In the Pietermaritzburg shooting, police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said some families had come forward to help identify victims. “It’s still too early to tell what the motive could have been and who could be behind the shooting because we are yet to identify the victims,” said Netshiunda.

events.title: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth
events.summary: Every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan. Savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete. Across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the new tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon . An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. Just 7% cited diversifying revenue streams. McKinsey’s 2026 research finds that AI high performers pursue growth or innovation alongside efficiency. In a 2025 study of software and reasoning tasks, METR found that the length of tasks AI agents could complete with 50% reliability had been doubling roughly every seven months. Those lengths reflect how long the tasks take human experts. AI is making ideas more abundant and early experimentation less expensive. For software-based concepts, it can help teams research a market, write and test code, and build an initial prototype before committing a larger team and budget. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Established companies can draw on existing expertise and capabilities to get started. Every established company has expertise in how its industry actually works. Customer knowledge: what people complain about, ask for, pay extra for, and work around. Capabilities built for one purpose that could serve another. Some also have patents, trade secrets, or research shelved because building on them was too expensive to staff. Startups would kill for these. AI can help you explore new uses. Turning those assets into revenue takes a method. At Idealab, we’ve spent three decades refining 31 ways to find business ideas, grouped into seven lenses. We’ve applied those methods with AI to create a database of more than 1.2 million potential business ideas, freely available at Idealab.ai . Four lenses start from demand, meaning what people suffer, want, or do: Start from a pain. Fix your own, fix someone else’s, or remove friction, waiting, waste, or danger. Your customer-support logs can reveal problems worth solving. Make it radically better. Ask what could become dramatically faster, simpler, more convenient, or automated. Open it to more people. Cut the cost of a premium service so a new customer group can afford it. What would that make possible? Read the signals people leave. Look for repeated questions and complaints, workarounds, misuse, broken trust, and ignored niches. Three lenses start from supply, meaning what just became possible: Harness a new capability. Apply new technology to an old problem, or pair an existing capability with a different business model. Get the timing right. Look for a falling cost curve, a platform shift, or a regulatory change. Exhume the graveyard: revisit projects shelved because they were right but too early. Think big. Reimagine a giant but static industry, or start from a bold vision of a better future. Consider a logistics company that can predict delivery disruptions. Could that expertise support a planning service for smaller shippers? AI can help explore the possibility. Customers still need to demonstrate that the problem matters enough to pay for a solution. Run these lenses against your expertise, customer knowledge, capabilities, and intellectual property. Use AI to identify and challenge the assumptions, then test demand directly with customers. Assign an accountable owner to the strongest opportunity. Use customer interviews, prototypes, or paid pilots to learn what people actually need and whether they will pay. Give the team clear milestones for deciding whether to invest further, change direction, or stop. One more thing. Put a revenue target next to the savings target in your next board deck. The goal is to build a stronger company by improving efficiency and creating new sources of growth. events.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
events.summary: The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. Under the interim rule , the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries. The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others. The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries. “This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.” The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions. Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S. The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group. The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S. Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect. Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media. The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies. “By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial
events.summary: Novo released full results from a late-stage trial showing Wegovy helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity significantly lower their body mass index. Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, but there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The drugmaker said it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids. Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index. Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial. When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications. "This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity. In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040. While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6. In Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea. But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September. "We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said. Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids. Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said. "That is something that is still an evidence gap," she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

events.title: Why Starshield limits are hurting Ukraine against jet-powered drones
events.summary: Ukraine’s military has been relying on the internet service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limits on SpaceX’s Starshield military-grade internet service are disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and hindering the country’s war effort against Russia. Over the weekend, two people were killed in a Russian jet-powered drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region. An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity. list 1 of 3 US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine list 2 of 3 Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia? list 3 of 3 Starshield restrictions help Russia’s energy attacks on Ukraine: Zelenskyy Zelenskyy linked the success of these Russian strikes to limits that he said had been placed on Ukraine’s use of Starshield. The country’s military has been relying on the service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones. Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, a network of 11,000 satellites launched into low Earth orbit by SpaceX to provide high-speed internet connectivity, even in remote areas. In a statement on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides often use to attack each other. He added that “many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there”. “We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this,” he added. Zelenskyy also accused Starlink’s sister service of throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations on Saturday. He said that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days. This is not the first time Ukrainian officials have complained about limits on Starshield hampering Kyiv’s defence efforts. Last month, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian missile and drone strikes, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning. How is slow-speed internet impacting Ukraine’s defences? According to a November 2 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Starshield is critical to Ukraine since it helps in encrypting satellite communications, which are needed to guide drones in order to carry out interceptions. “In addition to using Starshield service for strikes within Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, Ukraine uses Starshield-equipped drones to intercept and defend against Russian drones, such as new jet-powered drones taking aim at Ukrainian critical infrastructure and civilian targets,” the CSIS report noted. Without access to Starshield internet, these Ukrainian drones are unable to work as effectively. “Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered ‘shaheds’,” Zelenskyy said on X on Sunday. After last month’s disruptions, Zelenskyy said on X that “intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”. “This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he added. Last month, Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, had posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (161km/h). That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection. “Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he had said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”. Officials have said the restrictions have also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals. What are the jet-powered drones Russia is using? Jet-powered drones are high-speed uncrewed aerial vehicles equipped with small turbojet engines rather than traditional propellers or piston engines. In its war on Ukraine, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered variants such as the Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 models. These drones fly at much higher speeds than traditional propeller-powered drones, making them significantly harder for Ukrainian air defences to intercept. In August, 38 people were killed in the village of Myla in Ukraine, when a Russian drone attack struck an ammunition depot. Another 12 were killed in attacks across the country in September.

events.title: Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop
events.summary: Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users. The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day. Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions. For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop. When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop. Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. The incident, first reported by German broadcaster WDR, happened on Friday at Hotel Ling Bao, part of the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl, Germany, where a malfunctioning automatic dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the swimming pool. The hotel's monitoring system spotted the problem and emailed staff a warning about the excessive chlorine levels. Unfortunately, Microsoft's Outlook service was caught up in a global outage, meaning the warning never arrived. Brühl Fire Department said the problem started when a technical fault caused the pool's dosing equipment to pump in more chlorine than it should have. Chlorine gas then escaped into the swimming area, leaving guests needing medical attention. Paramedics checked over 15 people at the hotel, and five were taken to hospital. Four suffered minor injuries, while one was moderately injured and needed further treatment. The fire department sent about 40 personnel to the scene, and crews spent roughly two hours dealing with the incident. The incident came as Microsoft was battling a major outage that began on Thursday, November 12, and dragged well into Friday. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services were knocked offline, leaving businesses unable to access email and documents. The disruption wasn't confined to office workers unable to check their inboxes, with hospitals, police forces, and government departments reporting problems accessing the Microsoft services they use for day-to-day operations. Redmond has since blamed the outage on a bug introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade . It sat there until a later network change set it off, and the failures then spread across the company's infrastructure. Microsoft ruled out both cybercriminals and AI as culprits, and has issued the customary apology. At Phantasialand, though, a broken inbox was the least of anyone's worries. The chlorine dosing equipment went haywire independently of Microsoft's troubles, but the email warning staff about the problem apparently never arrived. Whether the hotel had a backup alarm, or anything capable of shutting off the chlorine supply automatically, remains unanswered. Why a hotel would rely on Outlook to deliver warnings about dangerous chlorine levels is anyone's guess.
