events.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
events.summary: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell , the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die . The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies , the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics , based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away. Christie Hemm Klok The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.” For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold. But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga , who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit. Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke As recently as the early ’90s , physicians who treated stroke struggled with “ therapeutic nihilism .” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery . In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event. Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right. The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.” Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter. Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray. I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. events.title: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem
events.summary: Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid. But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep. Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill. “Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch. Speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly. If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade. Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup said it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ F, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital. Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market. Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: A report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity. Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to 10 times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down. Accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail. High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan said. Instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle and rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit. “I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he said. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super-hot rock temperatures.” That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity. “What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he said. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Appliances can share 16 TB of DRAM and half a terabyte of HBM across up to 16 systems China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 52 minutes ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 3 hours ago Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed 6 hours ago Datacenters' share of UK planning applications nearly triples in three years 7 hours ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 8 hours ago Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric. Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth. “What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg. Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity. With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules. If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs. Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity. As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely. Memory godboxes could offer relief from the RAMpocalypse Amid the AI-fueled memory crunch, will Compute Express Link finally have its moment to shine? The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money. In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5. This mode essentially treats the HBM as a read/write cache. Frequently accessed files are written to and read from HBM first before being pushed into standard DDR5 as they get stale. Marvell and Penguin are positioning the new memory appliance as an alternative to storage-based key value (KV) cache offload. AI inference generates large KV caches, which are used to track model state across chat sessions, and long-running agents.

events.title: Americans are eating way less turkey than we used to
events.summary: Butterball Turkey Talk-Line experts take part in cooking and carving classes in 2009. AP Photo/M. Spencer Green One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm , Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays . I find turkeys fascinating , because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway . Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies , researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving . Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken , according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound , while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched . Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken . So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans . And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn . The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds . Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken . In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week . Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours , while a 4-pound chicken takes about two . That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society . In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut . He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one . They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take . I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. What will become of Nvidia now that its only leader in 33 years, and one whose vision shaped the company into one of the largest in the world, is gone? Who will take charge? events.title: Average diesel prices are under $6 per gallon for the first time in months
events.summary: Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Average U.S. diesel prices inched below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since Sept. 10 amid lower oil prices recently, per AAA data. Why it matters: Diesel soared even more than gasoline during the Iran war, and those costs rippled throughout the economy. Democrats featured high prices, especially for farmers, en route to midterm wins in typically red agricultural states. Zoom out: The worldwide diesel supply crunch remains acute even as the broader oil market is starting to fitfully stabilize. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, damage to Middle Eastern production and shipments, throttled oil supplies, and expanded U.S. exports to meet overseas demand helped raise domestic costs. The bottom line: Prices are now far below the Sept. 22 record of nearly $6.53 per gallon. The recent relief is real, but it's limited. events.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
events.summary: Salon owner: 'We have parents offering to pay their kids' wages' National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge. There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show. Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest. Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads". She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages. "I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said. Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters. "I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs." The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full. He has already unveiled some of his proposals including: Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits. Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000. This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100. Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase. Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank. Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money. But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing". Milburn told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers. "Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said. "The state has a responsibility to help them with that." On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit. People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales. McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029". events.title: After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public
events.summary: It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop. Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion. Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan. ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry , which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge. But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan. The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.) Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the company spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries. ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products. Many new grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry. Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives. The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs. My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck. “Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said. Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said. “Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.

events.title: Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings
events.summary: Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country. Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy , says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs. That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023. Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid. “We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.” Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments. Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models. The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said. To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added. Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said. The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures, with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital. events.title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
events.summary: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder. Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation. Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion. Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack? Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation. This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization. The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes. Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well? Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. events.title: Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed
events.summary: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon. During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators. NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size. Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation.” “It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained. Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained. In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems. A compute chameleon LANL is one of several labs tasked with ensuring that the US’ nuclear deterrent remains effective decades after underground testing was banned. The lab is also responsible for running simulations on energy sources like fuel candidates for future fusion reactors. Both of these workloads, Shipman tells us, fall into a category called multi-physics simulations. These workloads aren’t really one workload, but multiple simulations that can have wildly different compute requirements. A “good example is inertial confinement fusion. At the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, you're using lasers to implode a fuel capsule, and the goal is to generate more energy through yield than you do from depositing energy to the capsule,” Shipman explained. “That's inherently multiphysics.” There are simulations for the lasers, the hydrodynamics within the fuel capsule, and the chemistry and material interactions taking place during the fusion process. The problem, Shipman explains, is that a system that’s ideal for one of those simulations may not be well suited to others. “Identifying one specific platform that is optimal for that type of simulation is challenging.” CPUs, he says, are well suited to workloads with large serial sections, irregular access patterns, and jobs that benefit from deep cache hierarchies. Meanwhile, GPUs are fantastic for dense, matrix-multiplication heavy workloads. "Where NextSilicon fits in is being able to reconfigure to match the workload, on demand,” Shipman said. “The hope is that we won't have to make these rigid determinations upfront like, ‘we need this much CPU or we need this much GPU.’ We can use a much more adaptable, reconfigurable architecture to meet the workflow where it is at.” A closer look at Maverick 2 Despite some visual similarities to Nvidia’s current crop of GPUs, Maverick-2 is not a GPU. Instead it employs a dataflow architecture which overlaps communication and computation. Rather than waiting for load-store operations to shuffle data around as you would with a conventional CPU or GPU, the chips themselves comprise a grid of arithmetic logic units (ALUs) which are configured to perform an operation like addition or multiplication in the order that they’re needed. Data is computed as it moves from one ALU to the next, a bit like how a ball moves through a Rube Goldberg contraption. This can make dataflow architectures extremely efficient in bandwidth-bound scenarios, which has implications not only for HPC and scientific computing but also for AI. It’s why we’re seeing dataflow accelerators, like Nvidia’s Groq, Cerebras’ WSE-3, and SambaNova’s SN50, being deployed as decode accelerators in AI inference clusters. Where NextSilicon stands out is that its designs, so far, have been specifically tailored toward sparse double-precision FP64 workloads. Real FLOPS are rarely advertised Programming dataflow architectures, historically, has been a challenging endeavor. To overcome this, NextSilicon claims to have developed a compiler that can decompose any existing C, Python, Fortran, or CUDA codebases into a graph that can run directly on its chips. So far, NextSilicon has managed to validate its systems against the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the LAMMPS molecular dynamics test suite, and the Sparta Monte Carlo simulation suite. But as NextSilicon CEO Elad Raz notes, the roofline performance of Maverick-2 is different from one workload to another, and so the company has opted not to advertise peak theoretical performance the same way GPU vendors like Nvidia or AMD have traditionally done. That’s not to say NextSilicon is shy about Maverick’s performance characteristics. Rather than advertising peak performance that the chip may not be able to hit in the workloads its customers actually care most about, it published performance figures across a swath of HPC benchmarks. For example, in HPCG, one of the closest watched HPC benchmarks after High Performance Linpack (HPL), NextSilicon says a single Maverick achieves 600 gigaFLOPS of performance, which it says is on par with contemporary GPUs but at half the power. That’s just fine and dandy as far as Shipman is concerned. He tells us peak advertised performance is rarely a useful proxy for real-world performance. “The thing that my team spends the most time on is how do we generate representative proxies, representative kernels; how do we generate specifications that communicate our needs to the broader ecosystem so that vendors like NextSilicon can meet us and co-design with us.” ®

events.title: Who is Leo KoGuan, the Singapore-based billionaire backing Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Indonesia-born investor Leo KoGuan has also backed Elon Musk’s Tesla. Leo KoGuan, a Singapore-based billionaire, said he would not buy more Nvidia shares without Jensen Huang, whom he called “the supreme creator”. Huang’s exit after reported affairs and a 33-year run shook Nvidia, sent shares down 12.8%, and sparked calls from tech leaders for his return. KoGuan built his fortune through SHI International and Tesla, and has made major Singapore buys, including the Dysons’ Wallich Residence penthouse and 21 Carpenter hotel. SINGAPORE – Billionaire investor Leo KoGuan on Nov 13 said that he would not buy more Nvidia shares without co-founder Jensen Huang at the helm. This came a day after the US chipmaker announced Huang’s resignation. KoGuan, who called Huang “the supreme creator” in posts on X, argued that his achievements should count for more than his mistakes and said that he had invested about US$1.3 billion (S$1.7 billion) in Nvidia. The artificial intelligence and semicon heavyweight has a market capitalisation of about US$3.9 trillion as at Nov 16. KoGuan’s backing for Huang comes as prominent tech figures push for his return to Nvidia. Elon Musk, Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator president Garry Tan and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick were among the signatories of an open letter urging Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. More than 7,500 signatories reportedly identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia followed reports of three extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US authorities suspect of spying for China. His departure ended a 33-year run at the helm of Nvidia, the company he co-founded and whose chips now power much of the AI boom. The company named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive officer. Amid the turmoil, Nvidia shares fell 12.8% in the week to Nov 13, closing at US$162.85, even as chip stocks as a group rose about 8% the same week, noted Kenneth Goh, director of private wealth management at UOB Kay Hian. He added that the shares could remain under pressure until Nvidia’s board names a successor who has the confidence of key stakeholders. “KoGuan is saying out loud what a lot of investors feel. Many of them bought Nvidia because of Jensen Huang,” Goh said. “His own holding is small, well under 1% of the company. He has also only said he will stop adding. He has not said he is selling.” KoGuan first drew wider attention for his bet on Tesla. In Singapore, he made headlines for his high-profile property purchases, such as that of the Dysons’ Wallich Residence penthouse. KoGuan, 71, was born in Indonesia to Chinese parents. He moved to the US, where he earned a master’s degree in international affairs from Columbia University and a law degree from New York Law School. In 1989, he and his then wife, Thai Lee, paid less than US$1 million for a struggling New Jersey software reseller with five employees and about as many customers. The business became Software House International, now known as SHI International. SHI has since expanded beyond software reselling into hardware, cloud computing and cybersecurity services. It serves more than 17,000 customers, including Boeing, Johnson & Johnson and AT&T, and employs about 7,000 people worldwide. KoGuan told Bloomberg in 2021 that he had stepped back from day-to-day operations around the turn of the century. He remains chairman, while Lee is president and chief executive officer. In October 2025, SHI said it reached US$16 billion in gross sales over the preceding 12 months. It also announced an investment in AI engineering consultancy NStarX, giving clients of its New Jersey AI and cybersecurity lab access to NStarX’s data scientists. KoGuan began buying Tesla shares in 2019. He built a concentrated position through shares and options. Bank records showed that he held 6.3 million Tesla shares and 1.8 million options as at September 2021. The options gave him the right to buy Tesla shares at prices ranging from US$450 to US$550 apiece. He was one of the carmaker’s largest individual shareholders at the time. As the stock rallied, the value of his Tesla holdings climbed to more than US$7 billion by October 2021. In 2024, KoGuan said he was cutting his Tesla stake and buying three-month US Treasury bills. He said in a post on X that he still planned to hold Tesla for the long term but feared a stock market crash on the scale of 1929, which was the catalyst for the Great Depression. In March 2026, the 71-year-old said he was “still mostly in Tesla” and Treasury bills. He had grown more critical of Tesla and its CEO, Elon Musk, including over a pay package that could be worth up to US$1 trillion. He declined to say how much of his Tesla stake he had sold. On March 3, KoGuan said he bought one million Nvidia shares.

events.title: Ex-Barclays CEO Bob Diamond on investing in the Gulf and the irrelevancy of Bitcoin
events.summary: The News Speaking from the Bahrain capital Manama, which a few months earlier had been bombarded in Iranian attacks, Bob Diamond, chief executive of private equity firm Atlas Merchant Capital, says he’s still optimistic about the outlook for the Gulf’s future, the US economy, and the prospect to raise more capital to consolidate the banking industry around the world. Panmure Liberum, a UK investment bank he’s invested in, is expanding into the Gulf. Wall Street investors increasingly see the region as a place to invest, not just a place to raise money, and the war isn’t deterring that. “This is a really serious economy,” he said. Diamond has experience in the region spanning decades. His contacts in Abu Dhabi and Qatar helped secure a £11.8 billion bailout for Barclays during the Great Financial Crisis, enabling the bank to avoid a taxpayer-funded rescue. He left Barclays in 2012 in the wake of a scandal around its role in manipulating interbank rates, and has since reinvented himself as a private equity investor, backing bank consolidation deals and fintechs. He is also chairman of the advisory committee of the Export-Import Bank of the US and chairman of Abu Dhabi’s tokenization platform Finstreet. Diamond also said that Bitcoin, the most well-known and biggest digital asset by market capitalization, is “irrelevant” (though useful as a store of value untethered from governments) and that the future of finance is tokenization — an industry is being led by the US as well as the Middle East. Q&A Matthew Martin: You just announced Panmure Liberum, the UK investment bank you own, is expanding into the Gulf — how do you think about the opportunities in the Gulf now, particularly with the conflict that’s still going on? Bob Diamond: I don’t mean to be dismissive of the severity of the situation here for a second, with the invasion of Iran, but when you’re here, as you and I are today, it feels pretty normal. For people who have not spent time in this region, I don’t think there’s a recognition of how developed the economies are, how developed the leadership is. And then I’d say that since we started Atlas Merchant Capital just over 10 years ago, I’ve been as interested in investing Middle Eastern money in other parts of the world as I have been in how we can find ways to help develop business here on the ground. I think there’s just a tremendous opportunity in this region for an on-the-ground advisory and M&A business for middle-market and family-owned businesses, because, as we are seeing here, the entrepreneurial spirit is very, very strong in many of these countries. Financial services here is a great example of an industry where the vast majority of banks are ultimately state-controlled. As governments need to redirect capital to other things in the wake of the war, is there an opportunity for private equity investors to come in and play more of a role in the financial services industry in the Gulf? One hundred percent. But I think you hit on a key issue, which is that traditionally that state control made things more opaque, so you couldn’t get outside investment because it was opaque. And two, it was intrusive and more focused on subsidized business. And you can see why, right? Because as the Middle East was growing, much of the commercial real estate, for example, had to be “if we build it, they will come.” So some of the unbelievable commercial real estate, whether it’s in Abu Dhabi or Dubai or Qatar, or the financial services center that was built in Riyadh, was done really with strategic impetus, if you will, as opposed to pure commercial activity. And I think that’s changing, because a lot of those initial strategic investments have been done. I think it was the same in the early days of the development of Singapore. You could say the same thing, that it was strategic investing, but if you go to Singapore today, it’s a very commercial city. You don’t see commercial buildings being put up. What impact do you see the conflict in the region having on how Wall Street sees the Gulf? I think sometime around 2024, 2025, we hit an inflection point where the Middle East being seen purely as a source of funding for the Western world changed to “this is a really serious economy.” Going forward the Gulf will be focused much more on inward investment, as well as outward investment. I think it probably happened already with Saudi Arabia, and they’ve been a little bit ahead of it. But I think it’s really true across the region. But there are still significant pools of capital in this region — if you just look at the sovereign wealth funds, that’s the best example but not the only example — for investment in good ideas wherever they happen to be. Dubai and Abu Dhabi are both making this big play into fintech and tokenization. How much are you getting involved in that, and what do you see as the chances of centers in the region becoming hubs for this new asset class? I feel very strongly. Bitcoin’s irrelevant. It’s not that Bitcoin isn’t going to go up or down, and I’m not questioning whether Bitcoin’s going to have a significantly higher price or not. I’m personally not an investor, but I have a number of close associates who believe strongly. My point is different. In its best version, Bitcoin is a store of value away from a government, much as gold is. And if it doubles or triples or quadruples in value, it doesn’t have a single strategic implication for financial services. It’s just made somebody money, and it’s a good store of value. Compare and contrast that to stablecoins, basically making payments electronic institutionally for the major currencies around the world. Compare and contrast that to blockchain, which is 24/7, instantaneous settlement, a permanent record of every transaction that happens, everything at the speed of the internet and a fraction of the cost of conventional financial services. That’s the future. That’s the underpinning of financial services going forward: blockchain, and finally tokenization. In the last two to three years, the US has moved very, very aggressively forward in terms of recognizing Circle, USDC, stablecoins, payments. Under Gensler at the SEC, it was just ignored. Nothing was approved. Outside of the US, we’re not seeing the same kind of attitude in London or Europe, but we are seeing it in the Emirates and in the Middle East. Abu Dhabi’s only a few hours’ time difference from London and Europe, and I think it has a real chance to emerge as a more important financial center with the progress of tokenization and the advance of digital. What do you have planned for the future of your digital asset business Hyperliquid Strategies? I’m very, very positive on Hyperliquid. events.title: Africa’s power drive is short of developers, Gridworks CEO says
events.summary: The News Africa has plenty of investors ready to finance much-needed electricity projects, but too few developers with the expertise and early funding to get them off the ground, the head of a UK government-backed power developer told Semafor. More than 40% of sub-Saharan Africans lack electricity, with private investment central to a World Bank and African Development Bank push to connect 300 million across the whole continent by 2030. “People spend a lot of time talking about a lack of capital for infrastructure projects in Africa. There is not a lack of capital,” said Chris Flavin, chief executive of Gridworks, which develops and invests in electricity networks across Africa. The issue for him is that investors generally want to get involved once projects are ready for construction, leaving the four or five years of preparatory work harder to finance. Gridworks, which has electricity projects in countries including Uganda and Mozambique, is set to become the majority shareholder in a planned $300 million power line linking Zambia’s grid to DR Congo’s copper-mining region, under an agreement signed in October. Lenders have shown “very strong interest” in the line, Flavin said. When it develops its own projects, though, Gridworks faces the same hurdles as others despite its UK backing, he added, from permits and environmental approvals to years of planning “before you even get close to the financing.” In DR Congo, for example, commercial banks will not lend at that stage, said Archip Lobo, co-founder of Nuru, a solar mini-grid operator in the country’s east. “They will take the risk on something that exists,” he told Semafor. Instead, Lobo highlighted the existence of state support for early development costs and World Bank Group insurance against political risks. But the World Bank’s own evaluators are less sure capital is plentiful. They found in a recent review that private financing remained too limited to meet Africa’s electrification needs. The narrow pool of investors, such as development lenders’ private arms, government-sponsored funds, foundations, and impact funds “are unlikely to meet the scale of financing needed for electrification growth,” the group said. Industrial advantage Private power projects in Africa are easier to develop when they serve large industrial buyers, such as mines, rather than households and small businesses, Flavin said. A mine with a strong balance sheet and known electricity consumption gives developers a clear customer to design around. For projects aimed at individual customers “the challenge is one of guaranteed demand.” In southeastern DR Congo, CrossBoundary Energy, a Mauritius-based power producer, commissioned a 233-megawatt solar farm with battery storage in August to supply Kamoa-Kakula, a copper complex co-owned by Ivanhoe Mines. “Kamoa’s books are very good,” Auguy Bakome, a project manager at the mine, told Semafor in an earlier interview. He said its expected 40-year operating life and a 15-year contract to buy the electricity helped reassure lenders. Utilities must estimate consumption across tens of thousands of customers. Building networks to serve them is “at the much harder end of the spectrum, full stop,” Flavin said. Moyi Power, a Gridworks-backed utility planned for three cities in northern DR Congo, relies on donor grants for about a quarter of its $190 million first phase and is not expected to deliver electricity before 2029. Notable Africa’s shortage of reliable power is stalling its industrialization , Bloomberg reported, citing World Bank data that put manufacturing at 11% of sub-Saharan Africa’s GDP , half East Asia’s share.

events.title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
events.summary: Dreamteam , a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge. The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation. Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring. Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said. That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks. At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers. Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers. The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.” Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them. Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software. “We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms. Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products. Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code. Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue. The catch was a remarkable achievement: Starship returned to the same launch tower it had left almost a day earlier, settling into its giant mechanical arms. Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale. Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day. Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left. Many more development flights remain before SpaceX can deliver its promised fully reusable launch system. NASA's Space Shuttle came close, but the large external tank was expended with every launch, and the orbiters never matched the cadence SpaceX reckons it can achieve with Starship. SpaceX boss Elon Musk admitted that "many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)." Cadence will be key if Starship is going to meet NASA's needs for the Artemis missions. Somewhere between 6 and 22 launches (depending on who you ask) will be required for a lunar mission, and SpaceX has yet to demonstrate in-space propellant transfer between vehicles. Next year's Artemis III mission also calls for docking tests between NASA's Orion spacecraft and a test version of SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System (HLS) in low Earth orbit. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Councils waving through majority of proposals as government turns on the AI-friendly planning taps Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric 5 hours ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 7 hours ago Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis 3 days ago US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity 5 days ago AMD winds up Zen 6 cores for faster clock speeds 6 days ago Datacenters made up nearly three times as large a share of UK planning applications in the year to September 2026 as they did three years earlier, with councils receiving 59 submissions. The figures come from planning data site Plota, whose Q3 2026 Planning Index draws on applications from every council across the UK. Plota has logged 416 datacenter applications since 2016, though these include extensions and alterations, not just new bit barns. Estimates put Britain's existing fleet at between 477 and 602 facilities. The peak for volume came in the 12 months to March 2021, when 63 campus applications were filed. However, overall planning applications were also higher then, so datacenters accounted for just 1.1 in every 10,000 filed. In the current period they equate to 1.4 in every 10,000. The figures show that applications for building new server halls are about as high as they have been over the past decade, and close to their recent peak as a share of all applications. Even so, the application numbers don't show the dramatic jump that the steady stream of bit barn announcements might suggest. Nor do they tell us how many facilities are actually being built. Applications did bounce around the middle of 2024, when the current government - and its fetish for all things AI - was elected. But it didn't publish the AI Opportunities Action Plan , which recommended "AI Growth Zones" with streamlined planning to speed up datacenter builds, until the start of 2025. Plota links the rise to datacenters being recognized as critical national infrastructure (CNI) in September 2024, and a December 2024 update to the planning framework that told councils to identify suitable sites for them. The facilities are getting larger. One site being built for Equinix near London's M25 motorway will feature three data halls with more than 250 MW capacity, while another planned for Havering in East London could go up to 600 MW. Both were billed as being among Europe's largest campuses. According to Plota, just 3.3 percent of datacenter applications decided between 2016 and 2024 were refused, against 11.3 percent across all applications. The government has also overturned some local council refusals, controversially, as at a site near Abbots Langley in Hertfordshire last year. Slough leads Plota's tally of applications since 2016 with 28, followed by Tower Hamlets in East London with 16, Leeds with 12, and West Northamptonshire with 11. Developers in England can also ask ministers to bring qualifying datacenter projects into the nationally significant infrastructure planning regime , shifting the consent decision from the council to central government. Projects taking that route fall outside Plota's council-based figures. events.title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year
events.summary: Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis. The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs. Renewable energy projects built between 2003 and 2014 are expected to claim £4.5bn in subsidies over the next financial year, on top of £4.2bn in wholesale market revenue. The analysis showed developers will receive almost 50% more than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent gas prices soaring in 2022. The analysis by the Energy Competitiveness Unit (ECU), a non-partisan research and policy project, said the legacy support scheme – which is paid via taxes and energy bills – must be reformed “if we are serious about getting costs of the electricity system down in the short and medium term”. Unlike newer renewable energy projects that earn fixed-price subsidies for their generation, older projects access support via the renewables obligation (RO) scheme, which provides payments on top of what developers earn via the wholesale market, meaning that higher gas market prices lead to higher subsidy costs for renewables. The scheme was credited with kickstarting the UK’s renewable energy industry when it was put in place almost 25 years ago, but the ECU said it “has been allowed to persist unsustainably”. Andrew O’Brien, the ECU director, told the Guardian that the rise in wholesale prices over recent years has meant that many renewable energy developers are earning “well above what they could reasonably have expected” when first taking the decision to invest in the projects. The government announced last year that it would remove three-quarters of the RO scheme’s costs from home energy bills, and move these levies into general taxation from April 2026 to help temper the steep rise in energy bills. The government later warned that legacy generators could face higher windfall taxes unless they give up the existing RO scheme in favour of a new partially fixed subsidy contract as part of its plans to protect bill payers. The ECU believes that the government’s consultation on plans to fix the generators’ wholesale revenues to help to weaken the link between volatile global gas markets and the UK’s electricity costs “falls short”. It argues ministers should go further to fix their subsidy payments and create a new scheme. Since 2013, renewable energy developers have been required to compete in an auction to secure a contract for a fixed price for each megawatt-hour of electricity generated, known as a contract for difference (CfD), which means costs remain fixed regardless of global markets. Under an alternative proposal set out in the ECU’s research, the government could cut electricity costs by £3.8bn next year, and £9.2bn over 10 years, if all generators moved on to an entirely fixed-price contract, which it calls a fair value CfD. The new private law contracts could also offer a degree of legal protection against the political risk that any potential future net zero sceptic government could dismantle renewable energy support through the government’s RO scheme, a threat signalled by the rightwing populist Reform UK party . Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “It is in the interests of everyone – investors, generators, businesses, households and government – to get a credible long-term plan in place that can withstand shocks in this increasingly uncertain world,” the ECU said. In his budget speech last month, the chancellor, John Healey, said : “We will further break the grip of international gas prices on our bills by moving more of our old renewables on to fixed-price contracts.” Tara Singh, the chief executive of RenewableUK, said the renewable energy projects were still helping to keep a lid on bills by “pushing expensive gas off the system”. Singh said: “UCL found wind has saved consumers £100bn since 2010 even allowing for support schemes like the RO by reducing the need for expensive imports.” She added that the government’s windfall tax, which took effect from July, has meant that renewable energy projects using the RO scheme pay the Treasury up to 80p of every additional pound it earns from market prices above £82.61 per megawatt hour. “To put this into context, the average wholesale price of electricity over the last 12 months is over £100 per megawatt hour, and frequently higher than that,” she said. “The fastest way to protect consumers from future price shocks is to build more cheap, homegrown renewable power.”
