events.title: Zambia's mining investor seeks to borrow $700M
events.summary: The News Zambia’s majority state-owned mining and energy investor plans to borrow about $700 million by 2028 to expand its business, its CEO told Semafor, as Africa’s second-largest copper producer seeks a bigger share of the wealth from its minerals. The money, which ZCCM Investments Holdings has yet to secure, will help fund a $2.7 billion investment proposal it unveiled on Monday. Over the next decade, the company looks to back new infrastructure including a coal-fired power plant in southern Zambia and to raise its stakes in copper mines , among them a project led by Bill Gates-backed Kobold Metals. “We don’t want to be a quiet minority shareholder,” CEO Kakenenwa Muyangwa said. He added that any changes would be negotiated on commercial terms, and that “investors who share the ambition will find us a committed long-term partner.” ZCCM-IH holds stakes in mines run by other companies and earns much of its income from their dividends, which depend on what is left after the mines pay their costs and debts. “For a country that owns a share of its mines, that is not good enough,” Muyangwa said. The company now aims to earn more from royalties, a share of a mine’s sales that is paid regardless of profit. Its only such arrangement, with Canadian miner First Quantum’s Kansanshi mine, will bring in more than $990 million over the next decade, the company forecasts. ZCCM-IH aims to add at least one more later this decade. The investment company said it now owes $5 for every $100 of its own capital, down from about $66 in 2021. Muyangwa said a cleaner balance sheet had put ZCCM-IH in a strong position to fund its expansion. Trading ambitions ZCCM-IH also plans to negotiate with its mining partners to get a share of the copper produced at each mine, which it would then sell directly. That would give the company “a trading income on top of its investment income” and build “the skills to market Zambian metal from Zambia,” Muyangwa said. The plan comes as state-backed companies across Africa’s copper belt seek a more influential role over the trade of the metal. In neighboring DR Congo, state miner Gécamines sells copper through a venture with Swiss trader Mercuria. Zambia’s state-owned Industrial Development Corporation also has a trading venture with Mercuria, which last month named ZCCM-IH as a regional partner. The goal is greater control over the money countries earn from their minerals, Ekpen Omonbude, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, told Semafor. As demand for critical minerals grows, governments are looking to take a more active role in their sale, an approach he said is more common in oil and gas than in mining. Notable Zambia’s copper output rose just 1.5% in the first nine months of the year , far short of what it needs to meet its goal of 3 million tons a year by 2031.

events.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. “We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.” Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.” “If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.” The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada. Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs. The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market. Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant. Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained. events.summary: London-listed real estate developer Dar Global is launching a new mixed-use development in Jeddah , with an estimated value of about 1 billion Saudi riyals ($267 million) as part of its expansion plans in the kingdom. The project will be developed on a plot of land acquired for $56 million and forms part of Dar Global's programme to expand its Saudi Arabia portfolio by up to 4 billion riyals, the company said on Monday. On completion of the programme, the company's worldwide development pipeline is expected to reach about $24 billion, it added. A new international luxury brand will be introduced to Jeddah as part of the development, as the company plans to announce more land acquisitions in the kingdom. Dar Global has partnerships with more than 10 brands, including the Trump Organisation, Aston Martin, Automobili Lamborghini, Missoni, Pagani Automobili and W Hotels, among others at its developments. “With buyers from 61 nationalities already investing in our Saudi portfolio, we are witnessing accelerating international confidence in the country's real estate sector,” said Ziad El Chaar, chief executive of Dar Global. “This new development marks another significant milestone in our global expansion strategy.” The Arab world’s largest economy is looking to boost home ownership for Saudi citizens as part of its Vision 2030 programme. It has also opened up the property sector to foreign ownership, a move expected to attract increased demand. However, buyers remained “selective” in the kingdom during the third quarter amid regional uncertainty triggered by Iran war, a recent report by JLL said. In the July to September period, sale transaction volumes in Riyadh fell by about 30 per cent year-on-year to 9,100, while values decreased 51.8 per cent to 8.5 billion riyals. Residential transaction volumes in Jeddah fell by 25.8 per cent on an annual basis to 3,100. Transaction values fell by 5.8 per cent to 3.9 billion riyals, JLL said. With a presence in 14 international cities across nine countries, Dar Global’s portfolio of 4,200 units completed or under construction, spans the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, the UK, Spain and Greece. It is building three residential projects in Saudi Arabia in partnership with the Trump Organisation, including a $1 billion Trump Tower in Jeddah and a Trump-branded ​luxury project in Wadi Safar in the capital. Dar Global and the US President are also in partnership for the development of a $1 billion Trump Tower on Dubai 's Sheikh Zayed Road. Other international developers, including UAE-based Arada, are also expanding to Saudi Arabia. Last month, Arada unveiled a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh, with plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years. Up to 3,500 villas and townhouses will be built in Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a 2.5 million-square-metre plot.

An open letter addressed to Nvidia's board had attracted more than 173,000 signatures at the time of writing, just four days after Huang's departure following revelations about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The campaign, launched under the banner "Stand with Jensen," calls on Nvidia to reinstate its co-founder and former CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, give him a chance to respond to the allegations, and publicly explain why he was forced out. "For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," the letter reads. "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes. "Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took. This company is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now." Among the supporters are Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator boss Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. More than 8,000 signatories also identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to roughly a fifth of its workforce. However, how many of those signatures are genuine is anyone's guess. The site doesn't verify names or employers, so there's nothing stopping someone from signing as Musk, Huang, or Nvidia's entire board if they fancy it. The campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12 , ending his 33-year reign at the GPU giant he co-founded in 1993. His departure came after reports of an affair with Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, and a separate alleged relationship with an Nvidia employee. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been handed the unenviable job of running the company while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Huang's departure has left the chipmaker facing something of an identity crisis , with rivals undoubtedly watching the chaos with interest. Huang himself may not be ready to hang up his leather jacket. According to the Financial Times , the former CEO has discussed a possible comeback with associates, while an ally is reportedly assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. The effort could even involve seeking support from the White House, although Washington appears rather less enthusiastic about the prospect. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shake-up" and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also wants answers about whether Nvidia knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach China in breach of US export restrictions. None of that seems to have put off Huang's supporters. "He has erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company," Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick said.

events.title: SIA logs 3.5% rise in October passenger traffic; sees ‘healthy’ demand for semiconductor shipments
events.summary: SIA and its budget arm Scoot carried 3.7 million passengers during the month, up 4.5% from a year ago, the group said in a bourse filing. SIA reported a 3.5% rise in October passenger traffic, with 3.7 million travellers and an 87.8% passenger load factor, showing resilient demand for air travel. Scoot kept strong momentum, with a 91.6% load factor for its fourth straight month above 90%, while both airlines added new services to Madrid and Guiyang. Cargo traffic rose 10.1% as demand stayed healthy, especially for semiconductor and cloud-computing shipments, lifting cargo load factor to 59.1% despite slightly lower capacity. SINGAPORE – Singapore Airlines on Nov 16 reported a 3.5% rise in passenger traffic in October from the year-ago period amid “resilient” demand for air travel. The group’s October passenger capacity concurrently rose 2.9%, while the passenger load factor (PLF) – the percentage of available seating capacity occupied by passengers – was up 0.5 percentage point at 87.8%. SIA recorded a monthly PLF of 86.8%, thanks to “robust growth” across all regions, including East Asia, Europe and the South-west Pacific, where “traffic marginally trailed capacity increase”. Scoot’s PLF stood at 91.6%, making October its fourth consecutive month with a PLF exceeding 90%. Both airlines had launched new services during the month: SIA to Madrid in Spain, and Scoot to Guiyang in mainland China. Cargo loads rose 10.1% in October amid “healthy, broad-based demand across all verticals, particularly for semiconductor and cloud-computing shipments across the Pacific”, SIA said. Cargo capacity for the month was lower by 0.4%, translating to a rise in cargo load factor of 5.6 percentage points to 59.1%. The group’s passenger network as at end-October covers 138 destinations in 35 countries and territories; SIA serves 79 destinations, while Scoot serves 85 destinations. The cargo network comprises 141 destinations in 36 countries and territories.

events.title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix
events.summary: Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email. According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued. It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored. The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues. At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in. It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over. "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons." Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action. By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled. However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation – an update that reverted the defective change." At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update. A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control? The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®

events.title: Americans relying on heating oil brace for harsh winter: ‘We’re often cold in our own home’
events.summary: Surge in prices is forcing many to cut back on spending, with a projected 21% increase in costs of those households Millions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil. The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases. About 3% of US households rely on heating oil as their primary heat source. In the winter of 2023-2024, 4.79m US households used heating oil as their primary heat source, 82% of which were households in the north-east. A recent report from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association found that overall, heating costs are expected to climb over 7% nationwide, with average heating bills rising 16.9% in the north-east. Residents in Maine , where the temperatures can reach below 0F in many parts of the state, said they are bracing themselves for a pricey winter. “My home heating oil costs have doubled this year,” said Heidi Unruh, 61, of Kittery, Maine, where the winter chill comes in December and lasts through the end of March. “They were already impossibly high in Maine before Trump took office, and I will feel serious pain as the Maine weather dives to it’s typical winter chill” It costs more than $1,500 to fill her 250-gallon tank at home, which has to be refilled every 47 days when the temperatures are low. The increase in costs has forced her to try to cut back on other expenses. “Between oil prices, tariffs, and rising food and energy prices, it will be an especially difficult winter,” Unruh said. “Mainers everywhere will struggle along with me. To compensate, I grew a lot of my own food this year. I have cut back on unnecessary expenses, and am trying overall to need less.” Nikki Papadopoulos, who lives in Piscataquis, a county in the central part of the state, said that her family has started to use a wood stove because the cost of propane has also been high. They have also cut back on hot water, trying to use cold water to wash dishes, as the water heater also uses oil. “We keep our thermostat turned down to the absolute lowest setting available, and honestly, we’re often cold in our own home. We’re wearing layers, sweaters and jackets indoors just to stay warm,” Papadopoulos said. “We’ve cut out pretty much all unnecessary spending. We’re down to the bare essentials.” Though her husband recently received a pay increase, it’s been nearly eaten up by the higher cost of heating. “We’re essentially making compromises in our everyday routines just to stretch what’s in the tank,” she added. “We’re taking the hit from every direction.” Around 50% of households in Maine relied on heating oil in 2024, a reliance that has declined in recent years, though Maine still has the highest proportion of homes using heating oil in the US. “It’s a necessity. For people in colder regions of America, they need it, it’s what they keep themselves warm with,” said Justin Barnes, a fuel delivery driver in the Bangor, Maine region, who has had to give residents bills that have been much higher compared with recent years. “It seems like these politicians ain’t doing a lick to lower the prices or make our lives easier, which is their responsibility.” Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger and former state senator, won his election against longtime Republican senator Susan Collins in the recent midterm elections, where Republicans across the country lost their races in what was largely seen as a repudiation against the rising cost of living. Much of it has been driven by the war in Iran, where the closure of a key oil trading route has led to a prolonged spike in energy prices. Gas prices at the pump have risen over 30% compared with last year. Other oil products, such as diesel and heating oil, have gone up even higher. Recent data showed that heating oil saw a 74.2% increase from September 2025 to September 2026, costing over $6 a gallon on average. Russia’s export ban on diesel, which is similar to heating oil, amid the country’s war with Ukraine has also affected energy prices, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. In 2025, Russia exported 10% of internationally traded diesel. The Trump administration has attempted to strike a deal with Russia to export some diesel to the US, but the effort has failed so far. Bob Carpenter, an electrician in Greenville, Rhode Island, relies on heating oil to heat his home and has had to save up, bracing for the price hikes to refill his home’s oil tank. When his heating oil was delivered last month, it was $1,425 for roughly 240 gallons – about $600 more than he paid in previous years. The higher cost of heating oil comes atop other bills that have gotten more expensive, including electricity bills. “Two years ago, I thought $250 was expensive.

events.title: Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement
events.summary: In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis. In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work. In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling. What You Will Learn: How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects Register now for this free webinar!

events.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
events.summary: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success.

events.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
events.summary: President Donald Trump announces tariffs at the White House in April 2025. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.  Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:  Its own leaders.  The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies. Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies. Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.   “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.” The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.  Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries. “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.” Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.  That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.  The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year. The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president , asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”  Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event. Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.  “The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference . “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.” “I got a feeling the American people won’t see” the refund money. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs. Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx , have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. events.title: Boots to begin prescribing medical cannabis in UK
events.summary: Online service will be offered to patients with eligible conditions, in a first for a British high street pharmacy Boots is to start prescribing medical cannabis, it has announced, in a first for a UK high street pharmacy. The online service is being offered to patients in the UK aged 25 and older who have an eligible condition such as chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia. The chain is launching its SureLeaf service alongside a collaborative research programme with the University of Nottingham that will examine patient outcomes, prescribing practices and experience in the treatment of chronic pain. Patients will be invited to start an assessment online. Their suitability will then be reviewed by a clinical team, before they are invited to a video consultation with a consultant, according to Boots. Boots said any prescription would be “independently reviewed by a multidisciplinary clinical team that includes a second, independent consultant, before treatment begins”. It said any patient wishing to be prescribed medical cannabis must first have tried conventional treatments without success. And the pharmacy said patients would be regularly reviewed. Boots’ chief healthcare officer, Jamie Kerruish, said: “Millions of people live with ongoing pain and, for some, conventional treatments do not provide adequate symptom relief. This can have a significant impact on everyday life, from working and sleeping well to spending time with family and doing the things they enjoy. “Ultimately, it’s about helping people explore appropriate options that could help them better manage their symptoms and improve their quality of life.” Dr David Gwynne, the medical director of Boots’ online service, said: “Medical cannabis is not appropriate for everyone and prescribing decisions need to be made carefully on an individual patient basis. “SureLeaf has, therefore, been designed with strong clinical safeguards and specialist oversight at every stage, so treatment is only considered for patients where it is clinically appropriate. Our priority is to ensure patients receive responsible, clinically led care, from their initial specialist assessment through to ongoing monitoring and review once treatment begins.” The prescription of cannabis-derived medicines was legalised in 2018 after the mother of a young boy from Northern Ireland with severe epilepsy had cannabis oil seized at airport customs . Many private clinics have been treating patients with them for years. Hopes have been expressed that cannabis could revolutionise some areas of medicine. Only people with rare forms of epilepsy, those dealing with certain side-effects of chemotherapy, and those with certain multiple sclerosis symptoms, can get it on the NHS. But, besides chronic pain, private clinics have also been prescribing the medicines for various psychiatric disorders and neurological conditions. This year , researchers from universities in Sydney, Brisbane and Melbourne in Australia, and Bath in England, found “very little evidence” that cannabis was effective in treating anxiety, anorexia nervosa, psychotic disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder or opioid use disorder. They found some evidence the medical products could reduce dependence on cannabis, relieve the symptoms of Tourette syndrome and help insomniacs sleep better.

events.title: Thai central bank pushes back against proposed legal changes
events.summary: “No changes can be made that would undermine the next governor’s independence,” Bank of Thailand governor Vitai Ratanakorn told a briefing. Thailand’s central bank said the 2025 review found the Bank of Thailand Act still fits international standards and does not need changes. It warned that linking governor performance reviews to dismissal grounds could weaken independence and invite pressure from political or interest groups. Governor Vitai Ratanakorn said, “No changes can be made that would undermine the next governor’s independence,” while Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the government should not interfere but must coordinate. BANGKOK – Thailand’s central bank on Nov 16 defended its current governing rules and warned against changes that could undermine the governor’s independence, as it responded to criticism from its board chairman over the slow progress of legal reforms. The Bank of Thailand (BOT) said its 2025 review found the current Bank of Thailand Act remained appropriate and in line with international standards, with no need for changes. It said the BOT board had not approved any amendments to the act, though chairman Somchai Sajjapongse later pushed for changes. Among the issues previously raised and studied was whether the governor’s performance assessment could be used when seeking grounds for dismissal. Under the current law, performance assessments and grounds for dismissal are separate. The BOT said linking performance reviews to grounds for dismissal could undermine the central bank’s independence and expose it to pressures from political or interest groups. “No changes can be made that would undermine the next governor’s independence,” BOT governor Vitai Ratanakorn told a briefing. On Nov 14 , Somchai said the board called for a legal review last June, but after 18 months only one section had been proposed. He said the review should have involved outside agencies, including the Finance Ministry and the Council of State, not just BOT officials. On Nov 16 , Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the government should not interfere with the central bank’s operations, but the two sides need to coordinate. REUTERS

events.title: Employer health cost crunch is worse than projected
events.summary: There's new evidence that double-digit health cost increases were hitting employers well before the forecasts of big spikes for 2027 — forcing big changes in workplace coverage for millions of Americans. Why it matters: The findings offer a higher-resolution view of how much health spending is putting a drag on the labor market and increasing affordability concerns for the approximately 160 million Americans who get coverage through work. They also show how factors like surprise billing disputes, more cancer diagnoses and expensive specialty drugs are combining to exert cost pressure, with no immediate relief in sight. Driving the news: A new Gallagher benefits survey of more than 3,700 firms found 36% of the companies reported premium increases of 10% or more during their most recent renewal. Pharmacy costs account for a quarter or more of some companies' total health spending. Cancer care is the No. 1 cost driver for about 7 in 10 firms. The survey, fielded from January to March, also found employers are trying to avoid saddling workers with a disproportionate share of rising costs while struggling to balance the quality of care with their financial risk. "The last two renewal cycles have been unlike anything we've ever seen before," said Robby White, Gallagher's U.S. benefits business line leader. "It's unsustainable, obviously. Every additional dollar that an employer spends on health care, they can't spend on their employees." Between the lines: The 2027 coverage year was already shaping up to be painful for many employers. Projections are showing premium spikes due to rising demand for health services, more chronic disease and increased use of drugs like GLP-1s. In fact, double-digit premium increases for both the 2026 and 2027 plan years suggest there are more underlying causes, according to benefits experts. One leading factor is chronic disease: More people are being diagnosed with cancer at a younger age, and advanced treatments and related care can result in $10,000 a month in expenses or claims. Drug costs also are surging — and not just because of demand for GLP-1s. The high cost of specialty drugs for chronic or rare conditions is prompting companies to scrutinize the way formularies are designed and how well pharmacy benefit managers administer their benefits. White said another big cost driver is the No Surprises Act, which shielded consumers from large, unexpected medical bills but also created an expensive arbitration process. The arbitration has added administrative costs and is giving providers big payouts, which add millions in costs for large employers that self-fund their health plans. That's an assessment shared by big health insurers, which say the surprise billing law is creating unintended financial consequences. "The [independent dispute resolution] process has now become a top-three single driver of health care cost increases for employers," Aetna president Steve Nelson told Axios, adding the company wants to work with Congress to overhaul the system. The big picture: In a volatile health market, more employers are self-insuring and directly paying medical claims to have greater visibility and control over health costs, the Gallagher survey finds. As workers get tired of high deductibles, some employers are testing copay-only plans, which vary out-of-pocket costs by medical service and steer workers to providers deemed to be providing the most value. Part of this involves more digital tools to help patients decide. They're also re-evaluating their relationships with pharmacy benefit managers in response to rising drug costs, leading to what White says is a "huge shift" away from the big three PBMs — CVS Caremark, Optum Rx and Express Scripts. On GLP-1s, Gallagher says the question isn't whether the drugs are effective, but whether coverage is financially sustainable. More companies are exploring direct-to-consumer sales through outside vendors and giving employees debit cards or defined subsidies. What we're watching: Benefits experts are waiting to see how much congressionally mandated changes to PBMs' business practices bring down drug prices and improve transparency. They're also watching the growing number of worker lawsuits against plan sponsors, alleging they breached their fiduciary duty by failing to negotiate reasonable prescription drug prices or keep fees reasonable. Caitlin Owens contributed to this story .

events.title: South Korea faces an AI cheating scandal days before its national college entrance exams
events.summary: South Korea’s top scorer on the national tax accountant qualification exam has admitted to using AI to cheat.  Han Won-seok revealed in a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel that he used a small camera to photograph exam questions, sent the images to an AI tool, and checked the answers on his smartphone. He wore a face mask in the 14-minute long video, which has garnered more than 1.5 million views since being posted on Nov. 15. The Ministry of Economy and Finance will move to suspend Han’s qualifications. Under Korean law, candidates that cheat on their exam results are barred from taking the test again for five years, according to the Korea Herald. South Korea’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin said during a committee meeting on Monday that the ministry would inspect every pair of glasses worn by students during this week’s national college entrance exams. Reuters reported that smart devices were added to a list of banned items in July. Han acknowledged that his top ranking was fraudulent and apologized to fellow candidates, tax professionals, and exam officials. He also admitted to using the same method to cheat on a separate certified public accountant exam. “I deeply regret what I did,” Han said. Han said he is cooperating with authorities and would turn over his electronic equipment. He said he hoped an investigation might prevent similar incidents. Asked by his lawyer why he cheated, Han said he was worried about his future and wanted to make his parents proud. He said he later felt overwhelmed by guilt, particularly toward the runner up. Han scored perfect scores in three of the four subjects tested in the exam, including in introductory tax law, a subject where most candidates got an average of score of just 30 points out of 100, according to the Korea Herald. South Korea’s presidential office, Cheong Wa Dae, said it was following the case “very seriously,” with the nationwide college entrance exam scheduled for Nov. 19, Yonhap News Agency reported. It’s not the country’s first brush with AI-assisted cheating. In October 2025, at least 40 students at Korea’s Yonsei University used ChatGPT and other AI tools to cheat during a midterm test, The Korea Herald reported . It said that an additional 10 students were suspected of using AI during the test. In Japan, local media reported that an 18-year-old was referred to prosecutors after using smart glasses and recruiting tutors to help answer questions during a university entrance exam. In June 2025, several AI providers including Tencent , Alibaba , Moonshot AI, and ByteDance suspended some functions during the gaokao, the make-or-break exam that governs where students go to university. The providers suspended features including photo recognition and question-answering. Exams and education can become a flashpoint in Asia, where credentials can be critical for a successful career. In India, the leak of a medical entrance exam led to mass protests in New Delhi, forcing the education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Inside Acwa’s clean power battle plan
events.summary: The Scene Samir Serhan had an unenviable start at the helm of Acwa, one of the world’s top clean energy developers: The day before saw the first fusillades of the war in Iran. Acwa, which is part-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, operates power and desalination plants across the Gulf, and Serhan quickly understood they could become targets. Sure enough, some of the company’s assets were damaged in the war, although for security reasons it hasn’t disclosed exactly what was hit. Acwa’s net income rose 0.6% in the first nine months of the year compared to the same period last year, but was held back as the war slowed its pipeline of new projects and raised its shipping costs in the region ten-fold. But Serhan remains defiant: “You take the cards you’re dealt and make the best out of it,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye. Acwa operates nearly 100 gigawatts of gas and renewable power projects in more than a dozen countries, as well as the world’s largest privately held fleet of water desalination plants. At the summit, it was involved in one of the summit’s biggest clean power announcements, a commitment by eight financial institutions to back two gigawatts of solar plants Acwa will build in Türkiye. That plan followed Serhan’s belief that the key to global electrification, COP’s main theme this year, is to go as big as possible, so the unavoidable headaches of project development lead to a worthwhile payoff for investors and consumers. But Serhan is clear-eyed about the challenges ahead, including investors skeptical about its extensive reliance on Chinese supply chains. And only a few weeks after Acwa jointly launched a $4 billion plan to buy and build clean power projects in the US, with a focus on AI infrastructure, it ran into more unexpected headwinds: A new Congress adversarial to data centers, and an industry shaken by Jensen Huang’s ignominious departure from Nvidia. But Serhan still isn’t worried: “The demand is massive, and these things will be built.” The View From Acwa Tim McDonnell: Let’s start with Plenum, your initiative with EIG to invest $4 billion in US power projects with a focus on data centers. Since that was announced in October we’ve had the US election, which involved a lot of pushback against data centers, and then Jensen Huang stepping down from Nvidia, both of which have raised questions about a possible slowdown in the pace of the AI buildout. Is that a risk for Plenum? Samir Serhan: We’re operating today in five regions in the world, and with Plenum we’re entering the US market. The drive behind it is really the demand for clean electricity. Our main focus right now is to acquire immediately operating assets, instead of building greenfield projects, which take a lot longer. I know the stock market is reacting in a negative way to what’s happening with the Democratic majority and with the personal affairs of the CEO of Nvidia. It’s a shame, but I think this is just going to be a blip. The demand is there. People are seeing the value of AI and of industrial growth, which all need electricity. There might be some little bit of a slowdown in the US, but it will really happen. So none of this news has changed your capital allocation strategy. We are committing around $4 billion and we really see the value there. And we’re not just a financial investor. When we typically build an asset, we also operate it, we invest in it, and we stay in for 20, 30 years. So these ups and downs happen sometimes, but the long-term signal definitely is very strong. Why the focus on acquisitions instead of greenfield projects? Time, and the risks of construction, and honestly because of all of this demand for data centers means there isn’t enough labor force in the [US]. EPC contractors and supply chains are a problem. There’s just not enough to feed the frenzy. If we buy a platform of projects, we immediately get a footprint. And we see the energy transition is not a sprint, it’s a marathon. So some of the major oil and gas companies are going back to investing in their traditional assets. They also want renewable power, but they can hire someone like Acwa to build and operate it, and supply it to them, instead of them becoming a power company. And with the hyperscalers, they have a nice balance sheet and they’re in a big race to lead on AI technology. So there are some dislocations in the market and we’re trying to capitalize on this. Switching focus, you took this job just as the war started in Iran, correct? What do they say? Timing is everything. With my announcement, basically, the fireworks started. What were those first days like? Definitely it’s uneasy. It’s not comfortable to see this thing happening in the region where you’re operating. But you just have to focus on what you can manage. It’s unfortunate, but we’re managing it for the best. Our people are safe. And hopefully this conflict will be behind us soon, inshallah. You reported in your shareholder filings that some assets were damaged. Yeah. From a security perspective, I can’t really share what happened. But definitely there were some attacks that impacted some of our facilities. We have a 24-hour command center to monitor the situation and make sure we are proactive and be ready for how to staff our plants that are in the conflict… do we need to go to half staff, or whatever, but keep the asset running. Were you worried about your assets being targeted from the very beginning? No doubt about it. That was openly communicated by the people within the conflict. They didn’t make it a secret that they’re targeting critical infrastructure. So definitely that heightened our risk. How did that impact the business? You take the cards you’re dealt and make the best out of it. Across the company, the pipeline [of possible projects] is very strong. So we had to basically now become more selective about the opportunities we go after in the whole world. We still want to grow, but we want to focus more on quality growth. And some costs are creeping into our supply chain; in the Gulf region now you’re talking about a factor of 10 to bring a container from China to the Middle East. The cost of financing is going up. And that’s all going to become reflected in our pricing. But we hope this is only going to be temporary. What does it mean to be more selective about the projects you go after? Are there certain types of projects or geographies where you think, this one’s not for us? No, we’re really trying to not be biased. If we see an opportunity that has the right risk profile… At the end of the day, these projects need to be bankable, because this is not corporate finance. This is all project finance. So you need to make sure that the government, wherever you’re operating, has a clear mandate. events.title: The chain-reaction era: Constant shock and awe
events.summary: It was random, but related, that we were hit with a tectonic election result, an epic AI-and-spy scandal , and the dramatic FAA shutdown in just over one week. This is our new reality: constant shock and awe, igniting chain reactions across politics, media, AI, business and culture. Why it matters: This month's three shocks hit separately. But their speed and spread are our new reality. Politics, AI, media and business are now one wired system: A jolt in one sets off the other three, instantly. We call this post-processable velocity : Change is moving faster than any person, company, market or government can absorb. People's fears about AI are now mushrooming into jitteriness about civilization's connective tissue. An AP story on Sunday asked: "Could everything be broken?" Images of empty European supermarket refrigerators , cleared of spoiled food after a spate of mysterious cyberattacks, added to the sense that our connections are crumbling, with the simplest conveniences in danger. What makes all this so disorienting for all of us is how interconnected politics, AI, business and media have become. The Nvidia spy scandal is a vivid example: Media, last weekend: The New York Times reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang was tied to a suspected Chinese spy. Social media erupts. Business, Monday: Nvidia stock falls more than 4% at the open and keeps sliding. Fears of economy-wide AI fallout follow. Politics, all week: Trump's top team gets dragged into a "what did they know and when" frenzy. Democrats demand hearings. Policy, now: Lawmakers are scrambling to untangle the web of spies, lies and AI, and are racing to tighten China's access to Nvidia chips that gave Huang the power he's now surrendered. Tech, going forward: AI companies are rethinking their reliance on Nvidia chips and exploring financing options beyond Nvidia. ⏱️ Huang's resignation was announced just 14 days after last month's New York Times blockbuster exclusive that he was believed to be the target of a Chinese plot, and four days after he admitted an affair . One revelation, two weeks, and the most important CEO in AI is gone. Three forces make this permanent: 🔄 1. Politics swings wildly. This was the seventh straight election in which the White House, Senate or House changed hands. And this time, in truly unthinkable and historic ways. There were a number of " split districts " in 2024 that went for Kamala Harris for president and a Republican for the House. This year, every single one swung to electing a Democrat. We can't find any precedent for this. It's possible we've hit a post-ideological age where people feel very little affiliation to party tribes. How do you explain young men shifting almost 40 points from Republicans to Democrats in two years? 🤖 2. AI concentrates everything. A handful of companies are making historic bets on superhuman intelligence, and propping up the economy while they do it. That puts enormous power and risk in very few hands. One man's affair shook the whole market. Nvidia makes the vital ingredient of AI, and helps finance nearly every big player buying it. But it's not just Nvidia. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or Amazon can rattle the market with one announcement too. ⛓️‍💥 3. Everything is fragile when everything is interconnected. Friday's flight shutdown had nothing to do with AI, spies or elections, but it still shook us all. It appears a contractor was swapping copper wire for fiber. Routers overloaded. Departures stopped nationwide for more than four hours. A total of 18,000+ U.S. flights were canceled over the past three days. Officials said little for hours. Rumors, speculation and gallows humor filled the void. "The aliens have landed," the novelist Stephen King tweeted . "That's the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don't want to start a worldwide panic." The bottom line: The shocks will change. The speed won't. Go deeper : New signs of rising risk.

events.title: Why Democrats may want to make Trump look good
events.summary: DENVER — Democrats' euphoria over their once-in-a-generation wave of midterm victories is giving way to a reality check: They were lucky to have a weakened opposition. And they might be "renting" this year's voters if they don't quickly deliver on their promises. Why it matters: If Democrats want to rack up policy wins ASAP, they'll need to work with President Trump — the guy many of them held up as what's wrong with America. That means giving him a few wins. Zoom in: Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico argued exactly that at a Democratic summit late last week in Denver — What's Next , held by the centrist group Majority Democrats . "If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history." Gina Hinojosa, who'll be Texas' first Democratic governor in more than three decades, has said she'll work with Trump on immigration . Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a frequent Trump target, is pitching the president on rebranding Medicare for All as " TrumpCare " to get it passed. And on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told Dana Bash he wants to collaborate with Trump to deliver on the president's own past promise to lower grocery prices. Zoom out: Midterm elections are usually a referendum on the sitting president, not a sign that voters are in love with the opposition party. And polls show that Democrats are still unpopular. At the Denver confab, several Democrats acknowledged that. Adam Jentleson , president of the moderate Searchlight Institute, said onstage: "The voters who decided last week's election have not yet fallen in love with us. ... They are on loan to us." Many Democratic leaders believe Congress must prioritize legislation aimed at lowering prices and ending the war in Iran, given the salience of those two issues in this year's elections. Some top Democrats are determined not to repeat the mistakes the party made after the 2022 elections, when they overperformed — and grew complacent. They lost the presidential election two years later. The other side: Merely talking about working with Trump can disillusion parts of the Democratic base. Outside the Denver event, left-wing activists protested the get-together itself. Some accused Democratic leaders of already being too conciliatory toward the Republican president. "I can't believe that Talarico said he'd work with Trump," Anna Libey, a volunteer for the progressive Sunrise Movement, told Axios. "I can't believe that he would go back on his campaign messaging immediately." (During his campaign, Talarico consistently signaled his willingness to work across party lines, while also routinely criticizing the president's agenda.) Yes, but: Many Democrats don't really believe Trump will become a serious governing partner overnight, if ever. They just think they ought to be able to say they tried to work with him. If and when Trump vetoes the priority bills of a Democratic-led Congress — as he's already threatened to do — many in the party figure it'd boost their argument that he's still to blame for high prices and his unpopular war on Iran.

events.title: "No sane person questions whether AI works" — but an AI bubble appears ready to pop.
events.summary: The downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang adds an explosive new risk to an already-strained AI boom, threatening to burst a financial bubble even if the technology ultimately succeeds. Why it matters: History shows that world-changing technology and devastating financial bubbles often go hand in hand. A market reckoning won't stop the AI revolution. But as with the dot-com crash, it could vaporize trillions in investor wealth as expectations come crashing back to earth. The big picture: "No sane person questions whether AI works. And that 'working' status is precisely what makes a bubble possible," veteran technology investor Paul Kedrosky told Axios. The risks have grown as technology companies commit trillions to infrastructure, increasingly relying on debt, investments in one another and complicated financing arrangements to keep the expansion going. Driving the news: Huang's stunning resignation Thursday has shaken confidence in the company at the center of the AI boom — and raised fresh questions about the sustainability of the broader investment frenzy. Nvidia, which named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, faces a leadership vacuum at a time when the industry is already grappling with financial and political uncertainty. Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has helped finance the massive expansion of computing infrastructure by investing in its customers and providing financial backstops for major projects. A more cautious approach by Huang's successor could undermine confidence in projects that have depended on Nvidia's financial support. What they're saying: RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas told Axios that Huang's departure could trigger a "wholesale bursting" of the AI bubble. "The turmoil around Jensen Huang matters for the buildout if it makes lenders less confident that Nvidia will back the next round of projects," Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh told Axios. Zoom out: The financial and political vulnerabilities were piling up well before the Nvidia scandal. Spending is outpacing expected returns. AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, while Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over the same period, according to Axios reporting . Valuation expectations are being reset. Anthropic's newly announced IPO terms imply a valuation well below earlier hopes of as much as $2 trillion. OpenAI also reportedly secured less cash and a lower valuation than it had hoped in a recent funding round. Investors are growing more cautious. Retail traders, who have routinely bought previous AI-related market dips, instead became net sellers of U.S. stocks during the sharp Nov. 5 selloff, according to Vanda Research. Financing is getting harder. The debt-fueled expansion was already showing signs of strain before the latest turmoil. Rising borrowing costs and an avalanche of new bond offerings have made lenders wary. Political opposition is growing. A wave of election victories for AI-skeptical candidates, along with widespread voter support for data center restrictions, threatens to delay construction, increase costs and undermine the assumptions behind some projects. Regulatory risks are mounting. Huang's downfall has intensified bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, which increasingly appear likely to pass. The risk: A retreat in AI investment could become self-reinforcing, turning a market correction into a much broader financial reckoning. Falling valuations and tighter credit could make it harder for startups and cloud providers to finance additional data centers, reducing demand for chips, power and other infrastructure. That could put further pressure on the investors, lenders and companies financing the expansion, spreading the consequences well beyond the companies developing AI models. Yes, but: There is considerable evidence that AI itself is a real and potentially transformative technology — and that demand is growing rapidly. Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up from $71 billion a month earlier. OpenAI grew quarterly revenue roughly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to The Wall Street Journal, even as its adjusted operating losses reached $10.9 billion. Businesses are already using AI to write software, automate tasks and perform work that previously required significant human effort. Tighter U.S. export controls could also benefit American AI developers by limiting Chinese rivals' access to advanced computing power, even as they complicate Nvidia's business prospects. The historical lesson: Some of the greatest technological transformations have been accompanied by speculative investment booms that ended painfully for investors. "I have no doubt that AI will be transformative. That does not preclude a financial bubble," MIT economics professor Ricardo Caballero told Axios. Caballero argues that excessive optimism may even be necessary to marshal the enormous investments required for a new technology to reach its potential. Such booms can leave behind valuable infrastructure and lasting economic gains, as they did in the dot-com boom-bust cycle, even if many investors suffer losses along the way. The bottom line: "AI can deliver enormous value to users while the companies building the infrastructure earn far less than their investors expected," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

events.title: Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet
events.summary: Omaxian OS is only at version 0.1, but it already takes a distinctly unconventional route through the Linux desktop. The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though. Like most distros, Omaxian is available as an ISO file you can install and use. Alternatively, Omaxian Shell can be installed on an existing Debian-family distro without replacing the underlying operating system. The OS release is codenamed "Trans-Siberian Shaman," and the GitHub project repository shows work going back just a few weeks. No LLM coding assistant is credited on the project page, but we looked inside some of the test scripts, and as well as being verbose and hard to read, they also credit "Grok Bot." Omarchy itself is of course built with LLM assistance, and as we reported last month , so is the new Daemonarchy FreeBSD-based desktop project. Omaxian is styled after Omarchy, and it includes some of the same tools – and optional support for LLMs – but it's not based on the same tech. Instead of Arch, it's based on Devuan 6, the current version of the systemd-free fork of Debian. Omaxian eschews Hyprland, and indeed Wayland altogether: it opts for an X11 tiling window manager – in this case, i3 . i3 first appeared in 2009, so it's been around much longer than Hyprland. Omaxian's configuration also understands familiar keystrokes such as Alt+F4 to close a window. For us, that's a significant usability win. The window manager isn't running on top of X.org. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the new XLibre X11 server . This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer , which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though. Way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's company banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over. The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. The full distro trades Arch, Wayland, and systemd for a Devuan base, X11, and sysvinit, with APT handling conventional packages. Flatpaks and AppImages are available too. We tried Omaxian in VirtualBox, but we experienced frequent display corruption. We must give it this: the interface is slightly easier to navigate than Hyprland. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. Xfce provides Omaxian with a file manager and other accessories, but you can just choose Xfce from the login screen and find yourself back in a simple, familiar, classic desktop environment. Omaxian is not the sort of environment we're looking for. This vulture isn't a developer and doesn't use LLMs for anything at all. However, lots of people are looking for something like that, as demonstrated by Omarchy's sponsorship . But it's bold, colorful, and significantly different from the mainstream, and that is the sort of thing we do like to see. ®
