events.title: Most UAE salaries flat but top-tier roles to see rises
events.summary: A majority of UAE organisations are expected to keep salaries flat or offer modest increases next year amid economic uncertainty driven by the Iran war, according to a new report. A total of 77 per cent of organisations plan to hold salary ranges steady (42 per cent), or award rises of 1 per cent to 5 per cent (35 per cent), a Cooper Fitch survey found. Midsized firms – those with 251 to 1,000 employees – are expected to keep salaries flat, while large organisations will offer pay rises in 2027, it said. The survey covered more than 1,091 organisations in the Gulf region, representing over 450,000 employees, with questions focusing on recruitment activity, workforce headcounts, and salary trends for 2026 and projections for 2027. Information technology has the highest share of respondents planning salary increases, at 63 per cent, followed by telecoms with 60 per cent, and heavy industry and manufacturing at 59 per cent. Other sectors, including banking, financial services and insurance; and retail, e-commerce and luxury goods, are also expected to raise salaries next year. Salaries in government and the public sector are the most likely to remain unchanged, according to 70 per cent of those organisations. Economic uncertainty has continued across the Gulf region since the start of the Iran war in February. The Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil supplies, remains technically shut, disrupting trade and other activities. The International Monetary Fund projects the UAE 's economy will contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the strait. The projections by the Washington-based lender in October reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Companies are also planning to expand their workforce next year, with 42 per cent of respondents expecting to increase their headcount as the economy rebounds from the effects of the war. A staffing increase of 1 per cent to 5 per cent is the most common rate, selected by 24 per cent of respondents, while 32 per cent expect no change. Only 7 per cent anticipate reductions of 10 per cent or more next year, compared with 16 per cent in 2026. Real estate, construction and architecture are most positive about increasing staff numbers followed by retail, e-commerce and luxury goods, and banking, financial services and insurance. Talent outlook Most UAE respondents believe the local market has sufficient talent to meet their organisation’s hiring needs for 2027, while 25 per cent report insufficient talent and 11 per cent are unsure. Views vary by department, with 55 per cent of technology respondents reporting insufficient talent, compared with 16 per cent in human resources. Among the sectors shown, aviation, defence and aerospace has the highest share citing insufficient talent at 60 per cent, followed by information technology and hospitality (40 per cent each), and real estate and construction at 33 per cent. Government and public sector respondents are the most likely to report sufficient talent, at 91 per cent. The survey also that found sales and business development roles were the most difficult to fill, followed by technical and engineering roles and those requiring AI, data and technology skills. or this year’s report, Fitch Insights surveyed business leaders responsible for key decisions across more than 1,091 organisations in the Gulf region, representing over 450,000 employees. The survey comprised of twenty questions focusing on recruitment activity, workforce headcounts, and salary trends for 2026 and projections for 2027. Hiring stabilises LinkedIn, in a separate report on Monday, said hiring in the UAE was stabilising after war-related disruption earlier this year. Hiring fell to 40 per cent below 2025 levels in April, but by August the decline had narrowed to 18 per cent, and 15 out of 17 major industries posted monthly growth, it said. “The sharpest phase of the downturn appears to have passed, although hiring activity remains below 2025,” it added. AI is rapidly changing what employers need, LinkedIn found, with demand for artificial intelligence engineering jobs rising 232.4 per cent year-on-year in August. “The UAE is committed to developing national capabilities while attracting the world’s best talent, creating an agile workforce that can translate technological change into higher productivity, new industries and sustainable opportunities in the UAE,” Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade of the UAE, said.

events.title: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost
events.summary: Currencies such as the Japanese yen or the euro have tried and failed to loosen the U.S. dollar’s grip on world trade , unable to outweigh the U.S.’s deep and open financial markets. But now, Japanese bankers think that the rise of digital currencies could give the yen a new path to worldwide use. “The currency competition is now a software competition,” Tomoya Hasebe, global head of digital and innovation at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), said at a roundtable organized by FinCity Tokyo in Singapore on Nov. 16. “Currency dominance is increasingly determined not only by central bank policy or regulatory policy, but by which currency is easiest to use as code.” The yen is the world’s third most-used currency, after the U.S. dollar and the euro. Japan was the first country among G7 economies to roll out a comprehensive framework to regulate stablecoins. Yet yen-pegged stablecoins have barely enjoyed much usage, with U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins accounting for more than 97% of the market . The country’s three megabanks— Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, and the Mizuho Financial Group—are planning to change that with a jointly-issued yen-backed stablecoin set to begin transactions next March . The new stablecoin is meant to streamline cross-border payments and boost the appeal of the yen for global business. Several Asian economies are rolling out their own stablecoins to cater to firms seeking alternatives to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong, for example, issued its first two Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin issuer licenses in April , to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture by Standard Chartered Bank, HKT, and Web3 firm Animoca Brands.  “The majority of global trade is still in USD, but there is certainly a group of firms around the world that want to not use U.S. dollars for trade,” said Tim Way, senior director of global banking at digital asset infrastructure firm Fireblocks. “It’s an opportunity for Asia to stand up and have more trade in Asia running in Asian currencies.” Startups are entering a financial ecosystem that’s long been dominated by incumbents. JPYC, a Japanese startup, launched the country’s first yen-pegged stablecoin in October 2025. “More private enterprises and start-ups are starting to enter the stablecoin area,” Makoto Shibata, the head of Finolab, a Japanese fintech accelerator, said. Yet, it remains to be seen if yen-backed stablecoins—whether by on-chain start-ups or trad-fi institutions—will be able to gain traction. Unlike U.S. dollar stablecoins that generate returns from high-yielding treasury bills, yen-pegged stablecoins operate on razor-thin margins. Since JPYC was founded in 2019, it has faced steep growth bottlenecks , as users frequently redeem the token for traditional fiat, rather than hold it in their digital wallets.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.summary: Prominent conservative thinkers and MAGA figures are seizing on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy to pull President Trump away from his alliance with the tech right. Why it matters: The Nvidia scandal highlights some of the political weaknesses for Trump in allowing himself to be defined by his connections to an increasingly unpopular group of companies. Right-wing players are hoping the bombshell revelations about Huang's affairs will chip away at the president's embrace of the tech industry and offer an opening for anti-tech voices in his administration. What they're saying : They view the midterm elections as proof that people across the political spectrum hate AI, data centers and view Silicon Valley as too powerful. President Trump's perception of China "has always been entirely commercial and transactional. His view was, 'we're getting screwed. I'm going to get a better deal,'" Oren Cass, founder of conservative think tank American Compass, said. Cass, who has warned about Nvidia risks for more than a year, said the allegations of espionage are the strongest evidence yet that China is not a commercial partner but an adversary that is going to "subvert the American political process in ways that end up humiliating the President." MAGA figure Steve Bannon, meanwhile, said in a text he has called Jensen Huang "a CCP 'Agent of Influence' a thousand times." and that it's an OPEN SECRET." He backtracked on a suggestion that Jensen could go on a trip to China later this month. Other than that, he has kept it friendly. The president earlier this week called him "honorable" and on Thursday, following Jensen's resignation, the president said he "has done a fantastic job" and called him a "Legend." On Thursday, he said in an interview with Stephen Smith that Jensen is "a tremendous talent" who's done "incredible" and "brilliant" work at Nvidia. What we're watching: Supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying the White House to support his reinstatement as CEO, according to the Financial Times. events.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
events.summary: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “ Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .”

events.title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
events.summary: Illustration by Matt Rota for ProPublica. Animation by Henrike Lendowski for ProPublica. When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top.  Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children.  Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds.  No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt. New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show. According to all four of the major Wall Street credit-rating agencies, New York’s and Los Angeles’ fiscal health make them much better choices for investors. Chicago’s history of questionable borrowing and budgeting — it chose to either ignore or short its pension payments for years — has undermined its credibility.  Its credit rating now sits just two or three levels above junk status, making the cost of borrowing even more onerous. And the city’s chief financial officer, tasked with managing city debt and relationships with credit agencies, resigned last week in stunning fashion , saying she no longer could continue in the role because it would compromise her “integrity and professional obligations.” She had come from Fitch Ratings, a credit agency, and had been on the job for only three months. Chicago’s Pension Systems Are Less than 50% Funded The city is an outlier among other large cities, where most pensions are at least 75% funded. Note: Most cities have multiple pension funds. This chart displays the range between the pension fund with the least funding and the most funding within each city. Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number. Source: 2025 city budgets and pension reports (data as of September 2026) Lucas Waldron/ProPublica Options for a financial rescue are limited or unpalatable. Pension obligations, locked in by law and political realities, remain untouchable. There is little public or political appetite to raise property taxes or cut city jobs, particularly among the ranks of police, the city’s largest workforce. A windfall from the city’s still-under-construction casino grows more unlikely than ever.  The office of Mayor Brandon Johnson, who is finishing up his first term in office, blames “reckless financing methods” from past administrations for the city’s financial bind.  “Savings and efficiencies alone cannot solve the city’s persistent structural gap,” the city’s Office of Budget and Management wrote to WTTW and ProPublica in response to questions for this story. In searching for revenue streams, Johnson has sought to impose new taxes on the city’s biggest corporations — an effort that has met stiff resistance. Tackling the pension crisis, the city since 2023 has paid an additional $1 billion into its four pension funds above what is required by state law, records show, an infusion that the city touts as a stabilizing force.  But, like his predecessors, Johnson continues to rely on borrowing. Since taking office in 2023, Johnson has added $1.9 billion to the city’s debt obligations, according to city data. That borrowing has “advanced desperately needed investment in economic development and affordable housing in historically underserved communities on the South and West sides,” according to Johnson’s spokesperson. It also has been used to keep the city functioning. In 2026, for example, Chicago borrowed $166 million to pay firefighters what they were owed for working without a contract — and annual raises — for four years. Officials acknowledged they failed to set enough cash aside annually to cover those widely anticipated costs. The city borrowed an additional $267 million to cover the soaring cost of lawsuits alleging Chicago police officers committed a wide range of misconduct.  In some cases, the Johnson administration has negotiated agreements with its lenders that allow the city to pay only interest for several years, backloading its debt burden. Source: 2026 Chicago city budget Lucas Waldron/ProPublica With so much of the city budget dedicated to debt and pensions — and more cordoned off by federal and state laws that mandate spending for specific purposes, such as transportation —  Chicago officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of its annual budget, records show.  The result for residents: Restaurant inspections are lagging. Complaints about crumbling sidewalks and injuries from those hazards pile up, without timely repairs. The city’s Public Health Department doesn’t have enough caseworkers to handle the intensive intervention needed for children suffering from lead poisoning.   The budget pressures are unrelenting. In August, Johnson announced another borrowing plan to fix a budget shortfall that emerged midyear. He blamed the City Council for overestimating the impact of new revenue streams while his council foes accused him of continuing a pattern of questionable borrowing habits.  Amid the finger-pointing, Johnson acknowledged the bind facing his administration and the city as a whole. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch,” he said. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch.” Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson Watching the annual struggles of city officials to climb out of its money pit leaves many residents feeling more than a little uneasy about what comes next. “It is the feeling that people get when they max out their credit card and they’re barely paying the minimum,” said Alderperson Andre Vasquez, who represents the 40th Ward and speaks often of growing up in a family that struggled to pay the rent every month. “You’re behind on your utilities. events.title: More Americans see DC as safe, poll finds
events.summary: More Americans now say Washington, DC, is safe than have said so in 36 years, a statistic that the White House will likely view as a testament to President Donald Trump’s federal crime crackdown in the nation’s capital. Sixty-four percent of US adults currently view DC as a safe place, according to Gallup, a 12-point increase since 2023. That’s been driven by Republicans: In 2023, 77% of Democrats and only 29% of Republicans said DC was safe; today 70% of Democrats and 63% of Republicans say so. The poll was taken before a recent shooting in DC’s Logan Circle made national headlines. Crime has generally been on the decline in DC, though at least one study found that Trump’s National Guard deployment had minimal effect on violent crime. Another city seeing its highest perceived safety rating since 1990: New York City. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Democrats plan probes into Africa minerals deals
events.summary: Democrats plan to use their incoming majorities to investigate possible corruption in the Trump administration’s critical minerals deals in Africa, after months of what they said was administration stonewalling of their inquiries about the negotiations. Democrats have a mandate to “open formal investigations and commission public reports to map which individuals and companies are receiving lucrative critical-minerals deals,” Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., told Semafor. Jackson, along with Reps. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., and Jared Huffman, D-Calif., led an August letter to four agencies pressing them on the pacts, which Jackson said were struck in near-total secrecy. The administration’s response “dodged almost all of the questions we asked,” he said. Sánchez called the response “little more than something AI would write,” accusing the Republican majority of refusing “to conduct any oversight” of Trump’s trade deals. “That changes in January,” she said. Democrats are also targeting a reported State Department threat to withhold HIV aid to push Zambia into a minerals deal back in March. Using lifesaving aid “to extract unrelated economic concessions is what Russia, Iran, or [China] have traditionally done,” said Rep. Jimmy Panetta, D-Calif., who has separately pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio for details on the new global health agreements the US has signed with 36 countries . A State Department spokesperson said “our health assistance is not conditional on any commercial agreements,” adding that the health pacts contain nothing related to critical minerals. “As the president has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.” — Adrian Elimian

events.title: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
events.summary: Published 16 November 2026, 00:50 GMT This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you. That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year. Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information. Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out. Is it really HMRC? Here's how to tell If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January. Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC. Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email , external , text message , external or phone call , external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine. "Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer. New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October. There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information. To avoid being caught out, HMRC says: it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest Is it a real deal? Here's how to check In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered. Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy. "When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check. "No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy." The bank also advises doing these four things: Pause and check , rather than being blinded by a countdown timer Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed Doing these things now will help you save money at Christmas Published 7 days ago Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams Published 19 October Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC 0:18 Robert Pattinson asked about playing Bond in 2010. 00:00:18, play video Robert Pattinson asked about playing Bond in 2010 1:14 Would it really cost £750m a week for the UK to rejoin the EU? events.title: Pro-tech initiative adds Biden, Fetterman advisers
events.summary: The tech association Chamber of Progress is expanding an initiative launched last year to improve the relationship between the tech industry and Democrats, adding a former adviser to former President Joe Biden and former aide to Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., as senior advisers. Steve Benjamin, Biden’s former director of the White House Office of Public Engagement, is joining the Blue Horizon Project, along with former Fetterman chief of staff Krysta Juris, according to an announcement shared first with Semafor. The group is trying to steer the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress away from heavily regulating and investigating the tech industry; a poll it commissioned from Morning Consult found 84% of voters want Democrats to focus on fighting inflation rather than regulating AI and technology. “Tech and Democrats had a long honeymoon in the Obama era. There was a divorce in the Biden era, and now Democrats have to craft a relationship that’s somewhere in between,” Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, told Semafor. The group is among a handful trying to influence Democrats as they take power and weigh policy positions ahead of 2028. Who Decides, an outfit founded by unsuccessful New York congressional candidate Alex Bores that is calling for more stringent AI regulation, is already organizing across battleground states.

events.title: Democrats debate who gets oversight of AI
events.summary: Democrats are debating who will have a piece of investigating and overseeing AI and chip export controls next Congress in the wake of the controversy enveloping Nvidia. Incoming House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., is floating creating a subpanel on chips and AI, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said Meeks and incoming Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., are taking the lead on the Nvidia fallout. But other committees have jurisdiction and also want to lead on AI — including the House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, or Science, Space and Technology Committees. “It seems like every chairman … or chairwoman is wanting a piece of the pie with AI now,” grumbled one congressional aide, who questioned how that would work logistically, “considering it’s going to be spread out over — how many different committees?” One solution to settle the jurisdictional issues would be to set up a select panel overseeing AI, though a key committee chair has already registered his opposition to that idea. It’s also possible that multiple committees will pursue their own investigative efforts within their jurisdictions anyway, regardless of the turf wars that creates. — Nicholas Wu and Ashley Gold

events.title: Democrats’ leadership fight collides with Iran funding debate
events.summary: Senate Democrats’ leadership fight between Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is taking place against the backdrop of a major policy decision: how hard to push to include a spending prohibition on the Iran war in a broader funding bill. Schumer lists the “power of the purse” as an option for curbing the conflict, while Van Hollen is a leading proponent of a funding restriction. This could all lead to a shutdown on Dec. 11, the current funding deadline. It’s important to remember that the anti-Schumer sentiment among progressive activists increased when he supported advancing a spending bill early on in Donald Trump’s second term, after House Democrats came out in blanket opposition. Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., said that he wants to figure out what the “strategy is to get us out of the war, and it is understanding the differences between what takes place now and what takes place when we are back in charge.”

events.title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
events.summary: Matt Rota for ProPublica Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.  The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.  The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund.  Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole. Pension Holiday Snowballs Into Peril In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in pension debt. First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.  Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was actually needed to pay retirees. As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters, laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to comment for this story. Former Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley in 2006 Julio Cortez/AP Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation of the current pension crisis facing the city.   In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its skipped payments — no excuses allowed. Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement caused a spike in the city’s annual payments. Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began work on or after January 1, 2011. But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically. Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security. In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the minimum required by law.  Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the 90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the objections of city officials. Long-Term Lease, Long-Lasting Regrets Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s financial woes.  They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase. A Chicago resident feeds a new parking meter in 2009. The city privatized its parking meters in a $1.1 billion, 75-year deal as a way to get a cash infusion. Charles Rex Arbogast/AP But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially. The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park, infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for reelection. By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease. The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.” The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion purchase.  Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking meters in 2008. But even as the gap between the city’s revenues and its expenses continues to widen, property tax hikes remain the third rail of Chicago politics. Chicagoans’ property taxes last jumped in 2021, when former Mayor Lori Lightfoot raised them by $93.9 million and passed a budget that automatically hiked property taxes to keep pace with inflation. Johnson campaigned against those automatic property tax increases, forcing Lightfoot to drop a proposal to hike taxes by $42.7 million in 2023, just months before she lost her bid for reelection. The automatic property tax hike was eliminated, even though it could have prevented the city’s credit rating from being downgraded repeatedly and significantly reduced the annual budget gaps. In a postscript to the parking meter debacle, Chicago Parking Meters LLC sold the meters contract earlier this year to an investment firm, triggering a one-time payment to the city of $75 million. The City Council and Johnson then battled over how best to use that money for pension costs, creating a temporary hole in the 2027 city budget. The Financial Toll of Police Misconduct The 2014 police murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald changed nearly every aspect of City Hall politics around policing. Despite decades of scandals, misconduct and brutality, the Police Department had managed to fend off reform. But that ended with McDonald’s death, even as city leaders continued to fear a backlash from residents concerned about crime rates and a politically powerful police union. events.title: We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone
events.summary: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. It is quite natural, when being bent over a barrel ceases to be an amusing pastime, to seek a less barrel-shaped position. In this case, the pressure to find alternatives has many elements. As well as the cost, support for Macs and Chromebooks becomes problematic. Both platforms are heavily represented in education at various levels, with the Macbook Neo thundering onto the battlefield with colors flying. Add to that the pressure towards digital sovereignty in Microsoft's own colonial outposts, the accelerants for an Old World version of the Boston Tea Party are only building. We even have a Boston of our very own . It's very nice. Microsoft isn't threatening anyone with guns and rapine, not yet anyway, and the whipping away of free student access to email and Teams only feels like extortion because of the misery it is causing across the sector. It is perfectly legal for Microsoft to cause as much suffering coated in balderdash as it likes. It is also perfectly legal to return the favor by actively seeking a sector-wide migration strategy. There are pioneers to learn from, especially huge multi-state, multi-supply chain organizations like Airbus and the various European governmental entities that are some way down that path already. This growing pool of expertise may be the most important factor in being able to react to Microsoft's efforts to turn education into a science fair experiment in high velocity frog boiling — one where the frog most definitely feels the heat — that and the growing distaste for the antics of American big tech. It's not just the forcing of unwanted technology that makes the barrel increasingly unbearable, nor using that as an excuse to charge more, it's what the companies are actually trying to do in Europe. Google Chromebooks are nice. Google wolves invading your villages because the company illegally erased their ecosystem are not nice. You thought those Wi-Fi snooping Maps cars were bad? The Microsoft educational platform "evolution" is foolhardy, counterproductive, and hugely tone deaf. It will not make it new lifetime customers, it will increase the speed at which its already hostile constituency grows resentment and appetite for radical action. Colonies revolt when the time is right, and empires are lost when arrogance and under-estimation of the situation combine with mismanagement and strategic blindness. The US midterms showed how that storm is blowing in. To choose this time to provoke an entire global sector is functional illiteracy writ large. Perhaps Microsoft should get an education. ®

events.title: Mubadala and Centerbridge to acquire UK's Canaccord Wealth
events.summary: Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Company and US-based Centerbridge Partners have agreed to acquire UK-based Canaccord Wealth in an all-cash transaction. The transaction , which involves Canaccord Genuity’s wealth management business in the UK and Crown Dependencies, gives the business an enterprise value of approximately £1.17 billion ($1.54 billion), Mubadala said in a statement on Monday. Canaccord Wealth provides investment management and financial planning services to private clients, with £43.4 billion in assets under management and administration as of June 30. “We see significant opportunity in a market where growing wealth and increasing financial complexity are driving demand for expert advice,” said Yasir Badri, executive director of financial services at Mubadala. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Once completed, Mubadala and Centerbridge will jointly own Canaccord Wealth, with the existing management team retaining a “meaningful” ownership interest. “The UK wealth management sector continues to benefit from powerful structural tailwinds, as demand for high quality, personalised financial advice grows alongside increasing complexity in clients’ financial needs,” said Ben Langworthy, senior managing director and head of Europe at Centerbridge. Canaccord Wealth's assets under management and revenue have nearly tripled over the past decade, the statement said. The investment by Mubadala and Centerbridge will support the business’s next phase of growth, it added. Mubadala, which invests on behalf of the Abu Dhabi government, has been steadily expanding its global investment portfolio with a focus on sectors including renewables, mobility, advanced technology, artificial intelligence and life science. Last year, it reported a 17 per cent annual rise in assets to $385 billion, with its portfolio spanning six continents across asset classes. Last month, Mubadala's chief financial officer said it planned to maintain its annual investment with a focus on Asia. “Last year, we invested about $39 billion, which is roughly 10 per cent of our portfolio, and our aim is to continue doing that through all cycles. Every year, we want to deploy that same amount,” Carlos Obeid told the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore. In September, Mubadala announced a significant minority investment in Chinese coffee chain Luckin Coffee alongside its controlling shareholder, Centurium Capital, in a deal worth about $1 billion.

events.title: ASEAN to remain supply chain priority for US firms even as Trump’s tariffs face pushback
events.summary: US goods imports from ASEAN increased from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion (S$583.8 billion) in 2025. US firms are keeping ASEAN, especially Singapore, as a key supply chain base. They are diversifying away from China to reduce tariff, geopolitical and disruption risks. US imports from ASEAN rose from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion in 2025, up about 144%, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. Experts say tariff fights may continue, but companies are still strengthening traceability, audits and origin records. Smaller firms may return to China if South-east Asia loses its tariff advantage. SINGAPORE – The fate of US President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs may remain in limb o for the next two years after his party lost the majority in both houses of Congress, but American manufacturers reliant on Asian imports are not waiting for a resolution. Instead, they are busy bolstering supply chains painstakingly built over recent years to avoid getting blindsided by disruptions from protectionist measures or geopolitical tensions. And as US manufacturers seek to move sourcing of industrial components and supplies to more reliable, trustworthy and quality-conscious exporters, they are increasingly ending up in South-east Asia, including Singapore. US goods imports from ASEAN increased from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion (S$583.8 billion) in 2025, representing an increase of about 144%, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. When the US-China trade war started in earnest around 2018, large corporations and multinational companies pivoted from a just-in-time strategy to supply-chain resilience. A couple of years later, Covid-19 pandemic disruptions intensified the trend. In more recent years, however, smaller and mid-sized US manufacturers have turned to the just-in-case strategy, as trade disruptions turned into chaos amid Trump’s new and harsher tariffs, geopolitical conflicts and unending uncertainty over costs and pricing power. “Our clients aren’t unwinding diversification,” said Joseph Jurken, founder and managing director of US supply chain management firm The ABC Group. “They’re making it origin-defensible” to withstand US Customs scrutiny on tariff avoidance. US consultant Baker McKenzie believes the Democratic Party will use its congressional majority to try to undo certain tariffs. However, enacting legislation impervious to a presidential veto will require Republican support. While congressional committees may hold oversight hearings on how tariffs drive up consumer prices, trade enforcement and tariffs targeting unfair trade and China will continue to enjoy bipartisan support, it noted. “A Democratic-led Congress will likely push for tighter technology export restrictions, particularly regarding advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence, alongside broader limits on US investment in China,” Baker McKenzie said in a post-midterm commentary. In an interview with The Straits Times, Jurken said his firm is gradually adding to its offering qualified suppliers across South-east Asia, including Singapore, for clients looking to diversify outside of China. He added that India is becoming an increasingly important ex-China market. The ABC Group is a Milwaukee-based supply chain management firm that runs sourcing, quality control and supplier management in Asia for mid-market US manufacturers. It manages more than US$350 million in supply chain spend across six Asian markets. In the past few years in Singapore alone, ABC has helped insulate the supply chains of several clients from China-specific risks and disruptions in areas such as precision watch movements, complex injection mouldings, food and beverage processing, and high-end LED lighting. Jurken said: “With competition between the US and China intensifying around AI and robotics , markets like Singapore provide advanced manufacturing capabilities along with a way to reduce exposure to geopolitical risk in a single country.” However, for more price-conscious clients looking for low-end manufacturing products, Vietnam, Thailand and India remain in focus, he added. In Malaysia, factories in Johor with links to Singapore are also getting a lot of attention. While Jurken launched ABC only in 2021, he has been in the business of helping American companies navigate Asia for more than three decades. He said that cracks in the decades-old sourcing and supply management models had always been there. Tariffs and other trade distortions from 2018 onwards made them impossible to ignore. “The tariffs helped us broaden our market reach. It was the impetus for American firms to listen to why they should have a China-plus-one initiative,” he added. In fact, even before the US-China trade war began, ABC had started looking for alternative suppliers across South-east Asia.

events.title: Indonesian rupiah falls to record low as Fed bets boost dollar
events.summary: The rupiah dropped as much as 0.4% to 18,271 per US dollar on Nov 16. The Indonesian rupiah hit a record low of 18,271 per US dollar as a stronger dollar and higher Fed rate bets hit the currency. Investor worries grew over President Prabowo Subianto’s policy uncertainty, key policymaker exits, and MSCI’s warning of a possible market downgrade. Bank Indonesia said it will stay in markets to support stability, and it is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged on Nov 18. The Indonesian rupiah fell to a fresh record low, pressured by a stronger dollar amid hawkish US Federal Reserve expectations, lingering worries over domestic political stability and a potential market downgrade. The rupiah dropped as much as 0.4% to 18,271 per US dollar on Nov 16 . The currency has weakened about 9% in 2026 to underperform regional peers. Investors have soured on the nation’s assets in 2026 due to concerns over President Prabowo Subianto’s policy uncertainty, the exits of several key policymakers and MSCI’s warning that it could downgrade Indonesia’s equity market to standalone status. Most recently, the resignation of Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka compounded those worries, while growing bets on Fed interest rate hikes boosted the dollar and further pressured the rupiah. Bank Indonesia (BI) has said that it will remain present in the markets to maintain the rupiah stability. It regularly intervened in the currency’s spot market as well as offshore and onshore non-deliverable forwards. The central bank has also been buying government bonds in the secondary market to stem volatility. The central bank is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged on Nov 18 as the rupiah’s decline reflects tighter global financial conditions and bets on faster Fed rate hikes, according to Jeffrey Zhang, an emerging market strategist at Credit Agricole CIB. “We expect BI would judge the recent rupiah move to be in line with fundamentals, and don’t expect it to deviate from the current monetary policy stance,” he said. events.title: DWP glitch threatens my partner’s leave to remain
events.summary: Government department admits it is making a mistake that affects his immigration status but says it can’t put it right The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is knowingly paying me too much local housing allowance because of a system glitch and it could have serious implications for my partner’s immigration status. I am entitled to shared accommodation allowance as I am under 35 and claim universal credit. However, the DWP is paying me the higher one-bedroom rate for couples. Although we co-habit, my partner is an international student subject to immigration control and is not entitled to public funds. The DWP knows this, but insists a “recognised system defect” means it’s unable to implement the correct calculation. It told me that, until a technical solution is introduced, the system will continue calculating at the higher rate, and staff have been told not to correct accounts manually. It claims I will not be required to refund overpayments, but I’m more concerned about the wider implications for him. Your concerns are understandable. For the past 18 months, you have been receiving the higher rate (now £790 a month) because your partner lives with you, instead of the £586 to which you are entitled. That’s an overpayment of more than £3,600 and counting. If someone subject to immigration control benefits from public funds to which they are not entitled, the Home Office could curtail their leave to remain. You have been trying from the outset to correct the calculation. Your efforts were undermined by a tribunal last year which ruled your partner’s living arrangements entitled you to the higher rate. You appealed and in April another tribunal agreed a mistake had been made. It ordered your allowance be recalculated. When the DWP failed to do this, you involved your MP. That’s when you learned from the DWP of this extraordinary defect that prevents claims such as yours being automatically recalculated. Even more extraordinary was the “operational guidance” preventing staff from making the changes themselves. I submitted a freedom of information request asking how many claimants are affected and how much has been erroneously paid, but was told the information would be too expensive to collate. Almost certainly not as expensive as the sums being expended on ineligible recipients who do not wish to receive them. I asked the Home Office whether the issue might compromise the status of people in your partner’s situation, but it referred me back to the DWP. Despite having insisted it cannot manually override the system, the DWP did just that when I questioned it. It says: “We are aware of this issue, which involves an extremely small number of people. We will correct PJ’s case so she receives the right amount, and are working to ensure customers do not experience a similar issue.” I was assured that no one will be asked to refund the overpayments. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qantas cancellations leave remote island residents stranded on mainland Qantas operates the only air services between Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and the Australian mainland. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) An ongoing series of Qantas cancellations have left residents on Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands outraged. Twenty-five students from Christmas Island are among those stranded by the cancellations. Qantas says delays have been unavoidable for safety reasons. A group of school students are among residents left stranded on the Australian mainland after several weeks of Qantas flight cancellations to the country's most remote inhabited territories. Residents of Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands are reliant on the national carrier for their sole freight and transport link with Western Australia. But the delays have outraged residents of both islands, with some accusing Qantas of neglecting the critical route. A group of 25 Christmas Island students were part of those affected by the most recent disruptions, and have been stranded in Perth for two days. They were participating in a school camp on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, but found themselves diverted 2,700 kilometres away to Perth during the return journey. "Our kids weren't packed to go to the mainland," Christmas Islander Avin McKnight said. His son, Callum, is now staying with a relative. "They had no phones because part of school camp regulations was they weren't able to take their phones," Mr McKnight said. A spokesperson from the Department of Education said Qantas was providing accommodation for students and accompanying staff, while some had opted to stay with family. The students are expected to board a recovery flight home tomorrow. Avin McKnight's son Callum (right) has been stuck in Perth. ( Supplied: Avin McKnight ) Two days of flights to and from Perth were grounded last week due to forecast low-lying cloud, Qantas said. Another landed in Cocos only, skipping its layover in Christmas Island to return to the mainland. In the month prior, about half of flights were delayed or rescheduled for various reasons. A Qantas spokesperson said recent weather had proven a challenge. "The monsoon season is the most challenging time for flying from the mainland to the Indian Ocean Territories," the spokesperson said. "We thank customers for their patience; however, we will always prioritise safety over schedule." It adds to existing tensions between islanders and Qantas, which slashed baggage allowances and increased prices earlier this year. Mr McKnight, a Christmas Island resident of 30 years, said the problem had grown worse since Qantas took over the flights contract from Virgin Australia last year. "Everyone's just really had a real kick in the guts this weekend and it's just not good enough for that airline," he said. Hundreds of islanders gathered on both islands to protest about luggage cuts and price increases in September. ( Supplied: Khaliesha Amin ) Other residents took to social media to voice complaints over lost bookings, accommodation and hire cars. Christmas islander Mark Stein said three consecutive cancellations had forced him to push a specialist medical appointment. "[Qantas] should really remove the spirit of Australia from the side of the plane, because the Australian spirit is to try and give something a crack." Christmas Island relies on twice weekly flights for access to the mainland. ( Supplied: Chris Bray Photography ) Last week, a Productivity Commission interim report counted Christmas and Cocos (Keeling) Islands as two communities most impacted by skyrocketing regional airfares . Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients. It urged the federal government to reform subsidy arrangements like those in place on the Indian Ocean Territories to ensure they provide better value for money. Indian Ocean Territories administrator Farzian Zainal said she was urgently seeking a meeting with Qantas. "Reliable air services are essential for our community and I understand the consequences extend well beyond travel inconvenience," she said. The officials say they did not receive information about a car wash firebombing that had earlier been raised with the Transport Minister's office. The opposition has accused the minister's office of not passing on "critical information" to the department, but the government says the allegations put to them were "very broad and non-specific". The public servants leading the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project have defended the checks they conducted on a project contractor that was, five weeks later, suspended due to a court case alleging bikie involvement. The Department for Infrastructure and Transport's checks were prompted by a call from the Transport Minister's chief of staff on September 11 shortly after he met with the lawyer preparing the court claim. The opposition has used a parliamentary committee to question whether "critical information" was left out in that call between the minister's office and the department. But the government says the issues raised by the lawyer were "very broad and non-specific" with "no documents provided", and since then "more has come out" to prompt the government to kick the company off the project. The company, Career Boss Australia, had its contract to supply workers on the South Road upgrade suspended on October 18, after it was revealed in the media to be the subject of a civil claim alleging bikie Jamie Brown and another man had attempted to coerce the transfer of company shares. No criminal charges have been laid in relation to the case, and Brown has told the ABC he "denies ever threatening any shareholders". The Supreme Court claim was lodged on October 12 by businessman Robert Cammarano, who is claiming full ownership of Career Boss Australia. Robert Cammarano outside an Adelaide court. ( ABC News ) Five weeks before the court case was publicised, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, met with Transport Minister Joe Szakacs's chief of staff Daniel Wills and Child Protection Minister Alice Rolls. At the September 11 meeting, according to accounts from both Mr Jelbert and the government, Mr Jelbert raised matters regarding the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project, the Career Boss contract, Jamie Brown, the impending court action and a car wash in Malvern. The car wash, which Mr Cammarano claims to part-own, was destroyed in March after three firebombings. The ABC is not suggesting the destruction of the car wash is linked to any of the parties listed in the civil case, only that it was raised by Mr Jelbert at the September 11 meeting. Straight after the meeting, Mr Wills called Transport Department executive Paula Norman. Ms Norman said Mr Wills asked her to check with the private sector consortium leading the project, the T2D Alliance, whether "Jamie Brown had been a shareholder and whether Career Boss had raised any contractual issues with the T2D Alliance". Paula Norman appeared before a parliamentary committee. ( ABC News ) Ms Norman said Mr Wills did not pass on any mention of firebombings. "The advice that I got was to check for a shareholding related to Jamie Brown who was a bikie … and had any of these allegations or contractual issues been raised directly to the Alliance," she told parliament's budget and finance committee on Monday. Ms Norman said she phoned the general manager of the T2D Alliance, Stephen Shaddock, to investigate these two things and heard back on September 14. "He advised me that Jamie Brown was not a shareholder and, more importantly, that there were no contractual issues raised by Career Boss directly with the Alliance," Ms Norman said. Opposition questions information chain During the hearing, Liberal Party MLC Heidi Girolamo suggested to Ms Norman that Mr Wills and Ms Rolls did not pass on "pretty critical information" about firebombings that "may have changed the way you approached things going forward". Ms Norman replied that she was responsible for checking whether contractual issues with Career Boss Australia had been raised with the Alliance. "Career Boss Australia, if they had those allegations or any issues relating to the contract, should have raised it directly with the Alliance," she said.

events.title: What Is Acoustic Micro Imaging? A Quick Guide To This Inspection Process
events.summary: We all know how important inspection is for advanced packaging. Not only are these processes critical for ensuring higher yield, but they’re also integral for maintaining device reliability. As the industry pushes for smaller features and tighter spacing, even the smallest defects can pose major challenges. For instance, delaminations and air gaps can be detrimental in a market that demands increasingly complex devices. Such defects will lead to electrical or mechanical failures down the road. One technology that’s mitigating these issues is acoustic micro imaging (AMI). AMI is a high-frequency ultrasound technology, and it’s being used by the industry as an inspection method. How AMI works At the core of AMI technology is a transducer, or a device that turns energy from one form to another. It starts with a pulse of electrical energy, then converts it to mechanical energy, or a high-frequency ultrasound wave. Because ultrasound doesn’t travel through air, this allows inspectors to obtain clear images of gaps and delaminations in the device that could otherwise be difficult to see. However, the transducers used for AMI are not all the same. Each transducer handles a specific frequency, and they’re chosen based on the sample that needs to be inspected. By moving the transducer across the sample, the inspector can generate multiple images that can then be analyzed by the AMI software. Through this analysis, the inspector can choose to accept or reject parts based on the number of defects the package is found to have. So, how do these defects typically present themselves? The biggest difference between ideal and defective samples is that some defective samples will have very clear air gaps. However, another common defect is thinning of the attach material on solder pads. When this material is too thin, any stress that would be put on the device could lead to delamination. An uneven solder or thermal interface material (TIM) layer may also indicate a larger problem with the build process. When to use AMI – inspection, destructive testing, and X-rays With the ability to gather so much information without damaging the device, why would anyone choose to perform a destructive test to identify a defect, rather than simply use AMI inspection to check for them? One reason is for R&D purposes. Oftentimes, companies want to ensure that a process is fully developed before integrating it into their production cycle, and a destructive test can confirm proof of concept for AMI. An example of this in action is a standard capacitor inspection. New capacitor companies will often require a destructive test to confirm the presence of voids or delaminations found by the AMI software. Once the destructive proof of concept has been completed, the company can then integrate the software into their inspection process. There are some key differences between AMI and its transmission technology counterpart, which is more comparable to X-ray. Whereas AMI is an ultrasound technology, transmission scanning uses both a sending and receiving transducer positioned above and below the sample. Both transmission technology and X-ray create composite images, unlike AMI, which inspects layer-by-layer. Ultrasound and X-ray are complementary technologies. There are some things AMI can do that X-ray can’t, and vice versa. For certain applications, both technologies may be recommended. For example, composite images are preferable for inspecting spherical objects like ball grid arrays. The challenges and future of AMI Although AMI technology has tangible benefits, keeping up with the industry’s rapid pace is a hurdle that AMI must continually overcome. As applications become more complex, AMI software needs to quickly adapt to changing components. For instance, instead of scanning a single flip chip, AMI software could now be required to inspect multi-die stacks. One way this mounting complexity is being addressed is through machine learning algorithms. For example, some wafers have via patterns that look similar or identical to delamination, and humans have typically been responsible for distinguishing them. However, through advancements in machine learning, AMI software can now identify via patterns and exclude those from the defect count. As machine learning becomes more robust, it will open new doors for inspecting increasingly complicated devices. In addition, customer requirements for higher resolution and better throughput are also driving new developments for AMI software. To meet these rising demands, Nordson Test & Inspection developed its automated SpinSAM tool that can inspect four 300mm wafers at a time. Traditionally, acoustic microscopy systems move the transducer in a raster pattern, which is a small grid made up of individual pixels. This approach allows inspectors to collect data at every XY point, but it also requires decelerating to turn the transducer at the end of each line, thereby reducing throughput. Some acoustic microscopes address the need for better throughput by skipping lines and interpolating data points, or by using multiple transducers and stitching images together – both of which have their own drawbacks. In contrast, SpinSAM spins the wafer to move the transducer and the wafer continuously, allowing inspectors to scan each pixel faster, allowing for better throughput without image stitching distortion. events.title: Are AI Agents The New Semiconductor IP?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI agents could make customized design workflows faster and less expensive to develop. Multi-agent systems introduce new challenges for orchestration, verification, and tool integration. Consumption-based pricing could reshape EDA business models, but trust and proprietary data remain obstacles. AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs. At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge. Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. And they can do all of this much faster than a human, even though an experienced engineering team is needed to verify those results and recommendations. “We have in-house specialized AI agents to do different things, to do spec analysis, RTL generation for design, for formal and functional verification, and then CDC linking, and place-and-route,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents . “We provide our optimized agents to a customer, and sometimes a customer builds their own AI agent. But there are some similarities with the IP business. Sometimes we’re specifically building an agent for one customer for a particular flow, which is similar to what happens in the IP business. What’s different is that we can do it in a very short amount of time. With IP, you need 10 months. Our cycle is much shorter because AI agents are very easy to customize. In some cases we can give solutions to the customer the same day.” Those solutions still need to be verified and debugged. But the ability to sort through many different options quickly is an attractive formula, especially with rapid evolution of AI. “I draw parallels to the early 2000s gigahertz wars, where all of a sudden everything was multicore,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus . “Now we’ve gone from,’ Everything is going to be a GPU,’ to ‘Oh, no, it’s CPUs and GPUs, and this is a one-to-one ratio.’ So effectively we’re going through the same architectural churn that we go through every 10 to 15 years.” The business of agents Business models still need to solidify around agents. but they also need to be flexible enough to evolve at the same pace as the technology. “If you look at how the EDA industry has evolved, we’re not selling perpetual licenses anymore,” said Rob Knoth, senior group director of Strategy & New Ventures at Cadence . “We moved to time-based licenses many years ago. Now we see similar things as agents roll around. They’re hitting up the tool usage even more because they want to find answers quickly, and they’re trying lots of experiments. So putting together more of a consumption-based model is really good because customers know how to use that.” This isn’t a simple transition, though. While the promise of agents is significant, their adoption in chip design will take time. In addition, security and permissions aren’t always well-defined. “There are some things where you’d really rather sell an agent than sell the software,” said Wally Rhines, CEO of Silvaco . “People are trying to figure out if anybody in EDA is actually pricing based upon tokens rather than traditional pricing models. It doesn’t seem like anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it. I’m very much open to selling an agent that will automate [manufacturing equipment] calibration, then jump back to my store of synthetic simulated data against the physical data. We don’t get to see the physical data, but we do know how many tokens our agents consumed. It’s a way that EDA can sell a product, get the benefit, and no one ever sees the underlying data that companies want to keep proprietary.” Divide and conquer, but with caveats One of the big changes with the shift from generative AI to agentic AI is the need for orchestration, and this has broad business implications. Orchestration is basically a blueprint that defines how tasks are assigned, how agents access tools and data, and how that work is coordinated. But it’s especially challenging if multiple agents execute at the same time and their actions overlap. “What’s different about traditional AI and agentic AI is the coordination of multiple agents that are working in parallel, but doing different types of work,” said Robbie Williamson, vice president of customer engineering for cloud AI at Arm . “It’s not like there’s a unique workload that we haven’t seen before. It’s more about how do you coordinate all of these at the CPU level, and have enough bandwidth, memory, etc., to do all of this at scale. Instead of an individual making a request and driving AI, we have computers that can do it much faster. The transition that we see when we talk to hyperscalers is now about what they need from the CPU. With training, that wasn’t as important because you’re just batching the job and waiting for it to come back.” That creates a new hierarchy in the design flow. “What has happened with this multi-agent workflow is that, in an organization, you’re trying to design a chip,” said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at Synopsys . “When they’re having a problem with the PPA, some engineers say they know exactly what changes to make to lower the power. They’ll do clock gating. But when you clock gate power, then it changes something else. It increases the area. So some area will come in — and this is exactly what happens in the real world with coordination when multiple people come together to design a system. The human manager is coordinating the activities of the human agents in the world of a multi-agent framework. We have agents for EDA tools and agents for the CAE (computer-aided engineering) tools. We have simulation with three core solvers — CFD (computational fluid dynamics), HFSS (high-frequency structure simulation) for the electromagnetics, and mechanical for the structural part. In the EDA world, we have things for the implementation, and things for sign-off. Each of these tools has sub-areas, and we have agents to do these things.
