events.title: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management and Emaar team up for Dh8 billion projects
events.summary: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management is teaming up with Emaar Hospitality to launch five property projects worth Dh8 billion ($2.17 billion) in Abu Dhabi amid continued demand for property in the emirate. The first project, consisting of 452 apartment units and some penthouses, will be built on Al Maryah Island , according to its group chief executive. Timelines and locations of other projects were not disclosed. The five projects will be built in an area spanning 4.7 million square feet, with Al Maryah Island project to be built in one million square feet. The starting price for a one-bedroom home will be Dh3.7 million and “sales will begin very soon,” Rabih Karam told The National. “It’s a standalone project in one of the most strategic areas of Al Maryah Island, directly connected to the mall, ADGM and Cleveland Clinic,” he said. The launch of the new projects comes as demand for property remains strong in the emirate, despite Iran-war-driven uncertainty. A total of 38,483 property transactions worth Dh171.26 billion were registered in Abu Dhabi in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 76.1 per cent increase in value and a 32.8 per cent rise in volume on an annual basis, according to data from the Abu Dhabi Real Estate Centre. A growing number of companies are setting up their base at the ADGM, boosting demand for property in and around the international financial centre, including Reem Island. Reem Island recorded the highest transaction value at Dh29.86 billion during the period, followed by Al Hudayriyat Island (Dh28.62 billion), Al Saadiyat Island (Dh18.69 billion), Yas Island (Dh13.4 billion) and Zayed City (Dh5.36 billion), ADREC data shows. Assets under management at ADGM grew 54 per cent annually in the first six months of 2026, with 49,027 professionals now based at Al Maryah Island and Reem Island, an increase of 34 per cent on the same period last year. “Demand has been amazing in Abu Dhabi. We are witnessing it in our other projects that we are selling currently," Mr Karam said. The company sold two mansions for Dh350 million each in one of its developments on Saadiyat Island this summer, he added. He, however, did not say who bought these villas, but he said, “these are profile of people that they can choose to be any place in the world, and they are choosing to be in UAE and in Abu Dhabi”. The privately owned company is chaired by Sheikh Hamdan bin Zayed. The latest partnership with Emaar follows the launch of Address Beach Resort and Residences in Dubai in JBR by the two companies in 2016, Mr Karam said. The collaboration has since expanded with the launch of Vida Residences Saadiyat Island, which introduced the Vida brand to Abu Dhabi for the first time. The company did not disclose how it planned to fund the new developments. Emaar is looking forward to introducing more of its hospitality brands to Abu Dhabi, Mohamed Alabbar, founder and managing director of Emaar, said in a statement on Monday.

events.title: Small regional town fights back against proposed AI data centre
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Small regional Victorian town fights back against proposed AI data centre Dozens of people travelled from the Ballarat region to protest the proposal of a data centre in Miners Rest. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Thousands of Victorians protested against data centres on Saturday including dozens from the small town of Miners Rest. Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people and is the proposed location for a data centre to be constructed by Resi Ventures. Protesters are calling for a statewide moratorium on the construction of AI data centres. The small regional town of Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people. Locals say their quiet country life might be about to change after developer Resi Ventures announced to the Australian Stock Exchange in June its intention to build an AI data centre at the town's old quarry. Volunteer firefighter and First Nations man Jedd Willis said the proposal on a 67 hectare plot of land in his town had been overwhelming. "There been a complete lack of care for country which disturbs me as a First Nations person," Mr Willis said. "[The site] has a very valuable resource for water and for firefighting." Jedd Willis (left) says he often uses water from the proposed site to fill firefighting tankers. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Mr Willis, who is a CFA volunteer, said firefighters would often use the water at the proposed site for fighting bushfires. "Along that, the concerns around the lack of water availability across the state as a whole, let alone just this region and with the upcoming fire season being forecasted to be quite treacherous is concerning." On Saturday, dozens of Miners Rest locals joined thousands from across the state at the steps of the state library in Melbourne to protest against the rise of AI data centres in Victoria. As of September this year, there were 50 data centres operating across Victoria with another 18 in the pipeline. Protesters called for a statewide moratorium on their construction. Chris Phillips says the data centre proposed for Miners Rest could be up to 350 metres long. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Secretary for the No Data Centre Miners Rest group, Chris Phillips said the developer had not been open about its plans. He said locals learned about this proposal through the media, rather than consultation with the community. "The benefit to the community would be very little." Mr Phillips said one of his concerns was whether the company would be making use of an aquifer at the site. "There's an aquifer [at the site] that goes many hundreds of kilometres underground and people draw water out of that to grow food like, potato farmers," he said. 'Nervously watching' upcoming election Miners Rest locals say they are concerned about the light and noise pollution the proposed data centre may emit. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Mr Phillips said locals were also concerned about the noise pollution that could come from the centre. "It's going to have a noise transmission of 63 to 65 decibels, which will be heard up to 1 kilometre away, over a constant 24 hours," he said. He said he would be anxiously watching the upcoming election and hoped politicians were listening to the local community. "I think if [politicians] don't listen to people they're going to get a very, very rude shock come this election," he said. "We are very nervously watching and we've had commitments from various political parties but we are also very nervous as to what could happen once the party is elected we could be steam rolled." Locals say there has been no consultation from the developer regarding the proposed data centre. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) In a statement Ripon MP, Martha Haylett said Miners Rest families deserved to be consulted before decisions were made that could fundamentally change their local area. "There has been no planning approval, no permits issued, and no meaningful consultation with the community," Ms Haylett said. "A project of this scale and significance cannot be imposed on a community without proper scrutiny, transparency, and engagement." The City of Ballarat said in a statement it had not received any planning applications for the proposal. "While Council officers have had early conversations with the developer, no formal applications have been lodged," it said. "All planning applications are subject to a thorough assessment process." The ABC has contacted Resi Ventures for comment.

events.title: AIX investors urged to register claims before creditors' meeting in December
events.summary: Investors in AIX Investment Group's liquidated unit have been urged to register their claims by December 4, as its liquidators plan to hold the first creditors' meeting four days later. AIX Secure SPV, the Cayman-registered issuer of fixed-income notes linked to Dubai-based AIX Investment Group, was placed into liquidation on October 30 by the Grand Court of the Cayman Islands. The court appointed Angela Barkhouse of Kroll (Cayman) and Michael Byrne of Kroll Middle East Consultancy in the Dubai International Financial Centre as joint official liquidators. Claims must be filed online through the liquidation website, said law firm ALBM Excello Law, whose clients were among the creditors who supported the winding-up petition, in a statement on Monday. The firm is helping AIX investors file claims, appoint proxies and put forward members for the liquidation committee. “Many AIX investors are based in the UAE, and the liquidators have been authorised by the Cayman Islands Court to pursue proceedings before the DIFC Courts and the Dubai courts,” said Sujith Mathew, partner at ALBM Excello Law. “We will continue to monitor developments and keep investors informed as the liquidation progresses.” What went wrong AIX Secure SPV, which was registered in the Cayman Islands on December 9, 2022, was established to issue debt notes to raise funds for investment activities, either directly or through affiliated entities. However, investors alleged that AIX Secure SPV failed to make interest payments when due and filed claims against them. According to the Financial Times , investors have filed claims seeking to recover about $10 million, including two individual claims for almost $2 million and $8 million. The company reportedly suspended payments to thousands of investors after promising annual returns of up to 30 per cent. AIX on its website said that “a period of exceptional geopolitical uncertainty and significant volatility across global financial markets has affected valuations and investment realisation cycles within a limited part of AIX’s product offering”. Last month, the UAE's Capital Market Authority said it was reviewing AIX Financial Consultations' activities after receiving information that the company had delayed or even missed payouts. Without disclosing the details of the information it received or the nature of the review, the CMA said it would keep the matter confidential to ensure a thorough, fair and impartial assessment. Following the Cayman Islands ruling, AIX said it had written to its investors directly, explaining why it was proposing a restructuring rather than a forced sale of assets in the current market conditions. “AIX intends to apply to the court for a stay of the order within the period permitted, and will ask the court to consider in full the alternative to liquidation presented to investors in October,” it said on November 4. Steps for investors The liquidators have “determined that AIX Secure SPV should be treated as insolvent, so the liquidation committee must have between three and five creditors”, the latest statement said. While late claims will still be accepted, those creditors may be shut out of the meeting. “A claim admitted for voting is not yet admitted for payment; the liquidators will assess claims for distribution later,” it added. The liquidators have also asked investors not to visit their offices. According to the letter to creditors, nominations for the liquidation committee close on November 26. Submission of claim information for voting, notice of attendance and proxy forms are due by December 4. The creditors’ meeting will be held virtually on December 8. The committee will advise the liquidators on strategy and approve the basis of their fees.

events.title: Techie rigged off-spec fan near flammable liquid and an exposed motherboard, then left it to run for days
events.summary: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®

events.title: Labour hire syndicates have 'little fear of consequence', watchdog says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NSW anti-slavery commissioner criticises policing of labour hire syndicates exploiting migrants Topic: Business and Industry Regulation The Coffs Coast in NSW is Australia's largest blueberry-growing region. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor ) The NSW anti-slavery commissioner has released a report into labour hire firms, alleging a slew of illegal practices including extortion, blackmail and more. The report comes only a week after the government responded to 31 recommendations made by the Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery, which recommended urgent reform to the industry. James Cockayne has referred multiple allegations to NSW Police and the AFP. The New South Wales anti-slavery commissioner says he has seen no sign of proactive, intelligence-led policing of labour hire syndicates accused of exploiting migrant workers in regional NSW. James Cockayne made the comments in his formal response to a parliamentary inquiry into the modern slavery risks faced by temporary migrant workers, which handed down its final report in August. His response, tabled in parliament today, includes allegations that labour hire syndicates in the Riverina and on the Mid North Coast have underpaid workers and been involved in identity theft, money laundering and tax fraud. These cases have been referred to state and federal police. In a statement, NSW Police directed the ABC to the Australian Federal Police, which has also been contacted for comment. Dr Cockayne said the state government was not doing enough to combat issues in the labour hire industry, which supplied migrant workers to farms across the state. "For years, we pretended not to see the elephant in the room. The Committee changed that. Now the task is to move that elephant out of our homes and communities, and out of our supply -chains," Dr Cockayne said in a statement. James Cockayne has released a report on modern slavery. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) Dr Cockayne said multiple sources told him workers were moved off farms just before surprise inspections. He also reported unverified allegations that some had been moved out of the region involuntarily, for weeks or longer. The report said policing remained reactive, with fewer than 10 per cent of trafficking and modern slavery reports to the AFP reaching prosecution, according to Australian Institute of Criminology figures cited in the report. Only about 1 to 4 per cent end in a trial, guilty plea or conviction. The labour hire industry has been under intense scrutiny from advocates and government agencies for many months. In August, a Four Corners investigation highlighted how migrant workers had been exploited by labour hire firms , with some fruit pickers saying they were treated like "animals". During the same week, the NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery released its final report , detailing "harrowing stories of mistreatment" faced by workers and making 31 recommendations to the government. The report highlighted exploitation in the Coffs Harbour and Nambucca Valley regions on the Mid North Coast, asking for an investigation into allegations of systemic labour exploitation. In its response on November 9, the state government said it was working with state and federal agencies on a range of measures and had improved information sharing. Meanwhile, agencies have worked together to carry out surprise inspections on farms, while unions and migrant support groups ramped up their presence in affected regions. Migrant workers have seen increased assistance and resources from support organisations in recent months. ( ABC News: Lucy Cooper ) Dr Cockayne recommended police step up proactive investigations into labour hire syndicates and publish their national protocol for combating human trafficking and slavery. He also called for a plan to move high-risk industries away from exploitative labour hire, including support for worker-run cooperatives. He said major buyers need to do due diligence on supply chains to ensure they were not contributing to modern slavery. "Until licensing is in place, responsibility falls squarely on business," Dr Cockayne said. "The biggest players in these supply chains have the most weight with which to leverage the system. "They can afford to use it — and probably should, given big business may soon face criminal penalties for failure to prevent modern slavery in its supply chain. "This is not only about doing the right thing. Responsible businesses are being undercut by operators who cheat workers and dodge tax. Acting now protects workers, and fair competition too.

events.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
events.summary: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen Published 16 November 2026, 06:24 GMT Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter. Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case. It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura. The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact. Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field Published 4 hours ago Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 21 October Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers. "It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security. "It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear." Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain". She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. "Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities." Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea". She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades". Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial? Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand. The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy. The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field. Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners. This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw. He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade". A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made. Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism". He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now." Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify". The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

events.title: India feels less threatened by AI than the US, official says
events.summary: Indians see AI as less of a threat than people in the US because fewer workers hold the “cognitive and office-oriented jobs” that the technology could replace, one of the country’s top tech officials said. Young Indians are drawn to technology and see AI as a way to raise productivity, reduce poverty, and help India become a developed country within two decades, S Krishnan, secretary of India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The gains, he predicts, could touch sectors such as agriculture, education, healthcare, and government. Krishnan told Semafor Deputy Editor-in-Chief Shelly Banjo that AI tools could help advise farmers with the expertise that’s only available to the largest companies, or screen chest X-rays for tuberculosis to enhance the productivity of the stressed healthcare sector. With around 6 million people in IT and related services, Krishnan said India has the workforce that can diffuse the technology throughout the economy. But the constraint, shared in many countries, is that “AI compute is still in short supply and expensive.” Krishnan said India and the US were “pretty close” to a trade deal, with one or two issues left to resolve. “We’d prefer to have it by yesterday, but, yes, as quickly as we can,” he said. Asked about a potential bilateral visit between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump, which hasn’t happened in Trump’s second term, he said: “Well, I think they still share a very good relationship.” — J.D. events.title: Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads
events.summary: Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads. Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud. Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for. In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service. In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux. Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads. Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here . Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

events.title: Thrift shop asks shoppers to nominate a charity
events.summary: Julie Rindam (front) and Jeanette Worthington (back) plan to be transparent with donors by having a book in the shop which will evidence where money is going. Published 16 November 2026, 06:03 GMT Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises. Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month. Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years. "The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on." Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes. "All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said. "We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting." Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month. "Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said. The owner hopes that the store will also be a centre for the community. Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed. As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available. Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities. "People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said. "We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time." Janet Smart had been a regular donater to the shop before it was taken over by the new team. Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community. "When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said. "You meet such nice people in here as well." She added that the social side of the shop was equally important. "I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them." Jack Spencer is managing to find clothes and items that he wouldn't be able to find in more mainstream stores. Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items. "It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said. "You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it." For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit. events.title: CNMC Goldmine shares plunge as gold falls below US$4,000
events.summary: SINGAPORE – Shares of CNMC Goldmine Holdings plunged on Nov 16, extending recent losses as gold prices dipped below US$4,000 an ounce following a sell-off in the precious metal. The mainboard-listed mining stock sank nearly 11% to 85 cents at the midday trading break on Nov 16, bringing its losses to about 20.56% over the past five trading sessions and almost 30% over the past month. About 5.5 million shares changed hands during the morning trading session on Nov 16. Spot gold, meanwhile, fell 0.24% to US$3,872 an ounce, as signs that the US Federal Reserve could raise rates weighed on sentiment. This came ahead of remarks by Fed chair Kevin Warsh at a Nov 16 US conference that could offer further clues on the direction of interest rates. Gold has fallen nearly 6% since the start of the year, as elevated US Treasury yields and a stronger greenback dampened demand for the precious metal. Hashim Osman, a research analyst at Phillip Securities Research, attributed CNMC’s share price decline to growing expectations of further US interest rate hikes. This follows stronger-than-expected inflation data last week and consensus among Fed officials that inflation remains too high. “In this environment, the key differentiator among miners is their ability to limit margin erosion as gold prices ease,” he said. Elevated fuel costs remain a concern for investors, particularly for miners investing in exploration and development, he added. CNMC’s net profit rose 17.8% to US$18.6 million (S$23.9 million) for the six months ended June 30, 2026, from US$15.8 million a year earlier. The Singapore-headquartered gold and base metals producer, which operates in Kelantan, Malaysia, generated US$65.2 million in revenue for the first half of 2026, up 23.4% from a year earlier, driven by higher gold, silver and zinc prices. Revenue from gold produced at its flagship Sokor mine’s carbon-in-leach plant rose 32% to US$49.8 million, even as production fell 6% to 11,105 ounces. Including gold produced from lead concentrate at its flotation plant, which is used primarily to recover base metals, the company generated total revenue of US$56.7 million from gold in the first half of 2026, a 27.4% increase from a year earlier. Still, CNMC’s all-in production cost is about US$2,000 per ounce, so margins would still be intact even if gold retreats further.

events.title: 'Break-in and rising costs could kill my business'
events.summary: Gordon Kidd says he is struggling with business-related costs and a recent break-in has not helped Published 16 November 2026, 05:57 GMT The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs. Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about £20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop. Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue. A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates. West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing. "They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation. "That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop." He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business. "I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it." Burglars stole three cycles and a frame and damaged the shop in the raid Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses. "I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said. "We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough." He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever". "A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said. Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded. He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy". "Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general." A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people. "We are also making the business environment work better through our £4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments. events.title: Taiwan deputy minister on Jensen Huang scandal: ‘We feel sad’
events.summary: The scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has sparked a wave of sadness in his native Taiwan, the island’s deputy digital minister said Sunday. Huang had a close relationship with Taiwanese tech companies, meeting with them every year, Isabel Hou said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World. “The relationship is very personal,” she told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. “The supply chain leaders, I think, were concerned about how this kind of trust can be replaced. It will be tough.” Those ties went beyond business: Hou referenced a New York Times article in which Huang’s longtime hairstylist admitted he was too upset to sleep , drank a bottle of red wine, and prayed for the former chip CEO after his resignation. “We feel sad,” she added. The Nvidia ordeal has fueled calls in Washington for tighter chip export controls, given Huang’s years of lobbying to sell chips to China, and the revelation that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials suspect spying for Beijing. US authorities are probing whether Megaspeed, the company the woman formerly led, smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Singapore-based Megaspeed has denied the allegations. US lawmakers from both parties have pushed for tougher export restrictions, and Democrats have opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Taipei has been aligning its export control policy with the US. Hou said Taiwanese don’t want frontier chips going to China, where they could end up in military equipment aimed at the island. Reading a line prepared by her staff, she called for a policy that’s “precise, predictable, and coordinated with partners.” China, once the destination for the vast majority of Taiwan’s outbound investment, now draws less than 1%, Hou said, as companies expand elsewhere, many in the US. In AI especially, Taiwan needs “trusted partners.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: US official says government needs to make a better case for AI
events.summary: The US government has a responsibility to explain AI’s benefits to the public after the midterm elections showed widespread antagonism to the technology, a top State Department official said Sunday. Jacob Helberg, the undersecretary for economic affairs, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World that the election, in which many voters were opposed to AI and data centers, should be seen as an “opportunity.” “The onus really is on everyone serving in government at all levels, local, state, and federal, to do a better job of communicating to the public the opportunity and the upside of this great technology,” Helberg told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. Helberg pointed to data showing that AI has helped prop up the US economy through investment and productivity gains. He said AI hasn’t caused mass job losses, and “we haven’t seen any evidence at all that super intelligence has had an inflationary effect,” using the Trump administration’s preferred alternative term for AI. Competitor obsession Helberg, who has spearheaded the Pax Silica effort with US allies to secure global supply chains for critical industries, also said US global tech policy shouldn’t “obsess” over China. “Great companies don’t try to succeed by obsessing over their competitors,” he said. “One of the temptations in policy roles is you spend so much time studying what competitors do that it almost becomes easy to over-obsess on them.” While Pax Silica is building a bloc of US-allied nations to reduce their dependence on China, Helberg said the effort is intended to be “an America-centric initiative, not a China-centric initiative.” — J.D. events.title: Goldman Sachs predicts ‘sizeable surplus’ for oil market in 2027
events.summary: The Paris-based International Energy Agency said last week the global oil market is set swing to a surplus for the first time since the US-Iran war began. Goldman Sachs says the oil market will face a “sizeable surplus” in 2027, with crude supply minus demand at 2 million barrels a day. It expects Brent to average US$88 a barrel in 2027, then fall to US$78 by year-end as the “risk premium” fades. China’s weak fuel demand may limit prices, and Goldman says its total oil demand likely peaked in 2025. SINGAPORE – The oil market faces a “sizeable surplus” in 2027 that will drag prices lower even as supply risks remain, Goldman Sachs Group said. Crude production minus so-called end-use demand will reach two million barrels a day in 2027, despite accounting for supply disruptions half that size, analysts including Daan Struyven said in a Nov 15 note outlining their base case. Brent futures are expected to average US$88 a barrel in 2027 , easing to US$78 by the year-end “as the risk premium gradually normalises”, they said. The worldwide crude market has been rocked in 2026 by the US-Iran war, which initially choked off regional production before suppliers tapped alternative export routes and restored flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The Paris-based International Energy Agency said last week the global oil market is set to swing to a surplus for the first time since the conflict began. “For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and increasing market adaptation,” they said. “Under our base case, Middle East supply rises above its 2025 average on ongoing adaptation through ship-to-ship transfers and pipeline additions, while supply growth elsewhere stalls.” China – typically the world’s largest crude importer – is unlikely to prop up prices, with “persistent weakness” in road-fuel usage to scar demand by 400,000 barrels a day, according to the Goldman analysts. All in, “we estimate that China’s total oil demand peaked in 2025”, they added. Brent traded below US$95 a barrel on Nov 16 after dropping more than 1%. The benchmark peaked in 2026 above US$126 a barrel in April, hitting the highest intra-day price since 2022. Year to date, it has averaged about US$91. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Coles investigates cyber attack but provides little detail
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supermarket group Coles investigates cybersecurity incident but provides little detail Coles advised customers to remain vigilant after disclosing a cybersecurity incident. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) Coles says it is investigating a cybersecurity incident but provided little further detail to customers or investors. The supermarket group is looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect. Coles says it will provide updates on the investigation "as appropriate". Supermarket group Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, but has provided little detail on what occurred. Coles disclosed the cyber attack in a statement to the stock exchange on Monday morning, saying it is currently not aware of any data being accessed or stolen as a result of the incident. "Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," the statement read. On its website, Coles Group listed gift cards as working as normal, "no indication" of an impact on Flybuys accounts and no issues identified with Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery or QuiteLike subscriptions. However, the retailer said it was looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect, which it was investigating. It said it was working with global cybersecurity experts to "contain and secure the Coles IT environment". Coles says no action needed by customers Coles told investors and customers on Monday morning that it was business as usual for its operations. "Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online," the company website said. The supermarket group said customers do not need to take any action at this time but advised caution. Woolworths probes reports of drained digital gift cards Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers. "We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information from you — including by email, phone, text, or post — and potential scam activity," Coles said. "We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reusing the same password across multiple services." It urged similar caution from suppliers. "We apologise for any concern this may cause our customers and key stakeholders at a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world," the company said. In recent weeks, European supermarkets have been hit by IT incidents affecting fridge and freezer temperatures , which were believed to be cyber attacks. Over the weekend, customers of Coles' major rival Woolworths reported digital gift cards being drained by unauthorised transactions . Woolworths told ABC News it was investigating. A number of major Australian corporations have been rocked by cyber attacks and data breaches this year, including Origin Energy . The hacking incident in July left about 900,000 current and former Origin customers' data exposed. Coles said further updates would be provided "as appropriate".

events.title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
events.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy. The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country. The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.” Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations. Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April. “We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another. One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.” The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings. Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others. “We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.” Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom. He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves. Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion . His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry. "While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said. Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report. events.title: DBS, JPMorgan launch US-Singapore tokenised deposit service for institutions
events.summary: The solution connects blockchain-based accounts on DBS Token Services and the Blockchain Deposit Account network by JPMorgan’s digital payments unit, Kinexys. DBS and JPMorgan Chase launched a cross-border tokenised deposit service for institutions, allowing 24/7 US dollar transfers between the US and Singapore. Ant International is the first client, using it for global treasury and liquidity management, as firms seek faster payment tools for digital businesses. The move follows wider tokenised money trials and standards work, including a DBS-Citi weekend transfer completed in minutes and Project Bloom under the Monetary Authority of Singapore. SINGAPORE – DBS Bank and JPMorgan Chase on Nov 16 announced the launch of its cross-border tokenised deposit solution, which allows institutions to make 24/7 US dollar transfers between the US and Singapore. The solution connects blockchain-based accounts on DBS Token Services and the Blockchain Deposit Account network by JPMorgan’s digital payments unit Kinexys. Ant International, the global arm of Chinese fintech company Ant, is the first client to use the solution for its global treasury and liquidity management. The announcement comes as financial institutions seek faster liquidity management tools to support digital industries 24/7 such as e-commerce and digital services. For example, a DBS report released on Oct 28 showed that 88% of 422 business leaders surveyed in 11 markets were already deploying or piloting tokenised money use cases. Tokenised money is becoming increasingly mainstream among large corporations seeking access to a wider range of markets and greater liquidity, added the report. Meanwhile, outbound cross-border payment volume in Asia is projected to nearly double to US$24 trillion (S$30.92 trillion) by 2033, from US$13.5 trillion in 2025, based on a report by conference platform Money20/20 and market research provider FXC intelligence. “Tokenised money is moving rapidly from experimentation to delivering live tangible value for clients,” said Rachel Chew, chief operating officer and co-head of digital assets, global transaction services at DBS, Singapore’s largest lender. Over a weekend in September, DBS and Citi announced their successful trial of a US dollar payment between Singapore and the US, using tokenised deposits via the Swift Digital Ledger. The transfer was completed in minutes, faster than regular cross-border settlements that can take up to two business days due to weekend closures and time-zone differences. The launch of the cross-border tokenised deposit service follows an interoperability framework by DBS and Kinexys released in November 2025. More broadly, the two banks are also co-leading a token interoperability work group under Project Bloom, an industry initiative led by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to enable the safe, seamless and scalable use of tokenised money. events.title: Thai GDP growth rebounds as AI drives investments, exports
events.summary: The pickup showed the growing impact of the global AI investment cycle on Thailand, where electronics exports and private investment have surged. BANGKOK – Thailand shed its place as South-east Asia’s slowest-growing major economy in the third quarter, with the artificial intelligence boom powering exports while masking persistent weakness in household spending and tourism. Gross domestic product in the three months through September rose 2.9% from a year earlier, the National Economic and Social Development Council said on Nov 16. That was below the 3.1% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey. Second-quarter growth was restated at 2.4% from 1.9%. The pickup partly reflected a favourable comparison with a year earlier, when US tariffs and a border conflict with Cambodia disrupted trade. But it also showed the growing impact of the global AI investment cycle on Thailand, where electronics exports and private investment have surged. Investment growth accelerated to 11.8% in the third quarter, while exports jumped 18.3%, the council said. Household consumption ticked up just 2.5%, while government spending shrank 1.6%. The economic data put Thailand ahead of the Philippines, which expanded 2.1% in the quarter. The country still trailed most regional peers, with Vietnam growing almost 10% and Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia all expanding more than 5%. Growth above 3% has become unusual for Thailand, an ageing tiger economy constrained by high household debt and limited fiscal room. The country last grew more than 3% in a quarter in early 2025 and has not recorded annual growth above that level since 2018. The stronger performance comes during a period of unusual political stability. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul leads one of Thailand’s strongest governing coalitions in decades, giving his administration more room to pursue investment and economic policies even with a no-confidence vote looming next month and street protests simmering. Thailand has also attracted a surge in investment tied to AI, data centres and advanced electronics, while foreign investors have returned to its bonds and stocks. BLOOMBERG

events.title: China’s economy misses forecasts with across-the-board slowdown
events.summary: The People’s Bank of China has signalled caution about cutting interest rates when borrowing demand is already weak. China’s growth weakened across the board in October as consumption and industrial output undershot expectations while investment unexpectedly worsened, in a sign Beijing’s latest stimulus measures have yet to feed through to the economy. Retail sales rose 0.4% from a year ago, far worse than the consensus forecast of 0.8% by economists polled by Bloomberg. That compares with an increase of 1.1% in September. Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first 10 months of 2026 from the same period in 2025 , lower than the 7% decline expected by economists. Investment dropped 7.2% in the January-September period. Industrial output grew 4.8% in October from a year ago, missing expectations for a 5.3% increase and slowing from September. The figures pointed to a downbeat picture of an economy that’s losing momentum, after Beijing stepped up efforts to bolster growth in late September. Officials rolled out a moderate stimulus package including mortgage subsidies and greater public borrowing quota, while accelerating measures to shore up investment. Separate data on Nov 16 showed residential prices continued to fall in October, extending a slump that has dragged on economic growth for more than five years. Property investment plunged 21.6% in the first 10 months of 2026 from a year earlier, compared with a 20.6% decline in January-September. The economy was “overall stable” and “extended a trend of renewing growth engines and improving its structure,” the National Bureau of Statistics said in a statement. The agency highlighted challenges faced by the economy, include an uncertain global environment, imbalances between supply and demand, as well as difficulties in some businesses’ operation. Despite indications that growth has come under pressure, the urban surveyed jobless rate unexpectedly slipped to 5.1% in October from 5.2% in September. Many economists see the official unemployment gauge as an incomplete reflection of the labour market because it excludes migrant workers who returned to the countryside after losing work. The economy rebounded in the third quarter, with growth reaching the lower end of Beijing’s annual target of 4.5% to 5%. But the recovery remained heavily reliant on overseas demand, with net exports contributing almost 40% of the increase in gross domestic product – the most for any quarter since the start of 2025. That dependence is becoming a bigger risk as questions mount over the sustainability of the global artificial intelligence investment boom, which has powered demand for Chinese electronics and other manufactured goods. A slowdown in exports would increase pressure on domestic consumption and investment to pick up the slack. The October figures will be closely scrutinised by top officials ahead of the Central Economic Work Conference, usually held in the first half of December. The gathering will offer clues on Beijing’s economic priorities for 2027 and the scale of any additional support. Policymakers may lean more heavily on fiscal measures if the economy loses further momentum. The People’s Bank of China has signalled caution about cutting interest rates when borrowing demand is already weak. BLOOMBERG

events.title: A new generation of media will shape the 2028 Democratic primary
events.summary: The Scoop Last week, while shouting out supporters at the Muslim Public Affairs Council gala in Washington, DC, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed singled out a figure in the crowd for special thanks: the founder of Zeteo, Mehdi Hasan, whose posts and videos pushed back against claims that progressives had underperformed more moderate candidates. Three days later, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told the anti-Trump digital outlet MeidasTouch that the network had given him a key boost at a moment when few people believed Mississippi would be in play for a Democratic candidate. “Thank you for giving me the opportunity very early on, when nobody thought Mississippi would be on the radar, to tell my story, tell my message,” Colom said. The first two years of President Donald Trump’s return to power were a waking nightmare for the Democratic Party. But in Trump’s shadow, oppositional media on the left has seen a period of extraordinary growth. Creators like Aaron Parnas, Keith Edwards, and Jack Cocchiarella gained millions of followers railing against Trump on YouTube. Independent media companies like The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and Zeteo gained millions of combined subscriptions on Substack, which grew from a platform largely favored by right-leaning or “heterodox” publishers to one dominated by left-leaning new media outlets and voices. Scarred by Trump’s 2024 podcast tours, Democratic donors are pouring money into the independent media space, and Democratic candidates have new media figures on speed dial. And now this ascendant new media ecosystem is positioning itself to help pick the next Democratic presidential nominee — or at least weed out a few of the duds. Progressive outlets are aiming to serve as a check on traditional media that they feel wants to knock out left-wing candidates, while moderate forces are starting up their own media to try and counter a zealous left flank that has shouted down moderates online. “That’s going to be the war more than anything: the attention fight… How can I, with the least amount of friction, get these people to start sharing clips?” Cocchiarella told Semafor. The Left While many legacy outlets that had experienced ratings and subscriptions growth during Trump’s first term have seen little to no meaningful gains in his second go-around, independent media outlets critical of Trump, the mainstream media, and Democratic Party leadership saw huge gains. Since the beginning of Trump’s presidency, Zeteo has added almost 2 million YouTube subscribers. The Bernie Sanders-ite outlet More Perfect Union has added 3 million. Hasan Piker, the leftist Twitch streamer who became a midterm campaign fixation, has gained millions of followers on YouTube and increased viewership of his stream. Now, both MPU and Zeteo are hoping to bring different issues — or candidates — to the front of the Democratic presidential primary debate. Over the last two years, Zeteo has provided early coverage and political air cover for left-wing and socialist candidates, particularly those that have expressed aggressive criticism of Israel. In an interview on Thursday, Hasan pointed to the company’s early interviews with then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani and El-Sayed as examples; both were able to gain exposure to like-minded voters while other outlets were skeptical of their candidacies. “From Zohran Mamdani’s race, to AOC’s rise, to Abdul El-Sayed’s victory, I think it’s been very clear — I’m not saying they wouldn’t have happened without us; that’s a little bit too arrogant and not accurate — but certainly they were aided and abetted and strengthened and bolstered by the fact that we exist,” he said. Hasan said potential 2028 candidates clearly have taken notice. Before the midterm elections, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a candid rare interview on Zeteo that he was considering running in 2028 , an admission he hadn’t made on-camera anywhere else. Hasan said although his political views are clear, multiple likely candidates who do not necessarily share Zeteo’s progressive, Israel-critical stance had nonetheless been in touch in recent days about appearing on the outlet’s show. “Democratic presidential [hopefuls] and their teams have reached out to us, not the other way around, even people we’ve criticized,” Hasan said, noting that he’s angling for an interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a pro-Israel Democrat. Other outlets are more interested in highlighting specific issues, but could end up tipping the conversation in favor of certain candidates that they choose to spotlight. More Perfect Union, the viral video channel founded by Sanders advisor Faiz Shakir, has not outright endorsed candidates in races, but its story selection and tone have bolstered candidates on the left. During the midterms, the organization published a video on then-Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner titled It was less investigatory (the piece did not uncover the various scandals that later led to Platner’s decision to drop out), and more complimentary; it gave space for Platner to explain his view on various media controversies, and showed working class Platner supporters who were unbothered by the unfolding scandals. Over the last few months, More Perfect Union has interviewed Sanders and Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. In an email, More Perfect Union Editor-in-Chief Josh Miller-Lewis told Semafor that although the organization had not finalized its 2028 plans yet, it was hoping to host multiple events with candidates. The organization also hopes to grow its More Perfect University program, which hosted town halls where candidates faced college student questioners. But primarily, Miller-Lewis said, it plans to create content that would “put candidates in conversation with working class audiences and force substantive policy discussions that are often lacking in election coverage,” citing videos the organization made with Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz during the 2024 election and El-Sayed during the 2026 Senate race. “Our goal will be to create spaces where our working class audience has the opportunity to challenge candidates in substantive, solutions driven conversations, candidates can outline the big ideas they’ll prioritize if elected and show viewers how candidates engage with the voters they need to persuade to win,” Miller-Lewis wrote. Beyond highlighting more ideologically aligned candidates, left-wing outlets also plan to highlight shortcomings of centrist and moderate candidates. Ryan Grim, a founder of the foreign policy-centric Drop Site News, noted that the investigative outlet will be expanding its domestic coverage to focus on spotlighting how three powerful interest groups hope to influence the Democratic presidential primary. “Crypto and AI, and to some extent AIPAC, are gonna wanna participate, which is wonderful, and we’re a big democracy, but we’re gonna make sure that the public knows who they’re support

events.title: Tug of war continues over mysterious foreign barge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts So-called Indonesian ghost barge rusts, months after running aground in Torres Strait The barge is almost as long as the island it washed up on. ( Supplied ) An Indonesian barge that ran aground on a rocky island in the Torres Strait will remain there until the tides are high enough for it to be salvaged. A marine expert has come up with a plan to do so, but he has not heard back from the barge owner's insurers. The salvage operation relies on 3.7-metre tides, which are due to occur between December and March. A 100-metre barge remains grounded on a rocky islet, 10 months after it mysteriously drifted through international waters and crashed in Australia's far north. Far North Queensland marine services specialist Vance Wallin has a plan to salvage the Indonesian barge. But first, he needs the green light from an overseas insurance company and almost 4-metre tides in the Torres Strait. "You only get those tides in the wet season and, unfortunately, you get cyclones in the same period," he said. "You've got to make sure … the conditions are good enough to get in there and do it." Nelly 112's hull was intact in March, but it is expected some compartments may now have been breached. ( Supplied ) Nelly 112 was not carrying any people or cargo when it washed up on Athikho Poji, near Badu Island, in late January, after going adrift in bad weather in Indonesia. Mr Wallin's company, Carpentaria Marine Service, put forward a salvage plan, but he said the barge owner had handed responsibility for the boat to an insurance company. "To date, they haven't come to the party on agreeing with us on that salvage," he said. Mr Wallin, whose company has performed about 60 to 70 salvages and wreck removals, said it would take two or three days to remove the barge from its position "high on the rocks". "We need about a 3.7-metre tide to look at a salvage attempt," he said. "With a fair bit of ballasting, we think we'll be able to get it off." He said there would be tides high enough to perform the salvage in January, February and March. The barge, Nelly 112, washed up on the small island in January. ( Supplied ) However, Mr Wallin's proposal hinges on selling the barge to a buyer in Papua New Guinea, who has agreed to pay the entire salvage cost so the barge can be towed there to be used as a floating dock. "I believe they need to make a decision in the next couple of months," Mr Wallin said. Edmund Tamwoy has also expressed interest in taking on the barge for his Indigenous-owned Badu Island quarry business, but has not had success in contacting its owners. Mr Tamwoy regularly spots the abandoned barge on his run to collect recycling waste from nearby Mabuiag Island. "It's just getting rusty, of course," he said. He estimated it would cost about $200,000 to remove the barge from the island, a price he said he was prepared to pay. "Giving the opportunity locally to someone I think is the best outcome for everyone else, even for the owner," he said. However, Mr Wallin argued the cost of registering the Indonesian-flagged barge in Australia would be "uneconomical" and exceed the barge's value. A spokesperson for Maritime Safety Queensland said it had not set a deadline for the barge's removal. The regulator, which has the power to take possession of abandoned or derelict boats, has remained in contact with the barge owner to monitor progress on a salvage plan.

events.title: Alibaba unveils new flagship AI model in riposte to US rivals
events.summary: Alibaba said its Qwen4-Max model outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro. Alibaba launched Qwen4-Max, saying it rivals Anthropic and OpenAI and scored near the top in coding tests, beating Claude Fable 5.1 and Kimi K3.1 Pro. The model is not open weight, but smaller versions will come soon. Alibaba is building a wider AI system with models, chips and more computing power. Chinese firms are pressing US AI leaders with rapid new releases. Alibaba also added stronger security after worries over open-weight model cyber risks. Alibaba Group has launched a new flagship AI model, claiming performance that rivals Anthropic and OpenAI in China’s latest challenge to US leaders. The e-commerce giant turned AI player said its Qwen4-Max model scored near the top of coding benchmarks, outperforming Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 as well as home-grown rival Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro. Alibaba did not make the model open weight, which would allow users to download and customise it, but said it would make smaller versions of the series available soon. Chinese firms including Alibaba, Moonshot and DeepSeek are challenging US dominance in artificial intelligence, unveiling a succession of new models with rapid improvements in coding and reasoning. The release on Nov 16 adds to a flurry of recent Chinese launches, including Tencent’s Hunyuan 4 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro. Alibaba’s Qwen series is so far the most downloaded open-weight AI model family in the world, following an ambitious push into the technology spearheaded by chief executive Eddie Wu. The company is building a full AI ecosystem, from models to AI chips. The CEO said in September that Alibaba’s T-Head chipmaking unit, which recently filed for an initial public offering in Hong Kong, would roll out China’s most powerful AI chips domestically. The Hangzhou, China-headquartered firm has made attaining artificial general intelligence, or AGI, its primary goal. It is also rapidly expanding its computing power, with Wu setting a target of building 20GW of data centre capacity globally by 2032 . The firm introduced upgraded security measures in its latest model, following a series of alarming incidents that have raised concerns over the cybersecurity risks of open-weight models. That follows similar moves from Tencent and Moonshot. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Intel sued by investors after PC sales slump hits share price
events.summary: Published 16 November 2026, 03:04 GMT Intel, the US chip giant, is being sued by its shareholders who accuse the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in its personal computer (PC) sales that caused its share price to plunge almost 29% in one day. Billions of dollars was knocked off the value of the company after it forecast disappointing revenues ahead of its latest earnings report. The BBC has contacted Intel for comment. In October, Intel firm announced its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from the chipmaker that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders. Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power. As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive. Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October. Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though its share price is still up by 51% overall this year.
