events.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
events.summary: Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption. The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent. Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers. Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday. By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America. Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge. Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? Published 3 days ago Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world Published 3 days ago In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected , as were some schools and police forces. UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network. In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails. In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook. Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday. In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook. The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals. Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill". His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that. "The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said. "We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible." Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally. It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world. By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region. Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review. Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services. "The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure. Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

events.title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
events.summary: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035 BENGALURU, India -- With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers. The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey. India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers nonfossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India’s existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States. Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy. The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure . The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced. “If the grid doesn’t catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target,” Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, said. “A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must.” The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan. Economist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian “electrostate,” in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products. “So now in India you have two assets — not only do you have cheap labor, you also have cheap energy,” Shah said. The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source. India’s clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas. Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses. However, India’s continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country’s electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember. India’s power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035. Ember energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining. Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power. Berkeley's Abhyankar warned that newly built coal plants could become stranded assets if the government meets its renewable energy targets. Meeting the 2035 target requires more than building more renewable power plants. Their electricity must be able to reach consumers. India’s rapid clean energy expansion is already testing the grid's limits.

events.title: FAA ends hours-long nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations. Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position. Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed. Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack. Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems. "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said. Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades. "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room. He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding. Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates." Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports. Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues. The developer of that tool denied any connection. By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations over the course of the day Friday. Many travelers are stuck at the airport or on their planes on the tarmac Friday evening. Editor's note: This story has been updated with details from a press briefing.

events.title: FAA lifts rare nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA on Friday lifted a rare nationwide ground stop that impacted more than 14,500 flights after a major outage affecting the US’ air communications system. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system,” and said the government didn’t suspect any nefarious causes, such as a terrorist or cyber attack. He said the issues were connected to old equipment that was overloaded, and that flights should start taking off again over the next day. “Hopefully tomorrow, we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said, while trying to reassure travelers that the US remains “the safest system in the world.” The stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, caused widespread disruption and prompted shares in airlines to drop. American Airlines shares dropped more than 2% in after-hours trading, while United shares fell 1.6%. Those airlines are now navigating thousands of rebookings and frustrated passengers. This is only the third time the agency has ever issued such an order. The most recent was in January 2023; before that, air traffic was halted nationwide on Sept. 11, 2001. Duffy used a large portion of a press conference on Friday evening to blame the Republican-controlled Congress for withholding funds for air-traffic control repairs. He urged lawmakers to approve $50 billion to upgrade infrastructure through an emergency funding bill. “I’ve asked, the president’s asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Mississippi River cruise crash has no fatalities, critical injuries
events.summary: Thirty-two people are in local hospitals and all passengers and crew are accounted for after a tanker collided with a Mississippi River cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans , officials said Friday. The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference. What they're saying: While the investigation remains ongoing, officials said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker appeared to have lost control, causing it to collide with the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking after the collision, the cruise ship began to sink and eventually toppled over and flipped — leaving people in the cold water. Video from the scene shows passengers, in life preservers, swimming in the river toward safety. The first 87 passengers got off while the ship was still afloat, Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. She added it "was normal conditions" on the river and that there wasn't a high current, despite how notoriously challenging that stretch of the Mississippi River usually is. "The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said. He added, "I've never been prouder of a group of people than those people that came off of that boat." Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans. A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate. Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11. Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October. Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side. Another dozen vessels were in the water nearby as a helicopter roamed overhead and sirens rang out over the water. Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

events.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
events.summary: A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips. For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets. With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years. Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns. But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips. It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. The city-state has had some success in policing this. It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places. They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties. In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore. The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere. Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed. But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department. Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months. Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case. Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing. In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times. Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses. Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness. In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

events.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
events.summary: The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January. Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that officials in many states warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage. A federal court last month struck down a portion of the rules that required chronically ill Medicaid recipients to prove their condition significantly impairs the ability to work in order to qualify for an exemption. Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said Friday there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience." Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times . The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that a chaotic rollout of the requirements will disenroll more people because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements. What they're saying: "States have made real progress, and they've been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term," said Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman. How it works: The first-ever work rules mean Medicaid enrollees must report at least 80 hours a month of work, school or volunteering or get an exemption. States were facing tight timetables for setting up systems to notify millions of recipients about the requirements — and to track whether they're complying. Nebraska's early rollout of the work requirements in May led to confusion and coverage denials due to unsubmitted paperwork, per KFF Health News . What we're watching: Democrats who will control Congress next year intend to push for more delays, or to scrap the work requirements altogether. events.title: FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring
events.summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. In a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy said it has yet to be determined whether the issue was incompetence or a faulty router. In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris said, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET. "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and said international flights would be dealt with individually. The notice said, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ® Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop. Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop. Updated to add at 2353 UTC CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” Updated to add at 2340 UTC Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

events.title: ‘The machine doesn’t stop’: Abu Dhabi’s wartime plan for keeping its cultural ambition alive
events.summary: The Signal Interview “We have plan A’s all the way to plan Z’s, from our best-case scenarios to our worst-case scenarios,” Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak says, when asked how the culture, tourism, and property groups he leads are preparing for what might happen next in the conflict that has shaken the Middle East. Many of those plans are contingent on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran ending, but “if this conflict gets worse, we also have a very clear route,” says the chairman of the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi. The manga-loving 44-year-old member of Abu Dhabi’s Executive Council, whose other interests include sneakers, rap music, and basketball, has spent more than a decade at the heart of the city’s strategy to diversify its economy using museums, UFC fights, and theme parks. Last year alone, the city opened five museums and welcomed a record 26.6 million visitors. Culture and tourism are “the building blocks of our future,” he says. But the conflict has forced him to craft a response that combines a strategic pivot, reassurance to local staff and foreign partners, and continued commitment to his city’s long-term aims. When the Iran war started in February, flights and events were canceled and the number of Western tourists to the Gulf plunged, emptying local hotels. “We had to basically rethink how we’re…promoting ourselves,” Al Mubarak says. But, he adds, “We always understood that, no matter what happens… the machine doesn’t stop.” A pivot to new growth markets Before the conflict, Abu Dhabi was working toward a goal of attracting 39.3 million visitors a year by 2030, up from 24 million in 2023. It projected that those tourists would contribute AED 90 billion a year to the city’s economy. Al Mubarak is still sticking to his 2030 goals, but he says the assumptions underlying them have changed. He now expects a 10-15% drop in visitors from the US and Europe compared to its original estimates, for example, with growth from other parts of the globe making up the difference. So he has changed the focus of Abu Dhabi’s marketing, looking to pull in far more visitors from its own region, and from Eastern Europe, India and the rest of Southeast Asia, and Africa. The city is already seeing 5-8% growth in visitors from “some of our Eastern geographies,” he says, and much larger numbers from around the Gulf. On Yas Island this summer, he says, “Some days I felt I was in Saudi, some days I felt I was in Qatar, some days I felt I was in Moscow.” He recalls talking to two tourists as they watched the smoke from a drone attack on a French navy base in the first week of the conflict: when he asked if they were alright, they replied: “We’re Russians, so this is nothing.” Abu Dhabi has been a magnet for wealthy Westerners, with its Formula 1 track and outpost of the Louvre. But Al Mubarak wants to use the current crisis to broaden its appeal to other parts of the world whose populations’ economic power is growing. Under his worst-case scenarios for the war’s outcome, his plans would focus Abu Dhabi’s culture and tourism strategy much more on its immediate region and the Global South. That grouping of poorer countries comprises more than 70% of the world’s population, he notes, and its people want “to experience a lot more than they have.” Westerners have been more put off by news coverage that he says exaggerates the security threat, but he has not stopped marketing to them, too. “We haven’t stopped acknowledging that they are a traveler and they are a future potential traveler,” he says. “We’ve kept [at the] front of their mind that the UAE is here and Abu Dhabi is here, and it’s going to continue to develop, it’s going to continue to grow. So when the time is right for you as a traveler, our doors are wide open.” Three-quarters of Abu Dhabi’s hotel rooms were full again by August, Al Mubarak notes. At Aldar Properties, the commercial real estate developer he also chairs, new sales dropped 34% in the first nine months of this year, but at AED 18.9 billion were still higher than for the same period in 2024. Overseas buyers — from China, the UK, Russia, and elsewhere — made up 28% of the total. After the first day of Iranian attacks, he maintains, “business has really been as usual.” Projecting normality, and an alluring vision Informed by its experience during the pandemic, Abu Dhabi kept cultural institutions open throughout the conflict to give residents places to connect and “a sense of comfort,” Al Mubarak says. To reassure his own teams, he set up daily management group meetings, and a stream of video conferences, emails, and helplines for employees. What mattered most was to show that leaders were listening rather than just talking, he says. “Small things like that make a difference,” he notes, adding that his strategy starts with Abu Dhabi’s own residents. The city wants to be a “home away from home” for the world’s culture-lovers, he says, but “we did not develop our cultural strategy and our cultural infrastructure for people to come [to Abu Dhabi]. We developed it for people that are here.” But Al Mubarak is equally keen to project a sense of normality for potential visitors who are contemplating Abu Dhabi from afar. “Imagine yourself in Abu Dhabi today,” he says. The weather’s good this time of year, so “you’d wake up in the morning and you’d sink your feet in beautiful white sand,” then maybe go for a swim, he suggests. Then a tourist could go for an AI-personalized museum tour, a round of golf, some shopping, a concert at the Sphere (a $1.7 billion entertainment venue opening in 2029), or a comedy show. It’s “an imaginary story,” he says, but one “that could be a reality” for a visitor. The next step in realizing that vision will come on Dec. 11, when a branch of New York’s Guggenheim Museum opens on Saadiyat Island. Some of Abu Dhabi’s partners have expressed fears about the region’s suitability as a home for their artwork in a period of conflict — “our French partners raised concerns on some of the loans that they’ve had at the Louvre,” Al Mubarak acknowledges — but he was able to reassure them that its buildings are “built to withstand things of this sort of nature.” The opening of the Frank Gehry-designed Guggenheim will be a symbolic and emotional moment for Abu Dhabi, he says, but also one that “highlights our aspirations.” The case for not outgrowing your imagination What outsiders looking at Abu Dhabi’s transformation often miss is what has powered its economic growth, Al Mubarak says. “What they don’t see is that just three generations ago — my grandfather and my great-grandfather — they lived a very, very difficult life. They went days where they couldn’t find food.” The city’s ambition “comes from hunger and it comes from struggle,” he says. Even as it builds ever more glittering projects, he adds, “That struggle I’m talking about, we feel it. That taste is still in our mouth.” Abu Dhabi is still “the new kid on the block,” he says — an underdog

events.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
events.summary: The Campaign Legal Center is calling for an investigation into whether Alicia Jackson, director of the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, violated ethics laws. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”  Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.  In a letter to the department’s inspector general , the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.  Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why. In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.  At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures . Read More Top U.S. Health Official Backed a Medication Policy Shift That Benefited a Company She Has Stock In It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025. Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.   The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.  “Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote. The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds. ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson . The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies. Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.  137 Ventures founders Alex Jacobson, left, and Justin Fishner-Wolfson Kimberly White/Getty Images for 137 Ventures The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said. Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.  HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote . President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term. ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”  Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses. Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database , a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased. events.title: Activists call for Pressley to launch House speaker bid against Jeffries
events.summary: House Democrats are all but certain to elect House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as their speaker designate next week. There could still be some turbulence, though , with progressive activists calling for Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., to launch a bid against Jeffries. Ricardo Sanchez, a Pressley spokesperson, said she was in “active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people. She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership.” Most Democrats don’t believe Pressley will actually launch a bid ahead of next week’s leadership elections. She’s privately denied interest in running to other lawmakers, according to people familiar with her comments, and she hasn’t laid the groundwork for a bid by sounding out support from other lawmakers. House Democrats are staring down brewing fights as younger lawmakers jostle for power and influence ahead of the party assuming its largest majority in decades. Once their leadership slate is set, the caucus will weigh major changes like implementing term limits, shaking up panel leaders, and standing up select committees on controversial policy issues. “We can have the fight about how many terms should be the limit, but I think the time is right — with all these new members coming into the caucus — to set some limits,” said Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. At the “What’s Next” conference on Friday, Jeffries said discussion about term limits was the “right conversation to have.” And Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., launched an effort this morning to change the seniority system for subcommittee leadership positions. Jeffries and Democratic leaders could face an influx of new members who aren’t as beholden to caucus traditions when it comes to picking leaders based on seniority. “I think it’s going to be important for the Democratic Caucus to make sure that the voices of this large, energetic, new class of members are included at the table, and in general, I think we, as a party and as a Congress, are healthier when we allow for new perspectives and more renewal,” said Rep.-elect Luke Bronin, who’s coming to office after unseating a longtime Democratic incumbent. Democrats are also weighing the future of the select panel on China and whether to stand up a select committee on AI. Some Democrats have argued for changing the China committee, keeping it as is , or sunsetting it altogether. Top House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., who is close to Jeffries, has advocated for folding the China committee into his panel, and for standing up a separate Foreign Affairs subpanel on AI and chips. Doing so could set off a turf war with other powerful committee leaders.

events.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
events.summary: US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer. Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models." "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model." It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea . And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act. On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI. Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China." These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed. How DePue reached his conclusion The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs. As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run. Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights. "I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," said DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems." Noting that this is the first time MiniMax and Ant Group have been publicly linked to usage of Nvidia's Blackwell, he also cited several limitations to his approach. One is that usage of Blackwell GPUs doesn't prove where the GPUs were located, so it's possible some of these Chinese labs used this hardware through US providers – a loophole the Cloud Security Act aims to close. DePue's report includes initial seed values that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Nvidia's Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, for those who wish to attempt to reproduce the results. DuPue claims that multiple senior researchers, both independent and inside frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, have confirmed the result. Coincidentally, OpenAI and Anthropic have each complained about Chinese labs copying their models through distillation, a pastime also noted by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ®

events.title: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
events.summary: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of the Comptroller of the Currency National Credit Union Administration The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16. The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding. When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed. Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks. events.title: Bessent knocks Lutnick on Megaspeed
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is coming under more friendly fire over his department’s policing of AI chip exports. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this morning publicly blamed Lutnick for the administration’s failure to blacklist AI firm Megaspeed, telling CNBC that Treasury “has been pushing for this for months” but Commerce “has the pen.” Lutnick, who’d initially competed for Bessent’s job, agreed this week to testify before Congress following the news of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The scrutiny has raised questions about Lutnick’s job security , but many Republicans are still publicly defending the close Trump ally, leaving few certain that he may really be on his way out. “This guy has nine lives,” a person close to the White House told Semafor. “How many does he have left?” — Eleanor Mueller and Shelby Talcott

events.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
events.summary: Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI. “It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register . “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?” As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before. “There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.” Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. “But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said. Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI . From CVE to KEV From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure. Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse . “It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe . “We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.” This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching. “We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.” What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit. “It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said. AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “ super close to my heart .” “You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.” Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry , in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale. Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance. Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “ avalanche of vulnerability reports ," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling. Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. “A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,” Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®

events.title: How Nvidia’s Jensen Huang – and Trump – jumped the guardrails
events.summary: The Scoop In January, the general counsel for what was then the world’s most valuable company delivered a blunt directive on chip export controls to more than a dozen government officials: What Donald Trump and his friend Jensen Huang want, goes. “I was with the president when he and Jensen discussed this so I want to let you know what the president wanted,” said Nvidia’s Tim Teter, according to people with access to a detailed account of the call. “He wants this to go fast.” People on the call fell silent. At issue were proposed conditions on licenses to export Nvidia’s H200 chips to China, which included requirements that chipsellers know who their cloud customers were before shipping and conduct know-your-customer checks on any buyers purchasing more than a few thousand chips. Nvidia objected, with Teter calling the cloud-customer requirement a “poison pill” for the company, the people said. Nvidia also wanted the threshold for the know-your-customer checks to be in the tens of thousands (the equivalent of billions of dollars of chips) and pushed for end-of-life conditions to only apply to chips that were facing export controls. While it’s not unusual for big corporations to work with US government agencies and Congressional staffers on legislation or agency rulemaking, or even to see draft regulation in advance, people familiar with Nvidia and its former CEO’s Washington connections say the chipmaker wielded an unprecedented level of influence in shaping guidelines with far-reaching global security and business implications for the entire industry. The previously unreported discussions have only taken on greater significance since Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded decades ago after media reports of extramarital affairs with two subordinates and one with a customer and suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia declined to comment. Spokespeople for the White House didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security, which is housed within the Department of Commerce, said it was “completely routine” for the department and other agencies to work with individual companies in this manner and that “often the conditions change in response to legitimate commercial considerations” raised by corporations. The final version of all license conditions are reviewed by the state, defense, energy, and commerce departments.“Nvidia would have gone through the same process for license conditions as any other license applicant. Nvidia consulting with non-political experts at multiple US government agencies regarding its proposed changes to the conditions is consistent with standard practice,” the spokesperson said. Invoking the president If Trump was Huang’s friend in the White House, Teter was his muscle in Washington. After more than two decades at law firm Cooley LLP, Teter joined Nvidia in 2017, soon after the chipmaker announced the beginning of the “ AI computing era .” Nvidia’s GPUs had sparked the “big bang” of modern AI, Huang wrote at the time, years before Nvidia would turn into the world’s most valuable company. But as Nvidia became a bigger geopolitical force — and Huang became a fixture alongside Trump at meetings, dinners and the Oval Office — Huang and Teter developed a “scorched earth, adversarial attitude,” according to a former government official familiar with their Washington presence. “They make things more personal, going after think tankers, government officials, and the like,” the former official said, referring to reports of Nvidia targeting critics of the company and proponents of export controls. As he bulldozed through Washington, Teter regularly invoked President Trump’s name to push Nvidia’s agenda. In one exchange viewed by Semafor, Teter accused government officials who were developing export restrictions of misrepresenting Nvidia’s products and President Trump’s policies, chiding them for not carrying out Trump’s agenda and insisting that Trump deserved their support. Teter and the team of Nvidia lobbyists would often capitalize on their implicit White House backing and on the fact that most Hill staffers didn’t have the technical expertise to fight back on the company’s claims that certain restrictions weren’t technically feasible, even if later they were proven wrong, current and former congressional staffers told Semafor. Staffers “were kind of just believing whatever they were told,” and Nvidia would get all sorts of bills watered down, one staffer said. Nvidia’s “MO has largely been gaslighting,” creating an “intense trust deficit between the government and the Hill and Nvidia,” a former staffer said. And “obviously, the canonical example at this point is Nvidia denying” improper chip sales to China, this person said. Huang has said there’s no evidence chips were getting diverted to China, but Bloomberg has reported that Nvidia undercounted the Megaspeed sales it reported to the US government by 50,000 chips, worth billions of dollars. Companies tied to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, have purchased at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips since 2023, The Information reported . But well before Nvidia came under fire for its relationship with Megaspeed, Nvidia told staffers that a provision in the 2025 Chip Security Act, which would require chipmakers to be able to locate their chips, was a nonstarter. “They basically said it was not technically feasible” the former staffer said, “they were like, ‘we would need completely new technology to do this, and even if we did it would be very easily spoofable.’” In meetings with committee staff, Nvidia lobbyists argued location verification would create security holes. They “ran this line of bullsh-t on how the Chip Security Act was going to create all these cyber vulnerabilities,” a second former staffer said. “We spent six months going behind them and having to unpack all of the bullsh-t that [they were] telling to other offices.” Then in December, Reuters reported a new location verification technology feature, which Nvidia had been demonstrating privately for months. The feature was launched in May, meaning the company had been “lying to Congress about the technical feasibility while you were literally baking it into your next chip generation,” this person said. Nvidia declined to comment on the location-verification technology. Willing partner Nvidia, though, found a willing partner in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who appeared to be more concerned with avoiding another painful trade war with China, as Trump was, and with staying on the president’s good side than with combing through the innards of chip regulations, according to people familiar with the matter. “Lutnick was fine with the H200s [being sold]. I think he’s just tried to be very careful to not rock the boat, and also it’s been convenient to make friends with industry allies like Jensen, especially since Trump likes Jensen as well,” a former Commerce official told Semafor

events.title: Why a new court ruling matters for press freedom and privacy
events.summary: Protecting privacy and press freedom: An important Fourth Circuit ruling Nov 11, 2026 | Jon Palmer, Corporate Vice President and Chief Legal Officer, Microsoft The free press in America depends on the ability of journalists to protect confidential sources. On November 10, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit underscored that principle. The court placed limits on secret government demands for journalists’ online data, and upheld the rights Microsoft and LinkedIn went to court to defend. LinkedIn, a Microsoft subsidiary, challenged two government orders: one, seeking journalists’ online data, and another that prevented the company from informing the journalists or their news organizations of the demand. The opinion, authored by Judge Harvie Wilkinson III, opens with the statement that “[i]t is part of the audacity of the American project to believe that collective security can coexist with individual freedom.” Writing that “[c]onfidentiality of sources is the lifeblood of a free press,” the court remanded the case to the district court to consider narrowing both the scope of the government’s demand for information and the restrictions on LinkedIn’s ability to disclose the demand. In a world where journalists routinely use digital platforms to identify sources, communicate privately, and gather information, this case provides key legal guidance. Overbroad requests for online data can expose confidential sources, including individuals who may have no connection to the investigation itself. As a technology provider, we believe we have an important responsibility both to follow the law and to protect the people and organizations that rely on our services. When users are unaware that the government is seeking their information, technology providers are the last line of defense. They alone are in a position to challenge overly broad demands and ensure users’ rights are protected. We were proud to be supported in this case by amicus briefs filed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the American Civil Liberties Union, and other technology providers including Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, and X. Microsoft has a long history of standing up for these protections across administrations led by both political parties. Our position has remained consistent: government demands should be appropriately tailored, secrecy is the exception, not the rule, and customers should receive notice unless the government demonstrates a specific need for nondisclosure. For well over a decade, we have challenged unnecessary secrecy orders, pressed for changes to Justice Department practices, and advocated for stronger legal safeguards regarding government access to customer data. We recognize the government’s legitimate responsibility to investigate crime and threats to national security. As the Court here recognized, those investigations must be conducted within appropriate legal limits and must still protect privacy and First Amendment rights. This ruling reinforces that balance, concluding with the statement: “Serious security and speech claims are in tension in this case. There is space under law for both.” Now Congress should finish the job. As Brad Smith, Microsoft’s Vice Chair and President, argued in calling for Congressional reform of nondisclosure orders. Favorable court decisions and changes in government policy are important, but they are no substitute for durable legal protections. Congress should strengthen the laws governing nondisclosure orders by ensuring that secrecy is appropriately limited, justified by specific circumstances, and subject to meaningful judicial review. These reforms would help protect the privacy of individuals and organizations while preserving the government’s ability to investigate crime. The Fourth Circuit’s decision is an important reminder that privacy, press freedom, and public safety need not be competing interests. Our laws should protect all three. Microsoft and its subsidiaries will continue to stand up for these principles and the rights of the people and organizations that rely on our services. Protecting customer privacy means standing up for transparency Keeping secrecy the exception, not the rule: An issue for both consumers and businesses DOJ acts to curb the overuse of secrecy orders. Now it’s Congress’ turn. House passes historic reforms to rein in secret surveillance Tags: Congress , data privacy , Data Protection , Government , Microsoft , Privacy , Privacy and Security Digital Crimes Unit: Leading the fight against cybercrime May 3, 2022 Keeping your vote safe and secure: A story from inside the 2020 election June 22, 2021 ‘It’s about doing the right thing’ – A tech diplomat on democracy and what motivates him May 7, 2021

events.title: From the first console to the next chapter, XBOX celebrates 25 years
events.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI Comes to XBOX One and XBOX Series X|S Through XBOX Cloud Gaming on November 19 XBOX 25th Anniversary Magazine: Explore 25 Years of Games, Stories, and Memories 25 Original XBOX Games Available Today on PC via XBOX Backward Compatibility Stories Untold Is Now Available For Xbox One XBOX Playback is Here: Look Back at Your XBOX Story An Alligator Swallowed an XBOX Series X – You Can Win It This message was just sent to Team XBOX employees globally. Microsoft was founded on the belief that computing could put extraordinary capabilities in the hands of ordinary people. Gaming has been part of that story since the company’s beginning. In 1979, we released Microsoft Adventure , a text-based game that looked more like MS-DOS than an early version of Minecraft . Adapted by a single programmer, Gordon Letwin, one of Microsoft’s first 13 employees and later an architect on OS/2, the game let players explore a digital world, collect treasure, solve puzzles, and encounter mythical creatures. A few years later, Bruce Artwick brought the magic of flight to the 16-bit IBM PC, making it possible to fly a plane from your desk. Over the following decade, Microsoft published dozens of other titles including Minesweeper , Age of Empires , and another four Microsoft Flight Simulators , while Windows helped usher in 3D gaming with partners such as id Software (which would join XBOX some 24 years later). In the mid-1990s, a small team working on DirectX, the technology that helped developers make games for Windows, had a big idea: using PC architecture to power the first American video game console in decades. Shortly thereafter, work began on the secret “Project Midway.” When the original XBOX launched in 2001, it was impossible to miss. It was 2-3x larger than rival consoles, with a giant X molded into a black enclosure and a bright alien green jewel at the center. It shipped with a hard drive when competitors asked players to buy standalone memory cards and an Ethernet jack when 9 in 10 households still used dial-up. It also boasted more than twice the processing power of the PlayStation and GameCube and pioneered dual analog controllers. A year later, Xbox Live revolutionized online play with persistent friend lists and matchmaking, as well as a common service for developers to build connected experiences. And bringing all of this together was Halo: Combat Evolved , a launch title that not only defined XBOX but proved its first advertising campaign: “Games Will Never Be The Same.” Twenty-five years later, XBOX has grown into one of the world’s largest gaming businesses. We’ve built four generations of XBOX consoles, with a fifth on the way. Today, our games reach more than a billion players every year spanning beloved and iconic franchises such as Call of Duty, Candy Crush, Diablo, Doom, Fable, Fallout, Forza, Gears of War, Halo, Minecraft, Overwatch, Sea of Thieves, The Elder Scrolls, StarCraft, Warcraft, Wolfenstein, and many more. XBOX has been built by generations of employees, studios, developers, and partners who believed in what gaming could become. To all of you, thank you. I especially want to recognize the 111 people across XBOX and our studios who have been here for 25 years or more. You’ve helped shape the history we’re celebrating today, and each of you will receive a special engraved console to commemorate what you’ve helped build. Since joining XBOX, I’ve heard stories of friendships that began over a session and lasted a lifetime, of people who met the person they would marry, and of parents now sharing the games they grew up on with their children. I’ve also heard about people who are no longer with us, and how much those hours spent playing together still mean to those who love them. Ultimately, this is why we exist. The story of XBOX has never been ours alone. Our fans have challenged us, cheered us on, held us accountable, and stuck with us. We’ve been celebrating this anniversary with fans around the world and special launches. Today, we are bringing the celebration home to Seattle. Gaming has always been an industry driven by dreams. Not just the desire to bring something imagined to life, but to share it with others. Sometimes that dream is of a game, other times a console, a character, or an entire universe. The history of XBOX is a testament to the power of these dreams and how they can grow over time. The first Microsoft Flight Simulator was just 160 KB, with 2D graphics, 16 colors, and 20 total airports. The 2024 version draws on more than 2.5 petabytes of data (more than 15 billion times the size of the original game). Its 200-million-square-mile map recreates almost every city, road, and landmark across the planet, with trillions of individually rendered trees and real-world weather reproduced in near real time. While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically. As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this. Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982. I believe the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays. Our responsibility is to deliver great games, unmistakable hardware, and give more people the chance to make something the world has never seen.

events.title: Meatbags suck at spotting lying LLMs, so let AI narc on itself
events.summary: The internet is full of schlock, from biased news and dubious hot takes to false factoids. LogicLens aims to separate fact from fiction using the very same technology behind some of that slop: AI. It’s a simple premise, really: LogicLens, which lives in Chrome as a browser extension , or on iOS in the form of a mobile app called Receipts , combs through articles, social media posts, and other content to check it not only for factual inaccuracies, but also for bad reasoning. LogicLens and Receipts claim to identify logical fallacies , flag reports that misrepresent information, detect content that attempts to polarize an issue, and the like. It also cites sources, so if, for example, you need to call someone out on their BS, you’ll have ammunition. Or, if you’re trying to fact-check something before sharing it, you can get a more accurate view of the situation, and maybe post something else instead. Using the Chrome extension is as simple as clicking on its icon in the list of extensions in the browser. On iOS, the Receipts app is found as a share option. Once it starts, LogicLens scans an article, post, video, etc. to find potential issues of factual or logical inconsistency and flags them for review. If the facts of the matter turn out to contradict your worldview, LogicLens’ creators say they’re not trying to be partisan - you may just not be as informed as you need to be, which hopefully their tool will assist with. “We're not trying to be the referee of truth,” the company’s about page states. “Instead, LogicLens helps uncover the context, so you can decide for yourself without the spin." Of course, AI is increasingly used for online analysis and content review, and LogicLens is no exception. LogicLens doesn't identify the AI models powering its service in its publicly available documentation, but AI is definitely the backbone of the system. According to LogicLens, it's using an AI system that's “Research-backed and custom designed to outperform general models like ChatGPT & even trained experts.” We’ll leave that up to anyone willing to give the tool a spin to decide, but one thing’s for certain: The world needs something. Large language models and image generation tools are increasingly being used to generate internet content slop, and not all of it is as harmless as poorly made commercials for drop-shipped garbage: Some of it is being used to craft very convincing misinformation. A 2024 study found that AI-generated misinformation was even more convincing than stuff crafted by humans - and that was two years ago. Just think how much worse it’s likely become since then. To make matters worse, concerns have been raised about critical thinking skills being on the decline , potentially making it harder for people to identify falsehoods on the internet. AI users are reportedly less likely to admit they don’t know something, even though use of AI has been found in studies to l essen brain activity , leading to poorer retention of facts and worse performance on tests. Is using more AI the solution to the problem? In an ideal world, we’d all just put the computers down and go touch grass, but we’re not in an ideal world: We’re living in the age of AI. LogicLens is free but requires sign-up and restricts nonpaying users to 15 analyses a day and 100 over the course of a month. A $4.99 monthly subscription removes those analysis caps. ®
